  32. 5 B 70 hand comparison 2026: six specimens extracted blind on the scribe-compare taxonomy and five pairs audited against the images; every pair returned the band ‘inconclusive’ — the note against the signatures (the h built on different limbs, pointed against rounded minims; the shared capital I is the period's standard form), against Tycho's specimens of 1583 and 1599 (the capital I without the J-descender, the final s at x-height against his descending final s), and against the two hands of the volume of 1561; the marginalia against Tycho's specimens (the u-marks and the looped g concordant; the e, the final s, the final i and the absence of the ſt/ct arch discordant). Sample lengths below the forensic floor; the facsimile's c. 15–20 px x-height for the note is the binding constraint. A photograph of the title foot at three to four times that resolution, and a Pratensis prose specimen, are what would decide it. ↩

4Register of entries

The full records, in alphabetical order of author (anonymous works under their title), numbered continuously for citation in this chapter. Each record gives status and grade, imprint, the attesting sources with their numbers, the ownership marks and annotations recorded, the surviving copy with its links, the road of dispersal where one is documented, the editorial note, and, where Norlind catalogued the work, a transcription of his entry. The record key printed with each entry is stable across versions and is the form to cite; the running number may change when entries are added.

No online catalogue record traced.
Road of dispersal
Road U, Route out of the library unknown. Route before the twentieth century unknown; never traced at the Clementinum. Bought in Germany by Sigurd Wandel; in Harald Mortensen's collection at Copenhagen by 1932; his gift to Frederiksborg in 1950.. The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Note
Prandtl Verzeichnis A no. 48, bound alone as Band XX — the parchment Prachtband with the gilt portrait-and-arms plaques, which Prandtl listed in 1932 in Harald Mortensen's collection at Copenhagen, not in Prague. Bought in Germany by professor Sigurd Wandel; Mortensen's by 1932; his gift to Det Nationalhistoriske Museum på Frederiksborg in 1950, when it was called the only Danish-owned volume from Tycho's library (Paulli & Dal 1959, p. 15); in the museum's Tycho Brahe case in 1955 (Mortensen 1955, p. 25). The museum confirmed on 28 September 2026 that the volume is inventory B3950a-b, kept in the museum library and not on display. An octavo, not a folio. Prandtl's Band XX and the Frederiksborg book are one volume; an earlier reading of Band XX as a separate Prague volume was a misreading of Prandtl. The suffix a-b names the volume (a) and the slipcase it is kept in (b), the museum's answer of 12 October 2026.
Norlind 1970, p. 336

  • Whether the text carries annotations in Tycho’s hand: the volume has not been searched leaf by leaf.

Status

Attested by

by 1576 (the year stamped on the binding)
Ownership marks
Inscription: Tycho's autograph monogram ‘T. Brahe 49.’ (front) and ‘Tres. M 49’ (rear); no year visible under flat light
Surviving copy
Sign. 44 F 38, National Library of the Czech Republic (Clementinum) · identification A · the year 1576 stamped into the front board, the leather stripped (Boldan & Kazanskii 2023, p. 28)
Tycho's autograph monogram ‘T. B.’ on the manuscript-supplied title leaf of the Imago mundi and his glosses (e.g. fol. dd1r), read as his hand by Boldan & Kazanskii 2023; the year 1576 stamped into the front pasteboard (leather stripped, board later papered); ‘Collegii Societatis Jesu Commotovien. catalogo inscriptus 1645’ on fol. <2>2r; a blacked-out note of the Kulm brethren on the Euclid's a1r, recovered under the VSC 8000 (fig. 5)
Links: catalogue record · the library's photographs of the front and rear boards (Aleph STT record, OBRAZ. PŘÍLOHA; session-bound links — open from the record)
Bound with: Euclid (Campanus recension), Elementa geometriae (the first printed Euclid) (Venice: Erhard Ratdolt, 1482)
Road of dispersal
Road I, The Jesuit road: the Clementinum (1642), the colleges at Chomutov and Krumlov and the professed house, reunited in the Clementinum after 1773. Jesuit college at Chomutov — ‘Collegii Societatis Jesu Commotovien. catalogo inscriptus 1645’ on fol. <2>2r — and after the suppression of 1773 the University Library at the Clementinum, the route of the other Chomutov Tychoniana; how it reached Chomutov by 1645 is not recorded.. The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Note
The lead work of the incunable Sammelband 44 F 38 at the National Library, published by Boldan and Kazanskii in 2023 among incunables whose defaced provenance notes were read with a video spectral comparator: the first edition of d'Ailly's Imago mundi with his astronomical treatises, bound with the Ratdolt Euclid of 1482. ‘The owner of the Sammelband until his death in 1601 was Tycho Brahe’, shown by his autograph monogram ‘T. B.’ on the title leaf, which was supplied in manuscript at the end of the sixteenth century after the printed first leaf had been torn out, and by his glosses, for example on fol. dd1r. The two incunables may have been joined only in 1576, the year stamped into the front board; the binding is of the Uraniborg furnishing year, and the manuscript title leaf of the kind Tycho supplied to other volumes. The volume belongs to the Chomutov stratum: the college entered it in its catalogue in 1645, nine years before Gabriel Crusius's gifts to the same college. Kleinschnitzová did not list it, and it escaped every later census because it is catalogued among the incunables, outside the old-prints owner index. With the Venice Ephemerides of 1481 (Kleinschnitzová 14), the Louvain cosmography of c. 1477–1483 and the Ratdolt Euclid of 1482 are the earliest printed books now known from the library.
Open questions
  • Whether the manuscript title leaf and the glosses are in Tycho's hand; whether the pasteboard binding of 1576 matches the dated T. B. O. bindings; and any trace of the route from the heirs to Chomutov before 1645 — questions for the volume.
  • 27 Oct 2026 — the binding half narrowed: the library's own photographs of the boards (Aleph MEDIA, 2833 × 3695 and 2768 × 3631 px) show both boards now covered in paper with no year, tooling or initials visible under flat light, so a die comparison with the T.B.O. 1576 bindings is impossible (the leather is gone) and only a raking-light reading of the year's figures remains; the hand half unchanged (never compared — photographs of the supplied title and fol. dd1r needed); the route half is chapter II's.
  • Whether the National Library's incunable collection (departments 39–44) holds further volumes with Tycho's marks: the library's former-owner index covers 1501–1800 only.
  • 27 Oct 2026 — unchanged from any source held; an enquiry to the incunable curator (chapter IV, rank 1) is the test.

Note
Prandtl Verzeichnis A no.1; bound in Band IV. Prandtl records numerous annotations in Tycho's hand, with leaves of horoscopes and astrological tables at the end. The attribution is Prandtl's, and it is not exhaustive: at least one pre-Tycho hand is also present in the volume, whose terminal leaves carry a personal chronicle headed Accidentia mea, dated 1535–1545, and a nativity headed natus Andreas Schoenerus, cast for Nuremberg on 21 June 1530 (dies Martis, as the figure says; reproduced by Studnička 1901, Bericht, p. 22, as Tycho's work) — both antedating Tycho's birth on 14 December 1546. Studnička read the cost note on the first leaf of the manuscript once bound in the volume, which lists the Gauricus, the Albubater, the Cardanus and the binder’s fee, as Tycho’s own account of the purchase and the binding (Bericht, pp. 20–21), and Kleinschnitzová read the binding instruction on the last leaf of the Glareanus 19 G 20, which names the Gauricus and the Albubater, as Tycho’s hand (1933, no. 42, p. 93); the cost note is headed with Schöner’s name. Whose hands the volume’s annotations are has not been established by a comparison of hands. Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C).

Note
The Alphonsine Tables at the Technische Universität Wien (Tresor 7704 I), heavily annotated by Tycho and dedicated to him in 1590 by Lave Urne til Bæltebjærg, landsdommer in Skåne; formerly in the Prague Jesuit College (Mortensen 1955, p. 30). The volume is distinct from the Paris edition of 1553 of the Tables that Herwart von Hohenburg sent Tycho from Munich on 10 December 1600, a copy marked ‘No. 43’ (Opera omnia VIII, pp. 393–394: ‘mitto Alphonsinas Tabulas recognitas, Parisijs A° 53 impressas, No. 43 signatas’). Norlind (1970, p. 337) prints the title-page notes: ‘Collegij Caesarei Societatis Iesu Pragae. I Bibl. min. Anno 1642. Ex Bibliotheca Tichoniana’ above the title, and below it ‘Hunc librum dono dedj singularj Amico meo Domino Tychoni Brahe de Knudstorp Amicitiae ergo Anno salutis 1590. Laue Vrne senior min hand’. Tycho’s notes and the Urne dedication are known from Teichl’s report to Mortensen and from the title-page inscriptions Norlind prints; neither describes the notes, and the library’s own record names no former owner. Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C). Lave (Lauge) Urne the elder, of Belteberga, landsdommer in Skåne from 1589, lived 1535/39 – 8 October 1623 (DBL), not to 1625 as Mortensen 1955 and the earlier record have it; the copy is not ‘the only one of this edition in Austria’ — GW 1258 (ISTC ia00535000) lists six other Austrian copies. The inscription in full: ‘Hunc librum dono dedj singularj Amico meo / Domino Tychoni Brahe de Knudstorp Amicitiae ergo / Anno salutis 1590. Laue urne senior / min hand.’ — the only dated presentation copy to Tycho known; reported by Teichl 1943 (Mortensen 1955, p. 30), transcribed by Norlind 1970 p. 337; not examined since; the TU Wien record carries no provenance (register dossier of 27 October 2026, §16-04).

Laue urne senior / min hand.» – Lave (Lage) Urne till Bälteberga, som alltså skänkte exemplaret till Tycho, var något äldre än denne och blev landsdomare i Skåne 1589, död 1623. Han kallar sig »senior» till skillnad från sin yngre broder med samma namn (död 1629).

Note
Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 16; NK Clementinum Sign. 14 J 28, in the original brown binding with the initials ‘T. B. O. 1580’ (Kleinschnitzová; Norlind 1970, p. 337). Regiomontanus’s Oratio introductoria and Melanchthon’s prefatory letter, which Šolc 2002 (p. 330) lists for the volume, are the front matter of the Nuremberg edition of 1537, not separate works. Tycho owned this edition and wanted a better text: he complained in August 1598 that the Latin translation teemed with errors (Opera omnia VIII, 102), asked Scaliger for the Arabic in April 1599 (VIII, 152), heard in March 1600 that Scaliger had neither it nor another Latin version (VIII, 264), and in November 1600 was offered a copy of the edition of 1537 by Herwart von Hohenburg (VIII, 386) (Norlind 1970, p. 337).
Norlind 1970, p. 337
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Originalbd med initialerna »T. B. O. 1580». – Albategnius' skrift, som f.ö. också utgavs separat, innehåller endast texten till hans berömda tabeller, vilka bl.a. upptogo stjärnpositioner för epoken 879,0. Texten är översatt av Plato från Tivoli med tillägg av Regiomontanus. Den arabiska texten återutgavs med latinsk översättning först av Nallino 1903–07. – Tycho skriver till Scaliger i april 1599 (VIII, 152), att han önskade den arabiska texten. Redan i aug. 1598 (VIII, 102) hade han klagat över, att den latinska översättningen vimlade av fel. Som svar på Tychos brev från april 1599, meddelar Scaliger, mars 1600 (VIII, 264), att han inte kunnat komma över någon arabisk text och f.n. inte har någon latinsk översättning. Tycho hänvände sig tydligen därefter till Herwart von Hohenburg i München. I nov. 1600 (VIII, 386) svarar denne, att uppl. 1537 är svår att skaffa och f.ö. betingar ett högt pris; den är inkorrekt på flera ställen. Ett exemplar har han emellertid förvärvat från ett bibliotek och han erbjuder sig att skicka det. Tycho, som dock ägde denna uppl., synes ha trott, att det skulle ha funnits ytterligare en latinsk översättning. En sådan existerade emellertid icke vid denna tid.

Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Ett astronomiskt praktverk med rörliga pappskivor till åskådliggörande av planeternas rörelser. »Ouvrage très intéressant pour connaître l'état de l'astronomie vers le milieu du XVIe siècle» (Houzeau & Lancaster); »the most sumptuous scientific book ever printed» (D. J. Price, »The equatories of the planetis», Cambr. 1955, s. 132). Dåtidens omdöme om verket S. A. Ionides, »Caesar's Astronomy», i: »Osiris» 1936, s. 356–389. Ett astronomiskt praktverk med rörliga pappskivor till åskådliggörande av planeternas rörelser. »Ouvrage très intéressant pour connaître l'état de l'astronomie vers le milieu du XVIe siècle» (Houzeau & Lancaster); »the most sumptuous scientific book ever printed» (D. J. Price, »The equatories of the planetis», Cambr. 1955, s. 132). Dåtidens omdöme om verket var emellertid ganska kritiskt. Hagecius skriver sålunda till Tycho i nov. 1588 (VII, 147): »Hunc eruditum pulverem, in quo nos versamur, ille [sc. Apianus] ne somniavit quidem. Eius artem sæpe Rheticus, bonæ memoriæ, vocare solitus erat faden Dunst.» Kepler beklagar i sin »De motibus stellæ Martis», kap. 14, den »miserabilem industriam» som Apianus nedlagt på sitt verk, men han menar ändå, att Apianus »palmam ... inde famæ perennis est adeptus, quicquid operibus ipsis fortuna ista detrimenti attulerit». Tycho ägde i varje fall ett exemplar (till Hagecius nov. 1589; VII, 212). Längre fram i brevet (215) omtalar han ett annat exemplar, som han en gång köpte för 20 fl. och sedermera skänkte Paul Wittich vid dennes besök på Hven 1580. Tycho ber nu Hagecius att, eftersom Wittich avlidit, underhandla med systern i Tychos namn angående förvärvande av dennes bibliotek, som tydligen måste ha varit synnerligen värdefullt. Lyckas Hagecius i sina underhandlingar, skall han få det exemplar, som Wittich erhöll av Tycho. – I Landesbibliothek i Gotha finnes ett exemplar, däri Tycho på ett tomt blad i början gjort en del anteckningar (se Chr. Rausch i: Zeitschr. f. Bücherfreunde, N.F. 5: 2, 1914, s. 223–224). De utgöras av några verser ur Davids 19:e psalm (»Cœli enarrant Gloriam Dei et opera manuum eius annunciat firmamentum») samt ett distikon: »Qui negat esse Deum cœlos et sidera spectet / Esse etenim monstrat stella vel una Deum.» Därunder: »Tycho Brahe / scripsi / Anno 1599 / Junii die 14 / quo Viteberga / discessi / Pragam / a Cæsare vocatus.» Pr. upptager exemplaret som tillhörigt Tycho (nr 1 i hans förteckning). Att det skulle ha varit Tychos, synes dock knappast sannolikt. Den handskrivna anteckningen påminner snarare om en stamboksautograf. Exemplaret kan mycket väl ha tillhört någon annan, kanske rent av hertig Fredrik Wilhelm av Sachsen-Altenburg, med vilken Tycho vid denna tid stod i förbindelse. Ortroy, Apianus förtecknar under nr 112 ett 30-tal kända exemplar. Till denna förteckning kan ytterligare läggas dels Gotha-exemplaret dels ett i UUB. – Apianus' handexemplar ägdes av Mæstlin i Tübingen, som i ett brev till Kepler (april 1613; Caspar nr 651, s. 57) omtalar, att änkan efter Petrus Apianus' son Philippus Apianus utan Mæstlins vetskap låtit försälja hela restupplagan.
Open questions
  • Whether the book was Tycho's own before 14 June 1599 or Duke Friedrich Wilhelm's book in which he wrote; the basis of the Gotha copy record's naming of the duke as recipient (probably Gehrt 2013 on the duke's library); and the sense of Rauch's remark that the book came to Gotha from Munich.

Tycho's presentation inscription, transcribed in the library's catalogue record: 'D[omi]no Paulo Witichio Wratislauiensj ob amicitam & comune[m] mathemati[cum] amorem d[ono] d[edit] Tÿcho Brahe Huanae anno 1580 29 Octobris.' — to Paul Wittich of Wrocław, for friendship and a shared love of mathematics, given at Hven on 29 October 1580 (on the title page according to Gingerich and Westman 1988, p. 17); Tycho's own account of the purchase for 20 florins and of the gift, in his letter to Hagecius of 1 November 1589
Links: catalogue record · The Newberry's page on the copy, with an image · The University of Chicago Library's Schaffner-collection exhibit page
Road of dispersal
Road 0, Left the library in Tycho’s lifetime: gifts and exchanges. The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Note
Now at the University of Chicago Library (Schaffner bequest, 1972; bib 146807). Tycho's gift to Wittich at his departure from Hven, inscribed 29 October 1580; Tycho had paid 20 florins for it and told Hagecius on 1 November 1589 that he did not reclaim it and had another copy to hand (TBOO VII, 212 and 215; Gingerich's benchmark of an expensive book against about one florin for a De revolutionibus, Annotated Census, p. xv). The book left Tycho's library by gift in his lifetime and never returned; the identification of the Chicago copy rests on the library's own catalogue of 1977 (entry 15) and exhibit page. See the volume record.
Norlind 1970, p. 337
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Ett astronomiskt praktverk med rörliga pappskivor till åskådliggörande av planeternas rörelser. »Ouvrage très intéressant pour connaître l'état de l'astronomie vers le milieu du XVIe siècle» (Houzeau & Lancaster); »the most sumptuous scientific book ever printed» (D. J. Price, »The equatories of the planetis», Cambr. 1955, s. 132). Dåtidens omdöme om verket S. A. Ionides, »Caesar's Astronomy», i: »Osiris» 1936, s. 356–389. Ett astronomiskt praktverk med rörliga pappskivor till åskådliggörande av planeternas rörelser. »Ouvrage très intéressant pour connaître l'état de l'astronomie vers le milieu du XVIe siècle» (Houzeau & Lancaster); »the most sumptuous scientific book ever printed» (D. J. Price, »The equatories of the planetis», Cambr. 1955, s. 132). Dåtidens omdöme om verket var emellertid ganska kritiskt. Hagecius skriver sålunda till Tycho i nov. 1588 (VII, 147): »Hunc eruditum pulverem, in quo nos versamur, ille [sc. Apianus] ne somniavit quidem. Eius artem sæpe Rheticus, bonæ memoriæ, vocare solitus erat faden Dunst.» Kepler beklagar i sin »De motibus stellæ Martis», kap. 14, den »miserabilem industriam» som Apianus nedlagt på sitt verk, men han menar ändå, att Apianus »palmam ... inde famæ perennis est adeptus, quicquid operibus ipsis fortuna ista detrimenti attulerit». Tycho ägde i varje fall ett exemplar (till Hagecius nov. 1589; VII, 212). Längre fram i brevet (215) omtalar han ett annat exemplar, som han en gång köpte för 20 fl. och sedermera skänkte Paul Wittich vid dennes besök på Hven 1580. Tycho ber nu Hagecius att, eftersom Wittich avlidit, underhandla med systern i Tychos namn angående förvärvande av dennes bibliotek, som tydligen måste ha varit synnerligen värdefullt. Lyckas Hagecius i sina underhandlingar, skall han få det exemplar, som Wittich erhöll av Tycho. – I Landesbibliothek i Gotha finnes ett exemplar, däri Tycho på ett tomt blad i början gjort en del anteckningar (se Chr. Rausch i: Zeitschr. f. Bücherfreunde, N.F. 5: 2, 1914, s. 223–224). De utgöras av några verser ur Davids 19:e psalm (»Cœli enarrant Gloriam Dei et opera manuum eius annunciat firmamentum») samt ett distikon: »Qui negat esse Deum cœlos et sidera spectet / Esse etenim monstrat stella vel una Deum.» Därunder: »Tycho Brahe / scripsi / Anno 1599 / Junii die 14 / quo Viteberga / discessi / Pragam / a Cæsare vocatus.» Pr. upptager exemplaret som tillhörigt Tycho (nr 1 i hans förteckning). Att det skulle ha varit Tychos, synes dock knappast sannolikt. Den handskrivna anteckningen påminner snarare om en stamboksautograf. Exemplaret kan mycket väl ha tillhört någon annan, kanske rent av hertig Fredrik Wilhelm av Sachsen-Altenburg, med vilken Tycho vid denna tid stod i förbindelse. Ortroy, Apianus förtecknar under nr 112 ett 30-tal kända exemplar. Till denna förteckning kan ytterligare läggas dels Gotha-exemplaret dels ett i UUB. – Apianus' handexemplar ägdes av Mæstlin i Tübingen, som i ett brev till Kepler (april 1613; Caspar nr 651, s. 57) omtalar, att änkan efter Petrus Apianus' son Philippus Apianus utan Mæstlins vetskap låtit försälja hela restupplagan.
Open questions
  • The owners between Wittich's sister at Wrocław and Louis H. Silver: the binding of 1686 is the only fixed point; Gingerich's survey of copies (Röttel 1995), the Sotheby's catalogue of 8–9 November 1965 (lot 4) and the Newberry's 1964 handlist of the Silver collection should carry the line.
  • The two annotating hands the record notes, and the underscoring: whether either is Wittich's (his annotated copies of De revolutionibus would serve for comparison) or Tycho's; and the readings 'amicitam' and 'Huanae' in the record's transcription of the inscription. Images of the title page and of the annotated leaves would settle it.

Surviving copy
private collection — Astronomicum Caesareum, Private hands · identification A · Period 3 (T.B.O. 1583; the binding is not otherwise described)
Binding stamped ‘T.B.O.’ above the date ‘1583’; Tycho's annotations in the comet section near the end of the Astronomicum Caesareum (Gingerich 2002, fig. 2: f. O1 verso, a marginal heading reading, in the reproduction, ‘Motus diurnus Cometae in suo circulo’ beside Apianus's table of the comet's daily motion)
No online catalogue record traced.
Bound with: Schöner, Johann, Aequatorium astronomicum (Nuremberg, 1521) — bound with Apianus's Astronomicum Caesareum of 1540 in the T.B.O. 1583 volume (1521)
Road of dispersal
Road U, Route out of the library unknown. The French and Dutch/Flemish annotations place the volume around Antwerp or Brussels for a very long time; until about 1960 it was in a monastery library there. Gingerich's suggestion: it migrated to the Low Countries by the same Jesuit hands that carried the Wittich Copernicus now in Liège.. The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Note
Tycho’s own retained Astronomicum Caesareum, bound for him in 1583 with Schöner’s equatorium of 1521 and stamped ‘T.B.O. 1583’; he gave a second copy to Paul Wittich (Chicago) and inscribed a third at Wittenberg on 14 June 1599 (Gotha, Prandtl Band VI). The volume surfaced about 2000 through an e-mail enquiry to Gingerich from its Belgian owner, who asked why books of 1521 and 1540 sat in a binding stamped 1583 with the initials TBO; Gingerich recognised the mark and learned of Tycho’s annotations in the comet section (2002, pp. 327–328, fig. 2 = f. O1 verso). Later annotations in French and in Dutch or Flemish place the volume around Antwerp or Brussels for a long period, in a monastery library until about 1960 — in Gingerich’s view carried there by the same Jesuit hands as the Wittich Copernicus now in Liège. It was sold about 2001–2002 to an anonymous American collector for, Gingerich reports, close to a million dollars. Gingerich (2002, p. 327) had known only the Wittich copy and presumed that Tycho had retained another, which he had not found among the more than a hundred copies he had examined. Tycho himself attests a second Astronomicum Caesareum at Hven in 1589: offering Hagecius the Wittich copy for his trouble, he wrote on 1 November 1589 that he did not want it back, ‘as I have another copy at hand’ (Opera omnia VII, pp. 214–215; Gingerich and Westman 1988, p. 21) — this volume, bound six years earlier, not the Gotha copy inscribed in 1599.
Open questions
  • Which monastery in the Low Countries held the volume until about 1960, who the Belgian owner of about 2000 was, and who bought it in about 2001–2002: Gingerich names none of them, and the dealer’s or the owner’s records would.
  • Which edition of Schöner’s equatorium of 1521 is bound with the Apianus: Gingerich gives neither title nor imprint, and a description of the volume would settle it.

Attested by

Apianus, Petrus); Handels- og Søfartsmuseet, Årbog 1957; Museernes Samlinger (M/S Museet for Søfart); Magasin 1987; Björklund 1992; Gingerich 2002; Museet for Søfart 2026; Maggs 582 (1933); Reichner, Catalogue 1 ([1939]); Royal Library, Håndskriftafdelingen, Aktuelt (November 2001); Helsingør examination 2026; Band II transcription and hand comparison 2026; Schöner, Luculentissima … descriptio (1515); Bjørnbo & Petersen, Claudius Clavus (1904); Bruun Rasmussen 186 (1965)
Acquisition
1561; bought as a student with the Regiomontanus in the same volume: the purchase note ‘Eptg [emptus] thalero & 4 Groshj’ stands on the volume’s fly-title and the binding is stamped ‘Anno 1561’ (Prandtl 1932, Band II; Klem, Årbog 1957, p. 8) (Direct purchase)
Ownership marks
Inscription: the ownership inscriptions and the purchase note stand on the fly-title of the Regiomontanus, first in the volume Annotations: fol. 53r–v: four places with their positions in an early hand, read by the museum as ‘Elzingborgum 35 46. 57 0 / Lunda Lundt 36 30 57 23 / Vesby Gotlandiæ 47 5. 59 50 / Rumefalche [?] 46 35 60 15’. The Helsingborg and Lund figures are the book's own printed values from the Scania table on fol. 41v (‘Elseburgum 35 46 | 57 0’, ‘Lundis vel Lunda 36 30 | 57 23’), transcribed beside the printed Zealand–Scania island entry; Visby and the fourth place, which the printed table lacks, stand beside the Gotland entry on fol. 53v, so the fourth place was taken for a Gotland or neighbouring-island locality; it is Schöner's ‘Rumefalche’ (Luculentissima quaedam terrae totius descriptio, 1515, fo. 34r: ‘Bespue 47.5.59.50. Rumefalche 46.35.60.15.’), a Clavus-derived pseudo-toponym of Gotland from the Ulm Ptolemy of 1486 (Bjørnbo and Petersen 1904, pp. 115, 118), identified 21 October 2026. The latitudes are the Ptolemaic values Tycho later corrected (Helsingborg 56 3, Lund 55 45: TBOO V, 309–312), so the entries predate his Danish latitude programme; the hand is undated and uncompared. Photographed 20 October 2026: the four lines are in one ink and ductus — ‘Elzingborgum’ with a superscript c above the name, ‘Lunda’, ‘Vesbÿ Gotlandiæ’, and a fourth whose letters read R-?-n-s-f-a-l-?-h-?; read again on 21 October 2026 as ‘Lůnda lůndt’, ‘Veſbÿ Gotlandiæ’ and ‘Rumefalche’ (the museum's reading stands; the tall letter is an f), the u-marks and the diaeresis being the writer's habit; Visby and Rumefalche are Schöner's two Gotland ‘cities’ with his figures, Helsingborg and Lund his figures as Apian reprinted them. Also by hand: ‘Octava sphaera’ at the ring of the Schema praemissae divisionis, and ‘Wittenberga’ underlined in the German place table Binding: Band II: brown calf, blind-ruled mirror panels on both boards, originally gilt floral stamps, TVCHO BRADE stamped on the front board, ANNO 1561 on the rear, three raised bands; on the spine the remnant of a label with a library shelfmark 204 (the museum's record, 1957:0030)
Norlind records
inscriptions: Tycho Brade; Anno 1561; copy located by Norlind at: Handels- og Söfartsmuseet på Kronborg, Helsingör
Surviving copy
1957:0030, M/S Museet for Søfart (Maritime Museum of Denmark) · identification A · Period 1 (student bindings, 1560–1567)
front board: TVCHO BRADE, rear board: ANNO 1561 (stamped, originally gilt); fly-title: ‘tico brade ven:’ (struck through), ‘Tycho Brade’ and further ownership inscriptions (leaf half torn, repaired); fly-title verso: ‘Sum Thÿchonis Brade’ [I am Tycho Brahe's] (struck through), ‘Eptg [emptus] thalero & 4 Groshj’ [bought for a thaler and 4 groschen], beneath it an astronomical note, partly lost; a note in ink on the front pastedown; fol. 53r–v of the Apianus: four places with their positions in Tycho's hand; on the spine the remnant of a label with a library shelfmark 204; Latin plant names at the head of a run of recto pages in a hand other than Tycho's, and small plant remains between leaves (Magasin 1987, p. 31; Björklund 1992, p. 26; confirmed 20 October 2026); at the head of the front pastedown the pencil figure ‘+125’, Maggs's price of 1933, and a second figure (the museum's photograph). Thykier (1985 inspection; report of 13 January 2003) reads the front of the fly-title (his ‘forperm’) as the autograph ‘Tyge Brahe’ struck through and ‘tico brahe ven’ struck through (‘en lidt barnlig skrift’ [a somewhat childish hand]), and in another hand ‘Sum Paul…’, the rest lost on the torn-off part; on its back, under a struck line where ‘Brade’ can be glimpsed, the price ‘… 4 taliro & 4 Gross.’; short astronomical notes in Tycho's hand inside the binding and on the back of the leaf, and one in the margin of the preface's tenth (unpaginated) page; Latin plant names at the head of 36 unpaginated pages in a hand other than Tycho's, plant remains in the gutter of 26 of them (microscoped by Jette Baagøe, re-housed in annotated envelopes of acid-free silk paper), further remains between pages without names, one plant name unattested before c. 1623 (Peter Wagner and Baagøe). Examined and photographed at the museum on 20 October 2026. Fly-title recto: ‘tico brade ven:’ in a thin early hand, struck through once in the same ink; beside it a name obliterated under heavy black strokes (Thykier: ‘Tyge Brahe’), ringed in pencil; to the right, in a firmer hand with a flourish, ‘Sum Pauli’ [I am Paul's], complete to its last letter, what followed lost with the torn-away part; above it a smudged short word in another ink, and at the head, right, a short word in a darker ink, both unread; at the head, left, pencil ‘Acc. 1986/116’. Fly-title verso: ‘Sum Thÿchonis Brade’ under a heavy bar, ‘Sum’ and ‘Brade’ legible beside it; below it the purchase note ‘Eptg thaliro & 4 Grossj’ [bought for a thaler and 4 groschen]; beneath that, intact, a two-branch memorandum in bracket form — ‘Decl: Merid: … obliqua {Adde / Subtr.} diff. asc. ab Ascensione Recta — Septen: … obliqua {Subtr. / Adde} diff. Asc. ab Asc. R.’, ‘obliqua’ struck and ‘Recta’ written above it — a rule for passing from right to oblique ascension by the sign of the declination. Front pastedown: an ink note in the same early hand (‘Ascens: decl: Merid: … ex Asc: Recta / Septm: Sub S … hoc modo’, a companion rule); a pencil collation in German (‘… 70 (von 1–74) … 31–34 … 1 Doppelbl. …’, the trace of the Munich trade); pencil ‘1986/116’. Spine: a paper slip in the second compartment with ‘20’ and a damaged third figure consistent with 4, the figures written by hand in ink; nothing else lettered, no label surviving at the tail. Rear flyleaf: a faint ‘N 36’ at the head and a small blind-stamped cartouche near the gutter, both unread. Rear pastedown: in ballpoint ‘Gave jan. 1957 fra civiling. Oskar Ekman’ [gift, January 1957, from the engineer Oskar Ekman], the stamp HANDELS- OG SØFARTSMUSEET PÅ KRONBORG HELSINGØR – DANMARK [the Trade and Maritime Museum at Kronborg, Helsingør, Denmark], and ‘30:57’ in blue. Box: brown cloth clamshell, its gilt spine label lettered in English — JOHANN DE MONTEREGIO TABULAE DIRECTIONUM 1550 BOUND WITH PETRUS APPIANUS COSMOGRAPHIA 1553. TYCHO BRAHE'S COPY WITH AUTOGRAPH OWNERSHIP NOTES, ETC. — with ‘30:57’ written on it. In the Apianus: ‘Octava sphaera’ written at the ring of the Schema praemissae divisionis, ‘Wittenberga’ underlined in the German place table; on fol. 53r ‘Elzingborgum 35 46. 57 0’ (a superscript c above the name) and ‘Lunda 36 30 57 23’, on fol. 53v ‘Vesbÿ Gotlandiæ 47 5. 59 50’ and the fourth place, its letters R-?-n-s-f-a-l-?-h-?, ‘46 35 60 15’, all four in one ink and ductus. The plant names stand at the head of the preface leaves (Pulmonaria, Ranunculus aquaticus, Hedera arborescens …) in a later hand, and the envelopes of plant remains lie at their openings; read letter by letter from the frames on 21 October 2026: the purchase note is ‘Eptꝰ thaliro & 4 Groſs.’ — emptus thalero et 4 grossis — the sign after ‘Ept’ being the -us abbreviation, not a g; the pastedown rule reads in full ‘Aſcens. decl {Merid. [Adde, blotted out by the writer] / Septen. Sub} ex Aſc. Recta / in deſcenſionibꝫ contrario modo’, the same rule as the verso's bracket memorandum, whose surviving case labels are ‘…rom:’ and ‘…nes’; above the rule a darker ‘Angl. 5.’, unexplained; the smudged word above ‘Sum Paüli’ reads ‘Brÿſſe’ or ‘Chrÿſſe’ and stands inside a wet-wiped erasure of an earlier inscription, the head-right word ‘to bra[h/n][e/o]’; the heavy black strokes through the recto name and through the verso's ‘Sum Thÿchonis Brade’ are one ink and one campaign, a later owner's cancellation of both Brahe names, while the thin stroke through ‘tico brade ven:’ is earlier and different; the herbarium hand also wrote ‘Lamiꝫ’, ‘Liſimachia flore luteo’ and ‘Hÿacinthꝰ’; on fol. 53 ‘Lůnda lůndt’ and ‘Veſbÿ Gotlandiæ’ carry the u-mark and the diaeresis, and the fourth place is the museum's ‘Rumefalche’ (the tall letter is an f with a cross-bar), identified on 21 October 2026 as Schöner's — Luculentissima quaedam terrae totius descriptio (Nuremberg 1515), fo. 34r, ‘Gotlandiae insu. civita.: Bespue 47.5.59.50. Rumefalche 46.35.60.15.’ — a Clavus-derived pseudo-toponym of Gotland from the Ulm Ptolemy of 1486, so that both added lines on fol. 53v are copied, name and figures, from Schöner or from his source; a pencil ‘choo’ on the rear pastedown
Links: catalogue record
Bound with: Regiomontanus, Johannes, Joannis de Monte Regio tabulae directionum profectionumque; ejusdem Regiomontani tabula sinuum (1550)
Road of dispersal
Road U, Route out of the library unknown. The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Note
Prandtl Verzeichnis A no. 3; bound in Band II. The volume is at M/S Museet for Søfart, Helsingør, inventory 1957:0030, the gift of Lia and Oscar Ekman in 1957. The museum’s record gives the Paris 1553 title with the colophon dated 1551, fol. 1–74, the cordiform map inserted between fol. 34 and 35, and the four added positions on fol. 53r–v. The volume is in the museum’s own keeping; the Royal Library deposit reported in 1987 and 1992 has ended (the museum’s confirmation of 13 October 2026). Gingerich 2002 (p. 325) still recorded ‘a copy of the 1561 edition of Petrus Apianus’ Cosmographia’ as sold by a Munich antiquariat to an undisclosed location: this is the present volume, whose binding is stamped 1561. Examined at the museum on 20 October 2026: the four places read on the leaf, the herbarium confirmed, the accession note read. The fol. 53 lines read letter by letter on 21 October 2026; the hand compared with the Graphonomicon's dated specimens (inconclusive). The fourth place identified on 21 October 2026 as Schöner's Rumefalche (1515, fo. 34r), Clavus's pseudo-toponym; the misreading of its fifth letter in the transcription withdrawn. Reviewed on 29 October 2026: of the six volumes the house has carried as the student’s, this is the one documented as Tycho’s before he left Denmark on 14 February 1562 — by the boards stamped with his name and the year 1561, and by nothing else: the purchase note and the ownership entries are undated, and no hand in the volume is attributed. Copenhagen as the place of purchase is an inference from the year (the Kronik of 1987 read the Leipzig register’s ‘16 October 1561’ as the matriculation; it is the winter-semester heading, Norlind 1970, p. 16, and Tycho and Vedel matriculated in the spring of 1562); the price in thaler and groschen is German money of account, which no source explains for a Copenhagen purchase; Klem’s ‘i 1561’ (Årbog 1957, p. 8) is the binding’s year, not the note’s. The volume came back to Denmark as Oscar Ekman’s bequest, entered in January 1957 by his widow Lia in the dead man’s name (he died 16 September 1956; the sale catalogue of 1965, lot 497: ‘according to the last will of ingeniør Ekman’, not for sale).

Apollonius of Perga, Conicorum libri IV (prob. Commandino, Bologna 1566; or Memmo, Venice 1537). Bologna, 1566

Attested, not locatedBrec-e-norlind-apollonius-conica
Status
Attested, not located · entry confidence B
Subject
Mathematics
Attested by
Norlind 1970, p. 338 (s.v. Apollonius Pergæus); Jardine & Segonds 2008
Norlind records
Opera omnia: VIII, 366
Note
Norlind (1970, pp. 338–339): ‘Vi veta, att biblioteket på Hven ägde ett exemplar av Apollonius’ verk (Bil. 6)’ — the library on Hven owned a copy, on the evidence of his Bilaga 6. Which of the two Latin translations it was, Memmo’s (Venice 1537) or Commandino’s (Bologna 1566, with Eutocius’s commentary), is not known; Norlind inclines to Commandino’s. The ‘Opera’ that Herwart von Hohenburg sent from Munich at Tycho’s request in September 1600 (Opera omnia VIII, 366) was a loan, its title that of the edition of 1537. Christian Hansen Riber’s deposition of 13/23 May 1598 adds the one witness to the shelf: the former students, ‘who examined your library whenever we liked’, attest that it never held any writing of Apollonius on hypotheses and that Tycho had no book of his but the Conics (Jardine & Segonds 2008, p. 169). The authors suppose that Kepler found the Commandino volume, which also carries Serenus, in Tycho’s library for the Contra Ursum, and conjecture that the ‘Apollonij Pergaei Opera’ Herwart sent on 23 September 1600 may be the copy Kepler used; their page prints the editions as Memmo 1527 and Commandino 1556, misprints for 1537 and 1566 (pp. 169–170 n. 4).
Norlind 1970, p. 338
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Av detta berömda verk funnos vid denna tid tvenne latinska översättningar (av bok I–IV, som äro de enda bevarade på grekiska; bok V–VII föreligga endast i arabisk övers.). Den ena översättningen av den venetianske patriciern Johannes Baptista Memus utgavs i Venedig 1537.2°. Den viktigaste var dock av Federicus Commandinus och den trycktes i Bologna 1566, 2°. Den innehåller bl.a. Eutocius' kommentar och var det första försöket att göra verket begripligt genom förklarande noter. Vi veta, att biblioteket på Hven ägde ett exemplar av Apollonius' verk (Bil. 6), men vilken upplaga det varit, är icke känt; man skulle emellertid med skäl kunna gissa på Commandinus' översättning. – I sept. 1600 (VIII, 366) skickade Herwart från München på Tychos begäran till låns Apollonius' »Opera», detta är titeln på den upplaga, som trycktes 1537. föreligga endast i arabisk övers.). Norlind records
Opera omnia: III, 290
Note
Norlind holds that Tycho must have owned the book (‘Tycho måste ha ägt boken’), since Tycho writes in the Progymnasmata (Opera omnia III, 290) that its figures are the same as those in Graminaeus’ tract on the new star, both printed by Theodorus Graminaeus. Norlind 1970, p. 339

Aslakssøn, Cort, De natura caeli triplicis libelli tres. Siegen, 1597, 4°

Attested, not locatedBrec-e-norlind-aslaksson-denatura
Status
Attested, not located · entry confidence B
Subject
Cosmology
Attested by
Norlind 1970, p. 339 (s.v. Aslakssön, Cort); Zinner no. 3699; VD16 A 3899
Acquisition
the author’s dedication to Tycho; a presentation copy is presumed, none is documented (Norlind 1970, p. 339) (Gift of an author or correspondent)
Dedication
dedicatee: Tycho Brahe de Knudstrup; incipit: Magnifico et amplissimo viro, virtute, eruditione, prudentia veré nobili Domino TYCHONI BRAHE de Knudstrup, fundatori Arcis Uraniburgicae in lectissima Hellesponti Danici Insula Huena; sideralis scientiae scrutatori, instauratori, conservatori unico, Domino & fautori meo summé colendo S.; place date: Basel (Basileae Rauracorum), 16 November 1596; signed: Tuae Excellentiae perpetuó studiosissimus Cunradus Aslachus Bergensis; content: Offers the book as 'primitiae' / a 'gratae recordationis symbolum' in return for Tycho's benefactions; hails him as 'indefessus ille Caeli scrutator & Atlas'; praises the Brahe family's nobility and Tycho's heroic-Herculean labours in sidereal science, his celestial Globe ('Globus ille caelestis, infinitis tuis lucubrationibus & vigiliis comparatus, Mundoque pridem concessus') and his astronomical instruments ('Machinae Astronomicae tua opera incredibili sumptu affabré elaboratae'). The preface (sig. A2v) thanks his Siegen/Herborn teachers Johannes Piscator and Johann Bisterfeld, and records submitting the work to Rudolph Goclenius the Elder at the Frankfurt fair; it defends views 'a communi scholarum opinione abhorrentia' (the cautiously-stated Copernican paradoxes). A separate epigram 'Ad authorem' by Johannes Piscator faces the title.; source: BSB Munich copy bsb10192622, sig. A2-A3 (pp. 3-6); read from the open MDZ/IIIF digitisation
English translation
title: The Description of Heaven. Or, A diuine and comfortable discourse of the nature of the eternall heaven, the habitation of God, and all the Elect.; translates: Book III only (De caelo perpetuo); by: composed in Latin by Cunradus Aslachus; converted into English by Raph (Ralph) Iennings; imprint: London: A[ugustine] Mathewes for John Brambridge, 1623; ref: STC; EEBO-TCP A22193; note: Dedicated by the translator to Richard Liggins, Gentleman; neither Tycho nor Copernicus is named in the English.
Note
Cort Aslakssøn (Cunradus Aslacus, Cort Axelsen; Bergen 1564–1624), Tycho’s famulus on Hven 1590–93 and later the first Norwegian professor at Copenhagen. Full title: De natura caeli triplicis libelli tres, quorum I. de caelo aëreo, II. de caelo sidereo, III. de caelo perpetuo, e sacrarum litterarum & praestantium philosophorum thesauris concinnati (Siegen [Sigenae Nassoviorum]: Christoph Rab, Christophorus Corvinus, 1597). VD16 A 3899; Zinner 3699; [7] leaves and 214 pages, octavo (VD16; the ‘4°’ at Norlind, p. 339, is an error). Written and printed while Aslakssøn was abroad as tutor to Otto Brahe (matriculated at Basel 1596/97). The book is dedicated to Tycho (Norlind, p. 339; Store norske leksikon), whence Norlind’s inference that it ‘har väl alltså befunnit sig i Tychos bibliotek’. The ownership rests on that inference alone: no copy with Tycho’s marks and no presentation copy is recorded in the inventories of Prandtl, Kleinschnitzová, Šolc or Mortensen, or in the trade. In the preface Aslakssøn declares for Copernicus, a position Tycho rejected, so that the dedication stands in tension with the book’s own position. The work is a ‘Mosaic physics’, a synthesis of astronomy and scripture on the three heavens (elemental or aerial, astronomical or sidereal, eternal or perpetual); Comenius later listed Aslakssøn among the Mosaic physicists who preceded him. Book III, De caelo perpetuo, was translated into English as ‘The Description of Heaven … Composed in Latine by Cunradus Aslachus, and conuerted into English by Raph [Ralph] Iennings’ (London 1623; EEBO A22193). Copies of the edition survive in Munich (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek), Vienna (Österreichische Nationalbibliothek) and Copenhagen (Royal Library); none is Tycho’s. The dedicatory epistle, read in the Munich copy, is addressed ‘Tychoni Brahe de Knudstrup, fundatori Arcis Uraniburgicae … sideralis scientiae scrutatori, instauratori, conservatori unico’, dated Basel, 16 November 1596, and signed ‘Cunradus Aslachus Bergensis’; it hails Tycho as ‘indefessus Caeli scrutator & Atlas’ and pays eyewitness homage to his celestial globe and astronomical instruments.
Copies of the edition examined
  • Bayerische Staatsbibliothek (BSB), Munich, see bsb10192622 — Siegen: Christoph Rab (Corvinus), 1597, 8° (VD16 A 3899; Zinner 3699). From an Augustinian Canons-Regular house ('Ex Bibliotheca... regularis... Augustanae... observantiae', ms. on title-page foot); to BSB after the 1803 Bavarian secularisation. Not Tycho's copy. Ms. provenance line on title-page foot; BSB classmarks on the pastedown.
  • Österreichische Nationalbibliothek (ÖNB), Vienna — Siegen: Christoph Rab (Corvinus), 1597, 8° (VD16 A 3899). Ordinary copy; not Tycho's.
  • Det Kongelige Bibliotek (Royal Library), Copenhagen — via ProQuest Early European Books, (EEB ‘Copenhagen’ collection) — Siegen: Christoph Rab (Corvinus), 1597, 8° (VD16 A 3899). Ordinary copy digitised in EEB from the Royal Library holdings; not Tycho's.
Norlind 1970, p. 339

Links: catalogue record

Road of dispersal

Note
Kleinschnitzová 1933 no.47; NK Clementinum Sign. 18 J 318. The library's record for 18 J 318 gives the imprint as Basel, Petrus Perna, 1560 (the survivor record for 18 J 318; Norlind p. 339 ‘Basileæ 1560’), and Šolc's Czech text of 2006 (p. 190) prints ‘Basileae 1560’; his German text of 1999 (§ 2.528, printed p. 149) prints ‘Basel 1559’, the year of the Macer bound with it — a slip, not a second edition, unless the title page says otherwise. The pressed ‘T. B. 1560’ of the binding is the year of the purchase in either case. The ‘T. B. 1560’ volume is the earliest dated binding of Tycho’s and, while the purchase note of the Ptolemy 5 B 70 is disputed, the earliest book securely his (Christianson 1967, pp. 200–201: ‘two of his own “textbooks”’). Ownership graded B on 28 October 2026: the attribution rests on the blind-stamped cipher T·B and the year 1560 on the binding alone — no inscription, no annotation, no 1642 or Chomutov mark, and Kleinschnitzová 1933 gives no argument. The cipher is consistent with Tycho's documented series of initial-and-year bindings 1561–1583 (Helsingør 1561, Uppsala 1563, Strahov and 10 G 47 1567, T.B.O. 1576–1583) and the contents fit the Copenhagen curriculum of 1560, but T·B alone identifies no one. The NK ČR photographs requested on 28 October 2026 (the three edges, both boards, the three title pages at 600 dpi) and an EBDB identification of the panel stamps are the tests. Reviewed again on 29 October 2026, the literature pack read whole: ownership graded C (was B). Beyond the cipher the literature holds nothing — no inscription, no annotation, no hand, no note of 1642. Kleinschnitzová (1933, pp. 76–78) herself sets the volume outside the twenty-three Clementinum volumes that carry the note of 1642 and says it ‘verirrt sich’, strayed, into the Jesuit professed house on the Malá Strana — an explanation that assumes what it should show; Norlind’s ‘T. B. O. 1560’ (1970, p. 339) reads a letter the board does not carry; the library’s record gives Tycho the year 1567 in its former-owner field without a basis; Šolc (1999, 2006, 2018), Christianson (1967, 2020), Thoren and Pařez all derive from Kleinschnitzová. If the cipher is Tycho’s, the year 1560 places the binding before his departure from Denmark; whether it is Tycho’s is the whole question, and the National Library’s photographs are the test. Decided on 29 October 2026.
Norlind 1970, p. 339

Note
Norlind 1970, p. 340: that Tycho owned a copy of some edition is probable, since the Progymnasmata (Opera omnia III, pp. 251–253) quote verbatim a letter of Benedetti to Raimondo of Verona against the view that the new star of 1572 was one of Cassiopeia’s stars; which edition cannot be settled (in the Turin edition of 1585 the letter stands at pp. 371–374). Norlind 1970, p. 340
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Att Tycho ägt ett exemplar av någon upplaga av detta verk, är sannolikt. I »Prog.» (III, 251–253) citerar han ordagrant ett ställe härur, ur ett brev från Benedictus till Raimundus från Verona, vari denne polemiserar mot Raimundus' åsikt, att den nya stjärnan i Cassiopeia icke vore »ny» utan en av stjärnorna där. Av Tychos ord framgår, att boken varit sällsynt. Vilken upplaga det varit, kan icke fastslås med säkerhet. I upplagan, tryckt i Torino 1585, 2°, står brevet på s. 371–374 (jfr G. Bordiga, »Giovanni Battista Benedetti», i: »Atti del R. Ist. Veneto di scienze» etc., 85, 1925–26, s. 613). Riccardi, »Biblioteca matematica italiana» uppger första upplagan tryckt i Torino 1580 och känner ingen upplaga från 1585 (endast ett omtryck av uppl. 1580). I ett brev till Rothmann, febr. 1589 (VI, 172) nämner Tycho ett annat brev från Benedictus (s. 256–257 i nyssnämnda upplaga) vari behandlas bl.a. månens ljus, Benedictus menar sålunda, att det sekundära ljuset förorsakas av planeten Venus – en åsikt som Tycho trodde sig ha bekräftat genom sina egna observationer.

Road I, The Jesuit road: the Clementinum (1642), the colleges at Chomutov and Krumlov and the professed house, reunited in the Clementinum after 1773. The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Note
Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 12:2, ‘Manuskript … Brahes Autograph’ (Truhlář no. 2761); Norlind 1970, p. 340; the National Library’s early-prints record 14 C 20/adl.1 enters it under the Uraniborg edition of 1591. Twenty quarto leaves in a professional copyist’s hand, the content Tycho’s (Šíma and Valeška 2002; Dreyer, Opera omnia I, p. 315, had already denied the hand), dated ‘Calend. Januar. 1591’, with a distich dated ‘A. C. 1595, 13 Cal. Xbris’ (Prusík 1901). Published in facsimile by Studnička (1886) and by Dreyer (Opera omnia I, pp. 283–293). Bound after the Rheticus Canon of 1551 in the volume 14 C 20, whose title carries the note ‘Vide in fine Dogmata Tychonis Brahe m. p. scripta’. Gingerich and Westman (1988, pp. 24–26) trace the misattribution: Studnička's facsimile of 1886 took the manuscript for Tycho's autograph; Dreyer, in the biography of 1890 (p. 362 n.) and in Opera omnia I, pp. 315–318, found the body not his and the title-page signature doubtful (‘neither the “T,” “B,” nor “h” were typical of Brahe's autograph’), his test the two-stroke M never used by Tycho; Studnička (1901) then argued from this manuscript to the De revolutionibus marginalia, and Horský's facsimile of 1971 rested on the same circle. The two hands are, in their judgement, different from each other and both unlike Tycho's. Tycho names the manuscript to Hagecius on 14 March 1592 as the pamphlet of rules that lay ‘open for teaching in our library on each table’ (Opera omnia VII, p. 325; 1988, p. 62).
Norlind 1970, p. 340

Norlind records

Note
Brasch sent the manuscript poem, which celebrates Melchior von Roedern’s defence of Grosswardein (Várad) in 1598, to Tycho twice: in August 1600, when it was lost in transit (Opera omnia VIII, 337), and as a replacement in September 1600 that ‘probably reached’ him (Opera omnia VIII, 380; Norlind p. 340); von Roedern died on 20 September 1600. No surviving manuscript codex has been located in any catalogue. Martin Brasch the Younger also published a printed Varadini Hungariae propugnaculi... anni 1598 (1598) on the same subject — plausibly the same matter in print beside an authorial manuscript redaction of 1600, though no source collates the two. The first copy never arrived, the replacement only ‘probably’ did, no codex survives, and no ownership mark that could be looked for attaches to the item; the entry therefore rests on the correspondence alone. Status lost since 20 October 2026: a unique manuscript sent and probably received, not a mass-survival text — the class retired as unlocatable does not fit it.
Norlind 1970, p. 340

Brasch besjunger här Melchior Rhederus' (von Rödern) segerrika försvar av Grosswardein (Nagy-Várad) mot turkarna. Note
Dedication copy sent to Tycho about 1588 (Šolc 2002, p. 331). NK Clementinum, Sign. XV K 22 (olim 8 I 70), catalogued at Chomutov in 1671. The epigram on Bruno’s name on the last page is in a hand that Šolc gives to Tycho and that the handwriting analysis of Šíma and Valeška leaves open; the attribution to Tycho is graded D. How the Acrotismus reached Uraniborg is not settled: Kořán (1969) and Horský (1975) proposed Hagecius as the intermediary; Sturlese (1985, pp. 324–325) objected that only one letter passed between Hagecius and Tycho in 1588 and suggested the carrier of Morsing's Diarium to Bruno (Westman 2011, pp. 304–305 and p. 568 n. 127). In the De immenso (1591) Bruno names Tycho on the comets and on the proper motion of the stars (p. 305). Hedged 27 October 2026 (register dossier §17-06): a dedication to Tycho on the title is secure — three faded, trimmed lines, ‘Omni nobilitatis genere [Kořán: gratiae] insigni et famosis.o illustri et excell.o D. Tichoni Dano in signum benevolentiae et obsequii’ (del Giudice 2008; Šíma & Valeška 2002, p. 158); that it is Bruno's own hand rests on the word ‘author’ Kořán read in 1969, now erased, on Šíma & Valeška's unargued statement and on del Giudice's unpublished comparison; the arrival ‘by 17 August 1588’ rests on ‘Iordanus Nullanus in quodam scripto de Mundo contra Peripateticos’ in a letter known only as printed in 1596 (Opera omnia VI 144–149), and Šíma & Valeška put the gift after 1597 ‘somewhere in Germany’; the carrier is unknown (Westman 2011, p. 304 n. 127). Hand, date and carrier are not secure.

Inscription: Tycho's dedication on the verso of the front free endpaper facing the Calvin title, read on the leaf 21 October 2026: ‘Johanni Lindenouio | Conſobrino suo | Tycho Brahe | ddt.’ — four lines on one rising diagonal in one ink, the last letter of the name e-shaped where the pen failed at the joint (Mortensen 1955, p. 26) and read o, one long s only, arc u-marks over ‘-ou-’ and ‘suo’, no diaeresis on the y, the display signature about 1.8 times the body, ‘ddt’ after the name under two long strokes with a point after — d(ono) d(edi)t (Fund og Forskning X, 1963, p. 155; Mortensen printed d(onum) d(onavit)); wholly in Tycho's hand, probable (the Graphonomicon specimen copenhagen-kb-calvin-lindenov-dedication, grade B) Annotations: no reader's marks seen in the leaves photographed; the volume's later marks (21 October 2026): the Royal Library's pencils ‘88,-201’, ‘1954 g. 230’, ‘Boghist. Saml.’, ‘BOX’, ‘S-1977’, a cancelled ‘D.A.?.?’, ‘1597’ on the Calvin title and ‘dupl’ on the Theocritus title; a continental ‘fol. 9781’ (the 7 crossed) and ‘36’ on the rear pastedown, the pencil code ‘fij’ at the foot of the Theocritus title, an erased pencil note on the free endpaper, removed labels on both pastedowns, a scraped inscription above the device on the Calvin title; a seventeenth-century ink spine title ‘Johannis Caluini | Epistolae et Respons[a] | Theocriti | Idyllia et Epigra[m]ata’ Binding: examined 21 October 2026: gilt parchment over stiff pasteboard, 175 × 120 × 75 mm (leaves 171 × 106 × 70 mm), three sewing supports laced through the covering at the joints, a flat untooled spine with a later ink title, two pairs of green silk ties (remnants in the slits), all edges stained red and plain, plaited natural-thread endbands; on each board a gilt leaf roll with a twisted central line (c. 7–8 mm wide, leaf pitch c. 5 mm, corners overrun) with four five-petalled double roses with hatched barbs, c. 11 mm, in the corners and the oval at centre — the portrait on the front, the arms on the back, both the small die, c. 58 × 42–43 mm on the ruler, the gilt mostly worn; concordant with Mortensen's 5.8 × 4.3 (1955, p. 25), Friis's 59 × 42.5 on the Vienna quartos (1868–69, p. 251) and Strahov Σ VI 3 (58 × 43, 18 September 2026); Mortensen's ‘Spor af grønne Bindebaand’, ‘Rullestempel’, ‘Rosetter’ and the later spine title confirmed; the place of binding undetermined but the tools of the Hven family — the laurel roll of Gigas's Epistolae and GKS 307, a rose punch unlike theirs and unlike Σ VI 3's star but near the Magini rose of Hven — so Wandsbek 1597–98 or Copenhagen 1597 before Prague; the rose punch is not the Hven presentation rose (c. 14.5 mm: Stockholm RAR 106 A, the Dibner and Johan Adolf Epistolae, the Hazmburk Mechanica) nor the Magini rose (9.5–10 mm) but a third punch of 11 mm — a binder with his own tools in the Hven idiom, place open (tested 21 October 2026 at one scale)

binding: original; copy located by Norlind at: Köpenhamn, Det kongelige Bibliotek; copy located by Norlind at: Köpenhamn, Det kgl. Bibliotek
Surviving copy
88, 201 01801 (eks. 2), Royal Danish Library (Det kongelige Bibliotek) · identification A · Period 4 (gilt supralibros)
Examined on 21 October 2026 (eks. 2, 88, 201 01801): both gilt supralibros in the small size — the portrait oval c. 58 × 42 mm and the arms oval c. 58 × 42.5 mm on the ruler (±1 mm), the one size, concordant with Mortensen's 5.8 × 4.3, Friis's 59 × 42.5 on the first twelve Vienna fair-copy quartos and Strahov Σ VI 3 (58 × 43) — the legends HIC PATET EXTERIOR TYCHONIS FORMA BRAHEI PVLCHRIVS ENITEAT QVAE LATET INTERIOR and ARMA GENVS FVNDI PEREVNT DVRABILE VIRTVS ET DOCTRINA DECVS NOBILITATIS HABENT legible in part, the gilt worn and best preserved on the back; and Tycho's dedication on the verso of the front free endpaper facing the Calvin title, read letter by letter: ‘Johanni Lindenouio | Conſobrino suo | Tycho Brahe | ddt.’ — four lines on one rising diagonal in one dark iron-gall-type ink and one nib width, the last letter of ‘Lindenouio’ e-shaped where the pen failed at the joint (Mortensen) and read o, one long s only (‘Conſobrino’, the s of ‘suo’ a round s), arc-shaped u-marks over the u of ‘-ou-’ and of ‘suo’, no diaeresis on the y, the display signature about 1.8 times the body, the formula ‘ddt’ after the name with both d-ascenders crossing two long strokes drawn above it and a full point after — d(ono) d(edi)t (Fund og Forskning X, 1963, p. 155), one Latin sentence in natural order. Wholly in Tycho's hand: probable — Mortensen's verdict (‘egenhændige Tilskrift’), the signature built as the secure Wittenberg leaf of 8 May 1599 and the Duodo dedication of 1600, the address sharing the father's own prose idioms (the u-mark, the hooked descending J, the looped d), no calligrapher's marks, one ink and one planned block; the alternative of an address written at the same desk by a secretary over Tycho's signature is not excluded by the photographs — though Jessenius, the one documented secretary of such an address, is disfavoured on a word-for-word comparison with his album entry of 8 January 1599, and the father's own prose in the same album shares the address's 5-shaped round s and its L — and the son (who signed ‘T.F.’, ‘Filius’, ‘junior’ and never had a channel to a Lindenov) is excluded on context
Links: catalogue record
Road of dispersal
Road 0, Left the library in Tycho’s lifetime: gifts and exchanges. The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Note
A Tycho Sammelband repatriated from the USA (through the ship-broker Hjalmar Bruhn); the only book from his own library at KB besides the autograph observations. Given by Tycho to his cousin Hans Lindenov after the Calvin edition of 1597 had appeared — probably before 1599, Mortensen supposes, unless the book was sent to him later (Mortensen 1955, pp. 26–27). Worn parchment binding, gilt portrait/arms supralibros. Mortensen 1955, pp. 25–27. The recipient is Hans Christoffersen Lindenov til Ørslevkloster (d. by 7 April 1610), lensmand at Bergenhus 1578–86 — the officer to whom the crown's four letters on Tycho's Nordfjord fief were addressed — and lastly at Hammershus 1594–1610; he was on Hven for one night, 3–5 July 1594 (the diary, pp. 218–219). Tycho's consobrinus in the strict sense: Mortensen corrected Danmarks Adels Aarbog 1902, which lists Hans under Christoffer Lindenov's second wife Ide Rantzau, to the first marriage with Margrethe Clausdatter Bille (b. 1525), Beate Bille's sister; DAA dates neither marriage, and the correction stands unrefuted (Mortensen 1955, p. 27; DAA 1902, pp. 286–287; DAA 1890, p. 87). The Calvin edition stood in the Frankfurt Lent-fair catalogue of 1597 under ‘Libri Calvinianorum’ (Lutz, A2v): Tycho, who in 1574 had called Calvin's tract against the astrologers learned and its author over-strict (TBOO I, pp. 170–172), and who praised Beza in the Progymnasmata (TBOO II, p. 325), acquired the Reformed letter-book in the months after his own Epistolarum astronomicarum liber and in the spring his Hven pastor was convicted for failing to admonish him (22 April 1597). The Royal Library's acquisition falls between January 1952 and the article of 1955; the copy to be examined on 21 October 2026 is 88, 201 01801 (eks. 2), the first copy being Scavenius's of 1665. A pre-visit dossier of 21 October 2026 prepared the examination. Examined in the Royal Library on 21 October 2026: the volume is eks. 2, 88, 201 01801, acquired in 1954 (the accession pencil ‘1954 g. 230’); the dedication read on the leaf and the hand assessed (wholly Tycho's, probable; the son excluded on context, a secretary at the same desk not excluded by the photographs); the dies measured and the binding described; the Theocritus is VD16 ZV 14910 with the Commelinus ‘Veritas’ device (ΑΛΗΘΕΙΑ ΠΑΝΔΑΜΑΤΩΡ), the Calvin VD16 C 304 with Antonius's later device, the pelican on the mountain; Kancelliets Brevbøger keep Hans Lindenov on Bornholm in 1597–1602, so the gift was handed over in Copenhagen in the spring of 1597 if at all in person, or sent.
Norlind 1970, p. 341

Open questions
  • Collate both constituents (Calvin [28] Bl., 804[=806] pp. and a final blank; Theocritus [8] Bl., 319, 30 pp., [1] Bl., 150 pp. in three parts) and record whether Scaliger's Emendationes and Casaubon's Theocriticarum lectionum libellus are bound in; the leaves photographed on 21 October 2026 were the titles, the end of the Calvin index and the dedication opening.
  • Whether the dedication's first two lines are Tycho's or a secretary's at his desk (see the volume's open questions): Jessenius disfavoured on his VI F 44 entry of 8 January 1599; Longomontanus and Tengnagel untested.

Carelli, Giovanni Battista, Ephemerides ad annos XIX (1557-1575). Venice, 1557, 4°

Attested, not locatedBrec-e-norlind-carelli-ephemerides
Status
Attested, not located · entry confidence B
Subject
Ephemerides/Tables
Attested by
Norlind 1970, p. 342 (s.v. Carellus, Johannes Baptista); Šolc 2006; Westman 2011
Norlind records
Opera omnia: X, 5 ff.
Note
Norlind (1970, p. 342), citing Dreyer, states that Tycho ‘skaffade sig under sin Leipzigvistelse’ this edition — acquired it during his Leipzig years — and cites it often in his earliest observation journal (Opera omnia X, 5 ff.). Dreyer’s sentence is narrower: ‘In his observations from 1563–64 he also mentions the Ephemerides of Carellus (Venice, 1557)’ (Tycho Brahe, Edinburgh 1890, p. 18, n. 1); the acquisition at Leipzig is Norlind’s inference. The edition is Venice: Vincenzo Valgrisi, 1557, 4to; its title runs ‘ad annos XIX’, 1557 to 1575, where Norlind prints ‘IX’. Three datings stand side by side: Šolc 2006 (printed p. 190) places the Carelli ephemerides for 1557 with the Stadius among the tables Tycho ‘procured at once’ after the eclipse of 21 August 1560, unsourced; Norlind's Leipzig purchase is an inference from Dreyer p. 18 n. 1 (the citations in the observations of 1563–64); and the loci record of the Copenhagen years (after Christianson 2020, pp. 19–22) has the Carelli bought with Jens Nilsson in Copenhagen about 1561. Šolc's 1560 is not adopted. Westman (2011, p. 240) writes that Tycho, like Hagecius, ‘owned and annotated’ a copy of Carelli's Ephemerides; his note (p. 557 n. 80) cites the edition only, and no copy is named.
Norlind 1970, p. 342

Norlind records
Opera omnia: VII, 100
Note
Brucaeus bought Tycho a copy of Clavius’s Gnomonices at Rostock in March 1586 (his letter of 15 March 1586: ‘emi et tibi Gnomonicen CLAVIJ Bambergensis’, valued at seven Joachimsthaler; Opera omnia VII, 100). The purchase was conditional: the bookseller had deposited the books with Brucaeus at the beginning of the winter and would take them back if Tycho did not want them or already had them (‘Emi autem hac conditione, ut si tibi forte non placerent, aut forte eosdem iam esses nactus, Bibliopola ad se recipiat … Iam enim libros ineunte hyeme apud me deposuit’, VII, 100); whether this copy reached Hven is not recorded (Norlind 1926, p. 214, no. 3). That Tycho had the work is his own statement to Rantzau of 22 February 1597: Clavius’s writings on Euclid, on Sacrobosco and on gnomonics ‘in promptu habeo, et iamdudum introspexi’ (VII, 381). In December 1584 the Rostock bookseller, back from Frankfurt without the books Tycho had ordered, had sold his one copy, valued at nearly five Joachimsthaler, to Heinrich Rantzau (Opera omnia VII, 88; Norlind 1926, p. 214, no. 3), so Tycho’s first order went unfilled.
Norlind 1970, p. 342

Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C).

Copernicus, Nicolaus, Commentariolus (De hypothesibus motuum coelestium ... commentariolus) — manuscript. , Manuskript

DisputedCVienna, Austrian National Libraryrec-e-onb-commentariolus
Status
Disputed · entry confidence C
Type
Manuscript
Subject
Astronomy
Attested by
Norlind 1970, p. 343 (s.v. Copernicus, Nicolaus); Walde 1938; Jardine & Segonds 2008; Vackářová 2026; Gingerich & Westman 1988; Westman 2011
Norlind records
Opera omnia: II, 428
Surviving copy
Cod. 10530, Austrian National Library (Österreichische Nationalbibliothek) · identification C
No Tycho mark. The ÖNB description records no former owner (only a 19th-c. half-parchment rebinding). The identification rests on Norlind's attribution and on the volume's Uraniborg-circle content — Longomontanus's 'Responsio ad Capnurianam apologiam' is bound in the same 16th-c. Sammelhandschrift — which is circumstantial, not a mark.
Links: catalogue record · digital facsimile (ÖNB)
Road of dispersal
Road U, Route out of the library unknown. The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Note
A manuscript of the Commentariolus in the Österreichische Nationalbibliothek, Vienna, attributed to Tycho’s library by Norlind. Tycho owned the text: Hagecius gave him a copy at Regensburg in 1575, and he printed it in the Progymnasmata (Opera omnia II, 428). Whether the Vienna manuscript is that copy rests on Norlind’s attribution and on the Uraniborg-circle contents of the same Sammelhandschrift; the volume carries no mark of his, and its catalogue record names no former owner, so both the entry and the identification of the copy are graded C. Walde (1938) showed the Vienna manuscript to have been Longomontanus’s gift to the amanuensis Johannes Eriksen at Benátky on 18 July 1600 and left open whether it passed from Eriksen to Tycho; Eriksen’s books otherwise went into Queen Christina’s library with the Prague booty. The witness therefore belongs to the Uraniborg circle rather than, on present evidence, to Tycho’s own shelves. Jardine and Segonds note the copy that came from Hagecius (2008, p. 187 n. 4). The National Library's account of 2026 adds two points to the Regensburg gift: that the original Hájek exemplar is untraced (the same object as Norlind's ‘Tycho's exemplar not located’ if the Regensburg transfer was a gift), and the conjecture that it was Tycho who had Copernicus's name — absent from the anonymous letter as it circulated — set at the head of the transcripts he distributed (Vackářová 2026, printed p. 22; ‘zřejmě’, her conjecture, not a documented fact). The three surviving transcripts she names (Vienna, Stockholm, Aberdeen; p. 20) are those the history essay already records. Status disputed since 20 October 2026: the witness belongs to the Uraniborg circle rather than, on present evidence, to Tycho's shelves (Walde 1938 against the transfer), and a located C with the ownership in doubt is the Definitions' disputed, not located. Westman (2011, p. 248) describes the Regensburg manuscript as one ‘that evidently had been in Hagecius's family for many years’, citing TBOO II 428, which records the gift and nothing of the manuscript's earlier history.
Norlind 1970, p. 343
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Copernicus' preliminära, endast i manuskript publicerade, förhandsmeddelande om de forskningsresultat han sedermera framlade för offentligheten i »De revolutionibus orbium cœlestium». – I »Prog.» (II, 428) skriver Tycho, att han erhöll ett exemplar av Hagecius vid deras möte i Regensburg 1575 och att han därpå lät göra avskrifter av detsamma, vilka han skickade till andra astronomer i Tyskland. En sådan avskrift var väl det exemplar som Longomontanus vid sin avresa från Benatky d. 18 juli 1600 skänkte Johannes Eriksen, en annan av Tychos lärjungar. Detta exemplar, ett av de få bevarade, finns nu i Wien. Ett annat, tidigare ägt av Hevelius i Danzig, som förmodligen förvärvat det med Keplers kvarlåtenskap, finnes nu i KVA.
Open questions
  • Whether the Österreichische Nationalbibliothek’s Commentariolus manuscript, Longomontanus’s gift to Johannes Eriksen in July 1600 (Walde 1938), ever passed from Eriksen to Tycho or reached Vienna by another route; a mark of Tycho’s in the volume or a record of its arrival in Vienna would decide.
  • Whether a second Commentariolus in the Tycho orbit — the quarto of 14 folios in Paul Wittich's own hand, received from his uncle Balthasar Sartorius of Breslau, which Dudith described to Praetorius on 12 February 1589 (Gingerich and Westman 1988, p. 10 n. 21) — came to Prague with the Wittich books in 1600 under Tycho's ‘other manuscripts, if there are any’ (1 November 1589), and how it relates to the Vienna manuscript and to Liddel's Aberdeen copy.

From Tycho’s library: Prandtl, Verzeichnis A no. 14, his Einzelband X (‘reichverzierter weißer Lederband’). Prandtl (1932) attributed the marginalia to Tycho; Gingerich and Westman showed them to be Paul Wittich’s. The acquisition is documented in the correspondence. After Wittich’s death (1586) two noble visitors, the barons Johann Septimius von Lichtenstein and Felician von Herberstein, took charge of Wittich’s books and papers in Tycho’s name (Tycho to Hagecius, 22 March 1589, Opera omnia VII 165–166) and pursued the purchase of Wittich’s whole library from the surviving sister for six years, 1589–1595 (Tycho’s letters of 1 November 1589 and 12 August 1595 — Hagecius’s reply of 10 May 1589 found the barons away from court and Dudith already rebuffed by the sister: ‘omnem eius supellectilem librariam... iusto pretio nanciscar’; ‘de libris VITICHIANIS... a sorore superstite... obtinere queam’). According to Mosley (2007, pp. 175–179; the despatch at p. 179, following Gingerich and Westman 1988) Jacob Monau is held to have succeeded in part: he is thought to have despatched three of Wittich’s four annotated De revolutionibus volumes to Prague, the fourth remaining in Wrocław — Gingerich’s Wrocław 9 (Biblioteka Uniwersytecka 437777), the copy Valentin von Sebisch transcribed c. 1604. Gingerich’s Annotated Census traces two of Wittich’s copies to Tycho through Monaw’s delivery of October 1600 — Prague 3, 14 B 16 (p. 23: ‘likely one brought to him in Prague from Wittich’s heirs in Wrocław by Jacob Monaw … in October of 1600’) and Vatican 1, Ottoboniana 1902 (p. 105: ‘presumably he got it in October 1600 through the help of Jacob Monaw’) — and gives the Liège copy, Res MS 69C, the provenance of an annotator from Reinhold’s circle, Wittich and the Université de Liège, with no Prague station (p. 8); in his essay of the same year Gingerich writes that ‘another of the Wittich/Tychonic copies was perhaps acquired by a Belgian Jesuit working in Prague, for today it is found in the University Library in Liège’ (Tycho Brahe and Prague, p. 325). Whether the Liège copy was among the books Monaw brought to Prague is thus left open between Gingerich’s two accounts and Mosley’s count of three. The pursuit was bound up with Tycho’s dispute with Ursus over plagiarism. This is the channel by which the Wittich-annotated De revolutionibus entered the Tychoniana. The count of Wittich’s annotated copies that reached Tycho stands at two values: Mosley has three despatched to Prague, Gingerich and Westman two of the four, as Jardine and Segonds cite them (2008, p. 3 n. 1); both stand until the Liège question below is settled. Gingerich and Westman describe the volume (1988, pp. 33–34): the blind-stamped pigskin binding carries roll-stamps dated 1550, which does not exclude Wittich's having had the book bound; 21 blank folios are bound before the text and 71 after it, never used; the year 1580 is used in a worked example on f. 93; slips are pasted over earlier notes on ff. 22v, 26 and 65; John Dee's Parallaticae commentationis of 1573 is cited on f. 124v; the star catalogue (ff. 46v–62v) is the one long stretch without notes. They take it as ‘one of three copies brought by Monaw to Tycho in October 1600, but the only one to have retained any connection with the Danish astronomer’ (p. 33). Westman (2011, p. 283 n. 7) counts the surviving Wittich copies as five — four treated in Gingerich & Westman 1988 and a fifth, with a single Wittich annotation, identified in Gingerich's census of 2002 — and records the efforts to obtain the library as continuing at Wandsbek in 1598, ‘in particular, the several copies of De Revolutionibus that he knew it contained’ (p. 349); his statement that Tycho sought the books ‘from his widow’ (p. 286) is at odds with Tycho's own letters, which name the surviving sister. No letter, inventory, Kepler or Tengnagel document records a price, a payment, a receipt or a delivery: the correspondence ends with Monau’s promise of 14 June 1600 (Opera omnia VIII 325–326), and Gingerich and Westman themselves write that ‘as far as the letters are concerned, this is unfortunately the end of the story’ (1988, p. 22); part of Wittich’s library was still being sold at Wrocław in 1606. The October 1600 delivery is carried as probable, not as documented (register dossier of 27 October 2026, §3 and §6).
Norlind 1970, p. 343
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Detta är andra upplagan av Copernicus' berömda verk, i vilken upplaga också ingår Rheticus' första preliminära rapport (»Narratio prima») om världssystemet. – Pr. nr 14. Kl. nr 11. – Prag, UB.
Open questions
  • Whether the Liège De revolutionibus (Université de Liège, Res MS 69C; Nuremberg 1543, annotated by an early reader of Reinhold’s circle and by Wittich) passed through Tycho’s hands: Mosley counts three Wittich volumes despatched to Prague, Gingerich’s Census gives the Liège copy no Prague station, and Gingerich’s essay of 2002 supposes it acquired in Prague by a Belgian Jesuit; evidence of a Prague station in the Liège volume itself would decide.
  • 27 Oct 2026 — nothing in 14 B 16 or its records bears on a Prague station of the Liège copy; the test remains the Liège volume itself (a Clementinum or Prague Jesuit mark) or a Liège record naming a Prague owner.
  • Lead, unadopted: the National Library's account names Andreas Dudith, with Hájek, Monau and Longomontanus, among those Tycho asked to secure Wittich's books (Vackářová 2026, printed p. 33, without a source). Dudith died in February 1589 at Breslau, where the Wittich estate lay, and Tycho was in correspondence with him (the Epistolarium's Dudith letters of 17 August 1588 and 10 May 1589; TBOO VII); the claim is plausible and would add a fourth agent to the three attempts Christianson counts, but it is not adopted until the letter is found — Gingerich & Westman 1988, pp. 17–22 (Desiderata row 4f) or the Dudith correspondence are the places to look.
  • 27 Oct 2026 — no source held this round adds to the Dudith lead; G&W 1988 pp. 17–22 and the Dudith letters in TBOO VII (17 Aug 1588, 10 May 1589) remain the places to look.

No Tycho autograph mark. The dense annotations are Paul Wittich's, not Tycho's -- Gingerich (Census, pp. 105-108) retracts the earlier Tycho-annotation belief, noting the flyleaf longitude list cites Vratislavia (Wittich's Wrocław) but neither Hven nor Copenhagen. Tycho ownership rests on Gingerich's documented acquisition history (one of the copies Monau brought to Prague for Tycho in Oct 1600 -- Gingerich, Census, pp. 105-108; Mosley p. 179 puts the number despatched at three), not on a Tycho mark.
Links: catalogue record · digital facsimile (Vatican Library) · the front board of the Pius IX binding (DigiVatLib canvas 1, piatto anteriore)
Road of dispersal
Road III, The Swedish booty of 1648 (Königsmarck’s capture of the west bank of Prague). Tycho (presumably acquired Oct 1600 via Monau) → Rudolf II → 1648 Swedish loot → Queen Christina → Rome 1655 → Ottoboni 1690 → BAV Ott. lat. 1902. The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Note
Scholarship argues that Tycho owned or used more than one De revolutionibus. This copy is the Nuremberg edition of 1543 now Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, Ott. lat. 1902 (Gingerich: Ottoboniana 1902), described by Gingerich, Annotated Census (2002), pp. 105–108 (I.98, ‘Vatican 1’). The copy is annotated by Wittich; Tycho ‘eagerly sought’ it ‘and presumably he got it in October 1600 through the help of Jacob Monaw’. Gingerich conjectures its later route: from Rudolf II to the Swedish booty of 1648, to Christina, to Rome in 1655, to the Ottoboni library and so to the Vatican. The annotations are Wittich’s, not Tycho’s: Gingerich retracts the older belief, the flyleaf longitudes citing Vratislavia rather than Hven or Copenhagen. Tycho’s ownership therefore rests on the documented acquisition through Monau, not on any mark of his. The copy is distinct from the Wittich copy in the Clementinum (Sign. 14 B 16, the Basel edition of 1566). Gingerich and Westman (1988, pp. 31–32, 140): the volume is bound in red-orange morocco with the arms of Pius IX on the spine, so that the physical evidence of its earlier provenance is lost; it is entered in Queen Christina's catalogue of 1655 (Vatican, MS lat. 1871, pp. 88–91), the stage from which the Prague-loot conjecture is argued (Callmer 1977, pp. 116 ff.); ‘Andreae Osiandri’ is added in red ink on the Ad lectorem; observations of 8 November 1572 (f. 57v) and 16 September 1574 (ff. 54, 163) recur in the Liège copy; the manuscript leaves ff. 197v–211v are dated between 27 January and 17 February 1578, ff. 211–211v carrying star positions for 1578 and 1580.
Open questions
  • Whether a third of Wittich’s annotated copies, the Liège De revolutionibus of 1543 (ResMS 69C), also reached Tycho: Mosley (2007, p. 179, after Gingerich and Westman 1988) has Monau despatch three of the four to Prague, whereas Gingerich’s Census (2002) counts two as reaching Tycho, this copy and 14 B 16, and places the Liège copy outside his hands.
