Note
Quercetanus (Joseph Du Chesne), Ad Iacobi Auberti … brevis responsio (Lyon 1575, 8vo): a Paracelsian book Tycho owned only briefly. Its preface is dated 1 April 1575, and he gave the copy to Thaddaeus Hagecius at their meeting in Regensburg in the autumn of that year; in August 1585 he asked Hagecius for another copy, unable to recall author or title (Tycho to Hagecius, August 1585, Opera omnia VII, 95). The work is identified from Hagecius’s marginal note ‘Libellus est Josephi Quercetani’ on Tycho’s letter (autograph in Vienna, Österreichische Nationalbibliothek), not from the book; Norlind gives the title as ‘med största sannolikhet’ (Norlind 1970, p. 359). The copy passed into Hagecius’s library; a copy recovered from it would carry his marks, not Tycho’s. Status attested, passed on, since 20 October 2026: the copy left the library in his lifetime as a gift to Hagecius (road 0), which is why no copy is sought — not a mass-survival text retired as unlocatable.
Norlind 1970, p. 359
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
[Preamble printed before the headword, leading into it:] I aug. 1585 (VII, 95) skriver Tycho till Hagecius, att denne vid deras sammanträffande i Regensburg hösten 1575 erhöll en bok, vars författare Tycho dock icke kan erinra sig. Boken handlade om beredning av »kemiska läkemedel» (»de Chymicis medicamentis præparandis»), titeln kan Tycho icke med bestämdhet uppge, men han minns, att formatet var oktav. Fastän han sökt efter den hos bokhandlare i Tyskland, har han inte lyckats komma över den, eftersom han inte kunnat uppge vare sig förf.-namnet eller titeln. Han ber nu Hagecius skicka ett exemplar, så vida ett sådant står att få köpa, eller också ge besked om författarens namn. Vi veta inte, om Hagecius lyckades tillmötesgå Tychos önskan, men i margen till Tychos brev (original i Wien) har han antecknat »Libellus est Josephi Quercetani». (»Quartani» i noten, VII, 407, är en felläsning av utg.) Den bok som här avses och som Tycho alltså en gång ägt är med största sannolikhet: [Here follows the entry line; text after the entry line:] Förf., vars franska namn var Joseph Du Chesne (1546–1609), ansågs som en framstående läkare och var sedan 1593 livmedikus hos Henrik IV. I sina talrika skrifter framträder han dock som en charlatan inom yrket. Att Tycho varit så intresserad av denna skrift, sammanhänger väl med den läkarverksamhet han bedrev på Hven. Quercetanus var en ivrig anhängare av Paracelsus, för vilken Tycho också hyste en viss böjelse. Bokens förord är daterat d. 1 april 1575, den var således alldeles nyutkommen, då Tycho skänkte den till Hagecius.

B.’ on the manuscript-supplied title leaf of the Imago mundi and his glosses (e.g. fol. dd1r), read as his hand by Boldan & Kazanskii 2023; the year 1576 stamped into the front pasteboard (leather stripped, board later papered); ‘Collegii Societatis Jesu Commotovien. catalogo inscriptus 1645’ on fol. <2>2r; a blacked-out note of the Kulm brethren on the Euclid's a1r, recovered under the VSC 8000 (fig. 5)
Links: catalogue record · the library's photographs of the front and rear boards (Aleph STT record, OBRAZ. PŘÍLOHA; session-bound links — open from the record)
Bound with: Ailly, Pierre d’, Imago mundi, with his astronomical treatises (the first edition) (Louvain: Johannes de Westfalia, c. 1477–1483 (GW M31954))
Road of dispersal
Road I, The Jesuit road: the Clementinum (1642), the colleges at Chomutov and Krumlov and the professed house, reunited in the Clementinum after 1773. With the Imago mundi: Chomutov college (catalogued 1645), then the Clementinum after 1773.. The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Note
The second piece of the Sammelband 44 F 38: Ratdolt's Euclid of 1482, the first printed edition, with its woodcut diagrams in the outer margins. On the blank recto of its first leaf a blacked-out ownership note, perhaps still of the late fifteenth century, read under the comparator as ‘Hic liber pertinet domui fratrum in Culmen’: the house of the Brethren of the Common Life at Kulm (Chełmno) in Royal Prussia, founded from Zwolle in 1473, with a school Copernicus probably attended before 1491 and, in the years about 1473 to 1478, one of the first presses of east-central Europe; its library was dispersed when the house ended in the 1530s or 1540s, and eleven volumes with twenty-six incunables are known from it (Boldan and Kazanskii 2023, p. 28, citing Szandorowska 1968 and 1973). How the Euclid came from Kulm to Tycho — bought, like his other student books, or through the Prussian connections of his circle — is not recorded; it was in his hands by 1576, when the binding was made. Boldan and Kazanskii call it the first scientific title recovered from the Kulm brethren's library.
Open questions
  • The route from the Brethren of the Common Life at Kulm to Tycho before 1576.
  • 27 Oct 2026 — no source held records it.

Status
Located · entry confidence A
Subject

Acquisition

Ownership marks
Inscription: No Jesuit inscription of 1642. Title leaf: the ink ‘Bibliotheca Strahoviensis’ and two round purple BIBLIOTHECA STRAHOVIENSIS stamps of the series the library introduced from the late eighteenth century (Hlinovský & Pišna 2018, pp. 10–12); lower left, in graphite, the large ‘G. Crusio ‹K›’ of Gabriel Crusius — the formula ‘G. Crusio inservio’ that Kleinschnitzová printed from the National Library's 5 G 92 (1933, p. 89), where it stands beside the year 1673 — and faint strokes of an earlier inscription, effaced (read on the volume, 18 September 2026). Annotations: marginal notes ‘in his hand’ (Pařez 2009: přípisky psané jeho rukou in margine; Pařez, 4 September 2026: a few notes, certainly Tycho's) — not yet examined graphonomically Binding: front board: a plain blind-stamped two-line TYCHO / BRAHE above the central ornament and the date 1567 below it, on a Renaissance blind-tooled frame-composition binding; no supralibros on the back (Pařez 2009, with photograph; Katalog Tritius: ‘Supralibros Tychona Brahe z roku 1567’). The earliest dated appearance of his full name on a binding, of the family of the ‘Tycho Brade 1561’ and ‘Ty Brad 1563’ name-stamps
Surviving copy
AV II 2, Strahov Library (Strahovská knihovna, Královská kanonie premonstrátů na Strahově) · identification A · Period 1 (student bindings, 1560–1567)
front board blind-stamped TYCHO / BRAHE with the date 1567 (Pařez 2009, photograph; Tritius: ‘Supralibros Tychona Brahe z roku 1567’); marginal notes attributed to his hand (Pařez)
Links: catalogue record · Gabriel Crusius’s inscriptions on the title of NK ČR 5 G 92, as the National Library’s record transcribes them (Manuscriptorium)
Road of dispersal
Road II, The heirs’ dispersal into private hands (after 1601). No 1642 inscription. The title carries Gabriel Crusius’s mark; the next recorded owner is Jan Josef Klauser (‘Clauser’ in the Tritius record), the Prague printer and gubernial archivist, whose library Strahov bought in 1775 (Neškudla 2021, p. 229). The book left Tycho’s library by a private route and bypassed the transfer of 1642: Crusius gave two other Tycho volumes (5 G 92, 5 J 103) to the Chomutov Jesuits on 5 August 1654, and Klauser died on 31 July 1771, so the book was on the private Prague market before the suppression of 1773.. The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Note
Found by Hedvika Kuchařová and published by Pařez in 2009. Not the Clavius Euclid that Norlind inferred (one of the editions of 1574–91, of which no copy has been located): this is the Zamberti–Campanus Elements of 1558, a working mathematician's Euclid a generation earlier. The 1567 date places the binding in the Rostock student years, nine years before the earliest dated T.B.O. cohort; Norlind (pp. 344, 363) already knew a ‘T. B.’ initials mark of 1567, so the year is not anomalous — the two-line full name is. Whether this is one of the eight books Mainx found in 1943 is tested by the mark: it is not the gilt portrait plaque Mortensen describes for all eight. The graphite ‘G. Crusio ‹K›’ on the title is Gabriel Crusius's (identified 19 September 2026 by the match of formula and ductus with the digitised title leaf of 5 G 92): the Euclid is the third or fourth known book of a named private collector of Tychoniana in mid-seventeenth-century Bohemia, whose holding scattered by more than one route. Munzar and Pařez already counted five books from Tycho's library at Strahov in 2002 (p. 369); whether that count includes this Euclid, found by Kuchařová between 1996 and 2009, or the Mechanica, is not stated.
Open questions
  • Whether the marginal notes — at Book I, prop. 4 and in the Campanus section — are in Tycho’s hand: Pařez (2009) gives them to him (‘přípisky psané jeho rukou in margine’); they have not been compared with his securely attributed specimens.
  • The effaced inscription beneath Crusius's mark on the title — ultraviolet or raking light may recover the earlier owner's name.
  • Klauser's printed ex-libris, which would confirm the 1775 route, has not been looked for on the endleaves; nor Strnad's name or stamp.
  • The trailing ‹K› glyph after Crusius's name on all three Prague instances — a second initial, a locative abbreviation, or a personal mark — is unresolved; if Gabriel Crusius was a Kraus z Krausenbergu the glyph has a candidate expansion.
  • Whether the ‘five books from Tycho's library’ Munzar and Pařez counted at Strahov in 2002 include this Euclid (Pařez 2009 credits its discovery to Kuchařová and calls it new) or the Mechanica.

Fincke, Thomas, Geometriae rotundi libri XIIII (Basel 1583). Basileæ, 1583, 4°

DisputedCrec-e-mort-kb-fincke
Status
Disputed · entry confidence C
Subject
Mathematics/Geometry
Attested by
Norlind 1970, p. 345 (s.v. Fincke, Thomas)
Ownership marks
Inscription: No Tycho mark on either KB copy (both examined on their surrogates). The Geometria rotundi is dedicated to King Frederik II; in the dedication Fincke praises 'in Mathematis excellentissimum virum Dn. Tychonem Brahe' (printed text, present in every copy) — this is Norlind's whole basis, not a copy-level Tycho mark.
Surviving copies
LN 599 4° (eks. 1), Royal Danish Library (Det kongelige Bibliotek) examined and ruled out · identification D
No Tycho mark. Title-page autograph 'Horrebow'; royal crowned cipher + BIBLIOTHECA REGIA HAFNIENSIS stamp; 18th-c marbled-board binding.
Links: catalogue record · digital facsimile (Early European Books)
Hielmst. 1661a 4°, Royal Danish Library (Det kongelige Bibliotek) examined and ruled out · identification D
No Tycho mark. Contemporary limp-vellum sammelband (gothic-MS pastedown). Flyleaf: 'Severinus Pauli[?]... Lipsiae Anno Dni 158[3]' + mottoes 'Superna curato, Humana contemnito' / 'Mens generosa ultra polos'. Title page: 'Christiernus Joannis Hafniensis Anno 1620' + motto 'Ex uno omnia'. Hielmstierne bookplate No.1661 + BRH stamp.
Links: digital facsimile (Early European Books)
Note
Thomas Fincke, Geometriae rotundi libri XIIII (Basel: S. Henricpetri, 1583), dedicated to Frederik II. Both copies in the Royal Library, Copenhagen, have been examined in digital reproduction, and neither bears any mark of Tycho’s ownership. The first copy (LN 599 4, ex. 1) carries the autograph ‘Horrebow’ (the eighteenth-century family of Danish Royal Astronomers) on the title page and royal-cipher and BRH stamps, in an eighteenth-century marbled-board binding. The second (Hielmst. 1661a 4, ex. 2) is a contemporary Sammelband (Fincke 1583 with Ursus, Fundamentum astronomicum, Strasbourg 1588) in limp vellum, inscribed ‘Severinus Pauli[?] … Lipsiae Anno Dni 158[3]’ (mottoes ‘Superna curato, Humana contemnito’ and ‘Mens generosa ultra polos’) and ‘Christiernus Joannis Hafniensis Anno 1620’ (motto ‘Ex uno omnia’), later Hielmstierne’s. Norlind nonetheless placed the book in Tycho’s library — ‘fanns säkerligen i biblioteket på Uraniborg’ (Bilaga I, p. 346) — but his whole basis is Fincke’s printed praise of Tycho in the preface, a compliment present in every copy rather than a mark in any copy. No inventory, inscription or ownership mark attests Tycho’s ownership, and neither surviving Copenhagen copy is his.
Norlind 1970, p. 345
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Fincke bedrev studier vid olika utländska universitet, bl.a. i Basel 1583, blev vid 30 års ålder professor i matematik i Köpenhamn 1591, i retorik 1602 och i medicin 1603. Erhöll 1597 uppdraget att jämte professor Iver Stub resa över till Hven för att undersöka om någon åverkan gjorts på Tychos instrument, vilket misstänkliggjorde dem i Tychos ögon. – Boken är tillägnad konung Fredrik II, men i förordet till läsaren, fol. 3r, talar Fincke mycket vänligt om Tycho och ber honom inte dölja, om det finns något lovvärt i den och icke spara kritik, om så behövs. Boken, som tillkommit under Finckes studievistelse i Basel, fanns säkerligen i biblioteket på Uraniborg.
Open questions
  • Who the two early owners of the second copy were — ‘Severinus Pauli[?]’, Leipzig c. 1583, and Christiern Jensen of Copenhagen, 1620 — is unknown beyond their inscriptions, and neither is Tycho; a full reading of the inscriptions and the university matriculation registers would identify them.

Flemløse, Peder Jacobsen, Ægloga de eclipsi solari anno 1574 ... futura. Hafniæ, 1574, 4°

Attested, not locatedBrec-e-mort-kb-flemlose
Status
Attested, not located · entry confidence B
Subject
Astronomy (eclipse)
Attested by
Norlind 1970, p. 346 (s.v. Flemlöse, Peder Jacobsen)
Ownership marks
Inscription: No Tycho ownership mark. Full 32-image EEB scan of KB Hielmst. 1226 4 read: only the Hielmstierne armorial bookplate (engr. C.M. Tuscher, datable 1743-51), the Bibliotheca Regia Hafniensis stamp, and plain 18th-c paper boards.
Surviving copy
Hielmst. 1226 4°, Royal Danish Library (Det kongelige Bibliotek) examined and ruled out · identification D
No Tycho mark: the only marks are eighteenth-century Hielmstierne -- the Tuscher bookplate (1743-51) and the Bibliotheca Regia Hafniensis stamp. It is nonetheless the sole surviving copy of the edition (unicum, L. Nielsen).
Links: catalogue record · digital facsimile (Early European Books)
Note
That Tycho owned the work is well founded: the Aegloga is dedicated to him (17 October 1574), and Flemløse came to Hven early in 1578 as one of his very first pupils (Norlind 1970, p. 346). This copy, however, is not demonstrably Tycho’s. The only surviving copy known (a unicum, according to L. Nielsen as cited by Norlind 1970, p. 346) is KB Hielmst. 1226 4, an eighteenth-century Hielmstierne Danica acquisition carrying no mark of Tycho’s. No Prague or Clementinum copy is known: the work appears in none of Kleinschnitzová, Prandtl or Šolc, and the Czech National Library’s index of former owners records no copy of Brahe’s. Norlind uses no verb of ownership: he infers only that a copy was ‘högst troligt’ on Hven, from the dedication, not that the Copenhagen copy is Tycho’s. The copy is therefore rejected as Tycho’s, while ownership of the work is retained at grade C. Status attested, B, since 20 October 2026: the work-level ownership is sound on the dedication; the Royal Library's copy, judged in its own volume record, is not shown to be his.
Norlind 1970, p. 346
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Flemlöse blev en högt betrodd assistent hos Tycho, kom till Hven i början av 1578 såsom en av hans allra första lärjungar. Redan dessförinnan hade han emellertid stått i förbindelse med den omkr. 8 år äldre Tycho, såsom framgår av, att han tillägnat denne sin bok. Den utgör en episk herdedikt, behandlande den stundande solförmörkelsen i nov. 1574, vilken enligt Flemlöse bebådar Kristi snara återkomst. Förordet är dat. Köpenhamn i mitten av okt. 1574. Han har alltså avslutat boken vid den tid, då Tycho höll sina föreläsningar vid universitetet där. På dessa föreläsningar syftar Flemlöse fol. A3r; förmodligen har han varit en av åhörarna. Det får anses som högst troligt, att ett exemplar av boken fanns i biblioteket på Hven. – Enligt Lauritz Nielsen är endast ett exemplar numera känt (i Det kgl. Bibliotek i Köpenhamn).

Gemma Frisius, Reiner, De astrolabo catholico liber. Antwerp, 1556, 8°

Inferred from Tycho's use (Norlind's principle), retired as unlocatableCrec-e-norlind-gemma-frisius-astrolabo
Status
Inferred from Tycho's use (Norlind's principle), retired as unlocatable · entry confidence C
Subject
Astronomy/Instruments
Attested by
Norlind 1970, p. 347 (s.v. Gemma Frisius, Rainerus)
Norlind records
Opera omnia: III, 74
Note
Norlind 1970, p. 347: listed among the books of the library because Tycho discusses the tract in the Progymnasmata (Opera omnia III, 74); no copy, receipt or mark is recorded. Norlind’s introduction states the principle on which such tracts enter his catalogue: it may be regarded as fairly certain that nearly all the writings on the new star of 1572 and the comet of 1577 that Tycho reviews in the Progymnasmata and the comet book stood in the library on Hven (p. 335). Norlind shows by textual comparison which edition Tycho used: the sentence ‘Quicquid alii de ea scribant’ stands in the edition of 1556, published after the author’s death by his son Cornelius Gemma, and in Tycho’s text, but not in Everaert’s compendium of 1583 (Ortroy, nos. 129–130). Use is shown; ownership is the inference. If Tycho’s copy survives, it would carry no known mark by which it could be recognised.
Norlind 1970, p. 347
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Efter denna upplaga, som utgavs efter förf:s död av sonen Cornelius Gemma, citerar Tycho i »Prog.» (III, 74) och icke efter det av Martinus Everhardus publicerade kompendiet, som trycktes i Antverpen 1583 (Ortroy, a.a. nr 130). Detta framgår av en jämförelse mellan de båda upplagorna och Tychos text. Såväl i uppl. 1556 som hos Tycho står så t.ex. satsen »Quicquid alii de ea scribant», som emellertid saknas i uppl. 1583.

LocatedAprivate collectionrec-e-ging-gemma-characterismis

Ownership marks
Annotations: Numerous annotations in Tycho's hand, from a word or two to virtually filling the available margin (Martayan Lan 2001, which supplied a list of the annotated locations and a partial transcription); on pp. 124–125 of Book II the long note in the lower margin was written with the book held upside down (the colour plate at the front of Martayan Lan's catalogue; Gingerich 2002, fig. 1: the opening headed ‘COSMOCRIT. LIB. II’ / ‘CAPVT III’, with further notes in the outer margins beside the printed glosses on the new star's motion and distance). Tycho annotated heavily the section on Muñoz's observations of the new star of 1572 and quoted this passage explicitly in the Progymnasmata (Gingerich 2002, p. 327). The hand confirmed as Tycho's by Owen Gingerich (per litteras, 25 May 2001); Anthony Grafton's preliminary report for the dealer found a genetic relation between the notes and the Astronomiae instauratae progymnasmata (Prague 1602) Binding: Contemporary flexible vellum with yapp edges: gilt medallion portrait of Tycho in the centre of the front cover, worn, with ‘Hic patet exterior Tychonis forma Brahei / pulchrius eniteat, quae latet interior’ in the surround; the back cover with the Brahe family arms and ‘Arma genus fundi pereunt durabile virtus / et doctrina decus nobilitatis habent’ in the surround; covers soiled, remnants of ties; an old shelfmark stencilled on the spine (Martayan Lan 2001; the same portrait-and-arms supralibros is illustrated by Prandtl 1932 and Christianson 2000, p. 139)
Norlind records
Opera omnia: III, 67–80
Surviving copy
private collection — De naturae divinis characterismis, Private hands · identification A · Period 4 (gilt supralibros): contemporary flexible vellum with yapp edges, the portrait-and-arms supralibros (Martayan Lan 2001)
Tycho's autograph annotations throughout, from a word or two to a note filling the margin, incl. the long note written upside down in the lower margin of Book II, pp. 124–125 (the hand confirmed by Owen Gingerich, per litteras 25 May 2001, and studied by Anthony Grafton); Tycho's gilt portrait supralibros with the motto ‘Hic patet exterior Tychonis forma Brahei / pulchrius eniteat, quae latet interior’ on the front cover and the Brahe arms with ‘Arma genus fundi pereunt durabile virtus / et doctrina decus nobilitatis habent’ on the back
No online catalogue record traced.
Road of dispersal
Road II, The heirs’ dispersal into private hands (after 1601). The copy carries a scored (cancelled) former ownership inscription and a later inscription dated 1647, both unread, unidentified later annotations on the front endleaf, and an old shelfmark stencilled on the spine (Martayan Lan 2001): the traces of its route between Tycho's heirs and Felix Mainx's purchase in Prague in 1938. Gingerich 2002 (p. 326) places the book ‘around 1955’ in Harald Mortensen's own collection: a misreading of Mortensen's paper, which reports Mainx's acquisition; Martayan Lan's provenance line (‘the private collection of a professor in Prague’) has it right.. The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Note
Tycho’s heavily annotated working copy of Gemma’s book on the new star of 1572, printed by Christopher Plantin at Antwerp in 1575. The notes on Muñoz’s observations are the passage he quotes in the Progymnasmata, and Grafton’s report for the dealer found a genetic relation between the marginalia and the printed work (Prague 1602). The copy was recorded as Tycho’s by Mortensen (1955, p. 30) on Felix Mainx’s report that he had acquired it in Prague in 1938, listed by Norlind (1970, p. 347) from Mortensen, and identified as annotated in Tycho’s hand only when Martayan Lan offered it in 2001 (Catalogue 28, item 55, US$ 300,000, with a colour plate of Book II, pp. 124–125); the hand was confirmed by Gingerich (per litteras, 25 May 2001) and is reproduced as fig. 1 of Gingerich 2002, p. 326, which records the sale to a private American collector. The binding is Tycho’s portrait-and-arms supralibros on flexible vellum. Mortensen’s own sentence says that Professor Felix Mainx acquired the Gemma in Prague in 1938 and told Mortensen of it; the book was never in Mortensen’s collection, and Gingerich’s ‘the same collector’ (2002, p. 326) misreads him.
Norlind 1970, p. 347
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Innehåller i 2:a tomen, s. 111 ff. bl.a. om den nya stjärnan; Gemmas observationer av denna diskuteras i »Prog.» (III, 67–80). Om ett exemplar som tillhört Tycho meddelar H. Mortensen, s. 30.
Open questions
  • Who now owns the book: the private American buyer of 2001 (from Martayan Lan) is unidentified; the dealer’s records or a later sale would name him.
  • In which library the book sat before Mainx bought it in Prague in 1938 — possibly the monastery in which he found the eight further Tycho volumes in 1943; the scored former ownership inscription, the later inscription dated 1647 and the old shelfmark stencilled on the spine (Martayan Lan 2001) would name it once read.
  • What the annotations contain in full: Martayan Lan’s list of the annotated locations with partial transcription and Anthony Grafton’s report of 2001 are unpublished, and their publication or an examination of the volume would settle it.

Open questions
  • The number 2781 that Studnička read on the spine in 1901: the spine now shows no number, label or lettering, in direct or in raking light (the Ransom Center’s photographs of 7 October 2026). Whether the number was inked on the parchment and has faded, stood on a paper label since lost, or was never where Studnička placed it cannot be settled from photographs; ultraviolet light on the spine would show faded ink, and the hand that Studnička attributed to Tycho can no longer be examined at all.
  • The pencil note ‘Aus Tycho Brahes Bibliothek!’ on the front flyleaf and the number 760 on the front pastedown: whose hands — Laube's, the Leipzig bookseller's or Prandtl's — is not known; a comparison with Laube's or Prandtl's known hand would settle the note.
  • When and from whom Prandtl bought the volume (after Laube's death in 1923?), and when the University of Texas acquired the Prandtl collection: the catalogue record gives no accession date, and the bookplate none.

Norlind 1970, p. 348 (s.v. Gesner, Conradus)
Norlind records
Opera omnia: VI, 231; VI, 240; VI, 244
Note
Norlind: ‘Tycho, som också hade Gesners Thierbuch’ — Tycho, who also had Gessner’s Thierbuch. The book is attested only by Tycho’s own letter to Landgrave Wilhelm of September 1591, which places the Oryx description on fol. 68 (Opera omnia VI, 244). No copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified. Whether his copy was the 1563 or the 1583 edition is unrecorded; Norlind holds it immaterial, the two editions being in his words identical: Zurich, Christoph Froschauer, 1563 (VD16 G 1728), reissued 1583 (VD16 G 1729), folio. It is a different book from the surviving Gessner, De omni rerum fossilium genere (Zurich 1565; Prandtl, Verzeichnis A no. 46; now at the University of Texas at Austin). The only Thierbuch physically traced in Tycho’s orbit is Landgrave Wilhelm’s own Kassel copy, not Tycho’s, destroyed in an air raid in September 1941.
Norlind 1970, p. 348
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Lantgreve Wilhelm ägde upplagan 1563, efter vad han skriver till Tycho maj 1591 (VI, 231). Han uppger, att »in dem Deutschen Exemplari Gesneri de Animalibus Quadrupedibus» skulle på fol. 85 stå en beskrivning med bild av ett djur, kallat Rix eller Oryx (till Tycho aug. s.å.; VI, 240). Tycho, som också hade Gesners Thierbuch (om uppl. 1563 eller 1583 få vi ej veta, men det är betydelselöst, då båda upplagorna äro identiska), finner fol. 68 en beskrivning dock utan bild av det märkliga djuret (till lantgreven sept. 1591; VI, 244). Han menar därför, att lantgreven måste ha en annan upplaga. Lantgrevens uppgift är emellertid oriktig, ty i de båda upplagorna står fol. 68ᵛ en beskrivning utan bild under rubriken »Von der wilden Geyss Oryx genannt». Fol. 85ʳ finnes däremot bild och beskrivning av en älg (»Von dem Pferdthirtz»). – Lantgrevens exemplar (i Kassel) gick förlorat vid ett bombangrepp i sept. 1941.

The note's present location (an undigitised leaf, the first leaf of the Apianus adligatum, or binding waste) must be asked of NK ČR before the hands can be compared.

Hagecius, Thaddaeus (Hájek), Apodixis physica et mathematica de cometis. Görlitz, 1581, 4°

Attested, not locatedBrec-e-norlind-hagecius-apodixis
Status
Attested, not located · entry confidence B
Subject
Astronomy (comet)
Attested by
Norlind 1970, p. 348 (s.v. Hagecius, Thaddæus); Zinner no. 2979 (after Norlind); Kleinschnitzová 1933
Acquisition
1581; a copy sent by Bartholomaeus Scultetus from Görlitz (Tycho to Hagecius, October 1581; Opera omnia VII, 64) (Gift of an author or correspondent)
Norlind records
Opera omnia: VII, 64; IV, 293-295
Note
A copy was sent to Tycho by Scultetus in Görlitz (Tycho to Hagecius, October 1581, Opera omnia VII, 64). Tycho discusses the work in his book on the comet (Opera omnia IV, 293–295). No copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified, and the work belongs to the Hagecius gap: Tycho owned at least four works of Hagecius, each documented by a letter, and not one survives in the Clementinum. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 78) remarked on the absence: among the Clementinum Tychoniana there is not a single work of Hagecius, though his long friendship with Tycho and Norlind’s list make it likely that Tycho had many if not all of his works, and none of the Clementinum’s Hagecius copies carries a provenance note pointing to him. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 80) names the mechanism by which such a copy could lose its provenance: composite volumes from Tycho’s library were broken up and rebound with pieces of other provenance (5 G 42, 14 J 164, 19 G 20, XII A 12), and Richard Kukula, director of the university library 1897–1918, had old Sammelbände dissolved as a matter of principle, among them, to judge by its modern binding, the Scultetus of 14 F 284. Whether Tycho’s Hagecius copies were lost or survive unrecognised remains an open question. The National Library of the Czech Republic holds three copies of the Görlitz 1581 edition — in a Luther convolute, in a convolute from the Jesuit college at Litoměřice, and as the host volume (record 000030653) of the Hagecius composite owned by the Jesuit college at Chomutov — and none bears a Tycho mark.
Norlind 1970, p. 348

Hájek sent Tycho a copy with many manuscript corrections and additions in his own hand, hoping that Tycho would print the revised text or take selections into his own account of the nova; Tycho discussed the revised text in the Progymnasmata and did not print it (Dreyer 1890, p. 58 n. 2; Mosley 2007, p. 124 n. 42; Opera omnia VII, 99). Tycho’s copy, which would carry Hájek’s autograph corrections, has not been identified. The National Library of the Czech Republic’s two copies of the Frankfurt 1574 edition — one inscribed for the Chomutov Jesuit college in 1671 (‘Collegij Soctis IESV Commotonij Ao. 1671’, record 000154680), one stamped ‘REGIAE BIBLIOTH: ACAD: PRAGEN.’ (record 000014579) — have no earlier owner in the library’s records.
Norlind 1970, p. 349

The volume never reached the Clementinum: it is at the Biblioteka Kórnicka (Cim.Qu.2812), whose record notes the supralibros and the arms plate and whose digitisation shows the volume. The one Prague copy of the Cracow edition of 1584 (Sign. 22 B 201) carries no mark of his. How the book went from Chomutov to Kórnik is not established.
Open questions
  • How the volume passed from the Chomutov college, which catalogued it in 1671, to Kórnik: the older shelfmarks ‘H. VI. 365.’ and ‘C: 157.’ on the pastedown and ‘hh: 310.’ on the flyleaf, and the red stamp ‘Z HANKOWYCH’ at the foot of the title, have not been identified, and the Kórnik record names no former owner. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 81) supposed that the Chomutov stock reached the Clementinum only in part; this is the first located volume that took another road.

Hipparchus (ed. Petrus Victorius), the copy annotated by Joseph Justus Scaliger, In Arati et Eudoxi Phaenomena libri III (the Greek editio princeps, with Scaliger’s annotations). Florence (Giunta), 1567, 2°

Attested, not locatedBrec-e-corr-scaliger-books
Status
Attested, not located · entry confidence B
Subject
Astronomy
Attested by
Norlind 1970, p. 349 (s.v. Hipparchus Bithynus); Tycho’s correspondence, letter of 17 April 1599 (tekstnet.dk); Kepler, GW XIX (1975)
Acquisition
1599; given by Scaliger — ‘pro utroque libro mihi tam benigne concesso’ and ‘libris mihi dono missis’ (Tycho to Scaliger, 17 April 1599, Opera omnia VIII 151): a gift, not a loan; the earlier ‘lent or given’ resolves (register dossier of 27 October 2026, §18) (Gift of an author or correspondent)
Norlind records
Opera omnia: VIII, 102; VIII, 151
Note
Hipparchus’s commentary on the Phaenomena of Aratus and Eudoxus in the Greek editio princeps of Petrus Victorius (Florence 1567), Scaliger’s own copy, annotated in his hand. Christiernus Johannis Ripensis, formerly in Tycho’s service on Hven, met Scaliger in Holland and reported that he owned the Greek text. Tycho asked in August 1598 for the book or for transcripts of the passages he needed (Opera omnia VIII, 102); Scaliger sent excerpts, acknowledged in March 1599 (Opera omnia VIII, 151); and in April 1599 Tycho thanked him for two books granted him (‘pro utroque autem libro mihi tam benigne concesso’), of which the Hipparchus is the one identified. Norlind (1970, p. 362) considers that the other may be the Cyclometrica elementa duo of 1594 with Scaliger’s dedication, now Sign. 14 A 59 (Prandtl A 42). That Tycho had the annotated book itself Kepler states to Herwart von Hohenburg in January 1603: Scaliger had once sent Tycho his Hipparchus with his own notes, and it was still in the possession of the heirs (Norlind 1970, p. 350, citing the letter as Caspar nr. 242, p. 354). On 16 November 1624 Kepler asked Tycho’s son Georg Brahe for ‘Hipparchum de fixis graecè, ist ein klains folium, vnd vil drinnen manu Scaligerj’ (KGW XIX, no. 7, pp. 202–203), so the annotated book was still with the heirs two years after Tengnagel’s death. Whether Kepler obtained it is not recorded, and no copy has been traced since.
Norlind 1970, p. 349
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Ed. princeps, utg. av Petrus Victorius, av det enda originalverk vi äga av antikens store astronom. – Christiernus Johannis Ripensis, tidigare i Tychos tjänst på Hven, hade under en resa i Holland träffat Scaliger. Ripensis meddelade Tycho, att Scaliger ägde en bok på grekiska om Hipparchus' observationer, tryckt »för några år sedan» i Italien. Att härmed avses ovanstående verk är otvivelaktigt. Tycho ber Scaliger (aug. 1598; VIII, 102), att antingen skicka boken eller ock en avskrift av vissa partier. Varför Tycho var så intresserad av Hipparchus' skrift, beror på att de häri meddelade noggranna uppgifterna om den heliakiska uppgången resp. nedgången för vissa stjärnor samt observationerna av deras läge på himmelssfären, jämförda med sådana uppgifter från följande århundraden, voro viktiga för hans undersökningar av precessionen. Scaliger måste ha tillmötesgått det ena alternativet i Tychos anhållan, eftersom denne i mars 1599 (VIII, 151) tackar honom bl.a. för hans besvär med excerpering av vissa ställen hos såväl Hipparchus som Ptolemeus. Härav framgår alltså icke, att Tycho erhållit boken utan endast Scaligers excerpter ur densamma. Men från annat håll veta vi, att Tycho verkligen ägt ett exemplar av boken med Scaligers egenhändiga anteckningar. I jan. 1603 (Caspar nr 242, s. 354) skriver nämligen Kepler till Herwart, att Scaliger en gång skickade till Tycho Hipparchus' skrift med sina egenhändiga anteckningar och att den ännu befinner sig i Tychos arvingars ägo. Kepler har tydligen varit mycket intresserad av att förvärva exemplaret, ty så sent som i nov. 1624 (Caspar till nr 242, s. 499) skriver han till Tychos son Jörgen Brahe: »Sonderlich hett ich gern Hipparchum de fixis græce, ist ein klains folium, und vil drinnen manu Scaligeri.»
Open questions
  • Where the Victorius Hipparchus of 1567 with Scaliger’s annotations went after November 1624, when it was last recorded with Tycho’s heirs; it has not been found.

Links: catalogue record · digital facsimile (Manuscriptorium) · the 1606 title with the 1642 line and 'Ex Bibliotheca Tÿchoniana' — the label is the college's, not proof of ownership (Manuscriptorium canvas 9)
Note
A Prague imprint of 1606, five years after Tycho’s death, carrying ‘Ex Biblioth. Tijchoniana’, the Clementinum inscription of 1642 and the Tychonian shelf-mark ‘T.B. 27’; bound with it is Kepler’s De Jesu Christi servatoris nostri vero anno natalitio (Frankfurt 1606). Kukula, who published the volume in 1906–07 (no. VII), took the two tracts as proof that the family and Kepler kept the library together and added to it after 1601 and 1604; Prandtl (1932, p. 16) read it the same way — the heirs had apparently left the working library to Kepler, who carried it on for some years. The volume belongs to the Tychoniana as the Jesuits marked them, not to Tycho’s own library. Šolc 2006 (printed p. 192) names the heirs' additions ‘for example’ as De Stella Nova in pede Serpentarii and De stella tertii honoris in Cygno (both Prague 1606) and the Frankfurt ‘pars altera’ of 1606 — the two Prague titles one book, the Frankfurt piece the De Jesu Christi … vero anno natalitio bound with it here, the identification being the house's — and has them given to the Clementinum Jesuits together with the harder-to-sell, predominantly astronomical part of the library.

Note
Kepler to Tycho, Graz, 13 December 1597 (Opera omnia VIII, 14–15), sent no copy of the Mysterium cosmographicum (Tübingen 1596), supposing that Tycho already had one: ‘Exemplaria non dubito, quin antea habeas: quare facile patior, ut difficultas transmittendi per tantum intervallum a mittendo me avocet’. Tycho to Kepler, Wandsbek, 1 April 1598 (Opera omnia VIII, 44), replied that he had seen and read the book before: ‘Librum tuum, quem Prodromum vocas Dissertationum Cosmographicarum, iam ante videram et … perlegeram’. So already Norlind 1970, p. 350. How and when his copy reached him is not recorded; no copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified.
Norlind 1970, p. 350
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Keplers berömda ungdomsverk. – Egendomligt är, att Tycho åtminstone icke till att börja med fick något dedikationsexemplar. Kepler skriver nämligen i sitt första brev till Tycho (dec. 1597; VIII, 14), att han förmodar, att Tycho redan förut äger boken; därför skickar han icke något exemplar. Tycho svarar från Wandsbek i april 1598 (VIII, 44), att han fick brevet från Helmstedt. Boken hade han förut och han hade tagit del av densamma. Tychos brev innehåller många lovord över boken. Jfr s. 199 ff.
Open questions

Attested by

Acquisition
after 30 June 1600; procured through Georg Rollenhagen in Magdeburg at Tycho's request of April 1600 (Opera omnia VIII, p. 295) (Gift of an author or correspondent)
Norlind records
inscriptions: Observationes aliquot Eclipsium Solis et Lunæ per Joh. Krabbe, mathematicum ducis H. Julii factæ; copy located by Norlind at: Gl. kgl. S. 2° 318, fol. 159r (a leaf among Tycho's own observations; Norlind prints only the shelfmark, i.e. Köpenhamn, KB, Gammel kongelig Samling); Opera omnia: VIII, 295
Surviving copy
GKS 318 2°, Royal Danish Library (Det kongelige Bibliotek) · identification A
sewn among Tycho's own observation books, in the codex of his observations of 1600–1601; Tycho's autograph marginal notes on the leaf
Links: catalogue record
Road of dispersal
Road VIII, With the observation books: Kepler, Ludwig Kepler, Frederik III (after 1604). The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Observation codex
The leaf is sewn into one of Tycho’s own observation volumes, the codex GKS 318 2°.
Note
Not a book: a single manuscript leaf of another astronomer’s eclipse observations, obtained by Tycho, annotated in his hand and kept among his own observation books. In April 1600 Tycho asked Georg Rollenhagen in Magdeburg to procure the eclipse observations that Johannes Krabbe, since 1585 mathematician to Duke Heinrich Julius of Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel, was said to have made, together with the method by which the times had been taken, so that a comparison with his own observations would give the difference in meridian between the observing places (Tycho to Rollenhagen, April 1600; Opera omnia VIII, 295). The leaf arrived. Headed ‘Observationes aliquot Eclipsium Solis et Lunae per Joh. Krabbe, mathematicum ducis H. Julii factae’, it records seven lunar and six solar eclipses of 1581–1600 observed at Helmstedt, Berlin, Braunschweig, Wolfenbüttel and Gröningen near Halberstadt, the times as a rule derived from star altitudes; the solar eclipse of September 1595 could not be observed. The last observation is dated 30 June 1600, so the leaf reached Tycho after that date. In the margin Tycho wrote the mean times for Krabbe’s observations and for his own. Dreyer did not print the leaf in the Opera omnia; his commentary records it as sewn among Tycho’s observations of 1600–1601 in the Royal Library’s codex GKS 318 2°, which his edition numbers codex I, with Tycho’s annotations (Opera omnia VIII, 438, note to p. 295 line 2), and Norlind describes it from the codex (Norlind 1970, p. 351). It is entered because Norlind’s list of Tycho’s books includes the manuscripts he is known to have possessed, and because the leaf is a text by another author that Tycho acquired, owned and annotated; the observation codices themselves, being Tycho’s own writing, are not entries.
Norlind 1970, p. 351
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
I april 1600 (VIII, 295) skriver Tycho till Rollenhagen i Magdeburg, att han fått veta, att Krabbe (som sedan 1585 var astronom hos hertigen av Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel) anställt noggranna observationer av sol- och månförmörkelser. Tycho ber Rollenhagen skaffa honom detta observationsmaterial. Det räcker emellertid inte endast med vederbörliga observationsresultat utan han måste också få veta på vad sätt dessa resultat erhållits (om genom stjärnhöjder eller på annat sätt). Anledningen till att Tycho önskade alla dessa uppgifter var, att han ur en jämförelse mellan Krabbes och sina egna observationer ville bestämma meridianskillnaden mellan de båda observationsorterna. Rollenhagen har tydligen lyckats skaffa materialet, eftersom det nu befinner sig på ett blad bland Tychos egna observationer (Gl. kgl. S. 2° 318, fol. 159r). Det är icke utg. av Dreyer. Under rubriken »Observationes aliquot Eclipsium Solis et Lunæ per Joh. Krabbe, mathematicum ducis H. Julii factæ» upptagas 7 månförmörkelser och 6 solförmörkelser (den ena i sept. 1595 kunde dock icke iakttagas) för tiden 1581–1600. Tycho har gjort egenhändiga anteckningar i manuskriptet. Den sista observerade förmörkelsen är för d. 30 juni 1600; någon gång efter detta datum har Tycho således mottagit materialet. Observationsorten är icke en och densamma, utan olika (Helmstedt, Berlin, Braunschweig, Wolfenbüttel och Gröningen, vid Halberstadt). Tiderna ha i regel bestämts ur stjärnhöjder. I margen har vidare Tycho antecknat medierna dels för Krabbes tider dels för sina egna.
Open questions
  • On which folio of GKS 318 2° the leaf is sewn: Dreyer’s commentary gives fol. 157, Norlind fol. 159; the codex itself would decide.

Note
Norlind 1970, p. 351 (Zinner 2632), lists the tract among the books of the library because Tycho discusses it in the Progymnasmata (Opera omnia III, 218–225); no copy, receipt or mark is recorded. Norlind’s introduction states the principle on which such tracts enter his catalogue: it may be regarded as fairly certain that nearly all the writings on the new star of 1572 and the comet of 1577 that Tycho reviews in the Progymnasmata and the comet book stood in the library on Hven (p. 335). The edition Tycho discusses is the Lauingen edition, not the reprint De nova stella iudicia … Leovitii et Gemmae (s. l. 1573, Zinner 2633). As an unbound tract, Tycho’s copy would carry no known mark by which it could be recognised, and none has been identified.

binding: original; copy located by Norlind at: Prag, UB
Surviving copy
Sign. 18 J 318, National Library of the Czech Republic (Clementinum) · identification A · Period 1 (student bindings, 1560–1567)
blind-stamped pigskin (alum-tawed; the compiler's reading of Šolc 2018 fig. 1a, 28 October 2026 — the literature says ‘white leather’: Kleinschnitzová ‘Weisser Lederband’, the library ‘Světlá kožená vazba’, Šolc ‘weißer Ledereinband’) with the initials and year ‘T. B. 1560’ blind-stamped, the earliest dated binding attributed to Tycho in Prague (Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 47; Norlind 1970, p. 339, reads the cipher as ‘T. B. O.’ with the same year; the library’s record gives the owner’s year as 1567); ‘Domus Professae Soc. Jesu ad S. Nicolaum Pragae Catal. inscript.’ on the title
Links: catalogue record
Bound with: Bayrus, Petrus, De medendis humani corporis malis Enchiridion (1560); Sacrobosco, Johannes de, Libellus de sphaera (1558)
Road of dispersal
Road I, The Jesuit road: the Clementinum (1642), the colleges at Chomutov and Krumlov and the professed house, reunited in the Clementinum after 1773. The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Note
Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 47:3; Norlind 1970, p. 352; the library’s record 18 J 318/adl.2. The third piece of the volume in the ‘T. B. 1560’ binding. The ‘T. B. 1560’ volume is the earliest dated binding of Tycho’s and, while the purchase note of the Ptolemy 5 B 70 is disputed, the earliest book securely his (Christianson 1967, pp. 200–201: ‘two of his own “textbooks”’). Ownership graded B on 28 October 2026: the attribution rests on the blind-stamped cipher T·B and the year 1560 on the binding alone — no inscription, no annotation, no 1642 or Chomutov mark, and Kleinschnitzová 1933 gives no argument. The cipher is consistent with Tycho's documented series of initial-and-year bindings 1561–1583 (Helsingør 1561, Uppsala 1563, Strahov and 10 G 47 1567, T.B.O. 1576–1583) and the contents fit the Copenhagen curriculum of 1560, but T·B alone identifies no one. The NK ČR photographs requested on 28 October 2026 (the three edges, both boards, the three title pages at 600 dpi) and an EBDB identification of the panel stamps are the tests. Reviewed again on 29 October 2026, the literature pack read whole: ownership graded C (was B). Beyond the cipher the literature holds nothing — no inscription, no annotation, no hand, no note of 1642. Kleinschnitzová (1933, pp. 76–78) herself sets the volume outside the twenty-three Clementinum volumes that carry the note of 1642 and says it ‘verirrt sich’, strayed, into the Jesuit professed house on the Malá Strana — an explanation that assumes what it should show; Norlind’s ‘T. B. O. 1560’ (1970, p. 339) reads a letter the board does not carry; the library’s record gives Tycho the year 1567 in its former-owner field without a basis; Šolc (1999, 2006, 2018), Christianson (1967, 2020), Thoren and Pařez all derive from Kleinschnitzová. If the cipher is Tycho’s, the year 1560 places the binding before his departure from Denmark; whether it is Tycho’s is the whole question, and the National Library’s photographs are the test. Decided on 29 October 2026.
Norlind 1970, p. 352

Astronomy (nova)

Norlind records
Opera omnia: III, 58–67
Note
Tycho reprinted Maestlin’s tract in full in the Progymnasmata (Opera omnia III, 58–67) and praised it (‘liten till omfånget men till innehållet mera betydande’). Reprinting the tract in full implies that the Frischlin volume containing it was in Tycho’s hands, but Norlind frames the passage as discussion rather than ownership, and the attestation is accordingly graded C. There is no documented receipt, no inventory entry, and no copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified.
Norlind 1970, p. 352
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Ingår på s. 27–32 i: Frischlin, Nicodemus: Consideratio novæ stellæ ... Tubingæ 1573.4°. Z. 2622. Tycho har avtryckt den lilla skriften helt i »Prog.» (III, 58–67), där han också diskuterar den; den är, skriver han, liten till omfånget men till innehållet mera betydande och gedigen än de flesta större avhandlingar i ämnet. Dock nämner han ej, att den ingår i Frischlins verk.
Norlind 1970, p. 347
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Se: Mæstlinus, M., Demonstratio ...
Open questions
  • Whether the Swedish words ‘liten till omfånget men till innehållet mera betydande’, given as Tycho’s praise of the tract, are Norlind’s own wording or his rendering of a passage of Tycho’s; Norlind’s page and the Progymnasmata passage (Opera omnia III, 58–67) would decide.

Tycho’s correspondence, letter of 10 December 1600 (tekstnet.dk)
Acquisition
1600; commissioned copy (Manuscript copying and transmission)
Note
Herwart had the Revelatio ascribed to Methodius transcribed for Tycho because the volume that contained it was too bulky to send, and despatched the copy from Munich with the Alphonsine tables (Herwart to Tycho, 10 December 1600; Opera omnia VIII, 393: ‘METHODIJ uti fertur Revelationem, quam describi curavi, cum liber, cui inserta fuerat, ob molem transferri nequeat’). The transcript is not among the Clementinum volumes and has not been identified at the Royal Library, Copenhagen, or the Austrian National Library; the text survives in many copies, and a transcript without Tycho’s own mark cannot be told from them. Status lost since 20 October 2026: a unique transcript made for Tycho and sent, not a mass-survival text.

Note
Norlind: ‘sannolikt denna första upplaga Tycho ägt’ — Tycho probably owned this first edition (1542), the work in which the ‘nonius’ auxiliary scale is described; in the comet book Tycho calls it ‘Libello de crepusculis dudum edito’ (Opera omnia IV, 327). Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C).

Härför talar, att han i kometboken (IV, 327) nämner den som »Libello de crepusculis dudum edito». Status

Attested by

Acquisition

Norlind records
Opera omnia: VII, 184; II, 421; VII, 121; VII, 147
Note
Norlind 1970, p. 355: Tycho received a copy of the printed book from Hagecius at their meeting at Regensburg in November 1575 (Opera omnia VII, 184; II, 421) and was particularly taken with its section on the planets’ influence at their varying distances from the earth; in May 1588 he wrote to Hagecius that he could no longer find the book in his library and asked him to procure another copy (VII, 121; Hagecius’s answers of November 1588 and May 1589, VII, 147 and 184). A book that left the library, or was mislaid in it, in Tycho’s own lifetime. Norlind adds that a copy stood in Queen Christina’s library which he could not find among the Reginenses in the Vatican — a lead he did not pursue, and one worth the question, since books from Prague reached her library in 1648. The store's separate entry for ‘Francius, De astris’ (the Regensburg gift of 1575, lost by 1589) was this book: Hagecius describes the book he gave as ‘librum … de astris … IO. FRANCI, Parisijs impressum, et Reginae Galliae dedicatum’ (20 May 1589, Opera omnia VII 184), ‘Io. Franci’ being Iofrancus, Offusius's given name; Tycho's account of its content (3 May 1588, VII 120–121) fits Offusius, and Norlind (p. 355) already read it so. The two entries were
Norlind 1970, p. 355
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Förordet är dat. d. 8 jan. 1556, men verket trycktes först 14 år senare. I Turin fanns före branden 1904 två manuskriptexemplar av verket (Thorndike, 6, s. 109²⁰). Ett exemplar fanns i drottning Kristinas bibliotek men kunde ej återfinnas av mig bland Reginenses i Vatikanbiblioteket. – Tycho erhöll ett exemplar av den tryckta boken genom Hagecius vid deras sammanträffande i Regensburg nov. 1575 (VII, 184, II, 421). Han var särskilt intresserad av det avsnitt som behandlade planeternas inverkan på jorden på olika avstånd från denna. Härom skriver han till Hagecius i maj 1588 (VII, 121). Han säger vidare, att han nu inte längre kan finna boken i sitt bibliotek och han ber Hagecius skaffa ett annat exemplar. Denne synes först inte ha vetat vad det gällde för bok (brev nov. s.å.; VII, 147); hans efterforskningar efter denna i biblioteken i Prag hade ej lett till något resultat. I ett senare brev maj 1589 (VII, 184) skriver han emellertid, att han nu minns, vilken bok det varit.
Open questions
  • Whether Hagecius sent the second copy Tycho asked for in 1588; and whether the Offusius Norlind records in Queen Christina’s library, unfound among the Reginenses, is a copy from Prague (Norlind 1970, p. 355).

Note
The only authority is Joachim Morsius, who in 1625 — in the dedication to the pseudo-Paracelsian lion-prophecy — reported on Cort Aslakssøn’s word that Tycho had owned a copy, and who further supposed that the manuscript was by then in Prague with Tycho’s heirs. Norlind relays both. No inventory and no Clementinum catalogue records it, and no copy has been identified: the ownership is attested at second hand only and remains unverified. Status attested, not located, since 20 October 2026: no one contests the ownership — Norlind relays only Morsius's report — so the Definitions' 'disputed' does not fit.
Norlind 1970, p. 356
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Enligt Cort Aslakssön skall Tycho ha ägt ett exemplar. Paracelsus' inflytande på Tycho har varit betydande bl.a. i kemi och medicin såsom framgår av brevsamlingen och även annorstädes. Se t.ex. Dreyer, s. XI och registret, S. Lindroth, »Paracelsismen i Sverige», Upps. & Sthm 1943, s. 68, not 9.

Patrizi, Francesco, Nova de universis philosophia. Ferrara, 1591, 2°

Attested, retired as unlocatableBrec-e-norlind-patrizi-novaphilosophia
Status
Attested, retired as unlocatable · entry confidence B
Subject
Natural philosophy
Attested by
Norlind 1970, p. 356 (s.v. Patritius, Franciscus)
Norlind records
Opera omnia: VIII, 206
Note
Norlind (1970, p. 356): ‘Ett exemplar har Tycho säkerligen ägt’ — of either the Ferrara edition of 1591 or the Venice edition of 1593, perhaps the later. His basis is a note in Tycho’s hand in the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences copy of the Progymnasmata (p. 165), naming Patritius among the authors whose writings reached him only after the chapters they belonged to were printed. Tycho complained to Kepler that Patrizi misrepresented his world-system (Tycho to Kepler, December 1599, Opera omnia VIII, 206). The only surviving evidence of Tycho’s ownership is that annotation in his own Progymnasmata, not a mark in a copy of Patrizi; the work is common, and no copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified.
Norlind 1970, p. 356
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Ett exemplar har Tycho säkerligen ägt av endera upplagan Ferrara 1591 eller Venedig 1593 (kanske den senare att döma av en hans anteckning i KVA:s exemplar av »Prog.», se ovan s. 165). Till Kepler skriver han i dec. 1599 (VIII, 206), att Patritius i sin bok lämnat en helt vilseledande framställning av Tychos världssystem. Tycho menar väl vad Patritius skriver fol. 91ʳ (=Pancosmia, liber XII), att enligt Tychos världssystem skulle Merkurius' och Venus' banor skära solbanan i två punkter. Enligt Tychos framställning i kometboken var det dock endast Mars-banan som skar solbanan.
Open questions
  • Which edition Tycho owned, the Ferrara folio of 1591 or the Venice issue of 1593: Norlind (1970, p. 356) inclines to the later on the strength of Tycho’s note in the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences copy of the Progymnasmata (p. 165), which names Patritius among the authors whose writings reached him only after the chapters they belonged to were printed.

LostBrec-e-norlind-paulus-alexandrinus
Status

Subject

Attested by
Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 78 n. 1; Norlind 1970, p. 356 (s.v. Paulus Alexandrinus); Zinner no. 3309 (after Norlind); Šolc 1999; Šolc 2006; Collijn 1933 (as Kleinschnitzová printed it); Falkenstein 1839; Šolc 2018; SLUB war-loss register; Mortensen 1955
Ownership marks
Inscription: Flyleaf: two distichs in the hand of M. Johannes Schmidt to a nobleman addressed ‘Doctissime Smile’ — ‘Promissum transmitto librum, Doctissime Smile, / Invenies, legito, quae Tibi forte placent, / Somnia pars narrat, sed somnia vera loquuntur / Interdum. Ast illis credere multa cave. — Generositatis tuae officioss. M. Johannes Schmidt’ (Falkenstein 1839, pp. 574–575, read on the page). Binding: Tychonic original binding (»in Tychonianischem Originaleinbande«, per Collijn/Kleinschnitzová): parchment, Tycho's portrait stamp with the distich on the front board and his arms on the back (Falkenstein 1839, pp. 574–575)
Norlind records
binding: Tychonic original binding
Bound with
Rantzau, Heinrich, Horoscopographia, sive de inveniendo stellarum situ astrologia (1588); Boiemus, Michael (Böhm), Historia de somniis (1587)
Dispersal
Sächsische Landesbibliothek Dresden; reported by the library as lost in the Second World War (Norlind 1970, p. 356).
Later owners
Sächsische Landesbibliothek Dresden
Note
A book by another author that Tycho owned (Paulus Alexandrinus, edited from Heinrich Rantzau’s library, Wittenberg 1588), in its original Tychonic binding. Reported by Isak Collijn to Flora Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 78 n. 1) as a Tychonianum in the Landesbibliothek Dresden, the companion to the Waldstein (Mnichovo Hradiště) copy of Tycho’s own De nova stella, which, as a copy of one of Tycho’s own works, lies outside this library. The volume is lost: Norlind (1970, p. 356) records the Dresden library’s own communication that the copy ‘gått förlorat under senaste världskrig’ — was lost in the Second World War. Šolc still lists the volume in Dresden — ‘befand sich … in der Sächsischen Landesbibliothek Dresden’ (1999, § 2.533, printed p. 150) and, in the present tense, ‘se nachází v Zemské knihovně v Drážďanech’ (2006, p. 192) — and nowhere mentions the loss Norlind reports from the library itself; neither text cites a sighting. The entry keeps ‘lost’ on Norlind's report; a question to the SLUB (its war-loss records, and whether a Paulus Alexandrinus, Wittenberg 1588, in a Tychonic binding has since been acquired) would close it. Falkenstein's description of the Dresden library (1839, pp. 574–575; quoted by Šolc 2018, pp. 194 and 201–202) shows what the volume was: a Sammelband of three works — this Paulus Alexandrinus first, then Rantzau's own Horoscopographia (Wittenberg 1588, 4°) and Michael Boiemus's Historia de somniis (Wittenberg 1587, 4°) — in a parchment binding with Tycho's portrait stamp on the front board (‘Hic patet exterior Tychonis forma Brahei. Pulchrius eniteat quae latet interior’) and his arms on the back, and on the flyleaf two distichs by a M. Johannes Schmidt sending the book to a nobleman he addresses as Smil (‘Promissum transmitto librum, Doctissime Smile, / Invenies, legito, quae Tibi forte placent, / Somnia pars narrat, sed somnia vera loquuntur / Interdum. Ast illis credere multa cave. — Generositatis tuae officioss. M. Johannes Schmidt’; read on the page image 29 October 2026 — the OCR's ‘Praemissum’ and the elided name corrected). The address is to a Smil, not to Tycho: Schmidt's leaf and Tycho's portrait binding are the two facts recorded on the object, and no source reconciles them. Šolc presents the Boiemus as a further Dresden volume; Falkenstein's ‘Daran:’ makes it the third piece of this one. The loss of 1945 therefore covers all three works, which this library enters as the two bound companions. The SLUB's war-loss register carries a card for the Boiemus — Lit.Graec.B.1976, earlier ‘Phil. gr. B. 93a. Misc. 3’, and ‘Misc. 3’ matches Falkenstein's order, in which the Boiemus is the third piece; no card was found under the other two headings, and the register does not say whether the volume was removed in 1945–46 or destroyed (Nachweiskatalog image 00504111, read 27 October 2026; the identification with the Tycho volume is inference, C). The whole literature on the volume was read on 29 October 2026 (the volumelit table, nine passages): the attribution is Collijn's, printed by Kleinschnitzová in 1933 on the binding alone and naming only the Paulus; Mortensen 1955 (p. 28, the ‘two books’ Collijn reported, no title), Norlind 1970 and Šolc 1999, 2006 and 2018 repeat her — Šolc copying her misprint ‘natalatiis’ in all three, writing ‘leather bindings’ in 2006 where Falkenstein has a parchment binding, and in 2018 counting the one volume as two (the Paulus–Rantzau pair on p. 194, the Boiemus as ‘ein weiteres Tychonisches Buch’ on p. 201) while omitting the verses. Falkenstein himself, the only writer who had the volume in hand, makes no statement about Tycho's library; nobody after 1839 reports seeing it. The Rantzau literature (Oestmann 2004, Zeeberg, Lohmeier 2000, Ilsøe 2005) and the Tycho biographies name the editions, not this copy.
Norlind 1970, p. 356
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Enligt Collijn hos Kl., s. 78 not 1, fanns ett exemplar, som tillhört Tycho, i Landesbibliothek, Dresden. Enligt benäget meddelande från detta har exemplaret gått förlorat under senaste världskrig.
Open questions
  • Who ‘Smil’ (Falkenstein's ‘Doctissime Smile’, addressed ‘Generositatis tuae’) and M. Johannes Schmidt were, and how a volume Schmidt sent to a Smil came to carry Tycho's portrait binding. The name is Bohemian/Moravian; a book-collecting Moravian nobleman of the right years, Smil Osovský z Doubravice (1548–1613), is a lead from the name alone, unverified, not an identification.

Norlind records

Note
Tycho treats the work at length in the comet book (Opera omnia IV, 356–358; cf. Progymnasmata, Opera omnia III, 153–157). Thorndike (History of Magic and Experimental Science VI, p. 84) held that neither Tycho nor Hagecius owned a copy. Norlind shows that Thorndike misread the three passages of the correspondence on which he relied (Opera omnia VII, 120, 147 and 212), which concern Apianus and Pena and not this book, and so defends Tycho’s ownership against Thorndike’s denial. The Czech National Library holds the work as the fourth tract of a Hagecius composite volume from the Jesuit college at Chomutov; its record notes no mark of Tycho’s.
Norlind 1970, p. 357

Thorndike har dock missförstått de tre ställen i Tychos korrespondens, där enligt honom detta skulle bekräftas. Samtliga ställen (VII, 120, 147, 212) avse Apianus och Pena.

Ptolemaeus, Claudius, Almagest (old Venetian edition, c. 1515). Venetiis, 1515, 2°

Attested, not locatedArec-e-letter-ptolemy-almagest-venice
Status
Attested, not located · entry confidence A
Subject
Astronomy
Attested by
Norlind 1970, p. 358 (s.v. Ptolemæus, Claudius); Tycho’s correspondence, letter of 20 January 1587 (tekstnet.dk); Fund og Forskning 1965
Norlind records
Opera omnia: VI, 95
Note
Tycho states that he owns an old Venetian Almagest, some seventy years old in 1587 (letter of 20 January 1587: ‘vetus quoddam exemplar Almagesti, ante annos proxime 70. Venetijs editum’), that is, the Latin Almagest printed at Venice by Petrus Liechtenstein in about 1515. It is distinct from the Ptolemy volumes among the Clementinum copies — the Opera (Basel), the Geographia (Cologne 1597) and the De analemmate (Rome 1562). Norlind identified the edition in print (Fund og Forskning XII, 1965, p. 156, ‘Efterslæt’): the Latin Almagest printed at Venice in 1515 (Petrus Liechtenstein; Gerard of Cremona’s version), whose prefatory life of Ptolemy — ‘indledningen til en oversættelse af Almagesten, trykt i Venedig 1515, som Tycho Brahe har ejet og nævner i et brev’ — is the source of the royal descent and the physical description of Ptolemy in Tycho’s elegy In effigiem Cl. Ptolemaei (Epistolae astronomicae, 1596, p. 239). No copy of the Venice Almagest with Tycho’s marks has been identified. Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C).
Norlind 1970, p. 358
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Detta är den första tryckta latinska översättningen. Den återgår på Gerards från Cremona översättning från arabiskan. – Tycho ägde säkerligen själv detta verk (till Rothmann jan. 1587; VI, 95: »adhibui ... vetus quoddam exemplar Almagesti, ante annos proxime 70. Venetiis editum ...»).
Open questions
  • Whether a copy of the Venice Almagest of 1515 with Tycho’s marks survives; such a copy coming to light would decide.

brown stamped leather with the blind initials ‘I. P. 1561’ (Johannes Pratensis); the purchase note ‘Emptus Haffniae 2 Joachimicis 1560 ultimo Novembris’ (hand disputed: Tycho — Dreyer, Studnička 1901; Pratensis — Boldan & Vackářová 2024); marginalia Kleinschnitzová gives to Tycho; on the title ‘Collegij Caesarei Societatis Jesu Pragae A°. 1642’, ‘NB. Marginales notae sunt Tichonis Brahe’ and, in another hand, ‘Bibliothecae Mathematicae’ (Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 4)
Links: catalogue record · digital facsimile (Manuscriptorium) · the title page with the Pratensis signatures, the purchase note of 1560, the Jesuit inscription of 1642 and the NB note (Manuscriptorium canvas 3, 2363 × 3611 px)
Road of dispersal
Road I, The Jesuit road: the Clementinum (1642), the colleges at Chomutov and Krumlov and the professed house, reunited in the Clementinum after 1773. The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Note
Prandtl Verzeichnis A no. 31; Kleinschnitzová no. 4; National Library of the Czech Republic (Clementinum), shelfmark 5 B 70, bound as Band I. Friis (1868–69, p. 267) and Dreyer (1890, p. 14) read the title-page note «emptus Haffniae 2 Joachimicis 1560 ultimo Novembris» (bought at Copenhagen for two Joachimsthaler on the last day of November 1560) as Tycho’s own hand, and Dreyer made this the first book of the library, procured after the predicted eclipse of 21 August 1560. The same title page carries the name of Johannes Pratensis (1543–1576) and the binding his stamped initials «I P 1561»: Studnička (1901, p. 39) took Pratensis for the seller; Boldan & Vackářová (2024, pp. 143–144) take him for the first owner and suppose the book passed to Tycho from his estate. The hand of the note has not been examined. Norlind (1970, p. 358) took the ‘Ptolemaeum Tychonis’ that Benjamin Ursinus asked Kepler to request from the Rožmberk librarian (March 1614; Caspar no. 681, p. 105) to be this copy, and found the work entered in Václav Březan’s catalogue of Peter Vok of Rožmberk’s library at Třeboň, drawn up 1602–08 and now in the Royal Library, Stockholm. The copy survives, is digitised, and carries an early note beside the 1642 inscription that the marginalia are Tycho’s. Šolc (2006, printed p. 190), explaining how the Ptolemy came from Pratensis ‘by 1576 at the latest, after the friend's death’, has Tycho visit him often and observe at his house ‘for example on 3 December 1573’ the lunar eclipse whose beginning and course he had computed from the Prutenic tables to within 20 minutes. Tycho's own observation note places that eclipse on 8 December 1573 at Knutstorp (‘Hanc ego Eclipsin in curia mea Knusdorpiana observavi’, TBOO X, 38–39), with the new gilt-brass quadrant and his sister Sophie's help (the loci record of the Knutstorp years); Šolc's date and place are not adopted, and the visit is not evidence for when the book passed to Tycho. Christianson (1967, p. 201 n. 13) wrote that the volume ‘has now been shown to have belonged to Johannes Pratensis, from whom Tycho probably inherited it in 1576’, and printed a note in Dreyer’s hand (Royal Library, NKS 3077 4°, p. 101) recording Friis’s later opinion that the marginalia are few, insignificant and Pratensis’s. The title page is image 3 of the Manuscriptorium facsimile. The hands were compared on the facsimile on 25 October 2026: the purchase note is not shown to be Tycho’s (the capital I without his J-descender, the final s at x-height) and not shown to be Pratensis’s (the h built on different limbs, the minims), every pair inconclusive at the facsimile’s resolution; the marginalia share Tycho’s u-marks and looped g but use a German-cursive e, final s and final i that his secure hands show nowhere, and lean away from him. Reviewed on 29 October 2026 in the lecture session, the six student volumes read through their literature packs: no positive evidence makes the volume Tycho’s before he left Denmark on 14 February 1562. The reading of the purchase note as his own hand began with Friis (1868–69) and Dreyer (1890) and was repeated without a comparison by Prusík (1901), Studnička (1901), Kukula (1906), Prandtl (1932) and Šolc (1999); Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 74) saw that a binding stamped for Pratensis in 1561 contradicts a purchase by Tycho in 1560 and called Studnička’s binder’s error improbable; Šolc (2006, 2018) and Boldan & Vackářová (2024) make Pratensis the purchaser and first owner; the National Library’s own record gives Pratensis the year 1561 and Tycho none; and the comparison of 25 October 2026 found nothing in the note that points to Tycho. The volume is carried from today as Pratensis’s purchase of 30 November 1560, bound for him in 1561, and Tycho’s later — not before 1561, probably after Pratensis’s death on 1 June 1576 — on the Jesuit note of 1642 that the marginalia are Tycho’s and on the college’s acquisition from his heirs; ownership graded B (was A), and the ‘first book’ of Dreyer’s account withdrawn. Decided on 29 October 2026.
Norlind 1970, p. 358
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
Det är väl på detta verk som Benjamin Ursinus syftar i ett brev till Kepler mars 1614 (Caspar nr 681, s. 105); exemplaret synes ha hamnat i Peter Vok Ursini Rosenbergs bibliotek: »Posce per me et literas a Bibliothecario Rosenbergiaco Ptolemæum Tychonis serio: spondeo te habiturum. Posce saltem. Egi iam cum eodem, ille tuas literas videre vult.» Det finns upptaget i den väldiga fyra folioband starka katalogen över det rosenbergska biblioteket på Třebon, uppgjord åren 1602–08 av Peter Vok Ursini Rosenbergs bibliotekarie Václav Březan och nu förvarad i KB., Sthm.

AG XIV 7, Strahov Library (Strahovská knihovna, Královská kanonie premonstrátů na Strahově) · identification A · Period 4 (gilt supralibros)
gilt portrait supralibros (front) and arms (back), 76 × 59 mm (Pařez 2009), on a gilt-tooled brown leather binding — not parchment (autopsy 18 September 2026)
Links: catalogue record · Gabriel Crusius’s inscriptions on the title of NK ČR 5 G 92, as the National Library’s record transcribes them (Manuscriptorium)
Road of dispersal
Road II, The heirs’ dispersal into private hands (after 1601). Route to Strahov undocumented beyond the Crusius layer: no Jesuit inscription, no Klauser ex-libris photographed, no later owner named in the catalogue. The same collector's other volumes went to the Chomutov Jesuits (1654) and, in the Euclid's case, to Klauser.. The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Note
One of the two Strahov volumes with the full-size portrait/arms supralibros (Pařez 2009); the other, the Opus palatinum Σ V 5/a, is bound in parchment, this one in gilt-tooled brown calf. Books carrying this plaque were printed 1584–1598 (Norlind) — this 1580 imprint sits at the lower edge, and Pařez leaves open whether the plaques were applied as the books came or in one campaign after 1598. The title inscription ‘G: Crusio ‹K› / inservio.’ is Gabriel Crusius's — the same hand and formula as on 5 G 92 (compared 19 September 2026 on the digitised leaf) — which ties this volume to the Euclid AV II 2 and to the two Chomutov gifts of 1654.
Open questions
  • The endleaves and spine for a Klauser ex-libris, Strnad's name or a Mathematical-Museum spine — the volume's last step into Strahov.

Note
Heinrich Rantzau's Horoscopographia (Wittenberg 1588, 4°), bound after the Paulus Alexandrinus in the Dresden Sammelband that Falkenstein described in 1839 (pp. 574–575: ‘Daran: Henrici Rancovii (v. Ranzau) Horoscopographia, Wit. 1588. 4.’) — the volume in Tycho's portrait-and-arms parchment binding that Collijn reported to Kleinschnitzová and that the Dresden library reported lost in the Second World War (Norlind 1970, p. 356). Rantzau's book of the same year as the Paulus edited from his library, in the same binding: a pair that reached Tycho together, by gift or purchase, in 1588 or soon after. Entered on 20 October 2026 from Šolc 2018 (p. 194) and Falkenstein's entry; grade B by the document rule — Tycho's binding described by a librarian, the copy not seen since 1945. The SLUB's war-loss register carries a card for the Boiemus — Lit.Graec.B.1976, earlier ‘Phil. gr. B. 93a. Misc. 3’, and ‘Misc. 3’ matches Falkenstein's order, in which the Boiemus is the third piece; no card was found under the other two headings, and the register does not say whether the volume was removed in 1945–46 or destroyed (Nachweiskatalog image 00504111, read 27 October 2026; the identification with the Tycho volume is inference, C). Šolc 2018 (p. 194) infers from the words ‘ex Henrici Rantzovii bibliotheca’ that the volume's ‘paths once led through both libraries’, Rantzau's and Tycho's; the words belong to the Paulus edition's title (its Greek text printed from a manuscript in Rantzau's library) and Falkenstein records no Rantzau mark on the volume, so nothing documents that this copy was ever Rantzau's.

Iohannis Rantzovii equitis aurati coniugis, conscripta; item Ecloga de eiusdem matronae obitu (1582)
Road of dispersal
Road I, The Jesuit road: the Clementinum (1642), the colleges at Chomutov and Krumlov and the professed house, reunited in the Clementinum after 1773. The chain of custody stands in the volume record.
Note
Prandtl Verzeichnis A no. 33; Prandtl Einzelband XXII (National Library of the Czech Republic, Clementinum, shelfmark 1 H 56; Kleinschnitzová no. 3). The volume carries Rantzau’s autograph dedication of 1584 to Henrik Ramel, who probably passed it to Tycho (Norlind 1970, p. 359). Šolc 2002 (p. 330) lists ‘Astrologicae quaedam praedictiones; adiectus est tractatus De annis climactericis’ as a second item of the volume; it is the continuation of this print’s title. Three further works are bound with it (Kleinschnitzová 3:2–4). Heinrich Rantzau’s own library of more than six thousand volumes reached the same National Library by another road: taken from Breitenburg by Wallenstein in 1627 (1626 in Walde), given to the Jesuit professed house on the Malá Strana, partly confiscated by the Swedes on 2 September 1648, and in the Clementinum since the suppression of 1773 (Veselá 2025, pp. 9–10, 180–183; Lohmeier 2000, pp. 103–104). This copy came by the road of 1642 from Tycho’s heirs; the two are not to be conflated. Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C). The earlier reading of the store and of the library-history — Rantzau's presentation copy to Tycho — is withdrawn (27 October 2026, register dossier §18-10): the dedication names Ramel, and only the Tycho step is inference.
Norlind 1970, p. 359
Norlind’s entry, transcribed (Swedish)
I ett saml.-bd. På försättsbladet egenhändig dedikation 1584 av Rantzau till sedermera riksrådet Henrik Ramel, som förmodligen har skänkt exemplaret till Tycho. Av en dikt, som Tycho skrev till Rantzau och som trycktes på Uraniborg 1585, daterad d. 1 mars d.å. (IX, 187–190), framgår, att Tycho blivit smått På försättsbladet egenhändig dedikation 1584 av Rantzau till sedermera riksrådet Henrik Ramel, som förmodligen har skänkt exemplaret till Tycho. Av en dikt, som Tycho skrev till Rantzau och som trycktes på Uraniborg 1585, daterad d. 1 mars d.å. (IX, 187–190), framgår, att Tycho blivit smått förargad över, att Rantzau i en bok kallat Uraniborg för »specula», varav det är uppenbart, menar Tycho, att Rantzau icke haft klart för sig, hur byggnaden såg ut: »Cuius fama tuas siquidem pervenit ad aures, Intuitu vero forte minora refert: Quippe vocas speculam, quas Divæ struximus Ædes, Vnde liquet, formam te latuisse domus.» Den bok av Rantzau som Tycho här åsyftar, är just hans »Catalogus». Första upplagan trycktes i Antwerpen 1580 och såväl här som i alla de senare upplagorna står om Uraniborg följande: »Tygonique Braden (cuius vix similem in disciplinis Mathematicis hic Septentrionalis tractus habet) rex insulam nomine Vueen cum omnibus reditibus inter Zelandiam et Schaniam ad tempus vitæ concessit, ingentemque speculam erigi curavit» etc. Detta står som sagt i alla upplagorna. Vi kunna således inte med säkerhet avgöra i vilken Tycho läste det, men det kan ha varit i upplagan 1584 (s. 75–76), vars förord är daterat d. 1 febr. 1584. Exemplaret i Prag fick han dock säkerligen först senare.

Subject
Calendar/Astrology
Attested by
Norlind 1970, p. 360 (s.v. Rantzau, Henrik); Zinner no. 3399 (after Norlind)
Acquisition
1590; from the author (Tycho to Rantzau, April 1590; Opera omnia VII, 243) (Gift of an author or correspondent)
Norlind records
Opera omnia: VII, 243; VIII, 63
Note
Norlind records the book as received from the author (‘Erhöll Tycho av förf.’), on the evidence of Tycho to Rantzau, April 1590 (Opera omnia VII, 243). Rantzau’s own copy, into which a transcript of Tycho’s elegy to Denmark was bound and which King Christian leafed through on a visit to Rantzau (Opera omnia VIII, 63), is a different book. Two copies of the 1590 edition in the Royal Library, Hielmst. 547 2° and Hielmst. 146 2°, examined in facsimile, descend from Henrik Hielmstierne and bear neither a mark of Tycho’s nor the bound-in transcript. No copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified.
Copies of the edition examined
  • Det Kongelige Bibliotek (Royal Library), Copenhagen, Hielmst. 547 2° [19,-167] — Hamburg: Jacob Wolf, 1590 (Zinner 3399; USTC 689799). Henrik Hielmstierne (1715–1780); his library to the Royal Library. Earlier: contemporary presentation inscription on the title-page foot, “Reverendo et Doctiss[imo] viro Johanni Fab[…]” — a gift to a clergyman named Johann, not Tycho. Title-page presentation inscription (16th/17th-c., to “Johann Fab[…]”); 18th-c. octagonal armorial ex-libris (harpy supporters) = Hielmstierne; interior printed calendar tables clean of annotation.
  • Det Kongelige Bibliotek (Royal Library), Copenhagen, Hielmst. 146 2° [19,-167] — Hamburg: Jacob Wolf, 1590 (Zinner 3399; USTC 689799). Henrik Hielmstierne (1715–1780); his library to the Royal Library. None of note: no inscription, no ex-libris, blank flyleaves.
Norlind 1970, p. 360

När konung Kristian vid ett besök hos Rantzau bläddrade i boken, fick han även se Tychos dikt, läste den och avlägsnade sig sedan utan att säga ett ord (VIII, 63). Jfr s. 265.
