Chain of custody
  1. Tycho’s heirs, Prague from 1601
    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970
  2. Gabriel Crusius (‘nobilis ac doctissimus Dominus Gabriel Crusius’) until 1654
    His inscription on the title of 5 G 92, with the formula ‘G. Crusio inservio’ (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 89–90; the library’s record). Who he was is not established. — Kleinschnitzová 1933; NKP, Staré tisky (Aleph)
  3. The Marian sodality at Chomutov (Sodalitas B. V. Mariae Assumptae) — a congregation attached to the Jesuit college, possibly the college's own body
    The National Library's record lists the Church of the Assumption at Chomutov among the former owners, from the inscription on a2 ‘Sodalitat[is?] in Co[???] B. V. MARIAE Assumptae’, undated and with its place-word illegible; Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 89) prints only ‘ein unleserlich gemachter Provenienzvermerk’. Whether the sodality held the book before or after Crusius's gift of 1654, and whether it was a body distinct from the college, the record does not say: a station of uncertain order, entered as the record names it. — NKP, Staré tisky (Aleph); Kleinschnitzová 1933
  4. Jesuit college, Chomutov (Komotau) 1654–1773
    Crusius’s gift of 5 August 1654 — the title carries, after an effaced note, ‘[Commotouij] 5. Augustj A. D. 1654 Nobilis ac Doctissimus Dominus Gabriel Crusius. — G. Crusio inservio’ (the ‘Donavit’ wording belongs to 5 J 103, not to this volume) — and the college’s catalogue entry of 1673 — ‘Collegii Societatis Jesu Commotovii catalogo inscriptus 1673 a tamtéž dole jinou rukou: Com[m]otovij.’ — as the National Library’s record transcribes them (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 76, 89–90). — NKP, Staré tisky (Aleph); Kleinschnitzová 1933
  5. The Clementinum library after the suppression of the Society: the public University Library, since 1990 the National Library of the Czech Republic, Prague from after 1773
    Brought to the Clementinum with the library of the dissolved Chomutov college after 1773; Kleinschnitzová counted nineteen volumes of that provenance in 1933 (p. 81). — Kleinschnitzová 1933

Kukula first published the volume in 1906–07 as no. III of the seven Tychoniana found since 1902, under the shelfmark V G 92: the four Synesius pieces of 1558, 1557, 1555 and 1567, ‘T. B. O. 1576’ on the upper board, ‘Nobilis ac Doctissimus Dns. Gabriel Crusius 1673’ on the first title. The volume is Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 26, Sign. 5 G 92. || The fourth piece (adl. 3, Canter's De dono … Hymni) is dated by its colophon 'BASILEAE EXCVDEBAT IOANNES OPORINVS, ANNO CIↃ. IↃ. LXVII. MENSE SEXTILI.' (Manuscriptorium canvas 1056, read 27 October 2026) — August 1567, as Kukula, Prandtl and Kleinschnitzová give it; the library's record (1563) is wrong. On the title the 1654 date ends a struck-through line (as the library's record itself describes), and 1673 stands on the line of the Crusius formula, not beside 'Catalogo inscriptus' — Kleinschnitzová's assignment (gift 5 August 1654, catalogue 1673) cannot be confirmed from the bitonal facsimile. Four June 2026 census 'notable' pages (canvases 49, 157, 892, 922) are printed side-notes and Greek variants, not manuscript; the full re-read is pending. The HOME surrogate's file name ('Rantzau, Heinrich') is a mislabel: the volume is the Synesius Sammelband.

Quoted below in the words and language of the record itself; the Notes row paraphrases it in English.
Tisk pochází z knihovny Tychona Brahe.
Na titulní straně kulaté razítko s dvojhlavým orlem a opisem REGIAE BIBLIOTH: ACAD: PRAGEN. a drobné fialové razítko ve tvaru erbu s dvojhlavým orlem a písmeny ZK.

Na titulní straně exlibris chomutovských jezuitů s rokem 1672. || The library's photograph (2026): the spine whitened by the Chomutov college, the title ‘Proclus de Sphaera’ in ink at the head, the painted shelfmark ‘N. II.’, the labels ‘T. Brahe 28’ and ‘I. 2.’; the library's Manuscriptorium record describes the edge of the text block as carrying a chiselled title (‘Ořízka s cizelovaným názvem’) || Read on the Manuscriptorium facsimile, 27 October 2026: the ink initials T and B stand at the head of the title (canvas 1) and again at the head of the first text leaf †2r, the Hopper dedication (canvas 3), in one ink and manner; the Chomutov inscription on the title reads ‘Collegij Societatis IESV Commotouij’ above and ‘Catalogo inscriptus A° 1672.’ below the second printed title; the round REGIAE BIBLIOTH: ACAD: PRAGEN. stamp and the small ZK stamp are on the title. The facsimile (1024 canvases, 1079–1191 × 1692–1760 px, licence NoC-NC) covers the text block only — canvas 1 is the title page and canvas 1024 a blank leaf — so neither the board stamp nor the chiselled edge title is in it.
Chain of custody
  1. Tycho’s heirs, Prague from 1601
    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970
  2. route unknown until 1672
    No owner is recorded between the heirs and the Chomutov college’s catalogue entry. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 76) supposed that the college came by Tycho’s books in a way similar to the Clementinum’s gift; Císařová Smítková, Paličková and Vackářová (2021, p. 30) suppose Clementinum duplicates passed on under Joannes Jüngling, who kept the Clementinum’s mathematical library in 1749 and was prefect of the Chomutov library in 1765–1766; the college’s dated catalogue entries on Tycho’s volumes are of 1645 to 1675. — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021
  3. Jesuit college, Chomutov (Komotau) 1672–1773
    The college’s catalogue inscription ‘Collegij Societatis Jesu Commotovii catalogo inscriptus A° 1672’ on the title (the library’s record). — NKP, Staré tisky (Aleph); Kleinschnitzová 1933
  4. The Clementinum library after the suppression of the Society: the public University Library, since 1990 the National Library of the Czech Republic, Prague from after 1773
    Brought to the Clementinum with the library of the dissolved Chomutov college after 1773; Kleinschnitzová counted nineteen volumes of that provenance in 1933 (p. 81). — Kleinschnitzová 1933

Westman reproduces fols 41 and 41v of the Naibod (2011, figs 47–48, ‘Courtesy National Library of the Czech Republic, Klementinum. 5.J.2’) and reports owner's marks at that opening, the only marks in the volume beyond the initials on the title; he reads the stamp on the board as ‘TBDO/1576’. || The June 2026 vision census (13 confident + 5 possible pages) is unreliable for this volume: the three confident pages re-read at full resolution on 27 October 2026 — canvases 948 and 954 (the precession notes ‘A Christi Dei natali annis 139 …’ and ‘Ante Natalē Christi Dei annis 889 …’) and 538 (the ‘S A C P D L’ series) — are printed side-notes of the Basel edition and the cropped edge of a facing column, not manuscript annotation; only the page-1 positive (the Chomutov inscription) is a manuscript mark. Notes
Prandtl’s Einzelband XXIII (J. C. Scaliger, De causis linguae Latinae, 1584) is a Sammelband of two prints, Joseph Scaliger’s Verrius Flaccus and Festus of 1575 bound after it (Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 8; the library’s record, 8 H 39 adl. 1). Studnička named it in 1901 among the newly found Tychoniana (Bericht, p. 54). Prusík 1901, group C (brown leather), no. 1: Sign. 8 H 39, Scaliger’s De causis linguae latinae (1584). || A genuinely annotated volume: the re-read of the June 2026 census (27 October 2026) confirms 40 manuscript pages of 51 positives — a continuous apparatus of red-ink marginal glosses, red underlining and red strike-throughs on Book I of De causis (canvases 17–67, printed pp. 1–51): topic headings and summaries of Scaliger's argument ('Duo modi docendi et discendi; Via resolutoria … Via compositiva', 'Litera a figura dicta … Obliterare a lituris non a literis', 'Labdacismus; Metacismus; Platyasmus; Lotacismus', the Greek pathe of letters, 'I pro E; E pro V …'), verified as manuscript on canvas 18; the apparatus stops after Book I. The hand is unattributed in every source and has never been compared; the re-read dates the script to the 17th century.

Links
digital facsimile (Google Books) · Google Books full view (NK digitisation NKP:1002614021)
Sources
Prandtl 1932; NKP, Staré tisky (Aleph); Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970; Kukula 1906–07; Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021; Volf 1932; Veselá 2025
Notes
Kukula first published the volume in 1906–07 as no. VI of the seven Tychoniana found since 1902, under the shelfmark XIV A 63: Stoeffler’s Calendarium Romanum magnum (‘Tubingae 1518’ in Kukula; the book was printed at Oppenheim by Jacob Köbel in 1518, as Kleinschnitzová, no. 33, and the library’s record give it), Peurbach’s Tabulae eclipsium (Vienna 1514), Apianus’s Pronunciata (Nuremberg 1541) and an Introductorium astronomicum (Paris 1517), with ‘T. B.’ on the first title; the binding is without special character. The volume is Prandtl’s Band VII of 1932: the library’s owner index lists it under Sign. 14 A 63, Kleinschnitzová’s 1933 shelfmark for the Stoeffler and the Peurbach is 14 A 63, and the Stoeffler, the Peurbach and the Apianus are confirmed as its constituents. The volume is digitised in full view in the National Library’s programme with Google Books, the whole Sammelband under one digitisation id attached to the library’s record and to the four adligata records; the Manuscriptorium record is catalogue-only. The National Library’s provenance survey of 2021 counts 215 volumes with Chomutov inscriptions and ‘at least four books from Tycho’s estate’ among them, all stamped ‘TBO 1576’; its authors suppose Clementinum duplicates passed on under P. Jan Jüngling in the eighteenth century; the dated Chomutov notes of 1645 (44 F 38) and 1654 (Crusius’s gifts) are earlier. || The library's record gives the title and flyleaf initials ‘T. B.’ as pencil (‘Na předsádce a na titulní straně tužkou iniciály: T. B. (Tycho Brahe)’), beside the pencil ‘T.B. 28.’ on the pastedown, while Kukula, Prandtl and Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 90: ‘eigenhändig von Brahe’) give the title initials as Tycho's own; which is right, or whether two sets exist, is not decidable from the records (27 October 2026). Kleinschnitzová's no. 33 lists four pieces and no Apianus; the library's record has the Apianus Instrumentum sinuum (1541) as adl. 2. The authority-field chronology ‘1576’ for Tycho on the record has no stated basis; Kukula and Prandtl call the binding plain.

Quoted below in the words and language of the record itself; the Notes row paraphrases it in English.
Tisk pochází z knihovny Tychona Brahe.
Na přídeští tužkou: T.B. 31. Na předsádce tužkou iniciály: T. B. (Tycho Brahe).
Na titulní straně přípisek: Collegij Societatis IESV Commotouiensis Catalogo inscriptus 1675. || Read on the Manuscriptorium facsimile, 27 October 2026: the Bellanti title (canvas 1) carries 'Collegij Societatis Jesu / Commotouiensis Catalogo inscriptus' followed by four figures in a 17th-century numeral form consistent with 1675 (the library's and Kleinschnitzová's reading), the round REGIAE BIBLIOTH: ACAD: PRAGEN. stamp and the small ZK stamp; it carries no handwritten T. B. The facsimile (312 canvases) holds the Bellanti only, from its title to the device leaf (canvas 312); the binding and the Bonatti are not digitised.
Chain of custody
  1. Tycho’s heirs, Prague from 1601
    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970
  2. route unknown until 1675
    No owner is recorded between the heirs and the Chomutov college’s catalogue entry. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 76) supposed that the college came by Tycho’s books in a way similar to the Clementinum’s gift; Císařová Smítková, Paličková and Vackářová (2021, p. 30) suppose Clementinum duplicates passed on under Joannes Jüngling, who kept the Clementinum’s mathematical library in 1749 and was prefect of the Chomutov library in 1765–1766; the college’s dated catalogue entries on Tycho’s volumes are of 1645 to 1675. — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021
  3. Jesuit college, Chomutov (Komotau) 1675–1773
    The inscription ‘Collegij Societatis IESV Commotouiensis Catalogo inscriptus 1675.’ on the title, as the National Library’s record transcribes it. — NKP, Staré tisky (Aleph); Kleinschnitzová 1933
  4. The Clementinum library after the suppression of the Society: the public University Library, since 1990 the National Library of the Czech Republic, Prague from after 1773
    Brought to the Clementinum with the library of the dissolved Chomutov college after 1773; Kleinschnitzová counted nineteen volumes of that provenance in 1933 (p. 81). — Kleinschnitzová 1933

Notes
The De revolutionibus mis-attribution copy; entered via the Wittich-library purchase. Friis had already denied the marginalia to Tycho in 1868: the notes ‘næsten paa hver Side’ cannot be attributed to him ‘som man hidtil har antaget’, though the book ‘kan hidrøre fra hans Samling’ (Friis 1868–69, pp. 266–267, citing Hanslik 1851, p. 274, and Hanuš, Zusätze, Prague 1863, p. 9); the hand was identified as Paul Wittich's by Gingerich and Westman in 1988. The library's own catalogue of 1851 (Hanslik, pp. 274–275) had given the glosses to Tycho; Prusík 1901 (group A, no. 6) and Kukula 1906–07 repeated the attribution, Kukula calling for a specialist's study of the glossed Copernicus; Prusík noted the quantity of blank paper bound in with the book. Binding, as the National Library describes and photographs it in 2026: pale leather over boards, blind-tooled with ornament rolls and a pictorial centre panel on each board — Christ on the cross under an arch, figures at the foot and a lettered plaque below, on the front board; the risen Christ with banner and soldiers beneath on the back — a binding that in its execution stands apart from the rest of Tycho's volumes (Vackářová 2026, printed p. 9, Obr. 5–6; the front board, a graphite frottage of the whole board made to bring out the blind stamp, and the two centre panels are reproduced). The description supports what the provenance already implies: the volume was bound before it reached Tycho, for Wittich or an earlier owner, and carries none of Tycho's marks. Exhibited: in the Copernicus year 1973 the volume was the principal exhibit of the Prague quincentenary exhibition, shown as Tycho's annotated copy and prized as from his estate — the showing that the reattribution of 1981–88 overtook (Vackářová 2026, printed p. 8; she names neither venue nor organiser). Facsimile: Horský's edition (Nicolai Copernici De revolutionibus … cum commentariis manu scriptis Tychonis Brahe, Cimelia Bohemica 16, Pragae 1971), printed for the Copernicus year 1973, is held by the National Library as BMMS Facs F 158: smooth leather boards with the gilt initials NC and TB in a line device, the spine lettered COPERNICUS · BRAHE · DE REVOLUTIONIBUS (Vackářová 2026, printed pp. 9–10, Obr. 7); its title perpetuates the attribution to Tycho that the Debunked Claims Register records as overturned. The first-person note on fol. 82 in which the annotator writes of a discovery he himself made — the note John Craig copied into the Edinburgh copy as made by ‘M. Witt’, the clue of 1977/78 — does not stand in this copy: the National Library's curator states expressly that the Clementinum volume lacks it (Vackářová 2026, printed p. 32), consistent with Gingerich's placing of that note, on the mean motion of precession, in the Liège copy at ff. 81–83v. || The volume carries no mark of Tycho's own: the one trace leading to him is the college's 1642 line ‘Ex Bibliotheca et Recognitione Tichoniana’ (Vackářová 2026, p. 25). The tail label ‘B. 15.’ is one number off the shelfmark 14 B 16, in the form of the old shelfmark labels (‘I. 2.’ on 5 J 2, ‘F. 8.’ on 14 F 8); no source explains it. The ‘Musei Mathematici’ line the library records on the title is not identifiable in the Obr. 30 reproduction.

Notes
Friis described the volume in 1868, brought forward for him by the custos Dambeck: the Rheticus of 1551 with the Jesuit inscription, and ‘en Snees Blade’ (a score of leaves) of manuscript appended — the Praxis, dated at the Calends of January 1591 and ‘A. C. 1595, 13 Cal. Xbris’ — in a hand ‘som man hidtil, men vistnok med Urette, har anseet for den berømte Astronom’; a photograph of the volume had been sent to Copenhagen in 1862 by Dr Joseph Böhm (Berlingske Tidende, 9 March 1863), and Hanslik's history of the library (1851, p. 612) had noticed it (Friis 1868–69, p. 266). Šíma and Valeška (2002) established the hand as a professional copyist's. Prusík listed the Praxis first among the four manuscripts in 1901: a paper manuscript of twenty quarto leaves bound as the first appendix to the printed work at 14 C 20, the binding of the earliest period without special character, ‘Tycho Brahe Calend. Jannuar. 1591’ and the distich dated ‘A. C. 1595. 13 Cal. Xbris’ under the title; its authenticity, doubted by Dreyer, he held proved by Studnička. Hanslik's catalogue of 1851 (pp. 612–613) already printed the appended manuscript as Tycho's autograph, ‘Dogmata geometrica’, found by the custos Dambeck in the mathematical section of the library. || The Praxis (14 C 20/adl.1) is not in the Manuscriptorium facsimile: 26 canvases = the Rheticus's 12 leaves + 2 blanks (verified 27 October 2026); the only reproductions remain Studnička's facsimile of 1886 and Opera omnia I pp. 283–293. The column heads 'sin', 'cos', 'sec' (canvas 12) and 'tg', 'cosec', 'cotg' (canvas 13) pencilled above the Rheticus table are modern function names, a later reader's.

Notes
Kukula first published the volume in 1906–07 (no. V of the seven found since 1902, Sign. XIV F 8): the Arithmetica communis with Peurbach’s and Gmunden’s algorithms (defective), Strabo’s Hortulus (Nuremberg 1512), the Liber diversarum rerum ascribed to Ptolemy (Venice 1509) and Faber’s Meteorologia Aristotelis (Nuremberg 1512), ‘T. B.’ on the first title; the binding without special character. The National Library’s owner index lists the volume under Sign. 14 F 8 with the Strabo, the Ptolemy and the Faber among its constituents. The National Library’s provenance survey of 2021 counts 215 volumes with Chomutov inscriptions and ‘at least four books from Tycho’s estate’ among them, all stamped ‘TBO 1576’; its authors suppose Clementinum duplicates passed on under P. Jan Jüngling in the eighteenth century; the dated Chomutov notes of 1645 (44 F 38) and 1654 (Crusius’s gifts) are earlier. There is no digital facsimile of the volume; the library’s record offers five photographs (title page, front pastedown, boards, spine). || The library's convolute record (Manuscriptorium NKCR__-NKCR__14_F_000008_17OOHAF-cs, from Aleph docs 000155813, 000155815, 000155817, 000155823) lists four prints bound together today — the Arithmetica communis host ([Vienna: Singriener, 1515], 'neúplné'), Strabo's Hortulus as adl. 1 ('neúplné'), the ps.-Ptolemy Liber diversarum rerum as adl. 2 and the Meteorologia as adl. 3 — in the order a–d in which Kukula described them in 1906–07 (Prandtl's Band V: 21, 47, 32, 7); Kleinschnitzová's no. 36 omits the Strabo. The volume is intact as described since 1906; an earlier worklog note that it was disbound across several 1933 shelfmarks is contradicted by every source. The library records red manuscript marginal notes and red-highlighted capitals in the ps.-Ptolemy (adl. 2), attributed by no source.

Chain of custody
  1. Tycho’s heirs, Prague from 1601
    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970
  2. route unknown
    No owner is recorded between the heirs and the Chomutov college’s catalogue entry. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 76) supposed that the college came by Tycho’s books in a way similar to the Clementinum’s gift; Císařová Smítková, Paličková and Vackářová (2021, p. 30) suppose Clementinum duplicates passed on under Joannes Jüngling, who kept the Clementinum’s mathematical library in 1749 and was prefect of the Chomutov library in 1765–1766; the college’s dated catalogue entries on Tycho’s volumes are of 1645 to 1675. — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021
  3. Jesuit college, Chomutov (Komotau) until 1773
    No accession inscription on the leaves; the college’s signature on the spine, which Kleinschnitzová read as the Chomutov provenance also written on the Glareanus 19 G 20, once part of the same Sammelband (1933, no. 37 and p. 93). — Kleinschnitzová 1933
  4. The Clementinum library after the suppression of the Society: the public University Library, since 1990 the National Library of the Czech Republic, Prague from after 1773
    Brought to the Clementinum with the library of the dissolved Chomutov college after 1773; Kleinschnitzová counted nineteen volumes of that provenance in 1933 (p. 81). — Kleinschnitzová 1933

Sources

Notes
Bound volume IV, in Studnička’s reconstruction of its original make-up four constituents, nos. 41, 20, 1 and 11: the Sacrobosco manuscript, the Gauricus, the Albubater and the Cardanus. The manuscript was separated from Sign. 14 F 16 before 1901, at an earlier revision of the manuscripts (Prusík 1901, pp. 198–199; Studnička 1901, p. 21; Kukula 1906–07, p. 22). Studnička described the volume in 1901 as Tycho’s astrological study-book, brought to his notice by the custos Josef Truhlář: a manuscript compendium of Sacrobosco’s Sphaera first (now Sign. VII E 29), then the Gauricus, the Albubater and the Cardanus (Bericht, pp. 17–18, 30). He reports ‘constat 5 lb 15 d.’ on the inside of the front board — the sum of the cost note on the first leaf of the manuscript, which lists a Glareanus, the Gauricus with Montulmo, the Albubater, the Cardanus and the binder’s fee (pp. 20–21; the boards are not in the facsimile) — and reproduces as Tycho’s own work eight pages from the leaves bound at the end of the Albubater (pp. 22–29) and a horoscope from the Cardanus with a line of manuscript above it (p. 30). The first page he reproduces is the nativity of Andreas Schöner, cast for Nuremberg (‘Anno M.D.XXX die XXI Junij … natus Andreas Schönerus. Dies Martis’; 21 June 1530 fell on a Tuesday), and the cost note is headed with the same name. Which of the annotations in the volume are Tycho’s has not been established by a comparison of hands. Prusík 1901, group A, no. 3: Sign. 14 F 16, ‘ein Sammelband ohne besonderen Wert’, to which the Sacrobosco manuscript (now MS VII E XXIX) originally belonged; Kukula told in 1906–07 how the custos Truhlář, finding the price list on the manuscript’s flyleaf, recovered the Sammelband it had been taken from, its upper board marked ‘constat 5 15’, the sum of the list. The National Library’s digital facsimile of Sign. 14 F 16 shows the volume as it now stands: the three Petreius imprints — the Gauricus, the Albubater and the Cardanus — and nothing else; the Sacrobosco manuscript is at Sign. VII E 29. || Re-read of the June 2026 census positives, 27 October 2026 (ch. III), complete in two parts: 211 manuscript pages, 1 possible, 6 printed only of 218. The nativity on canvas 304 reads ‘Anno M·D·X·X·X·’ with a fourth X overwritten by a dark mark; ‘Dies martis’ fits 21 June 1530 (Tuesday, Julian), not 1540 (Monday). Besides the Schöner layer the re-read finds at least three later annotating layers — the bridge leaf (canvas 314, a rapid German cursive), a red ‘An: 1560:’ (canvas 246) and ‘Locus Stellae ex Copernici Doctrina’ (canvas 329) — none compared with any hand.

The annotating hands are described neutrally as a bold brown Latin cursive (pp. 22–49 and p. 104), a smaller calculating hand in the same ink (pp. 12–22) and a redder ink on p. 33; their attribution to Tycho is Kleinschnitzová's and Gingerich's and has not been compared. Compared in session on 27 October 2026 (hand_14F284_vs_hven_pillars_2026-10-27.md): inconclusive band, consistent with the 1577 comet working hand of KB GKS 1826 leaf 56 (14 concordances, no discordance), the notes' wording tracking Tycho's printed critique of Scultetus — status candidate, not an identification.

Notes
Prusík (1901) lists the volume in group C (Prachtbände), white leather, no. 2, under the shelfmark Sign. 14 G 30: Maestlin’s Alterum examen (Tübingen 1586) with Clavius’s Apologia (Rome 1588), which Prusík notes Tycho had bound after it as the reply (p. 200). || One reader's note only: beside Clavius's account of Tycho's vernal equinox of 1586 (Apologia, Lib. I, p. 30; canvas 184 — 'TYCHO Brahe Danus quidam nobilis vir … deprehendit anno 1586 … Æquinoctium vernum … accidisse die 10. Martij. Hor. 9. Min. 2. post Meridiem', from Bartholomaeus Scultetus), an eight-line brown-ink note with a long brace: '[H]anc unicam habet / [a]uthor in toto hoc libro / obseruationem coelitus / [de]ductam[?], quâ Calen- / darii reformationem / […]ant temporis æqui- / noctii Verni rite fi[eri?] / [?]t probare potest.' — the one observation from the sky in the whole book by which the author can prove the reform. The hand is unidentified and has never been compared. The June 2026 'calendar-reform marginalia' at canvases 506 and 508 (and the note at 227) are Clavius's printed side-notes, and 518 is show-through: the re-read of 27 October 2026 leaves 3 manuscript pages of 71 positives.

Chain of custody
  1. Tycho’s heirs, Prague from 1601
    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970
  2. route unknown until 1671
    No owner is recorded between the heirs and the Chomutov college’s catalogue entry. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 76) supposed that the college came by Tycho’s books in a way similar to the Clementinum’s gift; Císařová Smítková, Paličková and Vackářová (2021, p. 30) suppose Clementinum duplicates passed on under Joannes Jüngling, who kept the Clementinum’s mathematical library in 1749 and was prefect of the Chomutov library in 1765–1766; the college’s dated catalogue entries on Tycho’s volumes are of 1645 to 1675. — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021
  3. Jesuit college, Chomutov (Komotau) 1671–1773
    The inscription ‘Collegij Societatis JESU Commotouij Cat. inscr. A. 1671.’ on the title, as the National Library’s record transcribes it. — NKP, Staré tisky (Aleph); Kleinschnitzová 1933
  4. The Clementinum library after the suppression of the Society: the public University Library, since 1990 the National Library of the Czech Republic, Prague from after 1773
    Brought to the Clementinum with the library of the dissolved Chomutov college after 1773; Kleinschnitzová counted nineteen volumes of that provenance in 1933 (p. 81). — Kleinschnitzová 1933

The library's record mentions no marginalia, describes no binding beyond the spine label 'T. Brahe 46', and records the host and the Erastus Epistolae as incomplete (the host's extent runs from p. 6 to p. 9). Kleinschnitzová places the volume in her group III, 'Andere Provenienzen'.

The June 2026 census 'marginalia' of pp. 16–18, 97, 101, 102 are Scheiner's printed side-notes (re-read 27 October 2026); no manuscript annotation is known in the volume.

Notes
Prandtl’s Band XXIX, Einzelband 40: Reinhold’s Prutenicae tabulae of 1551, the presentation copy to the Counts of Mansfeld, which Prandtl locates in the Prague University Library. Studnička described the volume in 1901 (Bericht, pp. 41–45) and reproduced Reinhold’s dedication and the two manuscript pieces on the flyleaf: a passage headed ‘Plato’ (‘Unum est naturae vinculum, doctrina numerorum, figurarum et motuum coelestium …’), and the draft of the epigram ‘Quamvis mortalis vescor mortalibus auris’, a first version corrected and struck through and a second written under ‘Aliter’. Dreyer and Ræder printed the epigram from this leaf (Opera omnia IX, p. 215; the cancelled version p. 316). Studnička supposed that Tycho had kept both pieces from an earlier time and inserted them here, and took the binding as proof that the stamps were Tycho’s own and had come with him to Prague (pp. 41, 45). Prusík 1901, group C (Prachtbände), white leather, no. 1, lists Sign. 14 J 176 as the Prutenicae with Reinhold’s dedication to the Counts of Mansfeld, Tycho’s note ‘Est manus Reinholdi. Emi Pragae anno 1601 mense Junio’, and a leaf of verses in his hand at the front; Kukula in 1906–07 described the two drafts of the distich with their deletions. Reproduced: the front board with the gilt portrait medallion — a faded red inscription above it — and the arms stamp of the back board, photographed by Zdeněk Rerych for the National Library's volume of 2026, which presents the binding as the ‘second variant’ of Tycho's bindings beside the ‘typical’ T·B·O leather of 14 J 190 (Vackářová 2026, printed p. 8, Obr. 4; she does not say there were only two). The photograph places the portrait die on the front board and the arms die on the back, as the Iconographia's supralibros records assume. Reproduced in colour by Šolc (2018, figs 3a–c, p. 197 (the portrait binding, Reinhold's dedication with Tycho's note, the title)). || The front pastedown (canvas 2) carries the library's marks in sequence: the printed label 'Veřejná a universitní knihovna v Praze' pasted over the German label of the k. k. Öffentliche und Universitäts-Bibliothek, 'T. B. 18.' in ink, the violet 'Tres.' with 'M 18' and a blue-crayon '10.', a struck-through '[?] D 83', the red-and-black 'XIV / J 176' and the modern NK barcode label 1002391364; a blue round stamp 'UNIVERS. PRAG. BIBL. C. R. PUBL.' stands on the dedication leaf and the Plato leaf. The re-read of 27 October 2026 finds 29 manuscript pages, beyond the preliminaries mostly red-ink corrections of the printed tables (hand unidentified) and pencil figures.

Chain of custody
  1. Tycho’s heirs, Prague 1601–1642
    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970
  2. Jesuit college in the Clementinum (Collegium Caesareum), Prague 1642–1773
    The inscription ‘Collegij Caesarei Societatis JESV Pragae A. 1642.’ on the title, as the National Library’s record transcribes it. — NKP, Staré tisky (Aleph)
  3. The Clementinum library after the suppression of the Society: the public University Library, since 1990 the National Library of the Czech Republic, Prague from 1773
    The college library passed to the state with the suppression of 1773 and became the public University Library in the Clementinum; the Tychoniana were mixed with the other mathematical books and reassembled by the librarians around 1900 (Šolc 2002, p. 329). — Šolc 2002

B. O. (Bericht, pp. 34–35). Prusík 1901, group B, no. 3, gives the volume under Sign. 14 J 190: Mizauld’s Cometographia (Paris 1549) with the Artis divinatricis encomia. Reproduced: the front board, orange-brown leather with a blind roll frame, corner stamps and a central foliate lozenge, ‘T·B·O’ tooled above it and ‘1576’ in spaced digits below, photographed for the National Library's volume of 2026 as the typical binding of Tycho's library (Vackářová 2026, printed p. 8, Obr. 3). The year stands plainly on the photograph and confirms Kleinschnitzová's reading over Prusík's undated cipher. || Annotation census, 27 October 2026 (ch. III), base the local PDF (270 pages): a pixel screen flagged 93 pages and a full-size vision re-read of those found one annotated page (canvas 182, brown underlining under ‘Quod dum dico … nepotum nostrorum immemores’, no words) and one possible stroke (canvas 230, beside ‘Cometa Niger dictus’) — the volume is essentially unannotated. The facsimile's 270 canvases equal the Cometographia's own collation (2 flyleaves + 265 + 3 pages): Marstaller's Artis divinatricis encomia, which Aleph lists as adl. 1 under the same Manuscriptorium pid, appears not to be digitised.

Notes
Prandtl’s volume XV (Sammelband 28, 10); his third constituent, A 27, is Paduanus’s Viridarium, now 14 H 190, which Studnička named beside this volume. Studnička named the volume in 1901 among the newly found Tychoniana: ‘ein eleganter Band’ with Brucaeus and Peucer, and Paduanus’s Viridarium beside it (Bericht, p. 54). Prusík 1901, group B, no. 4: Sign. 14 K 70, Peucer’s Elementa doctrinae de circulis coelestibus (Wittenberg 1563) with Brucaeus’s De motu primo (Rostock 1573). || Canvas 2 is TYPESET: Joachim Camerarius's Greek poem 'Περὶ τῶν ἀστρονομικῶν εἰσαγωγῶν Κάσπαρος τοῦ Πευκήρου' printed with the 1563 Peucer, the name in type as the last line 'Ἰωαχείμου Καμερ.' — the June 2026 'signed Camerarius autograph' is debunked; there is no Camerarius autograph in the volume. The re-read of the June census (27 October 2026) leaves 5 manuscript pages of 16 positives: the two 1642 inscriptions (canvases 1, 327) and three short unattributed reader's notes — 'Joh: de Sacr[o] Bosc[o]' beside Alkindus/Alphonsus in the chronology (canvas 28), a faint 'non est, non credend[…]' beside the great circles (131), and '3 ortus [?] / & occ[asus?]' beside the three risings (Brucaeus f. 40, canvas 399). Prandtl's Band XV also lists A 27 (Paduanius, Viridarium), but that work is 14 H 190, bound with Maurolycus already when Prusík listed it in 1901.

Chain of custody
  1. Tycho’s heirs, Prague from 1601
    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970
  2. route unknown until 1671
    No owner is recorded between the heirs and the Chomutov college’s catalogue entry. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 76) supposed that the college came by Tycho’s books in a way similar to the Clementinum’s gift; Císařová Smítková, Paličková and Vackářová (2021, p. 30) suppose Clementinum duplicates passed on under Joannes Jüngling, who kept the Clementinum’s mathematical library in 1749 and was prefect of the Chomutov library in 1765–1766; the college’s dated catalogue entries on Tycho’s volumes are of 1645 to 1675. — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021
  3. Jesuit college, Chomutov (Komotau) 1671–1773
    The inscription ‘Na titulním listu rukou "Collegij Soc[ieta]tis IESV Commotovij Catalogo inscriptus A[nn]o 1671".’ on the title, as the National Library’s record transcribes it. — NKP, Staré tisky (Aleph); Kleinschnitzová 1933
  4. The Clementinum library after the suppression of the Society: the public University Library, since 1990 the National Library of the Czech Republic, Prague from after 1773
    Brought to the Clementinum with the library of the dissolved Chomutov college after 1773; Kleinschnitzová counted nineteen volumes of that provenance in 1933 (p. 81). — Kleinschnitzová 1933

Chain of custody
  1. Tycho’s heirs, Prague 1601–1642
    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970
  2. Jesuit college in the Clementinum (Collegium Caesareum), Prague 1642–1773
    The inscription ‘Collegij Caesarei Soc[ieta]tis JESV Pragae A[nn]o 1642.’ on the title, as the National Library’s record transcribes it. — NKP, Staré tisky (Aleph)
  3. The Clementinum library after the suppression of the Society: the public University Library, since 1990 the National Library of the Czech Republic, Prague from 1773
    The college library passed to the state with the suppression of 1773 and became the public University Library in the Clementinum; the Tychoniana were mixed with the other mathematical books and reassembled by the librarians around 1900 (Šolc 2002, p. 329). — Šolc 2002

O. 1576’, the title inscribed ‘Collegij Caesarei Soctis. Jesu Pragae. 1642. Ex bibliotheca Tychoniana’. The volume is Prandtl’s Band XVII of 1932: the library’s owner index lists it under Sign. 16 J 38, and all four of Prandtl’s constituents — Encelius, Fleischer, Stanhuf and Galateus (De Ferrariis) — are its contents; Kleinschnitzová’s 1933 shelfmark for the Encelius and the Fleischer is 16 J 38. || The Manuscriptorium digitisation of 16 J 38 (302 images) holds the host only: canvas 299 is Encelius p. 271 'FINIS', canvases 301–302 blanks, with the Fleischer title's 'DOC[T…]' showing faintly through canvas 302; the Fleischer, the Stanhufius and the Galateus (c. 1,000 pages) are not digitised, although the record lists all four parts under the one pid. The HOME surrogate named 'Fleischer, Johann (302pp)' is therefore the Encelius. The re-read of the June 2026 census (27 October 2026) leaves no reader's annotation in the host: its 'marginalia' are printed side-notes and show-through; the manuscript positives are the flyleaf numbers, the pencil 'MS 12 A 28' (the shelfmark of the manuscript XII A 28, Studnička's Brevissimum planimetriae compendium) and the 1642 title inscriptions.

Literature cited in the record
Kleinschnitzová, Flora. Ex Bibliotheca Tychoniana Collegii soc. Jesu Pragae ad S.K. Clementem. Uppsala: Almqvist & Wiksells Boktryckeri-A.-B., 1933, s. 24, č. 47
Sources
Kleinschnitzová 1933; NKP, Staré tisky (Aleph); Šolc 2018; Christianson 1967; Norlind 1970; Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021
Notes

The earliest dated binding attributed to Tycho anywhere — on the cipher T·B and the year alone, with no inscription, no annotation and no note of 1642, the one Tycho volume inscribed by the Jesuit professed house on the Malá Strana, so the ownership of its three works is graded C (29 October 2026; B on 28 October) — and, now that the Ptolemy 5 B 70 is carried as Pratensis’s, the earliest book attributed to him, if the cipher is his. Christianson (1967, pp. 200–201), reading the student volumes against the Copenhagen curriculum, counts it with the volume of 1561 as ‘two of his own “textbooks”’ still preserved, the Sacrobosco being the text Scavenius lectured on. Šolc’s photographs (2018, figs 1a–b) show on the front board the letters T and B, separated by small ornaments, above a panel stamp of a half-length figure, with the year 1560 below; on the rear board a second figured panel stamp and the paper label ‘Tres. M 47’. The library’s record reads the faint year on the board as 1560 and gives 1567 only in its former-owner field. The volume has no digital facsimile: the National Library’s catalogue record carries no link to a digitised copy, its Manuscriptorium record is a catalogue entry without images, and no copy at Google Books answers to the library’s digitisation identifier. Reproduced in colour by Šolc (2018, figs 1a–c, pp. 194–195 (the boards with ‘T.B. 1560’ and the label ‘Tres. M 47’, the Bayrus title)). Re-checked 25 October 2026: the Manuscriptorium image service answers ‘can’t get list of images’ for the record and the OAI repository does not hold it — there is no digital copy. || The binding's year 1560 rests on readings of the board (Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 94; the library: ‘málo znatelný letopočet 1560’; Šolc's text), not on an image: Šolc's plate does not resolve it at its printed size. Google Books returned no record for NKP:1002596125 on 27 October 2026.

Material: blind-stamped pigskin (alum-tawed), the compiler's reading of Šolc's photograph on 28 October 2026; every printed description says ‘white leather’. Photographs of the boards, the three edges and the three title pages at 600 dpi were requested from the National Library on 28 October 2026 (the reproduction request of 23 October, item 6).

|| 29 October 2026 — the literature pack read whole (39 passages, 24 documents): every author after 1933 derives from Kleinschnitzová (Norlind 1970 p. 339, adding a letter O the board does not carry; Šolc 1999, 2006, 2018, with the Bayrus misdated 1559 in two of the three; Christianson 1967 pp. 200–201 and 2020; Thoren 1990; Pařez 2009), and none adds a mark, a hand, a note or an argument. Kleinschnitzová herself (pp. 76–78) counts the twenty-three Clementinum volumes with the note of 1642 and lets this one ‘verirrt sich’ — stray — into the professed house, which is the conclusion restated as a route. The library’s former-owner field gives Tycho and the professed house the year 1567, unexplained beside its own binding note ‘málo znatelný letopočet 1560’. No source asks whether another T. B. owned a Basel 1560 imprint bound in 1560. Ownership C until the boards, edges, title pages and pastedowns are read on the photographs requested on 28 October 2026.

Sources

Notes
A cost note on the first leaf of the Sacrobosco manuscript Sign. VII E 29, which was once bound before the Gauricus of Sign. 14 F 16, is headed ‘Andreas Schöner’ and lists ‘Henricus Glareanus constat 21 ₰’, then the Gauricus and Montulmo, the Albubater, the Cardanus and the binder’s fee (reproduced by Studnička 1901, Bericht, p. 20); the binder's instruction on the last leaf of this volume names the Gauricus with Montulmo and the Albubater. Walde suggested in 1938 that the Glareanus, bought by Vedel in August 1564, may have come to Tycho in exchange for the Sammelband of 1563 now at Uppsala. The library’s records of the three adligata (docs 000082484–000082486, read 20 October 2026): Apianus, Cosmographia, ed. Gemma Frisius, Antwerp: Gregorius Bontius, 1545, inscribed on the title ‘Cubiculi Mathematici Pragae ad S. Clementem A[nn]o 1719’, with Joannes Walthrinus as an earlier owner; Theodosius, De sphaericis, ed. Vögelin, Vienna: Singriener, 1529, with the Charles College ex-libris ‘Col. Caroli IV Mathema. n° 30’; Stöffler, Cosmographicae aliquot descriptiones, ed. Dryander, Marburg: Cervicornus, 1537, inscribed ‘Dom[us] Professae Soc. Jesv ad S. Nicol. Pragae. Catalogo inscriptus 1733’. Each adligatum thus carries a later Prague provenance of its own, which indicates that the composite was assembled in the Clementinum after 1733 (an inference from the inscriptions; the records themselves say only that the three are bound with the Glareanus). Reproduced in colour by Šolc (2018, fig. 2, p. 196 (the Glareanus title with Vedel's note of 1564 and the Chomutov inscription of 1671)). || The endpapers facing the title (canvases 4 and 3) carry offsets of the 1671 Chomutov inscription — mirror-reversed on canvas 4, a faint ghost on canvas 3 — not a second inscription. The June census positives re-read on 27 October 2026 are all manuscript or possible (38 + 2): a red-ink glossator keyed to Euclid, Ptolemy and the sphere, with coordinates over the place-names, many notes struck through in red; a second black-brown hand on p. 50. No source held attributes these glosses.

Formerly XXXI H 26. Found by Šolc (2002) beyond Kleinschnitzová’s list and identified by Tycho’s handwritten initials. The library’s record describes the lead work as the Venice 1502 print of Vorrilong on the Sentences, 308 leaves, 8°, in a codex-form volume, carries a digitised facsimile of 808 images and names no former owner. || The volume is a Sammelband of manuscript and print (facsimile, re-read 27 October 2026): a 15th-century gothic-cursive scholastic treatise (pp. 3–95), the Vorrilong of 1502 (pp. 97–709; densely annotated above and below the title and on its verso; reader's marginalia elsewhere only on p. 463, on the printed side-note on anger in Christ, in a 16th-century gothic/German cursive), and a manuscript summary of Sentences III–IV (pp. 716–806; three leaves imaged twice — 754=764, 758=768, 760=770 — and the leaf order disturbed). Census base: not in the June census; of 254 stage-1 prefilter hits the re-read found 118 manuscript (most the manuscripts' own text), 6 possible, 130 printed only. No source and no re-reader claims a Tycho-period hand; no 1642 line is recorded or seen. The surrogate is in the per-machine cache on the office PC.

Sources
Kleinschnitzová 1933; Studnička 1901 (Bericht); TBOO; Šíma & Valeška 2002; Norlind 1970; Prusík 1901; Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021; Šolc 2002
Notes
Kleinschnitzová no. 2. Manuscript: six folio leaves, the third item of a volume of manuscripts which, according to Studnička, was made up when the Jesuit library was put in order in 1642, the lower and right margins folded in to fit the boards; headed in red ‘Cap. IIII. Quare his disciplinis prae ceteris prima et indubitata sit concludendi ratio’, with sections De puncto, De linea recta, De angulo and De figuris. Found by the custos Josef Truhlář and published by Studnička as Tycho’s autograph, the first page in facsimile in 1901 (Bericht, pp. 51–53) and the whole in 1903 as Brevissimum planimetriae compendium; Kleinschnitzová listed it as an autograph in 1933. Dreyer rejected the hand and the ownership alike — ‘manus non est Tychonis … neque ullum adest indicium, quod in hujus potestate libellum umquam fuisse ostendat’ — and reported from J. L. Heiberg that the text is taken from Proclus’s commentary on the first book of Euclid (Basel 1533) (Opera omnia I, p. 317). Šíma and Valeška (2002) assign the hand to a professional writer. Prusík listed the fragment in 1901 as the third manuscript, ‘eine mathematische Schrift ohne besonderen Titel’, beginning ‘Cap. IIII’, the binding without special character, under the shelfmark MS XII A XII (p. 198), the composite from which Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 83) reports it taken out and bound alone. The manuscript has not been digitised. || Truhlář's printed catalogue (retro-converted in Manuscriptorium, fetched 27 October 2026) places the six leaves at ff. 225–230 of the composite XII A 12 ('Fragmentum hoc manu scriptum nunc separatim asservatur sub sign. XII. A. 28.') and enters XII A 28 itself as 'manu Tychonis Brahaei propria exaratum', saec. XVI/XVII, ff. 6, 30 × 21 cm; Prusík (1901) still found it in XII A 12, so the separation falls between 1901 and 1905–06. Dreyer adds that the text is excerpted from Proclus's commentary on Euclid I (Basel 1533), interrupted by notes and drawings of sundials (Opera omnia I, p. 317).

45 images examined; 25 images with handwriting flagged (an automated survey of the facsimile; no hand attributed). Kinds: diagrams and tables (images 9, 11, 19, 21); corrections (images 6, 9, 11); marginal notes (images 6, 19, 21); ownership inscriptions (images 4); stamps or seals (images 4).

Kleinschnitzová no.1; Manuscript. A parchment manuscript in its original binding with the initials T. B. O. and the year 1582 (Norlind 1970, p. 340); Studnička counts it, in brown leather with the initials, to the second period of the bindings (Bericht, 1901, p. 7). He published the tables as Tycho's autograph and held them copied from Regiomontanus's sine tables of 1541 in the Archimedes volume, Sign. 5 C 31 (Bericht, p. 47); Norlind describes them as a copy and reworking of Copernicus's ‘Canon semissium subtensarum rectarum linearum in circulo’. Šíma and Valeška (2002) assign the tables to a professional writer; of the short inscriptions on the end leaves they conclude that they can neither prove them Tycho's nor exclude him. Prusík described the manuscript in 1901 as MS VI E IX: eighteen strong parchment leaves, the brown binding of the middle period full of ornament with ‘T. B. O.’ at the top of the upper board, the title ‘Tabulae sinuum 1582’, no distich on the title but at the lower right, added later in Tycho's hand, the words ‘οἰστέον καὶ ἐλπιστέον’; written for his own use and much worn; Kukula added Studnička's conjecture that the words were set down at the parting from the library on leaving Denmark. || The census re-read of 27 October 2026 counts 24 'manuscript' pages, but in this volume that includes the tables themselves; the added marks are the front-pastedown press-marks (canvas 2: 'Tres. M 1', the struck-through 'TB / [L]I cim. 52.', 'Cim D 82', the label 'E. VI. 9.'), the 1642 inscription and Greek line on f. 1r, 'Numerorum scientia' on f. Iv, the 'Tres. M 1' label on the back board and a short pen stroke above the table on canvas 29. The tables are seven-figure sines in 1' steps (sin 1° = 0174524 on canvas 5; sin 60° = 8660254 on canvas 29) with the differences written between the columns in the same hand.

Chain of custody
  1. Tycho’s heirs, Prague from 1601
    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970
  2. route unknown
    No owner is recorded between the heirs and the Chomutov college’s catalogue entry. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 76) supposed that the college came by Tycho’s books in a way similar to the Clementinum’s gift; Císařová Smítková, Paličková and Vackářová (2021, p. 30) suppose Clementinum duplicates passed on under Joannes Jüngling, who kept the Clementinum’s mathematical library in 1749 and was prefect of the Chomutov library in 1765–1766; the college’s dated catalogue entries on Tycho’s volumes are of 1645 to 1675. — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021
  3. Jesuit college, Chomutov (Komotau) until 1773
    As the first piece of the Sammelband 14 F 16, a Chomutov volume by the college’s signature on its spine (Kleinschnitzová 1933, nos. 24 and 37, p. 93). — Kleinschnitzová 1933
  4. The Clementinum library after the suppression of the Society: the public University Library, since 1990 the National Library of the Czech Republic, Prague from after 1773
    Brought to the Clementinum with the library of the dissolved Chomutov college after 1773; Kleinschnitzová counted nineteen volumes of that provenance in 1933 (p. 81). The manuscript was taken out of 14 F 16 and bound alone at a revision of the manuscripts before 1901 (Prusík 1901, pp. 198–199; Studnička 1901, p. 21). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Prusík 1901; Studnička 1901 (Bericht)

Notes
This Sacrobosco-commentary manuscript was separated from Sign. 14 F 16 before 1901, at an earlier revision of the manuscripts (Prusík 1901, pp. 198–199; Studnička 1901, p. 21; Kukula 1906–07, p. 22), and shelved as VII E 29, while the three printed constituents (Gauricus A 20, Albubater A 1, Cardano A 11) remain in 14 F 16; Prandtl’s four-part Band IV is Studnička’s reconstruction of the volume’s original make-up. The first leaf (f. 1r) carries a cost note headed ‘Andreas Schöner’: ‘Henricus Glareanus constat 21 d. / L. Gauricus & Jo: De monte ulmo constat 24 d. / Albubater 42 d. / Cardanus 42 d. / 36 d. Ligatori’, summed to 165 pfennigs, that is 5 lb 15 d. at thirty pfennigs to the pound; beside it a large monogram in ink, read as T B, with an astronomical diagram and pen trials of the planetary signs below; at the foot, in a later library hand, ‘Antea praeligatum Tractatui Lucae Gaurici Norimbergae a. 1540 edito, sign. 14. F. 16.’ On the verso: ‘Nota. Tribus rebus res comprobantur. I Ratione. II Autoritate. III Experientia’, and under it, in a larger hand, the conclusion drawn for astrology (‘Ergo etiam astrologia vera erit …’). Studnička reproduced the cost note and the upper note of the verso in 1901 as Tycho’s (Bericht, p. 20): the custos Josef Truhlář had concluded from the cost note that the works it lists must be in the library and found them in the Sammelband Sign. 14 F 16, where the removal of the manuscript had left a gap (p. 21). The hands have not been compared with Tycho’s or with Schöner’s. Prusík listed the manuscript in 1901 as the fourth, ‘Sphaera Johannis de Sacrobusto in compendium digesta, Anno salutis nostrae MDXXXIX’, formerly bound in the printed volume 14 F 16 and newly bound as MS VII E XXIX. || The front pastedown (canvas 2) carries 'Tres. M. 24.', the accession note 'A. B. 5/1900', 'T B. 24.' in blue crayon over an erased 6, and 'ms. VII. E. 29.' — the new binding entered in 1900 (inference from the accession note), consistent with the separation from 14 F 16 before 1901. The facsimile (73 canvases, CC BY-NC-SA) is complete, covers and spine included; its leaf labels (modern endleaf = 'Ir', old flyleaf = 'IIr') differ from the record's foliation (old flyleaf = f. Ir).

Notes
Walde showed in 1938 that the manuscript belonged to Johannes Eriksen of Hamburg, tutor to Tycho’s sons at Wittenberg in February 1598 and Tycho’s amanuensis at Prague in 1601: it carries the inscription, as Curtze transcribed it, ‘Dominus M. Christiernus Severinus Longomontanus reliquit amico suo Iohanni Ericksen [a Greek word] Benachia Bohemorum 18. Julii discedens A° 1600’ — Longomontanus’s parting gift at Benátky. Walde left open the assumption that it then passed to Tycho and with his papers to Vienna, observing that Eriksen’s other books and manuscripts went into Queen Christina’s library with the Prague booty (a Pitiscus of 1600 bought at Prague on 14 August 1601, now at Hanover; two chemical manuscripts at Leiden from Vossius’s share; a Lull of 1593 at Västerås with the Christina shelfmark), and supposed that his literary property came into Rudolf II’s hands. The manuscript is a sixteenth-century Latin Sammelhandschrift of 45 leaves containing the Commentariolus of Copernicus and the Responsio ad Capnurianam apologiam of Longomontanus, Tycho’s chief assistant. The Austrian National Library’s description records a nineteenth-century half-parchment rebinding and no former owner, and does not mention Brahe; Norlind’s attribution of the manuscript to Tycho’s library is not corroborated by the catalogue, and the link to Tycho rests on the Longomontanus text and the circle of Uraniborg. The library has published a full digitisation of the manuscript. || Chapter 3 state sheet, 27 October 2026: the National Library's facsimile has a IIIF v3 manifest (api.onb.ac.at/iiif/presentation/v3/manifest/DTL_2808861) of 100 canvases at 2257 × 2881 px, covers included; the cover-to-cover reading for a mark of ownership is the one test that can be made from home and is in progress.

Notes
The 1543 Nuremberg first edition, distinct from the Clementinum Wittich copy (Sign. 14 B 16, the 1566 Basel edition). Gingerich traces its passage (Census, pp. 105–108): from Wittich to his sister, and to Tycho, who ‘presumably he got it in October 1600 through the help of Jacob Monaw’; thence, by conjecture, to Rudolf II; taken in the Swedish plunder of the west bank of Prague under Königsmarck in July 1648; to Queen Christina, and with her to Rome in 1655; to Pope Alexander VIII (Pietro Ottoboni) in 1690; and so to the Vatican Library, the spine bearing the papal arms of Pius IX. Richly annotated by Wittich on four preliminary pages and on thirty pages after f. 196; the observation notes include a conjunction of Venus and Regulus on 16 September 1574 and of Jupiter and Fomalhaut on 8 November 1572, and ff. 197v–211v carry the proto-Tychonic geo-heliocentric diagrams dated 27 January to 17 February 1578 (Gingerich, ‘Vatican 1’). Digitised in full on the Vatican Library’s digital site as Ott. lat. 1902, with Wittich’s manuscript notes bound in at the end. || Chapter 3 state sheet, 27 October 2026: the DigiVatLib manifest (digi.vatlib.it/iiif/MSS_Ott.lat.1902/manifest.json) has 450 canvases at 1744–1962 × 2614–2618 px including the covers — canvas 1 is the front board of Pius IX's red-brown morocco with a gilt chain roll, canvas 3 a blank flyleaf; every image carries the library's 'ALL RIGHTS RESERVED' watermark.

B · identified by Rauch 1914, pp. 223–224 (the first publication of the entry); Prandtl 1932, Verzeichnis B, Band VI; the Forschungsbibliothek Gotha copy record (K10plus, revised 2024). Ownership doubted by Norlind 1970, pp. 337–338
Marks securing the identification
Tycho's autograph entry on the blank leaf after the pasted-in leaf of Apianus's later arms: Psalm 19:1, a distich of his own ('Cui negat esse Deum, coelos et sidera spectet / Esse etenim monstrat stella vel una Deum') and the subscription 'Tycho Brahe scripsi Anno 1599 Junij die 14, quo Vitebergâ discessi Pragam a Caesare vocatus'. A dated motto of the album kind, not an ownership mark; no owner's name on the title, no annotation in the text

rebound in plain brown calf at Gotha in 1967, after the volume was taken apart for the Edition Leipzig facsimile; the original leather was plain, with traces of ties

Chain of custody
  1. Friedrich Wilhelm I, Duke of Saxe-Weimar (1562–1602), Administrator of Electoral Saxony 1599–1602
    Tycho’s inscription of 14 June 1599, the day he left Wittenberg for Prague; the Gotha copy record names the Duke as the copy’s recipient and Tycho as donor. Norlind (1970, pp. 337–338) doubted that the book had been Tycho’s own; Rauch (1914) states instead that it came to Gotha from Munich. — Forschungsbibliothek Gotha, copy record (K10plus); Prandtl 1932; Rauch 1914; Norlind 1970
  2. The castle library at Altenburg 1602–1672
    Dissolved into the ducal library at Gotha in 1672 (the Gotha copy record). — Forschungsbibliothek Gotha, copy record (K10plus)
  3. Herzogliche Bibliothek Gotha, now the Forschungsbibliothek Gotha, Math gr2° 00038/02 from 1672
    The catalogue of Duke Friedrich III’s private library; the stamp and initial of Duke Ernst II (the Gotha copy record). — Forschungsbibliothek Gotha, copy record (K10plus)

Notes
What the volume shows. The only trace of Tycho is one inscription, on the recto of the blank leaf that follows the pasted-in leaf of Apianus’s later arms (image 123 of the Jena facsimile): Psalm 19:1 (‘Coeli enarrant gloriam Dei et opera manuum eius annunciat firmamentum’), a distich whose hexameter Tycho had used in his Copenhagen oration of 1574 (‘Cui negat esse Deum, coelos et sidera spectet’, here with the pentameter ‘Esse etenim monstrat stella vel una Deum’), and the subscription ‘Tycho Brahe scripsi Anno 1599 Junij die 14, quo Vitebergâ discessi Pragam a Caesare vocatus’ — written on the day he left Wittenberg for Prague. The hand is that of his Wittenberg album entries of 1598–99, and a separate album leaf of the same day carries the same departure formula. The title page bears no owner’s name, the text no annotation, and the binding is a Gotha rebinding of 1967, made after the volume had been taken apart for the Edition Leipzig facsimile; the restoration report pasted inside the lower board records that the original leather was plain. The copy also carries, in a sixteenth-century hand close to the Apian family, captions on the old and the new arms and red crossings through the old shield on the title — the apparatus of a copy completed after Apianus’s ennoblement of 1541. What it proves, and what it does not. The inscription proves that Tycho held the book on 14 June 1599 and wrote in it. It is a dated motto entry of the album-amicorum kind (‘scripsi’, not ‘emi’ or ‘possidet’), not an ownership mark, and nothing else in the volume connects it to his library. Prandtl listed the volume among Tycho’s books on the strength of the entry alone. Norlind thought it more likely the book of someone else, perhaps of Duke Friedrich Wilhelm of Saxe-Weimar, Administrator of Electoral Saxony and Tycho’s patron at Dresden in November 1598, in whose book Tycho would have written as in an album. The Gotha library records the volume as Tycho’s gift to the duke and the duke as its recipient; the duke’s other Tychoniana — the Mechanica Memb. I 110 and the star catalogue Chart. A 984, both with dedications to him — are in the same library, and the library of his line at Altenburg came to Gotha in 1672. On either reading the volume is a book that passed through Tycho’s hands, not one shown to have stood on his shelves; hence grade B. Rauch, who first published the entry in 1914 on information from the Gotha librarian Rudolf Ehwald, wrote that the book had come to Gotha from Munich; nothing later explains the remark. Gingerich, who examined the copy for the facsimile, reports the entry as ‘written in what is now the Gotha copy’. Catalogued by the Forschungsbibliothek Gotha at Math gr2° 00038/02; the copy record transcribes the inscription and names the duke as recipient. Digitised by the Forschungsbibliothek Gotha; the page-by-page facsimile is served in the ThULB Jena viewer (URN urn:nbn:de:urmel-ufb-191132). || Chapter 3 state sheet, 27 October 2026: the ThULB facsimile has a IIIF Presentation manifest (dhb.thulb.uni-jena.de/api/iiif/presentation/v2/ufb_derivate_00019113/manifest) and a level-2 Image API; image 123 is 4955 × 7256 px native — the sharpest reproduction of any Tycho writing among the surviving volumes' facsimiles — and its text was read in full on the image: DAVID REX PSAL. XIX / Cœli enarrant Gloriam DEI / et opera manuûm eiûs / annûnciat Firmamentûm. / Qui negat esse DEVM cælos et sidera spectet / Esse etenim monstrat Stella vel una DEVM. / Tycho Brahe / scripsj / Anno 1599 / Jûnij die 14 / quo Vitebergâ / discessj / Pragam / a CÆSARE vocatûs. (with a pen flourish). The entry served the same day as the comparator for the 14 J 176 purchase note of June 1601.

vol. 57

1957:0030 — Helsingør, Maritime Museum

Avol-s-band-ii
Earlier catalogues
Prandtl, Verz. B, Band II
Identification
A · identified by Prandtl, Die Bibliothek des Tycho Brahe (Verzeichnis B); the museum's record and photographs (the binding stamps, the inscriptions leaf by leaf, the purchase note, the added positions on fol. 53 of the Apianus); examined and photographed at the museum on 20 October 2026 (the stamps TVCHO BRADE and ANNO 1561, the fly-title's inscriptions and purchase note on both sides of the leaf, the fol. 53 entries, the museum's accession note)
Marks securing the identification

front board: TVCHO BRADE, rear board: ANNO 1561 (stamped, originally gilt); fly-title: ‘tico brade ven:’ (struck through), ‘Tycho Brade’ and further ownership inscriptions (leaf half torn, repaired); fly-title verso: ‘Sum Thÿchonis Brade’ [I am Tycho Brahe's] (struck through), ‘Eptg [emptus] thalero & 4 Groshj’ [bought for a thaler and 4 groschen], beneath it an astronomical note, partly lost; a note in ink on the front pastedown; fol. 53r–v of the Apianus: four places with their positions in Tycho's hand; on the spine the remnant of a label with a library shelfmark 204; Latin plant names at the head of a run of recto pages in a hand other than Tycho's, and small plant remains between leaves (Magasin 1987, p. 31; Björklund 1992, p. 26; confirmed 20 October 2026); at the head of the front pastedown the pencil figure ‘+125’, Maggs's price of 1933, and a second figure (the museum's photograph).

Thykier (1985 inspection; report of 13 January 2003) reads the front of the fly-title (his ‘forperm’) as the autograph ‘Tyge Brahe’ struck through and ‘tico brahe ven’ struck through (‘en lidt barnlig skrift’ [a somewhat childish hand]), and in another hand ‘Sum Paul…’, the rest lost on the torn-off part; on its back, under a struck line where ‘Brade’ can be glimpsed, the price ‘… 4 taliro & 4 Gross.’; short astronomical notes in Tycho's hand inside the binding and on the back of the leaf, and one in the margin of the preface's tenth (unpaginated) page; Latin plant names at the head of 36 unpaginated pages in a hand other than Tycho's, plant remains in the gutter of 26 of them (microscoped by Jette Baagøe, re-housed in annotated envelopes of acid-free silk paper), further remains between pages without names, one plant name unattested before c. 1623 (Peter Wagner and Baagøe).

Examined and photographed at the museum on 20 October 2026. Fly-title recto: ‘tico brade ven:’ in a thin early hand, struck through once in the same ink; beside it a name obliterated under heavy black strokes (Thykier: ‘Tyge Brahe’), ringed in pencil; to the right, in a firmer hand with a flourish, ‘Sum Pauli’ [I am Paul's], complete to its last letter, what followed lost with the torn-away part; above it a smudged short word in another ink, and at the head, right, a short word in a darker ink, both unread; at the head, left, pencil ‘Acc. 1986/116’. Fly-title verso: ‘Sum Thÿchonis Brade’ under a heavy bar, ‘Sum’ and ‘Brade’ legible beside it; below it the purchase note ‘Eptg thaliro & 4 Grossj’ [bought for a thaler and 4 groschen]; beneath that, intact, a two-branch memorandum in bracket form — ‘Decl: Merid: … obliqua {Adde / Subtr.} diff. asc. ab Ascensione Recta — Septen: … obliqua {Subtr. / Adde} diff. Asc. ab Asc. R.’, ‘obliqua’ struck and ‘Recta’ written above it — a rule for passing from right to oblique ascension by the sign of the declination. Front pastedown: an ink note in the same early hand (‘Ascens: decl: Merid: … ex Asc: Recta / Septm: Sub S … hoc modo’, a companion rule); a pencil collation in German (‘… 70 (von 1–74) … 31–34 … 1 Doppelbl. …’, the trace of the Munich trade); pencil ‘1986/116’. Spine: a paper slip in the second compartment with ‘20’ and a damaged third figure consistent with 4, the figures written by hand in ink; nothing else lettered, no label surviving at the tail. Rear flyleaf: a faint ‘N 36’ at the head and a small blind-stamped cartouche near the gutter, both unread. Rear pastedown: in ballpoint ‘Gave jan. 1957 fra civiling. Oskar Ekman’ [gift, January 1957, from the engineer Oskar Ekman], the stamp HANDELS- OG SØFARTSMUSEET PÅ KRONBORG HELSINGØR – DANMARK [the Trade and Maritime Museum at Kronborg, Helsingør, Denmark], and ‘30:57’ in blue. Box: brown cloth clamshell, its gilt spine label lettered in English — JOHANN DE MONTEREGIO TABULAE DIRECTIONUM 1550 BOUND WITH PETRUS APPIANUS COSMOGRAPHIA 1553. TYCHO BRAHE'S COPY WITH AUTOGRAPH OWNERSHIP NOTES, ETC. — with ‘30:57’ written on it.

Reader's marks in the Regiomontanus: a grey marginal note in an early hand on the Octavum problema page (‘pro g. m. / 60 / sec. / 15 / tert. / differentia’ — Thykier's note on the tenth page of the preface); tallies ij iij iiij beside ‘Ille autem numerus polaris’; a red-brown stepped line drawn through the Tabula declinationum; a large pen flourish at the head of the Tabula ascensionum rectarum. In the Apianus: ‘Octava sphaera’ written at the ring of the Schema praemissae divisionis, ‘Wittenberga’ underlined in the German place table; on fol. 53r ‘Elzingborgum 35 46. 57 0’ (a superscript c above the name) and ‘Lunda 36 30 57 23’, on fol. 53v ‘Vesbÿ Gotlandiæ 47 5. 59 50’ and the fourth place, its letters R-?-n-s-f-a-l-?-h-?, ‘46 35 60 15’, all four in one ink and ductus. The plant names stand at the head of the preface leaves (Pulmonaria, Ranunculus aquaticus, Hedera arborescens …) in a later hand, and the envelopes of plant remains lie at their openings; read letter by letter from the frames on 21 October 2026: the purchase note is ‘Eptꝰ thaliro & 4 Groſs.’ — emptus thalero et 4 grossis — the sign after ‘Ept’ being the -us abbreviation, not a g; the pastedown rule reads in full ‘Aſcens. decl {Merid. [Adde, blotted out by the writer] / Septen. Sub} ex Aſc. Recta / in deſcenſionibꝫ contrario modo’, the same rule as the verso's bracket memorandum, whose surviving case labels are ‘…rom:’ and ‘…nes’; above the rule a darker ‘Angl. 5.’, unexplained; the smudged word above ‘Sum Paüli’ reads ‘Brÿſſe’ or ‘Chrÿſſe’ and stands inside a wet-wiped erasure of an earlier inscription, the head-right word ‘to bra[h/n][e/o]’; the heavy black strokes through the recto name and through the verso's ‘Sum Thÿchonis Brade’ are one ink and one campaign, a later owner's cancellation of both Brahe names, while the thin stroke through ‘tico brade ven:’ is earlier and different; the herbarium hand also wrote ‘Lamiꝫ’, ‘Liſimachia flore luteo’ and ‘Hÿacinthꝰ’; on fol. 53 ‘Lůnda lůndt’ and ‘Veſbÿ Gotlandiæ’ carry the u-mark and the diaeresis, and the fourth place is the museum's ‘Rumefalche’ (the tall letter is an f with a cross-bar), identified on 21 October 2026 as Schöner's — Luculentissima quaedam terrae totius descriptio (Nuremberg 1515), fo. 34r, ‘Gotlandiae insu. civita.: Bespue 47.5.59.50. Rumefalche 46.35.60.15.’ — a Clavus-derived pseudo-toponym of Gotland from the Ulm Ptolemy of 1486, so that both added lines on fol. 53v are copied, name and figures, from Schöner or from his source; a pencil ‘choo’ on the rear pastedown

Binding
Period 1 (student bindings, 1560–1567)
Contents
  1. Apianus, Petrus, Cosmographia (per Gemma Frisium) (1553) (no. 15)
  2. Regiomontanus, Johannes, Joannis de Monte Regio tabulae directionum profectionumque; ejusdem Regiomontani tabula sinuum (1550) (no. 198)
Chain of custody
  1. route unknown
    The route out of Tycho's hands is undocumented. The fly-title (Thykier's ‘forperm’) carries two struck ownership lines — ‘tico brade ven:’ on the recto and ‘Sum Thÿchonis Brade’ [I am Tycho Brahe's] on the verso, as the museum reads them (Thykier 2003 read the recto's as ‘Tyge Brahe’ and ‘tico brahe ven’) — which may mark a transfer in his lifetime or a later owner's cancellation. A third inscription in a firmer hand, ‘Sum Pauli’ [I am Paul's], is the only name of a later owner the volume yields: Thykier read it as ‘Sum Paul…’ with the rest lost on the torn-off part of the leaf, but the examination of 20 October 2026 shows it complete to its last letter, so the owner's first name is all the leaf ever carried of him. The book was used as a herbarium by a hand other than Tycho's, one of whose plant names is unattested before c. 1623 (Thykier 2003, after Wagner and Baagøe), so it was in a plant-collector's hands after Tycho's death. It stands in no Prague catalogue and its first title carries none of the Jesuit, Chomutov or Crusius marks of the Bohemian roads. The spine label, a paper slip with the figures ‘20[4]’ written in ink, records a library between Tycho and the Munich trade that no source names (Thykier: ‘formodentlig katalognummeret i Tychos eller et senere bibliotek’ [presumably the catalogue number in Tycho's or a later library]; the dossier of 20 October 2026); the rear flyleaf adds a faint ‘N 36’ at the head and a small blind-stamped cartouche near its gutter — a second earlier number and a dealer's or restorer's mark, both unread (examined 20 October 2026). — Thykier 2003; Museernes Samlinger (M/S Museet for Søfart), the object record 1957:0030; Helsingør examination 2026
  2. Antiquariat Weiss & Co., Munich by 1932
    Prandtl 1932, the captions of his plates (pp. 2–3: ‘Seinerzeit im Besitze des Antiquariats Weiss & Co., München’ [at the time in the possession of the antiquarian firm Weiss & Co., Munich]) and p. 3 (‘kürzlich von München aus nach Amerika verkauft’ [recently sold from Munich to America] — wrong about the first step, see the next station); the Verzeichnis B entry for Band II names no location. The volume is in none of the firm's four digitised catalogues (1926–1930). — Prandtl 1932, pp. 292–293 (Sonderdruck pp. 2–3)
  3. Maggs Bros., London 1933–1938
    Catalogue 582 (1933), item 155, p. 92, £125, with every copy-specific identifier (the stamps, the half-torn fly-leaf, the purchase note, the Helsingborg note) and Prandtl cited for ‘our volume’; Catalogue 600 (1934), item 260, £125; Catalogue 666 (1938), item 451, p. 166, still £125, the entry reprinting Catalogue 600's text. The pencil ‘+125’ at the head of the front pastedown is this price. The firm's archive (British Library Add MS 89311) would name the seller. — Maggs 582 (1933), p. 92, item 155; Maggs 600 (1934), p. 208, item 260; Maggs 666 (1938), p. 166, item 451; New York Times Book Review, 28 May 1933, the issue (lending copy)
  4. Herbert Reichner, New York c. 1939–c. 1940
    Catalogue 1 ([1939]), item 72, probably $850 — Reichner was Prandtl's publisher in Vienna and emigrated to New York in 1938–39; the volume is in none of his Catalogues 2–9 (1940–48). — Reichner, Catalogue 1 ([1939]), the catalogue record (search-only; ‘Brade’ matches one page)
  5. route unknown from c. 1940
    The buyer from Reichner is not recorded; no American auction appearance 1930–58 (American Book Prices Current); Rare Book Hub has no record. Mortensen (1955, p. 25) knew of no such volume in Denmark, which bounds nothing: the volume was then in private hands, and the Tycho literature took no notice of the museum's report of 1957 until Norlind 1970. The one physical trace of the interval is the volume's box: a brown cloth clamshell box with a gilt spine label lettered in English (‘Tycho Brahe's copy with autograph ownership notes, etc.’), made in the English-speaking trade or for the American owner (examined 20 October 2026). — Mortensen 1955, p. 25; Helsingør examination 2026
  6. Oscar Ekman, engineer, and Lia Ekman, Copenhagen until 1957
    The museum's report of its acquisitions of 1956–57 (Klem, Årbog 1957, p. 8; Thykier 2003 dates the gift to January 1957 and names Oskar Ekman alone): ‘en gave fra fru Lia Ekman og afdøde ægtefælle, civilingeniør Oscar Ekman’ [a gift from Mrs Lia Ekman and her late husband, the engineer Oscar Ekman]. Oscar Ekman (b. Copenhagen 13 October 1885, owner of Nordisk Elektricitets Selskab from 1913, d. 16 September 1956) had been a life member of the museum's friends' society since 1944–45; Lia Ekman (née Pouplier, b. Hamburg 1894, d. 1965) remained one to her death. Their source for the volume is not recorded; at the sale of their library (Bruun Rasmussen 186, November 1965) it was shown as a withdrawn show-piece, as Erik Dal reported in Bogvennen 1966. The museum's accession note on the rear pastedown, ‘Gave jan. 1957 fra civiling. Oskar Ekman’ [gift, January 1957, from the engineer Oskar Ekman] (read 20 October 2026), enters the gift in January 1957 under Oscar's name, four months after his death: a gift in the dead man's name, made by his widow — which is what Klem's wording, Thykier's and Dal's ‘testamentarisk bortgivet’ [given away by bequest] each describe. The sale catalogue itself (Bruun Rasmussen 186, p. 111, lot 497, read 29 October 2026) lists the volume under ‘En Bog fra Tycho Brahe's Bibliotek’ for completeness only — ‘This copy will not be sold as it was given to the “Handels- og Søfartsmuseet” at Kronborg according to the last will of ingeniør Ekman’; the Danish text ‘foræret … af ingeniør Ekman og kan beses der i en af udstillingsmontrerne’ — so the gift was a bequest under Oscar's will, executed by his widow in January 1957, and the volume stood in a showcase at Kronborg in November 1965. — Handels- og Søfartsmuseet, Årbog 1957, p. 8; Kraks Blå Bog 1937, p. 276, s.v. Ekman; Bogvennen 1966, pp. 200–207, the passage on the Tycho volume; Thykier 2003; Helsingør examination 2026; Bruun Rasmussen 186 (1965)
  7. M/S Museet for Søfart (Handels- og Søfartsmuseet på Kronborg), Helsingør, inventory 1957:0030 from 1957
    The Ekmans' gift of 1956–57 (Årbog 1957; the museum's record); restored 1957 by Birgitte Dall. Deposited at the Royal Library's Håndskriftafdeling in 1986 as Acc. 1986/116 (the Kronik of 1987; the department's newsletter of November 2001), lent from there to the Ole Rømer Museum's exhibition ‘Tycho Brahes mange ansigter’ [Tycho Brahe's many faces], 25 October – 31 December 2001; in the museum's own keeping again, confirmed 13 October 2026, the date of return unrecorded. Examined and photographed at the museum on 20 October 2026: the Kronborg stamp and ‘30:57’ on the rear pastedown, ‘Acc. 1986/116’ in pencil on the fly-title and the pastedown and on the slip in the box, the plant envelopes in place, the box lettered in English. — Handels- og Søfartsmuseet, Årbog 1957, p. 8; Museernes Samlinger (M/S Museet for Søfart), the object record 1957:0030; Magasin 1987, pp. 31–33; Royal Library, Håndskriftafdelingen, Aktuelt (November 2001), ‘Udstillinger’, November 2001; Björklund 1992; Museet for Søfart 2026; Thykier 2003; Helsingør examination 2026
