Prandtl 1932; Norlind 1970; Handels- og Søfartsmuseet, Årbog 1957; Museernes Samlinger (M/S Museet for Søfart); Björklund 1992; Grinder-Hansen 2006; Gingerich 2002; Bogvennen 1966; Magasin 1987; Museet for Søfart 2026; Maggs 582 (1933); Maggs 600 (1934); Maggs 666 (1938); Reichner, Catalogue 1 ([1939]); Royal Library, Håndskriftafdelingen, Aktuelt (November 2001); Kraks Blå Bog 1937; New York Times Book Review, 28 May 1933; Christianson 1967; Mortensen 1955; Thykier 2003; Helsingør examination 2026; Band II transcription and hand comparison 2026; Schöner, Luculentissima … descriptio (1515); Bjørnbo & Petersen, Claudius Clavus (1904); Bruun Rasmussen 186 (1965)
Notes

Prandtl’s Band II, the student binding of 1561: Regiomontanus’s Tabulae directionum (Tübingen, Ulrich Morhart, 1550) bound before Apianus’s Cosmographia in Gemma Frisius’s recension (Paris, Vivant Gaultherot, 1553; the colophon dated 1551). Prandtl recorded it in 1932 at Antiquariat Weiss & Co., Munich, and as sold to America; Gingerich (2002, p. 325) still placed it at an undisclosed location, calling it ‘the 1561 edition’ of the Apianus after the date on the binding. It had in fact returned to Denmark within a generation: the Handels- og Søfartsmuseet på Kronborg reported it among the acquisitions of 1956–57 as the gift of Lia Ekman and her late husband, the engineer Oscar Ekman, and Norlind placed it there in 1970 (pp. 338 and 361).

The museum’s record (Museernes Samlinger, inventory 1957:0030, priref 400004307, revised 16 June 2026) describes the volume leaf by leaf. The Regiomontanus: title, [43] pp. text, [268] pp. tables, a few notes in the head margin. The Apianus: title woodcut, fol. 1–74 with the volvelles, the cordiform world map inserted between fol. 34 and 35, the tables of positions from fol. 37; on fol. 53r–v Tycho has added four places with their figures, which the museum reads ‘Elzingborgum 35 46. 57 0 / Lunda Lundt 36 30 57 23 / Vesby Gotlandiæ 47 5. 59 50 / Rumefalche [?] 46 35 60 15’ — Helsingborg, Lund, Visby, and a fourth place the museum could not read. Quarto; stained, water-stained and wormed. Brown calf, blind-ruled mirror panels on both boards with originally gilt floral stamps, TVCHO BRADE stamped on the front board and ANNO 1561 on the rear, three raised bands, and on the spine the remnant of a label with the library shelfmark 204 — an owner between Tycho and the Munich trade whom no source names. The inscriptions: a note in ink on the front pastedown; on the fly-title, struck through, ‘tico brade ven:’, then ‘Tycho Brade’ and further ownership inscriptions, the leaf half torn and repaired; on its verso ‘Sum Thÿchonis Brade’ [I am Tycho Brahe's], struck through, the purchase note ‘Eptg [emptus] thalero & 4 Groshj’ [bought for a thaler and 4 groschen], and beneath it an astronomical note, partly lost. Prandtl’s ‘Vorsatzblatt’ [endpaper] with the note and the name three times is thus placed: the purchase note is on the verso of the fly-title, not on the pastedown. Kept in a cloth-covered box; restored in 1957 by Birgitte Dall, Copenhagen. The record’s two photographs show the front board, and the volume open in its box at the Regiomontanus title with the fly-title raised, its verso with the purchase note and the astronomical note towards the camera. The record is filed in the museum’s case ‘Deponeringer div:’ (deposits), which agrees with the Royal Library deposit of 1986.

The Danish record of the volume, in order. Klem’s museum report for 1956–57 (Årbog 1957, p. 8) lists it among the year’s acquisitions as ‘en gave fra fru Lia Ekman og afdøde ægtefælle, civilingeniør Oscar Ekman’ [a gift from Mrs Lia Ekman and her late husband, the engineer Oscar Ekman], bought by Tycho ‘i 1561’ for ‘1 Thaler, 4 Groschen’. Erik Dal in Bogvennen (1966, p. 205), reviewing the Ekman sale (Bruun Rasmussen auction 186, 1–4 November 1965), names among the show-pieces withdrawn as bequests ‘en bog fra Tycho Brahes bibliotek (til Kronborg — Rundetaarn bød samtidig meget højt, men forgæves på en lignende hos Sotheby)’ [a book from Tycho Brahe's library (to Kronborg — Rundetaarn at the same time bid very high, but in vain, on a similar one at Sotheby's)]: the volume was still the museum’s in 1965. The Kronik of Magasin fra Det Kongelige Bibliotek (2:1, 1987, p. 31) records its deposit in the Royal Library’s Håndskriftafdeling, the contact arranged by museumsleder Claus Thykier of Ole Rømers Museum, the museum on Kronborg remaining the owner — an earlier witness to the deposit than Björklund 1992. The Kronik prints the front-board stamp as ‘Tycho Brahe’, a normalisation of the museum’s reading TVCHO BRADE; it reports ‘adskillige notater med flere hænder, deriblandt Tycho Brahes’ [several notes in more than one hand, among them Tycho Brahe's], and gives the herbarium use as a suggestion that had not been examined (‘foreslået … endnu ikke kunnet undersøges’ [suggested … not yet possible to examine], p. 33), which Björklund 1992 then states as fact. The Royal Library’s newsletter of November 2001 shows the volume still on deposit (Acc. 1986/116), lent to the Ole Rømer Museum’s exhibition of that autumn, and the Nationalmuseet catalogue of 2006 reproduced it from a Royal Library photograph. The deposit has ended: the museum’s curator, Thorbjørn Thaarup, confirmed in writing on 13 October 2026 that the volume is part of the museum’s collection and is kept at the museum (‘en del af vores samling og opbevares hos os’ [part of our collection and kept with us]); when it returned from the Royal Library is not stated.

The twentieth-century route, established on 20 October 2026: Prandtl’s ‘sold from Munich to America’ was wrong about the first step. Maggs Bros. of London offered the volume in Catalogue 582 (1933), item 155, at £125 — the entry collates both works, gives the stamps, transcribes ‘Sum Tychonis Brade / Epts thaliro & 4 Gross’ [I am Tycho Brahe's / bought for a thaler and 4 groschen], notes the half-torn fly-leaf and the Helsingborg note, and cites Prandtl for ‘our volume’ — again in Catalogue 600 (1934), item 260, and still in Catalogue 666 (1938), item 451, p. 166, always at £125, the figure pencilled on the front pastedown; the New York Times reviewed the 1933 catalogue on 28 May 1933. It reached New York only with Herbert Reichner’s first catalogue ([1939], item 72, probably $850) and is in none of his later ones. Between about 1940 and 1956 nothing is known.

Three published readings do not hold. The Kronik’s argument of 1987 that the price in thaler and groschen is Saxon coin and that the Leipzig matriculation register enters Tycho under 16 October 1561 fails on both points: the Copenhagen Ptolemy of 1560 is itself priced in Joachimsthaler, and 16 October is the winter-semester heading, the rector entering the term’s students at its end (Norlind 1970, p. 16); the binding’s ‘Anno 1561’ and every other witness put the purchase in Copenhagen. The Helsingborg and Lund figures on fol. 53r are the book’s own printed values from the Scania table on fol. 41v, transcribed beside the Zealand–Scania island entry; Visby and the fourth place stand beside the printed Gotland entry on fol. 53v. Christianson 1967 (Isis 58, p. 201), citing Prandtl, puts the ‘Anno 1561’ stamp on the spine — a slip; it is on the rear board. The provenance is set out in the deep-research dossier of 20 October 2026.

Claus Thykier’s report of 13 January 2003 (Ole Rømer Museet; absorbed 20 October 2026) is the examiner’s own account: he inspected the volume at the museum’s library in 1985, arranged its deposit at the Royal Library in 1986 (acc. 1986/116), and records the gift as January 1957 from civilingeniør Oskar Ekman with further provenance unknown. He reads the front of the fly-title (his ‘forperm’) as ‘Tyge Brahe’ struck through and ‘tico brahe ven’ struck through, and in another hand ‘Sum Paul…’, the rest lost on the torn-off part; the price, under a struck line where ‘Brade’ can be glimpsed, as ‘… 4 taliro & 4 Gross.’ in Saxon coin, which led him to leave open a journey abroad in 1561 or a book sent by courier (both answered by the semester convention: Norlind 1970, p. 16). He describes the herbarium: plant names at the head of 36 unpaginated pages in a hand not Tycho’s, remains in the gutter of 26 of them identified under the microscope by Jette Baagøe and re-housed in envelopes with the modern names, one name unattested before c. 1623 (Peter Wagner), so that the user ‘formentlig ikke har haft kontakt med Tycho’ [probably had no contact with Tycho]; and an astronomical note in Tycho’s hand in the margin of the preface’s tenth page. The book is to be kept horizontal in its capsule so that the plant remains do not fall out.

Examined and photographed at the museum on 20 October 2026, the volume, its box and the examiner’s report of 2003 brought from the store. What the leaves settle: the fly-title recto carries ‘tico brade ven:’ in a thin early hand, struck through once in the same ink; a name obliterated under heavy black strokes, which Thykier read as ‘Tyge Brahe’; and, in a firmer hand with a flourish, ‘Sum Pauli’ [I am Paul's] — complete to its final letter, so the owner’s first name is all the leaf ever carried of him, and what stood on the torn-away part was not the rest of it; two further short words, one smudged, one at the head right, stay unread. The verso’s struck line is the museum’s ‘Sum Thÿchonis Brade’ — ‘Sum’ and ‘Brade’ are legible beside the bar — so the museum’s transcription and Thykier’s ‘a struck line where Brade can be glimpsed’ describe one line, and the recto’s ‘Sum Pauli’ is one of the museum’s ‘further ownership inscriptions’: the three witnesses agree once the two sides of the leaf are told apart. Beneath the purchase note the astronomical memorandum is intact — a two-branch rule in bracket form for passing from right to oblique ascension by the sign of the declination, ‘obliqua’ struck and ‘Recta’ written above it — and the ink note on the front pastedown is a companion rule in the same early hand. The front pastedown also carries a pencil collation in German, the trace of the Munich trade, and the Royal Library’s accession number in pencil, which stands again as ‘Acc. 1986/116’ at the head of the fly-title and on the slip kept in the box.

The spine label is a paper slip with the figures written in ink, ‘20’ and a damaged third figure consistent with 4; nothing else is lettered on the spine, and the larger label or patch that Prandtl’s plate of 1932 showed at the tail is gone. The rear flyleaf carries a faint ‘N 36’ at the head and a small blind-stamped cartouche near the gutter — a second earlier number and a dealer’s or restorer’s mark, both unread. The box is a brown cloth clamshell box with a gilt spine label lettered in English, ‘Tycho Brahe’s copy with autograph ownership notes, etc.’ — made in the English-speaking trade or for the American owner between 1933 and 1956, the one physical trace of that interval. The rear pastedown has the museum’s accession note in ballpoint, ‘Gave jan. 1957 fra civiling. Oskar Ekman’ [gift, January 1957, from the engineer Oskar Ekman], with the Kronborg stamp and ‘30:57’, the inventory number in its old form: the gift was entered in January 1957 under Oscar Ekman’s name, four months after his death on 16 September 1956 — which reconciles Klem’s ‘fru Lia Ekman og afdøde ægtefælle’ [Mrs Lia Ekman and her late husband], Thykier’s ‘January 1957 from civilingeniør Oskar Ekman’ and Dal’s ‘testamentarisk bortgivet’ [given away by bequest]: a gift in the dead man’s name, made by his widow.

The herbarium is confirmed: the plant names stand at the head of the preface leaves (Pulmonaria, Ranunculus aquaticus, Hedera arborescens …) in a later hand, and the envelopes of plant remains lie at their openings, so the box must stay flat. The four places on fol. 53r–v are in one ink and ductus, written in one campaign: ‘Elzingborgum’ with a superscript c, ‘Lunda’, ‘Vesbÿ Gotlandiæ’, and the fourth, whose letters read R-?-n-s-f-a-l-?-h-? and whose figures, set against the printed values, put it about half a degree west of Visby and a little north — the Swedish coast opposite Gotland, if the figures are to be trusted; the name, not the figures, must decide. The reader’s marks — tallies, a red stepped line through the declination table, a pen flourish, ‘Octava sphaera’, ‘Wittenberga’ underlined — are of several hands and dates, and none is attributed. Nothing here has been compared with a dated specimen of Tycho’s hand: ‘Tycho’s hand’ remains the attribution of Prandtl, the museum and Thykier. Read letter by letter from the frames on 21 October 2026. The purchase note is ‘emptus thalero et 4 grossis’ — the sign that the museum, Thykier and the examination of 20 October took for a g is the 9-shaped -us abbreviation. The ink rule on the front pastedown reads in full: oblique ascension, for a southern declination add, for a northern subtract, the ascensional difference from the right ascension; in descensions the contrary way — the writer blotted out his first ‘Adde’ and wrote the rule again on the fly-title verso as a bracket table, there striking ‘obliqua’ and writing ‘Recta’ above it. The smudged word above ‘Sum Pauli’ stands inside a wet-wiped erasure of an earlier inscription and reads ‘Brÿſſe’ or ‘Chrÿſſe’; the heavy black strokes through the recto name and through the verso's ‘Sum Thÿchonis Brade’ are one ink and one campaign — a later owner cancelled both Brahe names, and the thin stroke through ‘tico brade ven:’ is an earlier, different cancellation. Three more plant names were read (Lamium, Lysimachia flore luteo, Hyacinthus), the Octavum problema column in full, and the fourth place on fol. 53v confirmed as the museum's ‘Rumefalche’ (the tall letter has a cross-bar: f, not a long ſ; a first reading of 21 October took it for ſ and is withdrawn). The same day the name was identified: ‘Bespue 47.5.59.50.’ and ‘Rumefalche 46.35.60.15.’ are the two ‘cities’ of Gotland on fo. 34r of Johannes Schöner's Luculentissima quaedam terrae totius descriptio (Nuremberg 1515), the text to his globe, and Schöner's northern towns come from the Ulm Ptolemy of 1486, whose Scandinavian names are Claudius Clavus's (Bjørnbo and Petersen 1904, pp. 115 and 118) — Rumefalche is one of Clavus's invented Gotland names, not a place, and its figures are a position on a map, not an observation. Helsingborg and Lund carry Schöner's figures too (Elebogum 35.46.57.0, Lunda 36.30.57.23), which Apian's printed Scania table repeats; so all four lines on fol. 53 are Schöner's values, copied by the student from Schöner, or from Apian and Schöner together. The Visby name form points to the exemplar: the 1515 printing reads ‘Bespue’ alone, the later Nuremberg reprint Bjørnbo used (undated, 1518) reads ‘Bespue uel wisbuy’, and the writer put the real name ‘Vesbÿ’ — so either the reprint or the Ulm Ptolemy itself stood on his desk at Leipzig; which, is open. The hands are labelled descriptively: A the thin early hand of ‘tico brade ven:’, B the grey-brown hand of ‘Sum Thÿchonis Brade’ and the purchase note, C the firm dark hand of the pastedown rule, the verso memorandum and the fol. 53 places, D ‘Sum Pauli’, E the herbarium hand, F the German pencil collation. Hand C was compared feature by feature with the dated specimens of the Graphonomicon of Tycho Brahe — the horoscope prose of 1583, the observation narrative of 1597, the album leaf of 1599 — and with the unattributed index of 1563–65 in the Uppsala volume of 1563: ten concordances with the atlas (the looped uncial d, the u-mark, the diaeresis on y, the single-storey a, the long-ſ/round-s distribution, the ſc connection, the looped e, the capital A, a slant of 15–24 degrees inside the atlas band) and no discordance, but none of high distinctiveness, and the display forms that would decide do not occur in a working memorandum; against the Uppsala index the concordances are preponderant, but that hand is itself unattributed between Tycho at Leipzig and Vedel. The verdicts are inconclusive on both pairings. No hand is attributed: ‘Tycho's hand’ remains the attribution of Prandtl, the museum and Thykier, now recorded as contradicted by no feature and supported in kind by every one; a secure Vedel autograph of the 1560s–80s is what would decide it. Christianson (1967, p. 201) counts it with the pigskin volume of 1560 ([[vol:s-kl-47|18 J 318]]) as ‘two of his own “textbooks”’ still preserved; it is the earliest book to carry a purchase note beside an ownership entry in Tycho’s name — the hands of both unattributed, the comparison of 21 October 2026 inconclusive. The volume is not digitised; the museum’s record carries its two photographs (the front board; the volume open at the Regiomontanus title), and the examination of 20 October 2026 photographed the boards, the edges and the inscribed leaves. || 29 October 2026 — the six student volumes judged in the lecture session (the literature pack of this volume: 175 passages, 84 documents): this is the one surviving volume documented as Tycho’s before he left Denmark on 14 February 1562, by the boards alone. The place of purchase is an inference from the year, not a document; the groschen of the price are German money of account, unexplained for Copenhagen by any source, the house’s Joachimsthaler argument answering only the thaler; the tools of the binding have not been set against the Uppsala binding of 1563; ‘Sum Pauli’ is an owner no source dates. The volume’s return to Denmark — Oscar Ekman’s bequest, entered in January 1957 by his widow Lia in the dead man’s name — makes the one Copenhagen student volume a Danish holding, at Helsingør. || 29 October 2026 — the Ekman sale catalogue read in a copy in a private collection (Bruun Rasmussen 186, p. 111, lot 497): the volume is entered under ‘En Bog fra Tycho Brahe's Bibliotek’ for completeness only, not for sale, ‘given to the Handels- og Søfartsmuseet at Kronborg according to the last will of ingeniør Ekman’, and on view there in a showcase in 1965. The catalogue repeats the trade's description (‘en af de første, Tycho Brahe har ejet … han har skrevet sit navn deri samt et par notater og den pris’); what it adds is custodial — the bequest — not palaeographic. The catalogue will be shown at the talk of 19 November 2026.

Avol-s-mort-frederiksborg-agrippa
Earlier catalogues
Prandtl, Verz. B, Band XX
Identification
A · identified by Prandtl 1932, Verzeichnis B, Band XX (‘Einzelband 48 (ca. 1550). Prachtband, Pergament. — Harald Mortensen, Kopenhagen’), the volume in Mortensen's own collection in 1932 (so also Gingerich 2002, p. 326); Mortensen 1955, p. 25 (‘nu i Tycho Brahe-Montren paa Det nationalhistoriske Museum paa Frederiksborg, tidligere i Forfatterens eje’); Paulli & Dal 1959, p. 15 (the gift of 1950, ‘i pergamentbind med Tychos portræt og våben i guld’); the museum's collections department, written answers of 28 September 2026 (inventory number B3950a-b, kept in the museum library, not on display) and 12 October 2026 (a = the volume, b = its slipcase)
Marks securing the identification
Prachtband: parchment with the gilt supralibros portrait and arms (‘Prachtband, Pergament’, Prandtl; ‘pergamentbind med Tychos portræt og våben i guld’, Paulli & Dal)
Binding
Period 4 (gilt supralibros)

Chain of custody
  1. route unknown from 1601
    The route out of the library is undocumented; never traced at the Clementinum.
  2. Sigurd Wandel, professor, Copenhagen (bought in Germany)
    Paulli & Dal 1959, pp. 15–16; Mortensen 1955, p. 25. — Paulli & Dal 1959; Mortensen 1955
  3. Harald Mortensen, Copenhagen by 1932–1950
    Prandtl 1932, Verzeichnis B, Band XX (‘Harald Mortensen, Kopenhagen’); Mortensen 1955, p. 25 (‘tidligere i Forfatterens eje’). — Prandtl 1932; Mortensen 1955
  4. Det Nationalhistoriske Museum på Frederiksborg, Hillerød, inventory B3950a-b from 1950
    Mortensen’s gift of 1950 (Paulli & Dal 1959, pp. 15–16); the museum’s written confirmation of 28 September 2026. — Paulli & Dal 1959; Frederiksborg 2026
Links
No online catalogue record traced; the location rests on the source named above.
Sources
Prandtl 1932; Mortensen 1955; Paulli & Dal 1959; Frederiksborg 2026; Gingerich 2002
Notes
Agrippa, Opera, tomus I (Lyon, c. 1550, 8vo): the parchment Prachtband with the gilt portrait-and-arms plaques that Prandtl listed in 1932 as Band XX in Harald Mortensen’s collection at Copenhagen. Bought in Germany by professor Sigurd Wandel, then Mortensen’s. Paulli and Dal (1959, pp. 15–16) print the letter to the museum’s director Otto Andrup of 30 December 1949 by which the testamentary promise became a gift in the donor’s lifetime: ‘selv om jeg hænger ved disse Ting, kan jeg jo have ligesaa megen Glæde af at se dem velforvaret udstillet paa Frederiksborg’. The gift was made in 1950, and the volume was shown in the museum’s Tycho Brahe case when Mortensen wrote in 1955. The museum confirmed in a communication of 28 September 2026 that it holds the volume in its library as inventory B3950a-b, not on display, and on 12 October 2026 that the suffix names two inventoried parts: the volume (a) and the slipcase it is kept in (b).

PAN Biblioteka Kórnicka (Kórnik Library of the Polish Academy of Sciences), Kórnik — 1 volume

vol. 56

Cim.Qu.2812 — Kórnik, Polish Academy of Sciences Library

Avol-s-kornik-heidenstein
Identification
A · identified by the copy itself, read in the Biblioteka Kórnicka’s digitisation (Wielkopolska Biblioteka Cyfrowa) on 18 October 2026
Marks securing the identification
white parchment (limp vellum) with the gilt oval portrait medallion on the upper cover, lettered ‘HIC PATET EXTERIOR TYCHONIS FORMA BRAHEI ✶ PVLCHRIVS ENITEAT QVAE LATET INTERIOR’, and the arms medallion on the lower, ‘ARMA GENVS FVNDI PEREVNT DVRABILE VIRTVS ✶ ET DOCTRINA DECVS NOBILITATIS HABENT’, gilt fleurons at the corners; on the title ‘Collegij Societatis IESV Commotouij Catalogo inscriptus A° 1671’ and, at its foot, the red stamp ‘Z HANKOWYCH’; on the verso the round stamp ‘BIBLIOTEKA KÓRNICKA’ (the scan, read 18 October 2026; the library’s record: ‘supereksl., plak., portret z napisem w otoku’)
Binding
Period 4 (gilt supralibros)
Contents
  1. Heidenstein, Reinhold, De bello Moscovitico quod Stephanus rex Poloniae gessit commentariorum libri VI (1588) (no. 120)
Chain of custody
  1. Tycho’s heirs, Prague from 1601
    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970
  2. route unknown until 1671
    No owner is recorded between the heirs and the Chomutov college’s catalogue entry. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 76) supposed that the college came by Tycho’s books in a way similar to the Clementinum’s gift; Císařová Smítková, Paličková and Vackářová (2021, p. 30) suppose Clementinum duplicates passed on under Joannes Jüngling, who kept the Clementinum’s mathematical library in 1749 and was prefect of the Chomutov library in 1765–1766; the college’s dated catalogue entries on Tycho’s volumes are of 1645 to 1675. — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021
  3. Jesuit college, Chomutov (Komotau) from 1671
    The inscription ‘Collegij Societatis IESV Commotouij Catalogo inscriptus A° 1671’ on the title (the scan), the formula of the Chomutov college found on 14 A 63, 14 H 225 and XV K 22. — Biblioteka Kórnicka (WBC); Kleinschnitzová 1933
  4. route unknown
    The volume did not come to the Clementinum with the Chomutov library after 1773. The red stamp ‘Z Hankowych’ on the title is read by the Kórnik cataloguer as Václav Hanka's (1791–1861) (Muszyński 1977, no. 583 and index p. 253), and the entry's mark ‘[A. T. Działyński-kat. Kiel.]’ places the volume in Kielisiński's card catalogue of 1840–c. 1847: it passed from Chomutov to Hanka in Prague and from him, in his lifetime, to Tytus Działyński's Kórnik. When and how it left Chomutov, how Hanka came by it, and what the older shelfmarks ‘H. VI. 365.’ and ‘C: 157.’ denote (Muszyński omits the concordance) remain undocumented. — Muszyński 1977
  5. Václav Hanka (1791–1861), Prague — his stamp ‘Z Hankowych’ by c. 1847
    The red stamp ‘Z Hankowych’ on the title, read as Hanka's by Muszyński 1977 (no. 583; index p. 253, after Encyklopedia Gutenberga 6, p. 86), who lists it on two further Kórnik volumes bound alike (Cim.Qu.2813–2814); the genitive plural (‘of the Hankas’) leaves a family stock possible (W4, 27 October 2026). — Muszyński 1977
  6. PAN Biblioteka Kórnicka, Kórnik, Cim.Qu.2812 from by c. 1847
    The library’s record and digitisation (Wielkopolska Biblioteka Cyfrowa, publication 518174). In Kielisiński's catalogue of 1840–c. 1847 (Muszyński 1977, no. 583, ‘kat. Kiel.’; Bolewska). — Biblioteka Kórnicka (WBC); Muszyński 1977; Bolewska (Kielisiński)
Links

Sources

Notes
Reinhold Heidenstein, De bello Moscovitico quod Stephanus rex Poloniae gessit commentariorum libri VI (Basel: Waldkirch, 1588), 184 pp., 4°; the library’s record (sygn. Cim.Qu.2812; Estreicher XVIII, 80) notes ‘supereksl., plak., portret z napisem w otoku’ and the arms plate ‘Arma, genus fundi pereunt …’. On the front pastedown the older shelfmarks ‘H. VI. 365.’ and ‘C: 157.’, a red label ‘XII’, the pencilled ‘Cim. Qu. 2812’ and ‘Dezynfekcja 2018’; on the flyleaf ‘hh: 310.’. Digitised by the library (publication 518174, edition 467724, DjVu); a copy of the scan is held in the house corpus. Muszyński 1977 (no. 583) reads the red stamp as Václav Hanka's and marks the entry ‘[A. T. Działyński-kat. Kiel.]’ — in Kielisiński's catalogue of 1840–c. 1847 (Bolewska); the same stamp stands on Cim.Qu.2813–2814, two Görlitz imprints of 1589–90 bound alike (W4, 27 October 2026).

Royal Danish Library (Det kongelige Bibliotek), Copenhagen — 2 volumes

vol. 54

88, 201 01801 (eks. 2) — Copenhagen, Royal Library

Avol-s-mort-kb-calvin
Identification
A · identified by Harald Mortensen 1955, pp. 25–27 (the volume acquired by the Royal Library from America through Hjalmar Bruhn: the small portrait-and-arms supralibros and Tycho's dedication to his cousin Hans Lindenov); Norlind 1970, p. 341, from Mortensen; examined and photographed in the Royal Library's reading room on 21 October 2026 — the library's copy eks. 2, 88, 201 01801, identified by the pencil catalogue signature 88,-201 on its front pastedown, the small dies on both boards, the dedication on the verso of the free endpaper and the Theocritus of 1596 bound second; the accession mark ‘1954 g. 230’ in pencil on the free endpaper
Marks securing the identification
Examined on 21 October 2026 (eks. 2, 88, 201 01801): both gilt supralibros in the small size — the portrait oval c. 58 × 42 mm and the arms oval c. 58 × 42.5 mm on the ruler (±1 mm), the one size, concordant with Mortensen's 5.8 × 4.3, Friis's 59 × 42.5 on the first twelve Vienna fair-copy quartos and Strahov Σ VI 3 (58 × 43) — the legends HIC PATET EXTERIOR TYCHONIS FORMA BRAHEI PVLCHRIVS ENITEAT QVAE LATET INTERIOR and ARMA GENVS FVNDI PEREVNT DVRABILE VIRTVS ET DOCTRINA DECVS NOBILITATIS HABENT legible in part, the gilt worn and best preserved on the back; and Tycho's dedication on the verso of the front free endpaper facing the Calvin title, read letter by letter: ‘Johanni Lindenouio | Conſobrino suo | Tycho Brahe | ddt.’ — four lines on one rising diagonal in one dark iron-gall-type ink and one nib width, the last letter of ‘Lindenouio’ e-shaped where the pen failed at the joint (Mortensen) and read o, one long s only (‘Conſobrino’, the s of ‘suo’ a round s), arc-shaped u-marks over the u of ‘-ou-’ and of ‘suo’, no diaeresis on the y, the display signature about 1.8 times the body, the formula ‘ddt’ after the name with both d-ascenders crossing two long strokes drawn above it and a full point after — d(ono) d(edi)t (Fund og Forskning X, 1963, p. 155), one Latin sentence in natural order. Wholly in Tycho's hand: probable — Mortensen's verdict (‘egenhændige Tilskrift’), the signature built as the secure Wittenberg leaf of 8 May 1599 and the Duodo dedication of 1600, the address sharing the father's own prose idioms (the u-mark, the hooked descending J, the looped d), no calligrapher's marks, one ink and one planned block; the alternative of an address written at the same desk by a secretary over Tycho's signature is not excluded by the photographs — though Jessenius, the one documented secretary of such an address, is disfavoured on a word-for-word comparison with his album entry of 8 January 1599, and the father's own prose in the same album shares the address's 5-shaped round s and its L — and the son (who signed ‘T.F.’, ‘Filius’, ‘junior’ and never had a channel to a Lindenov) is excluded on context
Binding
Period 4 (gilt supralibros)
Contents
  1. Calvin, Jean; bound with Theocritus, Calvini Epistolae & responsa, editio tertia, with Beza's Vita Calvini (Hanau: Wilhelm Antonius 1597, 8°, VD16 C 304) bound with Theocriti Idyllia & Epigrammata, with Moschus, Bion and Simmias, Greek and Latin ([Heidelberg]: Commelinus 1596, 8°, VD16 ZV 14910) (1597) (no. 43)
Chain of custody
  1. Hans Lindenov, Tycho’s cousin (Tycho’s gift) from 1597–1601
    Tycho’s dedication ‘Johanni Lindenouio consobrino suo Tycho Brahe ddt’ on the verso of the free endpaper facing the title. The recipient is Hans Christoffersen Lindenov til Ørslevkloster (d. by 7 April 1610): lensmand at Bergenhus 1578–86, where the four royal letters on Tycho's Nordfjord fief were addressed to him (29 May 1579, 10 August 1580, 8 January 1581, 16 March 1586; TBOO XIV, pp. 9, 14, 19; Friis 1871, p. 161), landsdommer in Nørrejylland from 1587, holder of Ørslev Kloster by exchange with the crown from 1584, lensmand at Hammershus 1594–1610, the fief withdrawn on 3 January 1610 for infirmity (DAA 1902, pp. 286–287; Bricka X, pp. 316–318). He crossed to Hven with Tycho in the night of 3–4 July 1594 and left on the 5th — ‘rediit D. T. cum Hans Lindenov et D. G.’, ‘Abiit Johannes Lindenow’ — his one visit in the diary (Friis ed. 1876, pp. 218–219). Tycho's consobrinus: Mortensen read the word strictly, Hans a son of Christoffer Lindenov's first marriage with Margrethe Clausdatter Bille (b. 1525), sister of Tycho's mother Beate, against DAA 1902, which lists him under the second wife Ide Rantzau; DAA dates neither marriage and no later Rettelser took the point up, so Mortensen's reading stands unrefuted (Mortensen 1955, p. 27; DAA 1890, p. 87). The Calvin edition was on sale at the Frankfurt Lent fair of 1597 (Lutz, A2v, under ‘Libri Calvinianorum’) and cannot have been among the books registered at Uraniborg on 21 March 1597 (the diary, p. 263; Mortensen prints 10 March); Mortensen puts the gift probably before 1599, unless the book was sent to Lindenov later (pp. 26–27: ‘sandsynligvis har han faaet Bogen i Tiden før 1599, hvis den da ikke paa et senere Tidspunkt er blevet sendt til ham’). Lindenov sat on Bornholm from 1594, so the book was handed over elsewhere or sent; the strict window is 1597 to October 1601. Examined 21 October 2026: the dedication read on the leaf (see the marks). Kancelliets Brevbøger place Lindenov on Bornholm throughout 1597–1602 — the lensbrev from 1 May 1597 (pp. 126–127), the missives of 20 June and 26 July 1597 (pp. 171, 187), the new lensbrev from 1 May 1599 (p. 419), the Gæsteri letters of November 1600 in which his castle clerk brought the account to Copenhagen (pp. 561, 563–564), the stranded munitions of 12 November 1601 (p. 684) — and record no summons to Copenhagen; no herredag met in 1597, and he had needed royal leave to go home in February 1596 (the 1593–96 volume, p. 585). A hand-over in Copenhagen in April–May 1597 is therefore possible but undocumented, and a sending to Bornholm or Ørslev from Wandsbek, Wittenberg or Prague the more economical reading; the chancery, Tycho's own papers (the index of the Opera omnia has no Hans Lindenov after 1586) and the son's album give no trace of him in Germany or Bohemia. The enfeoffment with Hammershus dates from 20 June 1594, two weeks before he crossed to Hven with Tycho; the landsdommer's office in Jutland was no longer his in 1597–1601, when the chancery addresses the landsdommere Mogens and Iver Juel separately. — Mortensen 1955; Fund og Forskning 1963; Danmarks Adels Aarbog 1902; Danmarks Adels Aarbog 1890; Bricka, DBL X (1896); Friis (ed.) 1876; TBOO; Lutz, Lent-fair catalogue 1597; Copenhagen examination 2026; Kancelliets Brevbøger 1596–1602; Kancelliets Brevbøger 1593–1596
  2. route unknown
    No owner is recorded between Lindenov and the volume’s appearance in America. Lindenov's widow Elsebe Jensdatter Juel held Ørslev to her death in 1626/27 and the estate stayed with his son and grandson to 1642 (DAA 1902); no sale of his books is recorded, no second volume with his name is known, and the auction databases hold no Tycho-marked Calvin or Theocritus at any date (Rare Book Hub transaction history, searched 21 October 2026). Mortensen's ‘fra Amerika’ names a place, not a dealer, an auction, a private owner or an institution. The object adds the first physical trace of the road: on the rear pastedown ‘fol. 9781’ in a continental hand of the nineteenth or early twentieth century (the 7 crossed) and a pencil ‘36’; at the foot of the Theocritus title the pencil code ‘fij’; an erased pencil note on the free endpaper; three label-shaped areas at the head of each pastedown where paper has been removed, earlier than the library's pencils of 1954–77; and a scraped inscription above the device on the Calvin title — one or more European trade or institutional passages before America, none named. The spine title in a seventeenth-century Danish hand stands between Lindenov and that road (examined 21 October 2026). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021; Danmarks Adels Aarbog 1902; Copenhagen examination 2026; Ilsøe 1998
  3. Royal Danish Library, Copenhagen from 1954
    Acquired from America with the support of the ship-broker Hjalmar Bruhn (Mortensen 1955, p. 25: ‘Ved virksom Støtte af Det kongelige Biblioteks altid redebonne Velgører Skibsmægler Hjalmar Bruhn er det lykkedes fra Amerika at hjemføre en Bog, der har tilhørt Tycho Brahe’); ‘for få år siden’ in 1959 (Paulli & Dal 1959, p. 15). The year is not stated anywhere: Bruhn (1881–1959) is already the library's benefactor in January 1952 (Paulli 1954, p. 7) and the volume is ‘det nu erhvervede’ in the article of 1955, so the purchase falls between 1952 and 1955 (Paulli & Dal 1958–59, p. 15: ‘for få år siden lykkedes Det kongelige Biblioteks at erhverve et tychonisk samlebind fra USA’). The accession mark in pencil on the free endpaper, ‘1954 g. 230’ (read 21 October 2026), gives the year — 1954, or the financial year 1954/55 — and the serial; the volume went into the Boghistorisk Studiesamling (‘Boghist. Saml.’), was moved to the box store (‘BOX’) in the security campaign of 1977 (‘S-1977’), an earlier location beginning ‘D.A.’ cancelled, and is catalogued as eks. 2 of the Hanau Calvin, 88, 201 01801, its Theocritus marked ‘dupl’ against the library's separate copy. Bruhn died on 21 December 1959 (‘Bruhn, Hj., Skibsmgl.’, Dødsfald i Danmark 1959); he had funded the library's purchases at the Maar auction of 1952 and given it a Steno quarto, a Pontoppidan psalm-book in a silver-filigree binding (1954) and two Andersen dedication copies (1955) — Danish-department benefactions, the Tycho volume the only Tychonian among them. — Mortensen 1955; Paulli & Dal 1959; Paulli 1954; DBL, ‘Dan Folke’; Copenhagen examination 2026; Royal Library, Opklaring af bogtyverierne (2005); Royal Library, Royal Identification Marks (2005); Royal Library archive registratur 1994; Dødsfald i Danmark 1959

Notes
A Tycho Sammelband, a Prachtband containing Calvin’s Epistolae et responsa (Hanau 1597) and the Theocritus of 1596, repatriated from the USA through the ship-broker (skibsmægler) Hjalmar Bruhn, the Royal Library’s benefactor (Mortensen 1955, p. 25: ‘Det kongelige Biblioteks altid redebonne Velgører Skibsmægler Hjalmar Bruhn’); the first book from Tycho’s own library to enter the Royal Library, which until then had owned none apart from the autograph observations (Mortensen 1955, p. 25: ‘har det hidtil ikke ejet en Bog fra hans egen Bogsamling (bortset fra de haandskrevne Observationer)’). Given by Tycho to his cousin Hans Lindenov after the Calvin edition of 1597 had appeared — probably before 1599, Mortensen supposes, unless the book was sent to Lindenov later (pp. 26–27). The dedication stands on the verso of the free endpaper facing the title; the supralibros is small. Mortensen describes the binding (1955, pp. 25–26): ‘et slidt Pergamentbind med Spor af grønne Bindebaand’, the portrait and arms plaques on the two boards, ‘derudenom en ret bred rektangulær Ramme trykt med Rullestempel, og inden i Rammens Hjørner Rosetter. Den udekorerede Ryg har haandskreven Titel fra senere Tid.’ His expansion of the dedication’s abbreviation is corrected by the corrigenda in Fund og Forskning X (1963), p. 155: ‘bør forkortelsen ddt opløses til dono dedit eller dedicavit’. The Royal Library’s catalogue lists two copies of the Hanau 1597 edition (VD16 C 304): 88, 201 01800, in the ordinary stacks, with the provenance of L. M. Schavenius, and 88, 201 01801, kept in the library’s store of rarities and lent only to the reading room, with no provenance or item note. The library’s copy of the Theocritus (Commelinus, 1596) at 168, 370 02401 is a separate copy; a constituent of the Sammelband would be shelved under the Calvin call number. The library has not confirmed that 88, 201 01801 is the volume acquired through Bruhn in 1954. Examined and photographed in the Forskningslæsesal on 21 October 2026: Photographed in the Forskningslæsesal on 21 October 2026, both Royal Library copies of the Hanau 1597 Calvin on the table: the Sammelband is eks. 2, 88, 201 01801 (barcode 201003563960), kept in the box store and, by the library's word, in Håndskriftsamlingens arkiv; eks. 1 is Scavenius's copy of 1665. Binding 175 × 120 × 75 mm, leaves 171 × 106 × 70 mm. What the volume carries beyond Tycho's marks, read on the object: the Royal Library's pencil catalogue signature ‘88,-201’ at the head of the front pastedown and again on the inner board edge (the Udenlandske Afdeling's Ældre Samling signature, two numbers with comma and dash); the accession mark ‘1954 g. 230’ in pencil along the fore-edge of the free endpaper — the accession year (or the financial year 1954/55) and a serial number, the letter unexplained, the only witness to the year of the purchase, which no printed source gives; ‘Boghist. Saml.’ (the Boghistorisk Studiesamling, the locked selection of the Ældre Samling started in the 1950s for books of provenance or annotation), ‘BOX’ (the climate-controlled box store funded in 1976 and filled in 1977–78), ‘S-1977’ (a marking of the security and revision campaign of 1977), and between them an earlier location of four pointed capitals beginning ‘D.A.’, struck through in the same pencil; ‘1597’ in pencil at the foot of the Calvin title; ‘dupl’ in pencil at the head of the Theocritus title — most simply the library's own duplicate check of 1954 against its separate Theocritus of 1596 (168, 370 02401), which is why the Sammelband is catalogued under the Calvin alone; the alternative, that the library had once owned and sold the volume as a duplicate and bought it back, is unsupported (duplicates were not signed before separation; Ilsøe records no Calvin of 1597 or Theocritus of 1596 in any duplicate sale; the catalogues of 1783 and 1786 are unread). Beneath the library's marks a continental layer of unknown origin: ‘fol. 9781’ at the foot of the rear pastedown, a graphite or ink number in a nineteenth- or early twentieth-century hand whose 7 is crossed (not the library's own pencil series of c. 1663, which runs only to c. 9200, has no prefix and covers Frederik III's stock), a pencil ‘36’ at its head, a two-letter pencil code ‘fij’ at the foot of the Theocritus title (a bookseller's cipher, or ‘ij’ for the second piece), an erased pencil note on the free endpaper, illegible even in the raw frames, three label-shaped areas at the head of each pastedown where paper has been removed (the library's pencils run over them, so they are earlier), and a scraped, thinned spot with brown specks immediately above the device on the Calvin title — the usual place for an owner's name, and not the library's practice, which stamped and did not erase; no library stamp is visible on either title. The spine carries an ink title in a round upright italic of the seventeenth century, ‘Johannis Caluini | Epistolae et Respons[a] | Theocriti | Idyllia et Epigra[m]ata’, not the dedication hand (Mortensen's ‘haandskreven Titel fra senere Tid’) and not the library's — a private owner of the Danish custody, to be set beside the Scavenius spine titles of eks. 1. No American mark is identifiable: the owner ‘fra Amerika’ either left none or removed it. The binding: gilt parchment over stiff pasteboard, three laced thongs, a flat untooled spine, two pairs of green silk ties (remnants in the slits at the fore-edge), all edges stained red and plain, plaited natural-thread endbands; on each board a gilt leaf roll with a twisted central line (band c. 7–8 mm, leaf pitch c. 5 mm, the corners overrun, not mitred) with four five-petalled heraldic double roses with hatched barbs, c. 11 mm, in the corners and the oval at centre, the gilt mostly worn. The dies place nothing (they were at Hven by 1588, in Prague after 1599 and in use after Tycho's death); the roll is a laurel garland of 6 mm pitch of the type Gigas saw on the Epistolae of 1596 and GKS 307, and the roll frame without a lozenge has its parallel in Gigas's plate of the Epistolae for Duke Johan Adolf; the rose punch is not that of GKS 307 (c. 18 mm) and probably not that of the Epistolae (c. 14 mm), nor the star-in-circle of Strahov Σ VI 3, the other small-die carrier; its nearest relative is the rose on the Magini De mundi of Hven, the same five-petalled barbed design a tenth smaller. The structure — stiff parchment, three laced thongs, flat spine, green ties, a rectangular frame with corner roses — is that of the Hven parchment family, not of the Prague leather bindings, so the evidence tilts to Tycho's own tool-kit used after Hven, at Wandsbek in 1597–98 or in Copenhagen in the spring of 1597, with Prague the less likely; the plain red edges have no parallel on any Hven binding the edition can see. The rose punch at 1:1 against the Magini rose and the rose on Astr. 1100 would decide. The dedication, read at native resolution and tested by refutation: one ink and one planned block (the ſ of the second line fitted into the space above the y of the third, the T's arch filling the indent of the second line); the signature constructed as the secure Wittenberg leaf of 8 May 1599 and the Duodo dedication of 1600; the address sharing the father's informal-prose idioms; no diaeresis on the y, as on two other secure specimens; the formula after the name, unparalleled among the store's dedications but explained by the sentence order; the doubled stroke over ‘ddt’ paralleled by the Duodo ‘DDt.’. The photographs cannot separate two writers sharing one inkwell at one desk, so an address written by a secretary over Tycho's own ‘Tycho Brahe ddt’ (the practice of the Mosbach Mechanica, where the signature came first and Jessenius added the address later at Wittenberg) remains the one live alternative, decided only by the order of the strokes where the second line crosses the third — and that alternative is now disfavoured for Jessenius himself: his own entry in the album of Tycho's son (Národní muzeum VI F 44, fol. 24r, Wittenberg, 8 January 1599), set word for word against the address, has an I in ‘Iohan:’ that is a straight oblique stroke without descender or foot where the address's J descends and hooks, an h whose right limb descends where the address's sits on the baseline, a sigma-form round s, a small hooked u-mark and a joined cursive ductus, while the father's own prose on the first leaf of the same album shares with the address the 5-shaped round s (‘suo’ beside ‘Sortis’), the construction of the capital L (‘Lindenouio’ beside ‘Laborem’), the arc u-mark, the baseline h and the lifted, letter-by-letter ductus, with no disagreement of construction found; the untested hands are Longomontanus and Tengnagel; the son, who in 1598 gave a cousin a Mechanica under a bare ‘Tycho Brahe’, is excluded on context — in Italy in 1601, Prague in 1602 and northern Bohemia from 1603, the only Copenhagen entry in his album dated 28 October 1599, no channel to any Lindenov, and every specimen of his own hand marked ‘T.F.’, ‘Filius’ or ‘junior’. Where and when the gift was made: Kancelliets Brevbøger reach Hans Lindenov on Bornholm throughout 1597–1602 — a new lensbrev from 1 May 1597, the Swedish-muster alert of 20 June 1597, the Bilde complaint of 26 July 1597, the new lensbrev from 1 May 1599, and in November 1600 his castle clerk, not he, ‘nu var her med Hans Lindenovs Regnskab’; no herredag met in 1597, no letter summons him to Copenhagen, and he had needed royal leave to go home in February 1596 — so a meeting in Copenhagen in the spring of 1597, when Tycho lodged there, is possible but undocumented, and a sending to Bornholm or Ørslev from Wandsbek, Wittenberg or Prague, through the Lindenov–Bille kin who were in letter contact with Tycho in 1598–1600, is the more economical reading. The Royal Library's own record of the acquisition (the file behind accession 1954 no. 230, which should name the seller) has not been asked for. The rose punch, tested the same evening against every Tycho binding imaged at a known scale: the rose of the Hven presentation bindings is a punch of about 14.5 mm with line-hatched outer petals and a seeded centre — on the Stockholm De mundi of 1588 (Dudith's copy, RAR 106 A, 14.1–14.9 mm against the ruler in the Swedish digitisation), on the Dibner Epistolae of 1596 (14.4–15.2 mm against the Kodak scale in the Smithsonian's photograph), on the Epistolae presented to Duke Johan Adolf (the Royal Library's LN 430 4°, eks. 1, the copy Gigas knew as Astr. 1100; 13.8–14.6 mm on the cover image in Early European Books, scaled on the large oval and checked on the roll's 6.4 mm pitch) and, by size, on the Mechanica presented to Jan Zbyněk z Hazmburka (Strahov AG XI 56, 14.2–15.0 mm); the rose on the Magini De mundi is a second punch of 9.5–10 mm; the rose on this volume, 11 mm with smooth petals and a bossed centre, is a third. The binding was therefore not made with Tycho's presentation tools: a binder working in the same idiom, with his own rose and a laurel roll of the same type and nearly the same pitch (6.0 against 6.2–6.6 mm), bound the two books. Where is still open — Copenhagen in 1597, Rostock, Wandsbek or Hamburg in 1597–98, Wittenberg in 1598–99 — with Prague low, since the other small-die carrier at Strahov has a star and raised bands; a dated Wandsbek binding imaged at high resolution (the Mechanica presentation copies, the Royal Library's LN 432) is now the comparator to seek.

GKS 318 2° — Copenhagen, Royal Library

Avol-s-krabbe-kb-gks318
Identification
A · identified by Dreyer, Opera omnia VIII (1925), p. 438, note to p. 295; Norlind 1970, p. 351. The two give different folios (157 and 159); neither has been checked on the codex
Marks securing the identification
sewn among Tycho's own observation books, in the codex of his observations of 1600–1601; Tycho's autograph marginal notes on the leaf
Contents
  1. Krabbe, Johannes, Observationes aliquot Eclipsium Solis et Lunae per Joh. Krabbe, mathematicum ducis H. Julii factae (1600) (no. 130)
Chain of custody
  1. Tycho’s heirs, Prague 1601–1604
    The heirs ceded Tycho’s instruments and manuscripts to Rudolf II by contract; the library stayed with them, while the instruments ‘cum libris observationum’ were ordered to Vienna in 1604 (Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 75). Kepler received the observations, originals and copies, under a contract with Tengnagel in 1604 (Dreyer 1890, Appendix, p. 370). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970; Dreyer 1890
  2. Johannes Kepler, with the observation books 1604–1630
    Kepler received Tycho’s observations, originals and copies, under a contract with Tengnagel of 1604 and never returned them (Dreyer 1890, Appendix, p. 370); the leaf is sewn into the codex of the observations of 1600–1601. — Dreyer 1890
  3. Ludwig Kepler, as a pledge against the court’s bond of 1633 1630–1655
    Mortensen 1955, pp. 31–32; Dreyer 1890, Appendix, p. 373 (by the beginning of 1662 at the latest). — Mortensen 1955; Dreyer 1890
  4. Frederik III of Denmark; the Royal Library, Copenhagen, GKS 318 2° from 1655
    Sold by Ludwig Kepler to Frederik III for 600 rigsdaler in 1655 (Mortensen 1955, pp. 31–32). — Mortensen 1955

Holding

Sources

Notes
One manuscript leaf, not a book. Its heading reads ‘Observationes aliquot Eclipsium Solis et Lunae per Joh. Krabbe, mathematicum ducis H. Julii factae’; it records seven lunar and six solar eclipses of 1581–1600 observed at Helmstedt, Berlin, Braunschweig, Wolfenbüttel and Gröningen, the times as a rule from star altitudes, and it carries in Tycho’s hand the mean times for Krabbe’s observations and for his own. Tycho had asked Georg Rollenhagen in Magdeburg in April 1600 to procure these observations and their method, in order to fix the meridian difference between Krabbe’s observing places and his own (Opera omnia VIII, 295); the last entry on the leaf is 30 June 1600. The leaf is sewn into the codex of Tycho’s observations of 1600–1601 and passed with the observation books from his heirs to Kepler, to Ludwig Kepler, and by sale to Frederik III in 1655 (Mortensen 1955, p. 31). The library’s record is that of the codex: it names Tycho’s Benátky and Prague observations and the observations Kepler sent from Styria, not the Krabbe leaf. The leaf is not printed in the Opera omnia; Dreyer’s commentary places it at fol. 157, Norlind at fol. 159. No digital facsimile of the codex exists: the library’s record for GKS 311–318 is a physical-only record, and of the observation codices only GKS 316 is digitised; the library’s microfilm is Ms. micro 555.

Göteborg, Röhsska Museum — Theatri humanae vitae volumen decimum-octavum — Göteborg, Röhsska Museum

Avol-s-mort-rohsska-prachtband
Earlier catalogues
Prandtl, Verz. B, Band XXV
Identification
A · identified by Prandtl 1932 (no.57 / Einzelband XXV); Mortensen 1955 (pp. 28–30)
Marks securing the identification
Tycho's gilt portrait+arms superexlibris — the finely struck, well-preserved exemplar figured in the Zeitschrift für Bücherfreunde X (1906/07). On a Renaissance binding: the 1906 notice took it for Basel work made for Tycho, Bargum for Danish work made under his direction, Mortensen (1955, p. 28) for a binding Tycho acquired bound and then stamped. The 1906 description: brown leather over wooden boards, two chased brass clasps, seven raised bands, three blind-tooled frames (the inner one with fourteen scholar-portrait medallions), four gilt rosettes, the two gilt medallions with the distichs.
Binding
Period 4 (gilt supralibros)
Contents
  1. Zwinger, Theodor, Theatri humanae vitae volumen decimum-octavum [the last tome, volumina XVIII–XXIX: 33 books, pp. 3251–4373 and the index] (1587) (no. 245)
Chain of custody
  1. route unknown from 1601
    The route out of the library and to Sweden is undocumented (possibly the Swedish sack of Prague in 1648, but no evidence places the volume on that road).
  2. Ludwig Rosenthal, antiquarian bookseller, Munich until 1906
    Rosenthal sent the volume to the Zeitschrift für Bücherfreunde, which reproduced its plaques in 1906. — ZfB 1906–07 (binding note)
  3. Per Hierta (1864–1924), Främmestad, Västergötland until 1915 or by 1924
    Prandtl 1932, Verzeichnis B, Band XXV (p. 14: ‘Per Hjerta, Frammestad, Schweden’); Mortensen 1955, p. 30: ‘tilhørte tidligere Per Hierta, Främmestad, Sverige’. Hierta's collection of bookbindings was bought by Hjalmar Wijk and given to the Röhsska in 1915 (SBL 19, p. 32; Nordisk familjebok, 4th ed., p. 528); Hierta died in 1924, so Prandtl's placing of the volume at Främmestad in 1932 was already stale (W9, 27 October 2026). — Prandtl 1932; Mortensen 1955; SBL (Hierta)
  4. Röhsska museum, Göteborg from 1915?
    There by 1955 (Mortensen 1955, p. 30: ‘findes nu i Röhsska Konstslöjdmuseet, Göteborg’; p. 28: one of the Nordic volumes ‘har skiftet Ejer siden Prandtls Liste udkom’); the museum’s accession is not documented. Most probably with Wijk's gift of Hierta's bindings in 1915 (C: neither source names the Zwinger). — Mortensen 1955; SBL (Hierta)
Links
No online catalogue record traced; the location rests on the source named above.
Sources
Mortensen 1955; Prandtl 1932; ZfB 1906–07 (binding note); Bargum 1906–07; SBL (Hierta)
Notes
Theatri humanae vitae vol. XVIII (Basel 1587). Mortensen 1955 (pp. 28–30) identifies the volume Prandtl catalogued as no. 57, ex Per Hierta, with the one now at the Röhsska museum, Göteborg. The modern inventory number and the museum’s accession are not recorded. The volume was first published in 1906, when Ludwig Rosenthal of Munich sent it to the Zeitschrift für Bücherfreunde: wooden boards covered in brown leather, two chased brass clasps, seven raised bands, three blind-tooled frames, the innermost with fourteen portrait medallions of scholars, four gilt rosettes, and the gilt portrait and arms medallions with their distichs; a manuscript note inside the board called it a ‘Schweizer Ledereinband mit Blinddruck und Goldmedaillons’, and the writer supposed the binding made at Basel for Tycho. Bargum answered from Copenhagen in the same volume that the binding was Danish work made under Tycho’s direction — though he could not match the fourteen medallions on any other Tycho binding — that Tycho was not at Basel in 1587, that Gellius Sascerides may have procured the book at Basel or at the Frankfurt fair after the summer of 1588, and that Tycho may have taken from Zwinger’s title the name of his projected Theatrum astronomicum. Mortensen in 1955 took the volume for a Renaissance binding that Tycho acquired bound and then stamped, the reading followed here. Neither notice names the volume’s owner between Rosenthal and Hierta. || Chapter 3 state sheet, 27 October 2026: the object has never been seen by the house and no image exists beyond the two plaques of 1906; the museum's inventory number is unknown and its online catalogue unreachable; the enquiry to the museum (one letter: the accession record for chapter II, photographs of boards with a rule, spine, edges, pastedowns and title for chapter III) is drafted in the talk folder, unsent.

Pařez (2009) prints the shelfmark as ‘AF XIV 7’; the catalogue has AG XIV 7 (Katalog Tritius record 1045270: ‘vazba se zlacenou podobou Tychona de Brahe’). The route by which the volume reached Strahov is not documented. The binding is not parchment, as Pařez’s ‘pergamenových vazbách’ for both mathematical works would have it, but brown leather (calf) over boards, with a wide gilt border roll of putti and foliage, a gilt lozenge frame of the same palmette roll as on the Opus palatinum, blind-tooled corner rosettes with a star, and remnants of green silk ties; Pařez’s description holds for Σ V 5/a only. The large portrait plaque stands in the lozenge on the front board and the arms plaque on the back (76 × 59 mm, Pařez 2009), with the shelf label at the foot of the back board. The title leaf carries the two Strahov stamps and, in ink beside the device, ‘G: Crusio ‹K› / inservio.’ (Gabriel Crusius). One reader’s note is recorded: p. 7, cap. V De divisione, ‘Divisio igitur’ underlined and ‘Analogia divisionis & multiplicationis’ in the margin; the hand has not been assessed.

The front board, of blind-tooled pigskin over wooden boards, bears the two-line TYCHO / BRAHE above and 1567 below a central panel showing a crowned shield with a radiant sun and the legend SOL·VIDET·OIA (a Sol-videt-omnia panel stamp); the Katalog Tritius describes it as ‘Supralibros Tychona Brahe z roku 1567’, and Pařez (2009) published a photograph. Crusio ‹K›’ of Gabriel Crusius, mid-seventeenth century. Examination of the volume found one annotated opening: Book I, prop. 4 (Theon’s exposition, ‘Si duo triangula …’), with marginal and head-of-page notes and a lettered triangle, together with a short jotting in the Campanus section — the ‘few notes’ of Pařez, who attributes them to Tycho’s hand. The hand has not been established as Tycho’s. The volume was found by Hedvika Kuchařová and published by Pařez (2009); the Katalog Tritius provenance note reads ‘Brahe, Tycho; Clauser, Jan Josef’ (record 993601).

O Tychonově vlastnictví (1546 - 1601) svědčí autografní zápis meteorologické povahy na fol. e14b (75v) druhého přívazku. Pak se konvolut stal součástí tzv. Matematického muzea v Klementinu, odkud přešel na Strahov (původní signatura AG VII 84). Cyril Straka: Zápis Tychona Brahe v knihovně Strahovské. Časopis Českého muzea 87, 1913, s. 382-384, zvl. 384 uvádí, že konvolut přešel na Strahov počátkem 19. století jakožto součást knihovny astronoma Antonína Strnada (1746 - 1799). To&nbsp;se však nezdá být pravděpodobné, neboť Seydl&nbsp;ani Kouklová&nbsp;v katalogu&nbsp;Strnadovy knihovny tuto položku neuvádějí. Je možné, že u Straky došlo k záměně s&nbsp;efemeridami, které sestavili Johann Stoeffler - Jakob Pflaum: Almanach nova plurimis annis&nbsp;[1499 - 1531] venturis inservientia. Venezia, Peter Liechtenstein 1507 (EDIT 16 CNCE 35579), v nichž se nachází Regiomontanova předmluva. Tyto efemeridy&nbsp;se do Strahovské knihovny&nbsp;dostaly skutečně ze Strnadova majetku a nesou signaturu AG VII 87 (srov. Kouklová, s. 217, č. 459, kde však záznam veden mylně jako prvotisk s odvoláním na H 15085, což je předchozí edice z Ulmu 1499).&nbsp;
Chybí 358 listů. Dochována je&nbsp;jen&nbsp;složka 1a4 s Ratdoltovou a Regiomontanovou předmluvou a ze&nbsp;složky 2a pouze fol. a5-6 Mariensüssova Expositia. ; Natištěné iniciály v červeno-černém tisku nekolorovány, rubriky nedoplněny. Před hlavním dílem předvázány [3] zachovalé předsádkové listy s matematickými výpočty, sahajícími až na nepotištěné fol. 1a1a, kde se jejich autor ca 1766 nad kresbičkou koše podepsal "Josephus Worel". Táž ruka nesoustavně pročíslovala listy celého konvolutu.
Hlavní dílo konvolutu v pozdně gotické vazbě na prkénkových deskách 230 x 150 potažených usní jen do jedné třetiny (přední deska mírně naprasklá). Přídeštní část usně, přibitá k deskám malými hřebíčky, byla zdobena dnes už zcela setřelým slepotiskem s rámovou kompozicí. U horního kapitálu poškozený hřbet nebyl zdoben. Na přední desce se zachoval sotva znatelný nápis "ALMANACH". Středová spona odstraněna. Žlutá ořízka.

Notes
Regiomontanus, Ephemerides 1492–1506 (Augsburg: Ratdolt 1492), with the prefatory gatherings a4 a10 of the Venice 1481 Ephemerides bound before it — the gatherings missing from the National Library’s copy (Kleinschnitzová 14). The identification as Tycho’s rests on the inscription at fol. a2r, ‘Collegij Caesarei Societatis Jesu Pragae Anno 1642. Ex Bibliotheca Tichoniana’ (Straka 1913; Boldan 2025, 33.c and 36.a; Tritius), the same basis as the Clementinum volumes; the authorship of the 34-line weather note at fol. e4v, which Straka (1913) attributed to Tycho’s hand, is the open question, and the note has not been subjected to a comparison of hands. Munzar and Pařez (2002, fig. 5) reproduce the weather note. The binding is a contemporary one, not from Tycho’s bindery: bare wooden boards with a strip of leather over the spine nailed to the boards with brass nails, the shelf label DR VII 19 at the foot; a marginal ink ‘156/2/1’ stands beside the Tabula regionum, above which is the reference-meridian note ‘Nota hec Ephemerides sunt supputate ad longitudinem …’. The Katalog Tritius (record 1064031) describes a late-gothic binding on wooden boards, 230 × 150 mm, leather over a third of the boards only, nailed, the blind-tooled frame worn away, ‘ALMANACH’ faintly on the front board, the clasp removed, yellow edges; the 1481 part reduced to gathering 1a4 and fol. a5–6 of 2a; three front flyleaves of mathematical calculations signed ‘Josephus Worel’ above a drawn basket, c. 1766, the same hand foliating the volume; a late-sixteenth-century ‘Ex libris Johanni Nachlovskij’ at fol. 1a1b, the 1642 formula at 1a2a, and Tycho’s ownership attested by an autograph note of meteorological character at fol. e14b (75v). The record states that the volume ‘then became part of the so-called Mathematical Museum in the Clementinum, from which it passed to Strahov’; the Strnad step of Straka (1913) is doubted because neither Seydl nor Kouklová lists it. The old shelfmark was AG VII 84.

Names in the record

Sources
Gingerich 2002; Schaffner catalogue 1977; Chicago, Schaffner exhibit; Newberry, Movable Mayhem; Gingerich & Westman 1988; Mosley 2007; Christianson 2000; TBOO; Bogvennen 1966; Newberry (Karr Schmidt 2023); University of Chicago Library, catalogue record 146807
Notes
The volume carries Tycho’s presentation inscription, which the library’s catalogue record transcribes: ‘D[omi]no Paulo Witichio Wratislauiensj ob amicitam & comune[m] mathemati[cum] amorem d[ono] d[edit] Tÿcho Brahe Huanae anno 1580 29 Octobris.’ — to Master Paul Wittich of Wrocław, for friendship and a shared love of mathematics, Tycho Brahe gave this, at Hven, on 29 October 1580 (a Saturday). The record’s ‘amicitam’ and ‘Huanae’ are its own readings. Gingerich and Westman, who examined the book, place the inscription on the title page. The record further notes former owners’ manuscript annotations in two hands with underscoring, a manuscript pagination 1–46 beginning on page [2], the original silk threads to the volvelles ending in small pearls or coloured glass beads, the volvelle on page [17] lacking its moving parts, a cancel slip over two lines of page [75], some initials hand-coloured by a former owner, a paper tab at the first page of the Meteoroscopion, Louis H. Silver’s book label and Joseph Halle Schaffner’s bookplate. The binding is half leather and marbled paper over boards, with an armorial device pasted to the front cover and the date 1686 tooled on it, and fabric ties, one missing. Tycho’s own words settle the ownership: writing to Hagecius on 1 November 1589 about Wittich’s library, he says that among the books will be found ‘that Astronomicum of Apianus, which I bought for 20 florins and gave to him when he was here; I do not reclaim it after his death unless it can be bought at a fair price’, and that he has another copy to hand. The book was therefore Tycho’s, left his library by his gift on 29 October 1580 — two days after his return from Helsingborg, in the weeks of the comet he and Wittich had observed — and did not come back: what Monaw brought from Wrocław in October 1600 were the annotated copies of Copernicus. It is a documented gift in Tycho’s lifetime, with his autograph, not a survivor of the posthumous dispersal. Whether one of the two annotating hands is Wittich’s, or Tycho’s, is not stated. The record names the owners the inscription does not: Louis H. Silver of Chicago, whose library the Newberry Library bought in 1964 and from which this volume, never accessioned, was sold at Sotheby’s in London on 8–9 November 1965 as lot 4 (‘Silver 4’ in the catalogue of 1977); Joseph Halle Schaffner, who bought at that sale through Warren Howell and whose science library came to the University of Chicago by bequest after his death in August 1972 (exhibited 1977, entry 15). The owners between Wittich’s sister at Wrocław and Silver are not recorded; the binding of 1686 is the one fixed point. Catalogued by the University of Chicago Library at alc ff QB41.A639 1540 (the exhibit label gives alc ff QB41.A63). The volume has not been digitised. Dal's note on the Ekman sale (Bogvennen 1966, p. 205) records that Rundetaarn ‘bød samtidig meget højt, men forgæves på en lignende hos Sotheby’ — a Tycho-library book at Sotheby's in November 1965; the one Sotheby sale of that month the note names is the Silver/Newberry duplicates sale, whose lot 4 is this volume, so this lot is the candidate for the underbid (C; no bidding record seen; added 27 October 2026). Dal's note goes on in its next sentences to name the sale — November 1965, Louis H. Silver, the Newberry Library — and the Newberry's own account (Karr Schmidt 2023) says the copy was never accessioned and was sold to help defray the costs of the Silver purchase; Bruun Rasmussen 186 ran 1–4 November and the Silver sale 8–9 November 1965 (W10, 27 October 2026). || Chapter 3 state sheet, 27 October 2026: the volume is a single work in a later binding (the 1686 owner's), so it stands 'rebound' in the constituents register; no image of any leaf, board, spine or edge is held, and the two annotating hands and the underscoring the record reports remain uncompared until the Special Collections Research Center's images are ordered (ten colour TIFFs per volume at USD 10 each, on Christian's list). The Danish side of the 1965 sale: Dal's note on the Ekman auction (Bogvennen 1966, p. 205) says Rundetaarn ‘bød samtidig meget højt, men forgæves på en lignende hos Sotheby’; the one Sotheby's sale of November 1965 the note names is the Newberry Library's Silver-duplicates sale (8–9 November 1965, 369 lots, £288,998), whose lot 4 is this volume, bought by Warren Howell for Joseph Halle Schaffner (Schaffner catalogue 1977, entry 15) — so Rundetaarn's underbid most probably fell on this volume (C; no bidding record seen-02).

Sources

Notes
Gesner, De omni rerum fossilium genere (Zürich 1565, 8vo): the parchment Prachtband that Prandtl owned himself and reproduced, spread open with both boards, as the frontispiece of his catalogue of 1932; his Verzeichnis B lists it as Band XXI, ‘Prachtband, Pergament’, with the previous owner Prof. Dr. G. C. Laube of Prague, who had bought it from a Leipzig antiquarian bookseller. The volume was first noticed in 1901 by Studnička, who saw it in Gustav Laube's possession and read the number 2781 written on the spine as Tycho's own shelf number in his hand, remarking that the binding, unlike those of the Clementinum volumes relabelled in 1642, was intact — the single datum behind every estimate of several thousand volumes for the library (Norlind 1970, p. 335; Gingerich 2002, p. 323, ‘at best speculative’); the hand is Studnička's attribution. Gingerich (2002, p. 325) places the volume at the University of Texas at Austin (Harry Ransom Center), acquired with Prandtl's collection in the 1950s; his ‘private hands in Moravia’ is a conjecture, Prandtl's own account being the Leipzig trade. Catalogued by the University of Texas Libraries at QE 362 G391d 1565, Harry Ransom Center Book Collection, with the local note ‘Wilhelm Prandtl Collection’; the record names neither Tycho nor the binding, and the volume is not digitised. Examined and photographed at the Ransom Center on 7 October 2026 (twenty photographs: both boards with a ruler, the spine straight on and in raking light, the pastedowns and flyleaves, the title page, and the leaves that carry marks). The boards, about 17.5 × 11.5 cm, are as in Prandtl's plate: the portrait oval with the distich Hic patet exterior Tychonis forma Brahei / pulchrius enitet quae latet interior on the upper board, the arms with its distich on the lower, each within a lozenge of gilt foliate roll, with corner fleurons and a border roll; the portrait oval measures about 8 × 6 cm against the ruler, which is the larger of Mortensen's two dies (7.6 × 5.8 cm), not the smaller (5.9 × 4.3 cm in Mortensen’s measurement of 1931, 5.8 × 4.3 in that of 1955). The spine, in four panels between gilt-ruled bands with a gilt foliate tool in each, carries no lettering, label or number at all, in direct or in raking light: the 2781 that Studnička read in 1901 is no longer visible, and whether it was inked on the parchment and has faded, or stood on a label since lost, cannot be told from photographs. The title page bears Laube's blue stamp ‘Prof. Dr. G. C. Laube, Prag’ at the foot and no other inscription; the Jesuit inscription of 1642 is absent, as Studnička's remark on the intact spine implied. The front flyleaf carries a pencil note in a modern German hand, ‘Aus Tycho Brahes Bibliothek!’, the front pastedown a pencilled ‘760’ within an oval (a bookseller's or collector's number), the title verso a pencilled ‘HS-67’ and the gutter of leaf a2 the Texas call number in pencil; the rear pastedown has the printed bookplate ‘The University of Texas — The Wilhelm Prandtl Collection — The History of Science Collection’; the rear flyleaf is blank. A leaf-through of the whole volume found one marginal entry, on p. 103 of Gesner's De figuris lapidum: beside the woodcut of the goat-engraved gem that Francesco Calzolari of Verona had sent Gesner, a pen drawing of a goat copying it, and below the paragraph a single word in a German cursive hand, apparently ‘mein’, with a long flourish — a reader's doodle in a German hand, with nothing in it to suggest Tycho, whose marginalia are Latin in a humanist cursive; pp. 16–17 of Cordus's De halosantho show only hair-thin curving lines without ink, a dry pen rather than writing. Prandtl, who noted Tycho's hand systematically in other volumes, recorded none here, and the examination confirms it: the volume carries no annotation attributable to Tycho. Walde noted in 1938 that whether the number 2781 came from Tycho himself or from some cataloguing in his library was undecided, and that if it did the library must have run to several thousand works. Prandtl's photograph of 1932 — the book opened flat, lower board, spine and upper board — shows the spine without a number (the journal impression, Philobiblon 5, p. 299, and the offprint's frontispiece agree), and Prandtl, who cites the Bericht, says nothing of one: the number was gone before he bought the book, 'some years' before 1932, that is between Laube's death on 12 April 1923 and the sale of his books. Studnička's page is specific — the number stood on the spine, written, in Tycho's manner — so something was there in 1901; what it was, a dealer's or an owner's pencil number or label cleaned off in the trade, or Tycho's own, the photographs cannot say. The three edges of the text block have not been photographed. || Chapter 3 state sheet, 27 October 2026: the 'about 80 × 60 mm' of the Ransom Center photographs is a reading in the ruler's plane before parallax correction (Gross's own caveat), not a third die size — the oval is the large die (76 × 58 mm of the six concordant sources); the volume is intact as bound for Tycho (one imprint, seven parts); the edges remain unphotographed and the spine untested under ultraviolet.

Identification

Marks securing the identification
upper board blind-stamped at the head TY ✿ BRAD, a rosette between the words (the library's photographs, October 2026; the year 1563 that Prandtl, Norlind and Mortensen read with the name is not legible in them — in raking light, 13 October 2026, the band beneath the panel shows only the remains of stamped forms on an abraded surface, a looped figure at its right end that may be the 6 — but is plain to the eye with the book in hand: the library's Rare Books Librarian, asked, read 1563 on the band without doubt, 14 October 2026; the LIBRIS note gives ‘TY BRAD 1563’); light tanned leather over boards, blind-tooled with a portrait-medallion roll of the Reformers type (one medallion lettered IOANNES HVS), a foliate roll and rules, an Annunciation panel on the upper board (legend VIRGO · MARIA · DEI · MATER · SANCTISSIMA · SALVATORVM) and a Baptism-of-Christ panel on the lower (HIC EST FILIVS MEVS DILECTVS IN QVO MIHI COMPLACITVM EST); two brass clasps, the catches on the upper board, the straps lost; five raised bands; edges plain. The numerals ‘1.’, ‘2.’, ‘3.’ on the three titles are the later librarian's, matching the contents note on the front flyleaf
Binding
Period 1 (student years, to 1565): a Saxon binding of the Wittenberg–Leipzig type, consistent with a Leipzig binder in 1563

Xenophontis libri de repub. Lacedaemoniorum & Atheniensium. Itemque de praefectura equestri, conversi in sermonem Latinum. Historia rei nummariae, sive de nomismatis Graecis & Latinis (1556) (no. 44)

Chain of custody
  1. Anders Sørensen Vedel (1542–1616), Tycho’s preceptor at Leipzig from 1563 disputed
    His name ‘Andreas Seuerinus Velleius’ at the head of the first title. Walde (1920) and Mortensen (1955) read the volume as Tycho’s gift or exchange to Vedel; Norlind (1970, p. 366) read it the other way, as Vedel’s book given to Tycho, who had it bound — in which case it did not leave the library in his lifetime and its road to Sweden is unknown. — Walde 1920; Mortensen 1955; Norlind 1970; Mortensen 1942

    No owner is recorded between Vedel and De la Gardie. A mechanism for the gap: in the Danish war of 1658–60 Magnus Gabriel De la Gardie ‘acquired … big parts of the collections of Gunde Rosenkrantz (1604–1675), in which large portions of books previously owned by Holger Rosencrantz (1574–1642) and Anders Sörensen Vedel (1542–1616) could be found’ (Sjökvist 2024, p. 35) — Vedel's books as a body, not this volume, are named; a Rosenkrantz mark in the volume would raise it (C-04). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021; Sjökvist 2024
