Handwriting survey
680 images examined; 31 images with handwriting flagged, 7 uncertain (an automated survey of the facsimile; no hand attributed). Kinds: marginal notes (images 19, 20, 21, 22, 24, 30…); diagrams and tables (images 33, 34, 129, 143, 155); underlining or marks (images 90, 176); corrections (images 124).
Sources
Prandtl 1932; Walde 1920; Walde 1938; Norlind 1970; Mortensen 1955; Thoren 1990; Uppsala UB 2026 — catalogue, photographs, EOD facsimile; Uppsala UB, Alvin record 805325; Sjökvist 2024; Mortensen 1942; Kleinschnitzová 1933; Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021
Notes

Prandtl’s Band III, the Sammelband of 1563: Camerarius’s Hippocomicus with his Latin Xenophon (Leipzig 1556), Osius’s Historia excidii Hierosolymorum (Wittenberg 1558) and Garcaeus’s Tractatus de erigendis figuris coeli (Wittenberg 1556), in that order, the three titles numbered ‘1.’, ‘2.’, ‘3.’ in ink. Light tanned leather over boards with rich blind tooling and traces of clasps, the front board stamped TY BRAD and dated 1563; Vedel’s name ‘Andreas Seuerinus Velleius’ at the head of the first title; Magnus Gabriel De la Gardie’s red seal inside the front board; a handwritten index on the rear endleaf (the library’s catalogue; the LIBRIS note common to the three records: ‘På främre pärmen tryckt: "TY BRAD 1563"; på titelsidan handskrivet: "Andreas Seuerinus Welleius"; Magnus Gabiel De la Gardies röda sigill på främre pärmens insida’). Walde, who came upon the volume at Uppsala, took it for a book Tycho procured on the study journey of 1563 and soon gave or exchanged to Vedel, his companion on that journey — in an exchange Tycho may have received the Glareanus of 1536 that Vedel bought in August 1564, now at Prague (19 G 20); Mortensen followed him; Norlind read it the other way, as Vedel’s book given to Tycho, who had it bound with the two others.

The library’s facsimile of October 2026 (the text block only; binding, pastedowns and endleaves not photographed) shows the annotation leaf by leaf. The Camerarius carries a red-brown subject heading at the head of sig. A2 recto, red-brown underlining of the Greek style-terms in the preface (image 24) and of the opening of De nominibus equestribus (p. 97), and pen strokes against a passage on p. 141; the Osius nothing beyond its ‘2.’ and a small numeral ‘7’ at the foot of one page (image 58); the Garcaeus the ‘strödda marginalanteckningar’ of the catalogue — subject headings and section numbers in the calendar chapters (images 19–37 of the Garcaeus), the solar cycle for 1555 worked by long division (33), the dominical-letter table numbered by hand with the years 1488–1501 and a 1–7 counter (34), ‘obliquam’ correcting the misprint ‘aliquam’ (124), figures checking the Elector August’s nativity and part of fortune (129, 143, 155), the rule of the part of fortune written out (136), the revolution of 1556 recomputed from Reinhold’s tables (171: ‘Ego R[…] juxta Reinholdum ☉ in 16 37 ♌’), a note on the meridian of Reinhold’s equinox table (174: Königsberg at longitude 44¼ against 53½, ‘37 circiter min[uta]’), ‘Directionis finis’ with underlining at Propositio XXII (176) and a faint unread note (152). These are two registers of a sixteenth-century hand, in brown and black ink; whether they are Tycho’s student hand of 1563–65 or Vedel’s is not decided. Thoren (1990, p. 17) and Christianson (2020, p. 24) record that Tycho, during his Leipzig studies, bought ‘an astrological work by Johannes Garcaeus’ and began a notebook of horoscopes on its model; Thoren’s note points to this copy.

The library’s photographs (Alvin record 805325) show the rest: the upper board with TY ✿ BRAD at the head and the Annunciation panel, the lower board with the Baptism-of-Christ panel, the Reformers roll, the brass catches of the lost clasps, five raised bands, plain edges; on the front pastedown the library’s labels (‘Script. graeci (Xenophon)’, ‘Pp. IX. 2. 398’) and Magnus Gabriel De la Gardie’s red wax seal; on the front flyleaf verso the older shelfmarks ‘V. XI. 4.’ and ‘238’ and a contents note in an eighteenth- or nineteenth-century library hand (‘Accedunt: 2. Hieron. Osius … Witeb. 1558. 3. Joh. Garcaeus Jun. … Witeb. 1556’), whose numbering is the ‘1.’, ‘2.’, ‘3.’ written on the three titles; and on the rear endleaf, in a sixteenth-century cursive, an unfinished index of the Garcaeus — ‘Index monstrans quid quaelibet propositio in hoc libello contineat’, propositions I to V with their signatures (B, C, D …), a pen flourish beneath. The index is in the same hand, and belongs to the same work, as the marginal headings and section numbers of the Garcaeus, and it was written in the bound volume: whoever annotated the Garcaeus did so after the binding of 1563 — the owner of the bound book, Tycho in 1563–65 or Vedel afterwards; the index is the longest specimen of that hand.

The year 1563, read on the upper board by Prandtl, Norlind and Mortensen, is not legible in the photographs, nor in the three raking-light photographs the library supplied on 13 October 2026: the band beneath the panel, where a Saxon binder stamps the year under the owner’s name, carries the remains of stamped forms — a looped figure at its right end that may be the 6, the rest on an abraded surface — but no numeral can be read from them. With the book in hand the year is plain: Peter Sjökvist, the library’s Rare Books Librarian, confirmed in October 2026 that 1563 is seen quite clearly with the naked eye and that there is no doubt that is what stands on the binding. The year therefore stands on four readings of the book itself — Prandtl, Mortensen, Norlind and Sjökvist — and on the library’s catalogue note; the photographs fail to reproduce it, they do not contradict it. The Alvin record names De la Gardie, Tycho Brahe and Vedel as former owners. A Sammelband at KB, RAR:142 A, bound with Peucer 1553, is a different volume. The volume is kept in Specialsamlingar; the Osius also carries the older control number Pp:398 (2). Sjökvist (2024, p. 35) supplies the mechanism the chain lacked: in the Danish war of 1658–60 De la Gardie ‘acquired … big parts of the collections of Gunde Rosenkrantz (1604–1675), in which large portions of books previously owned by Holger Rosencrantz (1574–1642) and Anders Sörensen Vedel (1542–1616) could be found’ — Vedel's books as a body, not this volume, are named (added 27 October 2026).

Chain of custody
  1. route unknown from 1601
    The route out of the library is undocumented: the library remained with Tycho’s heirs in 1601 (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76, 78), but nothing places this volume with them, and the first dated witness on the copy is the inscription of 1647.

  3. route unknown

  4. Felix Mainx, Prague from 1938
    Mainx told Mortensen in 1938 that he had acquired Tycho’s copy (Mortensen 1955, p. 30). — Mortensen 1955
  5. ‘A private European collector’ until 2001

Links
No online catalogue record traced; the location rests on the source named above.
Sources
Martayan Lan Cat. 28 (2001); Gingerich 2002; Mortensen 1955; Norlind 1970; Kleinschnitzová 1933
Notes
Martayan Lan’s description (Catalogue 28, item 55, pp. 66–67, headed ‘Tycho Brahe reads & annotates the new star of 1572: unpublished notes on “the greatest cosmological crisis in Western history” – Grafton’): 4to; 229, (1) pp., (5) ff., 284 pp., 18 ff.; three woodcut star charts and several depictions of constellations and related astronomical phenomena in the text. Binding: contemporary flexible vellum with yapp edges, a gilt medallion portrait of Tycho in the centre of the front cover, worn, with ‘Hic patet exterior Tychonis forma Brahei / pulchrius eniteat, quae latet interior’ in the surround; the back cover with the Brahe family arms and ‘Arma genus fundi pereunt durabile virtus / et doctrina decus nobilitatis habent’; covers soiled, remnants of ties; an old shelfmark stencilled on the spine. Condition: front endleaf soiled, with unidentified later annotations; waterstain and soiling in the upper right corner of the title and on scattered leaves; a scored former ownership inscription and a later inscription dated 1647; even toning, occasional light browning; ‘for a working copy, very good’. The price asked was US$ 300,000. The annotations in Tycho’s hand range from a word or two to notes virtually filling the margin; on pp. 124–125 of Book II the lower-margin note was entered with the copy held upside down (the colour plate at the front of the catalogue, captioned ‘Tycho Brahe’s Annotated Copy No. 55’; Gingerich 2002, fig. 1). The dealer supplied a list of the annotated locations with a partial transcription, and Anthony Grafton’s detailed but preliminary report, available on request, which found a genetic relation to the Progymnasmata (Prague 1602); Owen Gingerich confirmed the hand (per litteras, 25 May 2001) and wrote that the book ‘contains source material used directly by Tycho in composing his Progymnasmata … this is a working text that is feeding directly into his published work, and we have nothing else like this’. The dealer called it ‘one of only two known copies of any book owned by the astronomer in private hands’. Provenance as given: ‘a private European collector. In 1955, the Danish librarian H. Mortensen described the present copy as being in the private collection of a professor in Prague’ – that professor is Felix Mainx, who told Mortensen in 1938 that he had acquired Tycho’s copy (Mortensen 1955, p. 30); Gingerich 2002, p. 326, which places the book in Mortensen’s own collection about 1955, misreads Mortensen’s paper. Gingerich 2002, p. 327: Tycho annotated heavily the section on Muñoz’s observations of the new star of 1572 and quoted the passage in the Progymnasmata; n. 16: now in the hands of a private American collector. References cited by the dealer: Norlind 1970, p. 347; Adams G-373; Durling 2042; Warner, The Sky Explored, p. 92; Daston & Park, Wonders and the Order of Nature, p. 175; Christianson 2000, p. 139; Prandtl 1932 (cited by the offprint pagination, pp. 1–16).

O1 verso, a marginal heading reading, in the reproduction, ‘Motus diurnus Cometae in suo circulo’ beside Apianus's table of the comet's daily motion)

  2. Schöner, Johann, Aequatorium astronomicum (Nuremberg, 1521) — bound with Apianus's Astronomicum Caesareum of 1540 in the T.B.O. 1583 volume (1521) (no. 255)
Chain of custody
  1. route unknown from 1601
    The route out of the library is undocumented. The star names written in French on the planisphere and a note partly in Dutch, partly in Flemish place the volume around Antwerp or Brussels for a very long time; Gingerich supposed Jesuit hands, a conjecture (Gingerich 2002, pp. 327–328).
  2. A monastery library in the Low Countries c. 1960
    Gingerich 2002, p. 328. — Gingerich 2002
  3. A private owner in Belgium null–c. 2000
    Who wrote to Gingerich about the binding stamp about 2000 (Gingerich 2002, p. 327). — Gingerich 2002
  4. A private collector in the United States from c. 2001
    Gingerich 2002, p. 328. — Gingerich 2002
Links
No online catalogue record traced; the location rests on the source named above.
Sources
Gingerich 2002
Notes
Gingerich 2002, pp. 327–328: about two years before he wrote (so about 2000) an e-mail enquiry came from Belgium about a copy of Apianus's Astronomicum Caesareum bound with an even rarer equatorium, an earlier one by Johann Schöner: why, the owner asked, would books printed in 1521 and 1540 be in a binding stamped 1583, with the initials TBO above the date? Gingerich recognised Tycho's mark at once. Further enquiries showed several annotations by Tycho, all in the comet section near the end; fig. 2 (‘courtesy of another private collector’) is a detail of f. O1 verso with Tycho's marginalia beside the table of the comet's daily motion. Additional early annotations in other hands – the star names on the planisphere in French, a note on the facing page partly Dutch and partly Flemish – place the book around Antwerp or Brussels for a very long time; until about 1960 it was in a monastery library. Gingerich imagines it migrated to the Low Countries by the same Jesuit hands that brought the Wittich Copernicus to Liège. ‘This extraordinary volume has changed hands again, to an anonymous American collector who must have paid close to a million dollars for it.’ Gingerich, who had examined over a hundred copies of the Astronomicum Caesareum without finding one associated with Tycho, took this to be the copy Tycho retained when he gave Wittich his (the Chicago copy, with Tycho's presentation inscription; Tycho later complained it had cost him 20 florins). It is distinct from both the Chicago copy and the copy Tycho inscribed at Wittenberg on 14 June 1599, now at Gotha (Prandtl Band VI). Neither the monastery, the Belgian owner nor the American buyer is named.

Handwriting in the digitised volumes

An automated survey of the facsimile images of 29 digitised volumes locates handwriting and classifies it by kind (marginal notes, underlining, corrections, ownership inscriptions, stamps): 13,510 images examined, 1,023 of them carrying handwriting of some kind. It is not a leaf-by-leaf examination except where a record says so, and it attributes no hand. The Prague volumes carry, besides whatever Tycho wrote, the hands of earlier owners and the accession notes of the Jesuit houses, 1636–1675 (the Clementinum, Chomutov, Krumlov). Only the most informative images of each volume are listed, by image number, so that the facsimile can be opened at them; no reading of the annotations is offered here. The Uppsala volume’s facsimile is not online.

Notes
Marked Tychoniana, not his: a post-Tycho 1606 imprint in the Bibliotheca Tychoniana (Prandtl's Kepler-volume evidence). Kukula first published the volume in 1906–07 (no. VII of the seven found since 1902, Sign. XIV J 199): Kepler's De stella nova (Prague 1606) and De Jesu Christi vero anno natalitio (Frankfurt 1606), ‘Ex bibliotheca Tychoniana’ on the first title; he took the two tracts, printed five years after Tycho's death, as proof that the family and Kepler kept the library together after 1601 and 1604 and added to it. The inference is not followed here: the volume is a post-Tycho imprint that the Jesuits marked as Tychoniana. || The June 2026 census 'marginalia' (pp. 66–70, 205, 207, 265) are Kepler's printed side-notes, and its 'Sochs 1637' a misreading of 'Soc[ieta]tis' (re-read 27 October 2026): the volume carries no reader's annotation known and every manuscript mark on it is the college's or the library's.

6Concordance of the catalogues

The concordance takes a reference from the earlier literature (a number of Prandtl’s Verzeichnis A or B, a volume or an item of Kleinschnitzová, a page of Norlind’s Bilaga I, a record of the National Library, a shelfmark) and gives the entry it stands for in this edition and the place where the book is today. It is set out twice from this edition’s side, by work and by volume, and once from the side of each earlier catalogue, in that catalogue’s own order. Every table ends in the same two columns, This edition and Held today; a reference that answers to no entry says why.

Prandtl’s misprints and slips, as read against Prusík 1901 and Kleinschnitzová 1933:

  • A15 'FERNETIUS / Fernetii' for Fernelius (inherited from Studnička).
  • A27 Band XV constituents printed '(23, 10, 27)' for (28, 10, 27).
  • A30 Band XIX constituents printed '(30, 24)' for (30, 25).
  • A26 and A27 are one book (14 H 190); Band XV has two constituents.
  • A6 / Band IX is a doublet of A5 / Band VIII (Prusík’s ‘1548’).
  • A44 'Tubingae' for Oppenheim (Koebel) 1518.
  • A52 'libri tres' for libri tredecim; XXIII is a Sammelband, not an Einzelband.
  • A58 'Wittenberg' for Leipzig (Camerarius, Valentin Papst 1556).
  • XVI: Crusius inscription placed 'auf dem Titelblatt von 55' and dated 1673; it stands on the title of 54 (first in the volume) and is dated 5 August 1654, 1673 being the Chomutov catalogue entry.
  • XXII 'Einzelband' (a Sammelband of four Rantzau pieces); IV, XXVIII describe states that no longer existed in 1932 (the manuscript removed before 1901; the Christmann an adligat of Scheiner 1631 by 1901).
  • XXV: Per Hierta had died in 1924.

Kleinschnitzová 1933

Her 47 volumes with the 104 items she lists in them, one row to an item. Her three groups: I, Collegium Soc. Jesu Pragae ad S. Clementem, nos. 1–23; II, Collegium Soc. Jesu Commotovii, nos. 24–42; III, Andere Provenienzen, nos. 43–47.

e-letter-braun-theatrumGeorg Braun & Frans Hogenberg, Theatrum urbium / Civitates orbis terrarum (the city-atlas; sought the further volumes)18 October 2026The fourth part of the Civitates orbis terrarum that was at Hven in December 1588 was Rantzau’s loan (Norlind 1926, p. 218, among the loans; Opera omnia VII, 386; Rantzau’s own copy is at Augsburg, Gebele 1926), and Norlind found no evidence that Tycho owned parts I–III; a borrowed book is outside this catalogue.
e-letter-munoz-novastellaJerónimo Muñoz (Munosius), Libro del nuevo cometa / De nova stella (Spanish, Valencia 1573)18 October 2026No document attests the book as Tycho’s: he asked Hagecius for Muñoz’s Spanish tract on the new star on 25 January 1590 (Opera omnia VII, 224); Hagecius answered on 1/11 June 1590 that he had his own copy, the author’s gift, and no one to translate it (VII, 251: ‘MUNNOSIJ libellum de nova stella Hispanico idiomate, ab ipsomet olim mihi missum et donatum, habeo, qui tamen eum Latinum faciat, habeo neminem’) and sent nothing; Tycho withdrew the request on 3 August 1590 (VII, 270), and the Progymnasmata say he never saw the text (III, 80). The store had read Hagecius’s letter as a gift.

Where the located volumes are today. The National Library of the Czech Republic holds 52 of the 72 volumes — those the Clementinum college itself received as a gift, inscribed in 1642, and those gathered there from the other Jesuit houses after 1773; the remaining 20 are in 13 institutions in 8 countries and, for 2 of them, in private hands. The table counts only volumes identified as Tycho’s own; the map plots the institutions that hold them, so the privately held volumes are not on it.

8The ownership marks

Tycho’s books are recognised by the marks his binders and his own hand put on them. The bindings form a datable sequence. In the student years the name was stamped on the boards — TVCHO BRADE / ANNO 1561 on the volume now at Helsingør, TY BRAD 1563 on the Uppsala Sammelband, TYCHO / BRAHE 1567 on the Strahov Euclid — or the initials alone with the year, T. B. 1560 (18 J 318) and 1567 (10 G 47); all of these are earlier than Hven. From 1576, when Uraniborg was furnished, the gilt cipher T.B.O. (Tychonis Brahe Ottonidis — Prusík 1901, p. 198) stands on brown leather with the year beneath it, 1576 on most of the books, then 1580, 1582 (Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 81) and 1583 (Gingerich 2002); where these bindings were made is not settled — Prandtl places a binder on Hven (1932, p. 9), Kleinschnitzová argues a Copenhagen workshop from the stamps shared with Vedel’s bindings (1933, p. 82); she also recorded Danish waste in two boards — a Danish print, an arithmetic she supposed, with a Dutch gospel print in the T.B.O. 1576 binding of 14 A 66 (no. 34), and a Danish manuscript fragment of the seventeenth century in the rebinding of 40 F 39 (no. 14). From 1588 the presentation bindings carry the gilt portrait-and-arms supralibros, Prandtl’s Prachtband (1932, p. 11); one of them, the Strahov Opus palatinum, was struck after 1599 by a Prague binder of the Rudolfine circle (Voit 2020). Books received ready-bound, and gifts, may carry only his handwritten initials or a purchase-note. The four periods are Prandtl’s (Verzeichnis B, 1932, pp. 13–14), after Prusík (1901, p. 198 n.); the date ranges are this catalogue’s, from the dated stamps, and are the scale used in the volume records.

The dies of period 4 are dated by the presentation copies of De mundi (1588): the Sascerides copy, Royal Danish Library LN 428 4° ex. 1, its dedication dated 20 March 1588 (Norlind 1970, p. 122; the census of De mundi); the Scultetus copy at Görlitz, portrait and arms, dedication dated 8 May 1588 (Norlind 1970, p. 124); the Maestlin copy in the British Library, dedication dated 14 May 1588 (Norlind 1970, p. 122).

36 of the 72 volumes carry no binding period in their record: books in another owner’s binding or rebound after they left the library, manuscripts, bindings stripped of their covering, and bindings not described at first hand.

Recognition checklist

  • An oval gilt portrait medallion on the upper board, with the distich ‘Hic patet exterior Tychonis forma Brahei…’, in two sizes — about 76 × 58 and 58 × 43 mm, as measured in the table below — indicates a presentation binding of period 4, Prandtl’s Prachtband (1932, p. 11).
  • The arms oval on the lower board, with ‘Arma genus, fundi pereunt; durabile virtus…’, accompanies the portrait.
  • The gilt cipher T.B.O. on brown calf with a rhomboid arabesque and the year beneath indicates period 3; the same cipher with no year reported is Prandtl’s period 2.
  • Handwritten ‘T. B.’ initials or a purchase-note on the title-page mark gifts and copies received ready-bound.
  • The Jesuit accession inscription ‘A. 1642 / Ex Bibliotheca Tychoniana’, or a Chomutov, Krumlov or professed-house catalogue entry (Chomutov 1645–1675, two of them Crusius’s gifts of 1654), indicates the Jesuit road — the Clementinum, or a Jesuit house whose library came to it after 1773.

A caution. The Clementinum’s inscription Ex Bibliotheca Tychoniana is not by itself proof of Tycho’s ownership: the Jesuits went on adding to the Tychoniana after his death. Sign. 14 J 199, two Kepler tracts of 1606 bound together, carries the inscription. Kukula (1906–07, p. 25) and Prandtl (1932, p. 16) read it as a sign that the heirs and Kepler kept the library together and added to it; Kleinschnitzová excluded it from her census because Tycho died in 1601 (1933, p. 83). It is recorded here among the volumes marked Tychoniana but not his. Conversely, a volume bearing only the Jesuit inscription and no binding-stamp may still be Tycho’s where its imprint predates 1601: on that ground Kleinschnitzová admitted the plain-bound Clementinum volumes (1933, p. 83).

9Acquisition and dispersal

How the books came to Tycho, and by what roads they left the library — a few in his own lifetime, the rest after 1601. The acquisition channels are reconstructed from the correspondence and from the purchase-notes and dedications on the surviving copies. The roads of dispersal are the routes by which the volumes reached their present holders, each with the marks it leaves on a book; the chain of custody of every located volume is set out station by station, each step with the record that documents it, and where the record is silent the gap is stated as a gap. The figure reads the chains as one descent, from the library to the 14 institutions and the private hands that hold its volumes today.

How the books came to Tycho, as far as the correspondence and the purchase-notes and dedications on the copies show it; an entry is assigned to a channel only where a document names the route, so most entries carry none.

Road V has no located volume by definition, and the 108 titles without a located copy (§13) are not its measure: a title stands there because no copy has been identified, not because one is known to be lost.

The roads in detail

0 — Left the library in Tycho’s lifetime: gifts and exchanges 4 volumes

Books that left the library in Tycho’s lifetime: the Apianus he gave Paul Wittich at Hven on 29 October 1580, the Apianus at Gotha in which he wrote a dated motto for Duke Friedrich Wilhelm of Saxe-Weimar on leaving Wittenberg on 14 June 1599 — his own book given at parting, as the Gotha library reads the entry, or the duke’s book in which he wrote, as Norlind thought more likely —, the Calvin–Theocritus Sammelband dedicated to his cousin Hans Lindenov in exile, and — if Walde and Mortensen are right against Norlind — the Sammelband of 1563 that carries Vedel’s name. These volumes left the library before it was dispersed and reached their holders by roads of their own.

I — The Jesuit road: the Clementinum (1642), the colleges at Chomutov and Krumlov and the professed house, reunited in the Clementinum after 1773 51 volumes

Tycho's son-in-law Frans Gansneb Tengnagel — a Catholic convert who ran the posthumous editions — had intended to continue Tycho’s work and died in 1622 (Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 76); the heirs, pressed by the lawsuit over the unpaid purchase price, parted with their possessions piecemeal, the earliest dated step out of the library being of 1623 (p. 76); a part of the library came as a gift to the Jesuit Collegium Caesareum at the Clementinum in Prague (Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 76, after Volf). The volumes so given — twenty-three survive — carry on the title ‘Collegij Caesarei Societatis Jesu Pragae A° 1642’, in most cases with ‘Ex Bibliotheca Tijchoniana’ and ‘Musaei Mathematici’, and were shelved as the separately kept Musaeum Mathematicum, whose books are known by the red-brown double lines on their white spines (p. 78). A larger group came to the Jesuit college at Chomutov (Komotau), apparently in the same way (p. 76); a single volume each reached the college at Krumlov — by exchange in 1654 from Andreas Scherhackl of Budějovice, who had owned it since 1623 — and the professed house on Prague’s Malá Strana (pp. 76 and 78); the suppression of the Society in 1773 and the secularisation of the monasteries brought these fragments together again in the Clementinum (p. 78) — nineteen volumes of Chomutov provenance by 1933 (p. 81). Šolc's accounts of 1999 (§ 2.533, printed p. 150) and 2006 (printed p. 192) give the nineteen the Chomutov inscription ‘Collegij Societis JESU Commotouij Catalogo inscriptus A.’ with a year between 1671 and 1675 — the 1645 entry of 44 F 38 and Crusius's gifts of 1654 lie outside that range — and add that four further Tychonic volumes reached the Clementinum itself as gifts (‘Stiftungen’) of private persons whose names stand on their title pages; he names neither the donors nor the volumes. The store's Crusius volumes (5 G 92, 5 J 103) were gifts to the Chomutov college, not to the Clementinum, so they are not Šolc's four; which four he means is open (see lead-crusius-layer). The National Library’s provenance survey of its Jesuit stocks (Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021, p. 30) registers 215 volumes with Chomutov inscriptions, seven of them given to the college before 1600, and among them ‘minimálně čtyři knihy z pozůstalosti Tychona Brahe’, all with the supralibros ‘TBO 1576’ on the front board and the Chomutov inscription on the title; its authors connect the college’s unusual holding of mathematics and astronomy with P. Jan Jüngling (1705–1775), keeper of the Clementinum’s mathematical library in 1749 and prefect of the Chomutov library in 1765–1766, and suppose these books to have been duplicates of the Clementinum college’s library. The Museum itself was removed after 1773 to the lodging of its last keeper, Joseph Stepling, and returned only after his death in 1778, a custody in which losses occurred, at Karel Rafael Ungar's cataloguing of the 1780s the Tycho volumes were then distributed among the University Library's subject departments, predominantly department 14 (Šolc 2006, printed p. 192) — he does not say what the first element of a present shelfmark denotes —, and the librarians of the Clementinum later broke up some of Tycho's Sammelbände and bound his books with others' (p. 80), which is why some of his volumes now hold works that were never his. In the chains of custody the Mathematical Museum is named as a station only where the volume itself carries the words (‘Musaei Mathematici’, ‘Bibliothecae Mathematicae’ or the Museum's spine marking); the college alone is named otherwise. Gingerich's 2002 survey of the Clementinum volumes counts the marks as follows: sixteen carry the initials 'T.B.O.' tooled on the binding, six the gilt supralibros portrait, twelve the initials written in by hand, and two are author presentations (Bruno and Scaliger). Clear marginalia in Tycho's hand appear in only a few — among them the Ziegler In C. Plinii of 1531, in its Martianus Capella section, and Bartholomaeus Scultetus's Cometae of 1577. Šolc's own later wording (2006, p. 192) is ‘věnováno’ — donated — for the harder-to-sell, mostly astronomical remainder, with the Vitellio–Dürer volume reaching the Jesuits ‘probably by sale’ in 1636; the Handbuch's ‘gekauft’ (Faltysová 1999, § 1.13, after Tobolka) is the other reading, and neither cites a document. Two documents frame the Chomutov road without explaining it: in 1623 the heirs' claim on the Chamber was assigned to the tax arrears of four royal towns, Chomutov and Kadaň among them — the instructions to the towns dated Chomutov 26 September 1623 and Kadaň 3 July 1626 (Volf 1932, part 2, p. 23), and the college that received Tycho's volumes had lost its library to the Saxon plunder of 1631, partly bought back the next year (Veselá 2025, pp. 27–29), so that the first dated accession of 1645 entered a library being rebuilt. Whether either tie carried books is undocumented. The duplicates road under Jüngling cannot account for the dated Chomutov entries: he was prefect of the Chomutov library in 1765–66, a century after the inscriptions of 1645–1675, so for the inscribed volumes the choice is between the heirs, the college's own purchases and local private donors such as Crusius (the research round of 27 October 2026).

II — The heirs’ dispersal into private hands (after 1601) 4 volumes

During the lawsuit over the purchase price the heirs parted with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library with them: ‘so manches Werk wanderte auch in Privatbesitz’ (Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 76). The volumes placed here are those whose first recorded owner after Tycho is a private collector of the seventeenth century; what else left by this road is untraced. Since 20 October 2026 the road also carries the Strahov Euclid of 1558 (AV II 2), formerly on a road of its own (VII): it passed from the heirs to Gabriel Crusius — his graphite ‘G. Crusio ‹K›’ on the title, the formula his gift volumes at Chomutov carry in ink — and from him by private hands to Jan Josef Klauser (1705–1771), whose library Strahov bought in 1775; it carries no Jesuit inscription. The Ramus AG XIV 7 began the same way, Crusius giving it to the Chomutov college on 5 August 1654. Kleinschnitzová's 2 A 8 (e-kl-43), inscribed by Andreas Scherhackl of Budějovice in 1623 and given by him to the Krumlov Jesuits by exchange in 1654, belongs here too, not on the Jesuit road: its first owner after the heirs is a private man.

III — The Swedish booty of 1648 (Königsmarck’s capture of the west bank of Prague) 1 volume

The 1648 Swedish capture of Prague carried off Rudolfine/Bohemian holdings, including Tycho material, to Sweden. The first Tycho items documented on this road are not books of the library: two manuscripts — a parchment copy of the star catalogue and a Solis et Lunae motus diarii of 1598–99 — and a printed book in a presentation binding, from Rudolf II’s collection at the Castle, shipped with the Castle’s books in 1648–49 and entered in the Stockholm royal library’s catalogue of 1650–51 under Frans Tengnagel’s name, all three untraced (Veselá 2025, p. 142). The Castle was the one Prague collection the Swedes confiscated systematically; the Old Town Jesuit college and the university libraries were untouched, which is why the core of 1642 was never at risk (p. 256). The recataloguing at Stockholm in 1650–51 stripped the booty’s spine marks, and Vossius removed the royal library’s signatures from the books he took in 1654: a volume without a Swedish mark is not thereby excluded from this road (pp. 208–214, 228). The database of the Swedish book plunder (Knihovna AV ČR, searched in full on 19 October 2026: 4,367 records) holds no Tycho imprint from its Prague-Castle group of 79 records (47 under Rudolf II, 20 under Ferdinand III) and no book of Tycho's own; its three Tycho imprints came by other roads — Dudith's De mundi with the Dietrichstein library of Mikulov (Stockholm KB), Hermann Bulder's De mundi and Tycho's dedication copy of the Mechanica to Petr Vok with the Rožmberk library (Stockholm University Library; Copenhagen). Tengnagel's name returns nothing.

IV — Rudolfine-imperial absorption 0 volumes

Rudolf II had the instruments and the manuscript observations ceded to him by contract (Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 75), and books may have passed into the court’s orbit with them; none is documented. No located volume is placed on this road: the one candidate, the Vienna manuscript of the Commentariolus, enters the record by an undocumented step and stands on the road of unknown route. Veselá reads the three Stockholm items — two manuscripts and a print — as Tycho’s personal gift to Rudolf II on his arrival in Prague, an inference she marks as such (2025, p. 142). The one catalogue of the Castle library, of 1636 (Riegger 1795, pp. 214–230), is Ferdinand III’s library and not Rudolf’s, whose books had largely gone to Vienna after 1612, and a Habsburg supralibros is not proof of Rudolf’s ownership: any claim that a book of Tycho’s passed through Rudolf’s hands has to pass that test (pp. 140, 150).

V — Attrition / loss

War, fire and untraced dispersal account for the gap between the library as it stood at his death and the remnant located today — no single catastrophe, but a long attrition that left no mark to search by. No located volume belongs here by definition, and the titles without a located copy are not its measure: a title is unlocated because no copy has been identified, not because one is known to be lost; the size of the loss is bounded only by the size of the library, which is itself disputed.

VI — Out of the Jesuit stock after 1773 without staying in the Clementinum: Strahov (Strnad), Teplá, Kórnik 4 volumes

Two volumes carrying the 1642 inscription are now at Strahov, not in the Clementinum: Rheticus–Otho's Opus palatinum (Σ V 5/a) and the Regiomontanus Ephemerides (DR VII 19). The documented route out of the Clementinum is the one Boldan & Vackářová describe for the Mathematical Museum's library: after the suppression of 1773 Karel Rafael Ungar screened the incoming Jesuit and monastic books for duplicates, the observatory director Antonín Strnad bought part of the surplus astronomical volumes for himself, and from his estate they passed to Strahov, which bought the substantial part of his library after his death in 1799 (Munzar 2001). Straka gave exactly this chain for the Regiomontanus in 1913 — Clementinum → Strnad → Strahov — though Strahov's present cataloguer notes that the volume appears in neither published catalogue of Strnad's library (Seydl 1939; Kouklová 1989). The spine is the test: the Mathematical Museum's books carry no ex-libris, only red lines and an abbreviated title on the spine, and Strnad's books his handwritten name or name-stamp. Seydl identified the Strahov volumes from Strnad's library by matching his own book-list, in two hands, against the Strahov volume catalogue (Hyklová 2017, p. 49) — the method behind the cataloguer's finding that the Regiomontanus is in neither list. The library's own record of DR VII 19 nevertheless places the volume in the Clementinum's Mathematical Museum before it came to Strahov, and Munzar and Pařez (2002, p. 369) supposed the Strahov purchases from the Clementinum stock were made ‘probably not before’ 1773. Two volumes show the same leakage from other Jesuit stocks. The Bianchini of Teplá, inscribed at the Clementinum in 1642, is now in the Premonstratensians' library there by an undocumented step. Heidenstein's De bello Moscovitico (Basel 1588), in Tycho's portrait-and-arms binding and catalogued at Chomutov in 1671, never reached the Clementinum at all: it is at the Biblioteka Kórnicka (Cim.Qu.2812), its route there — the volume carries older shelfmarks and stamps not yet identified — still to be established. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 81) supposed that the Chomutov stock reached the Clementinum only in part; the Kórnik volume is the first located proof of it. The Bianchini's Teplá station closed in 2006–07, when the National Library bought the Teplá monastery's manuscripts, incunabula and paleotypes and the volume returned to the Clementinum (NK ČR STT 000005829, accession 07/ORST 394); the road keeps Teplá's name as the house it passed through.

VIII — With the observation books: Kepler, Ludwig Kepler, Frederik III (after 1604) 1 volume

The manuscript observations went a road of their own: Kepler received them under a contract with Tengnagel of 1604 and never returned them; after his death in 1630 his son Ludwig held them as a pledge against the court’s bond of 1633 and sold them to Frederik III of Denmark — in 1655 on Mortensen’s account (1955, pp. 31–32), ‘at the latest in the beginning of 1662’ on Dreyer’s (1890, Appendix, pp. 370, 373). A leaf of another man’s observations sewn into Tycho’s own codex travelled with them.

U — Route out of the library unknown 7 volumes

Volumes identified as Tycho’s by their marks that surfaced in the trade or in a later collection with no documented step between his library and their first recorded later owner. The chain of custody records the gap as a gap; the later stations are given with their sources.

The custody of the surviving volumes

For every located volume, one station per documented custodian, with the dates the record gives, the basis of each step and its source; a step the record does not document is a station of its own, set in red as “route unknown”, and a contested step is flagged “disputed”. The volumes stand by road and, within the Jesuit road, by the house whose inscription they carry; the grade is that of the volume’s identification.

  1. Hans Lindenov, Tycho’s cousin (Tycho’s gift) from 1597–1601
    Tycho’s dedication ‘Johanni Lindenouio consobrino suo Tycho Brahe ddt’ on the verso of the free endpaper facing the title. The recipient is Hans Christoffersen Lindenov til Ørslevkloster (d. by 7 April 1610): lensmand at Bergenhus 1578–86, where the four royal letters on Tycho's Nordfjord fief were addressed to him (29 May 1579, 10 August 1580, 8 January 1581, 16 March 1586; TBOO XIV, pp. 9, 14, 19; Friis 1871, p. 161), landsdommer in Nørrejylland from 1587, holder of Ørslev Kloster by exchange with the crown from 1584, lensmand at Hammershus 1594–1610, the fief withdrawn on 3 January 1610 for infirmity (DAA 1902, pp. 286–287; Bricka X, pp. 316–318). He crossed to Hven with Tycho in the night of 3–4 July 1594 and left on the 5th — ‘rediit D. T. cum Hans Lindenov et D. G.’, ‘Abiit Johannes Lindenow’ — his one visit in the diary (Friis ed. 1876, pp. 218–219). Tycho's consobrinus: Mortensen read the word strictly, Hans a son of Christoffer Lindenov's first marriage with Margrethe Clausdatter Bille (b. 1525), sister of Tycho's mother Beate, against DAA 1902, which lists him under the second wife Ide Rantzau; DAA dates neither marriage and no later Rettelser took the point up, so Mortensen's reading stands unrefuted (Mortensen 1955, p. 27; DAA 1890, p. 87). The Calvin edition was on sale at the Frankfurt Lent fair of 1597 (Lutz, A2v, under ‘Libri Calvinianorum’) and cannot have been among the books registered at Uraniborg on 21 March 1597 (the diary, p. 263; Mortensen prints 10 March); Mortensen puts the gift probably before 1599, unless the book was sent to Lindenov later (pp. 26–27: ‘sandsynligvis har han faaet Bogen i Tiden før 1599, hvis den da ikke paa et senere Tidspunkt er blevet sendt til ham’). Lindenov sat on Bornholm from 1594, so the book was handed over elsewhere or sent; the strict window is 1597 to October 1601. Examined 21 October 2026: the dedication read on the leaf (see the marks). Kancelliets Brevbøger place Lindenov on Bornholm throughout 1597–1602 — the lensbrev from 1 May 1597 (pp. 126–127), the missives of 20 June and 26 July 1597 (pp. 171, 187), the new lensbrev from 1 May 1599 (p. 419), the Gæsteri letters of November 1600 in which his castle clerk brought the account to Copenhagen (pp. 561, 563–564), the stranded munitions of 12 November 1601 (p. 684) — and record no summons to Copenhagen; no herredag met in 1597, and he had needed royal leave to go home in February 1596 (the 1593–96 volume, p. 585). A hand-over in Copenhagen in April–May 1597 is therefore possible but undocumented, and a sending to Bornholm or Ørslev from Wandsbek, Wittenberg or Prague the more economical reading; the chancery, Tycho's own papers (the index of the Opera omnia has no Hans Lindenov after 1586) and the son's album give no trace of him in Germany or Bohemia. The enfeoffment with Hammershus dates from 20 June 1594, two weeks before he crossed to Hven with Tycho; the landsdommer's office in Jutland was no longer his in 1597–1601, when the chancery addresses the landsdommere Mogens and Iver Juel separately. — Mortensen 1955; Fund og Forskning 1963; Danmarks Adels Aarbog 1902; Danmarks Adels Aarbog 1890; Bricka, DBL X (1896); Friis (ed.) 1876; TBOO; Lutz, Lent-fair catalogue 1597; Copenhagen examination 2026; Kancelliets Brevbøger 1596–1602; Kancelliets Brevbøger 1593–1596

  3. The Clementinum library after the suppression of the Society: the public University Library, since 1990 the National Library of the Czech Republic, Prague from 1773
    The college library passed to the state with the suppression of 1773 and became the public University Library in the Clementinum; the Tychoniana were mixed with the other mathematical books and reassembled by the librarians around 1900 (Šolc 2002, p. 329). — Šolc 2002

    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970
  2. route unknown until 1671
    No owner is recorded between the heirs and the Chomutov college’s catalogue entry. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 76) supposed that the college came by Tycho’s books in a way similar to the Clementinum’s gift; Císařová Smítková, Paličková and Vackářová (2021, p. 30) suppose Clementinum duplicates passed on under Joannes Jüngling, who kept the Clementinum’s mathematical library in 1749 and was prefect of the Chomutov library in 1765–1766; the college’s dated catalogue entries on Tycho’s volumes are of 1645 to 1675. — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021
  3. Jesuit college, Chomutov (Komotau) 1671–1773
    The inscription ‘Collegij Societatis JESU Commotouij Cat. inscr. A. 1671.’ on the title, as the National Library’s record transcribes it. — NKP, Staré tisky (Aleph); Kleinschnitzová 1933
  4. The Clementinum library after the suppression of the Society: the public University Library, since 1990 the National Library of the Czech Republic, Prague from after 1773
    Brought to the Clementinum with the library of the dissolved Chomutov college after 1773; Kleinschnitzová counted nineteen volumes of that provenance in 1933 (p. 81). — Kleinschnitzová 1933

  1. Tycho’s heirs, Prague from 1601
    The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Norlind 1970
  2. route unknown until 1671
    No owner is recorded between the heirs and the Chomutov college’s catalogue entry. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 76) supposed that the college came by Tycho’s books in a way similar to the Clementinum’s gift; Císařová Smítková, Paličková and Vackářová (2021, p. 30) suppose Clementinum duplicates passed on under Joannes Jüngling, who kept the Clementinum’s mathematical library in 1749 and was prefect of the Chomutov library in 1765–1766; the college’s dated catalogue entries on Tycho’s volumes are of 1645 to 1675. — Kleinschnitzová 1933; Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021

  4. route unknown
    The volume did not come to the Clementinum with the Chomutov library after 1773. The red stamp ‘Z Hankowych’ on the title is read by the Kórnik cataloguer as Václav Hanka's (1791–1861) (Muszyński 1977, no. 583 and index p. 253), and the entry's mark ‘[A. T. Działyński-kat. Kiel.]’ places the volume in Kielisiński's card catalogue of 1840–c. 1847: it passed from Chomutov to Hanka in Prague and from him, in his lifetime, to Tytus Działyński's Kórnik. When and how it left Chomutov, how Hanka came by it, and what the older shelfmarks ‘H. VI. 365.’ and ‘C: 157.’ denote (Muszyński omits the concordance) remain undocumented. — Muszyński 1977
  5. Václav Hanka (1791–1861), Prague — his stamp ‘Z Hankowych’ by c. 1847

1957:0030
Helsingør, Maritime Museum
AU
  1. route unknown
    The route out of Tycho's hands is undocumented. The fly-title (Thykier's ‘forperm’) carries two struck ownership lines — ‘tico brade ven:’ on the recto and ‘Sum Thÿchonis Brade’ [I am Tycho Brahe's] on the verso, as the museum reads them (Thykier 2003 read the recto's as ‘Tyge Brahe’ and ‘tico brahe ven’) — which may mark a transfer in his lifetime or a later owner's cancellation. A third inscription in a firmer hand, ‘Sum Pauli’ [I am Paul's], is the only name of a later owner the volume yields: Thykier read it as ‘Sum Paul…’ with the rest lost on the torn-off part of the leaf, but the examination of 20 October 2026 shows it complete to its last letter, so the owner's first name is all the leaf ever carried of him. The book was used as a herbarium by a hand other than Tycho's, one of whose plant names is unattested before c. 1623 (Thykier 2003, after Wagner and Baagøe), so it was in a plant-collector's hands after Tycho's death. It stands in no Prague catalogue and its first title carries none of the Jesuit, Chomutov or Crusius marks of the Bohemian roads. The spine label, a paper slip with the figures ‘20[4]’ written in ink, records a library between Tycho and the Munich trade that no source names (Thykier: ‘formodentlig katalognummeret i Tychos eller et senere bibliotek’ [presumably the catalogue number in Tycho's or a later library]; the dossier of 20 October 2026); the rear flyleaf adds a faint ‘N 36’ at the head and a small blind-stamped cartouche near its gutter — a second earlier number and a dealer's or restorer's mark, both unread (examined 20 October 2026). — Thykier 2003; Museernes Samlinger (M/S Museet for Søfart), the object record 1957:0030; Helsingør examination 2026
  2. Antiquariat Weiss & Co., Munich by 1932
    Prandtl 1932, the captions of his plates (pp. 2–3: ‘Seinerzeit im Besitze des Antiquariats Weiss & Co., München’ [at the time in the possession of the antiquarian firm Weiss & Co., Munich]) and p. 3 (‘kürzlich von München aus nach Amerika verkauft’ [recently sold from Munich to America] — wrong about the first step, see the next station); the Verzeichnis B entry for Band II names no location. The volume is in none of the firm's four digitised catalogues (1926–1930). — Prandtl 1932, pp. 292–293 (Sonderdruck pp. 2–3)
  3. Maggs Bros., London 1933–1938
    Catalogue 582 (1933), item 155, p. 92, £125, with every copy-specific identifier (the stamps, the half-torn fly-leaf, the purchase note, the Helsingborg note) and Prandtl cited for ‘our volume’; Catalogue 600 (1934), item 260, £125; Catalogue 666 (1938), item 451, p. 166, still £125, the entry reprinting Catalogue 600's text. The pencil ‘+125’ at the head of the front pastedown is this price. The firm's archive (British Library Add MS 89311) would name the seller. — Maggs 582 (1933), p. 92, item 155; Maggs 600 (1934), p. 208, item 260; Maggs 666 (1938), p. 166, item 451; New York Times Book Review, 28 May 1933, the issue (lending copy)
  4. Herbert Reichner, New York c. 1939–c. 1940
    Catalogue 1 ([1939]), item 72, probably $850 — Reichner was Prandtl's publisher in Vienna and emigrated to New York in 1938–39; the volume is in none of his Catalogues 2–9 (1940–48). — Reichner, Catalogue 1 ([1939]), the catalogue record (search-only; ‘Brade’ matches one page)
  5. route unknown from c. 1940
    The buyer from Reichner is not recorded; no American auction appearance 1930–58 (American Book Prices Current); Rare Book Hub has no record. Mortensen (1955, p. 25) knew of no such volume in Denmark, which bounds nothing: the volume was then in private hands, and the Tycho literature took no notice of the museum's report of 1957 until Norlind 1970. The one physical trace of the interval is the volume's box: a brown cloth clamshell box with a gilt spine label lettered in English (‘Tycho Brahe's copy with autograph ownership notes, etc.’), made in the English-speaking trade or for the American owner (examined 20 October 2026). — Mortensen 1955, p. 25; Helsingør examination 2026
  6. Oscar Ekman, engineer, and Lia Ekman, Copenhagen until 1957
    The museum's report of its acquisitions of 1956–57 (Klem, Årbog 1957, p. 8; Thykier 2003 dates the gift to January 1957 and names Oskar Ekman alone): ‘en gave fra fru Lia Ekman og afdøde ægtefælle, civilingeniør Oscar Ekman’ [a gift from Mrs Lia Ekman and her late husband, the engineer Oscar Ekman]. Oscar Ekman (b. Copenhagen 13 October 1885, owner of Nordisk Elektricitets Selskab from 1913, d. 16 September 1956) had been a life member of the museum's friends' society since 1944–45; Lia Ekman (née Pouplier, b. Hamburg 1894, d. 1965) remained one to her death. Their source for the volume is not recorded; at the sale of their library (Bruun Rasmussen 186, November 1965) it was shown as a withdrawn show-piece, as Erik Dal reported in Bogvennen 1966. The museum's accession note on the rear pastedown, ‘Gave jan. 1957 fra civiling. Oskar Ekman’ [gift, January 1957, from the engineer Oskar Ekman] (read 20 October 2026), enters the gift in January 1957 under Oscar's name, four months after his death: a gift in the dead man's name, made by his widow — which is what Klem's wording, Thykier's and Dal's ‘testamentarisk bortgivet’ [given away by bequest] each describe. The sale catalogue itself (Bruun Rasmussen 186, p. 111, lot 497, read 29 October 2026) lists the volume under ‘En Bog fra Tycho Brahe's Bibliotek’ for completeness only — ‘This copy will not be sold as it was given to the “Handels- og Søfartsmuseet” at Kronborg according to the last will of ingeniør Ekman’; the Danish text ‘foræret … af ingeniør Ekman og kan beses der i en af udstillingsmontrerne’ — so the gift was a bequest under Oscar's will, executed by his widow in January 1957, and the volume stood in a showcase at Kronborg in November 1965. — Handels- og Søfartsmuseet, Årbog 1957, p. 8; Kraks Blå Bog 1937, p. 276, s.v. Ekman; Bogvennen 1966, pp. 200–207, the passage on the Tycho volume; Thykier 2003; Helsingør examination 2026; Bruun Rasmussen 186 (1965)
  7. M/S Museet for Søfart (Handels- og Søfartsmuseet på Kronborg), Helsingør, inventory 1957:0030 from 1957
    The Ekmans' gift of 1956–57 (Årbog 1957; the museum's record); restored 1957 by Birgitte Dall. Deposited at the Royal Library's Håndskriftafdeling in 1986 as Acc. 1986/116 (the Kronik of 1987; the department's newsletter of November 2001), lent from there to the Ole Rømer Museum's exhibition ‘Tycho Brahes mange ansigter’ [Tycho Brahe's many faces], 25 October – 31 December 2001; in the museum's own keeping again, confirmed 13 October 2026, the date of return unrecorded. Examined and photographed at the museum on 20 October 2026: the Kronborg stamp and ‘30:57’ on the rear pastedown, ‘Acc. 1986/116’ in pencil on the fly-title and the pastedown and on the slip in the box, the plant envelopes in place, the box lettered in English. — Handels- og Søfartsmuseet, Årbog 1957, p. 8; Museernes Samlinger (M/S Museet for Søfart), the object record 1957:0030; Magasin 1987, pp. 31–33; Royal Library, Håndskriftafdelingen, Aktuelt (November 2001), ‘Udstillinger’, November 2001; Björklund 1992; Museet for Søfart 2026; Thykier 2003; Helsingør examination 2026

10Owners and custodians

Every person, house, firm and library through whose hands a surviving volume passed, from Tycho’s heirs to the holders today, in alphabetical order: the role, the dates the record gives, the volumes, and under each volume the basis of the step and its source. The names stand as the records give them — an owner not identified is listed as such, and the two American private collectors are two entries, not one. Where the Familia has the person, the name opens its record there.
