11Chronology

The dated events in the history of the library: its formation, the acquisition campaigns, the marks, the exile, the dispersal, and the rediscovery of the surviving volumes by modern scholarship. Each event carries the source it rests on, in the short form used throughout this chapter; the full references are in the sources section.

DatePhaseEventSourceEntries
14 December 1546LifeTycho Brahe born at KnutstorpChristianson 2000
1560FormationProcures the Ephemerides of Stadius after the eclipse of 21 August — the first book of Dreyer’s account, and the ‘few books, particularly ephemerides’ of Tycho’s own; no copy survivesDreyer 1890, p. 14; Christianson 1967, pp. 202–203Stadius, Johannes, Ephemerides novae et exactae
1560FormationSacrobosco’s Libellus de sphaera (Wittenberg 1558), Bayrus’s Enchiridion (Basel 1560) and Macer’s herbal (Basel 1559) bound in blind-stamped pigskin lettered ‘T. B. 1560’ (Prague, NK ČR 18 J 318) — the earliest dated binding attributed to Tycho, on the cipher alone — no inscription, no annotation, no note of 1642, the one Tycho volume from the Jesuit professed house (ownership C since 29 October 2026)Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 47; Christianson 1967, pp. 200–201; Šolc 2018, figs 1a–cBayrus, Petrus, De medendis humani corporis malis Enchiridion (1560); Sacrobosco, Johannes de, Libellus de sphaera (1558); Macer Floridus (Odo of Meung), De herbarum virtutibus Aemilii Macri Veronensis elegantissima poesis, cum … Georgii Pictorii … expositione (1559); 18 J 318
30 November 1560FormationThe Prague Ptolemy (Basel 1551) bought at Copenhagen for 2 thaler by Johannes Pratensis, whose name and 1561 binding it carries — Dreyer’s reading of the note as Tycho’s own, repeated from Friis to Šolc 1999 without a comparison, has no positive support (the hands compared 2026); Tycho’s later, probably from Pratensis’s estate after 1576 (ownership B since 29 October 2026)Dreyer 1890, p. 14; Friis 1868–69, p. 267; Studnička 1901, p. 39; Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 74; Boldan & Vackářová 2024, pp. 144–145; the hand comparison of 25 October 2026Ptolemaeus, Claudius, Claudii Ptolemaei Pelusiensis Alexandrini omnia quae extant opera praeter geographiam (1551)
1561FormationRegiomontanus’s Tabulae directionum (Tübingen 1550) and Apianus’s Cosmographia (Paris 1553) bound in calf stamped ‘TVCHO BRADE’ and ‘ANNO 1561’, bought for a thaler and four groschen — the earliest purchase note, beside an ownership entry in Tycho’s name; the one surviving volume documented as Tycho’s before he left Denmark on 14 February 1562, the place of purchase an inference from the year (Helsingør, M/S Museet for Søfart 1957:0030)Prandtl 1932, Band II; Museernes Samlinger 1957:0030; Christianson 1967, p. 201Regiomontanus, Johannes, Joannis de Monte Regio tabulae directionum profectionumque; ejusdem Regiomontani tabula sinuum (1550); Apianus, Petrus, Cosmographia (per Gemma Frisium) (1553); 1957:0030
1562FormationTo Leipzig to read law; buys astronomical books and instruments with money accounted for to his tutorDreyer 1890, pp. 15–17
1563Formation‘Ty Brad 1563’ sammelband (later gifted to Vedel; now Uppsala)Prandtl 1932, Verz. B, Band III; Mortensen 1955, p. 27Garcaeus, Johannes, Tractatus brevis et utilis de erigendis figuris coeli (1556); Osius, Hieronymus, Historia excidii Hierosolymorum longe luctuosissimi, cuius exemplum & memoria his temporibus maxime videtur accommodata & necessaria. Item historia Ioseph filii Iacob versibus enarrata (1558); Camerarius, Joachim, In hoc libro haec insunt: Hippocomicus, quae est disputatio de curandis equis. Xenophontis liber de re equestri Latinus factus. Nomina equestria Graeca & Latina. Xenophontis libri de repub. Lacedaemoniorum & Atheniensium. Itemque de praefectura equestri, conversi in sermonem Latinum. Historia rei nummariae, sive de nomismatis Graecis & Latinis (1556); Script. Graeci
1567FormationThe Strahov Euclid (Basel 1558) bound with TYCHO / BRAHE 1567 stamped on the board — the latest of the three dated name-stamps of the student years (after TVCHO BRADE 1561 and TY BRAD 1563) and the only one in the spelling BRAHEPařez 2009; Strahov Katalog Tritius, record 993601Euclid (ed. Bartolomeo Zamberti and Campanus of Novara; comm. Theon, Hypsicles), Euclidis Megarensis mathematici clarissimi Elementorum geometricorum libri XV. Cum expositione Theonis in priores XIII a Barthol. Zamberto Veneto latinitate donata, Campani in omnes, et Hypsiclis Alexandrini in duos postremos (1558)
1574-autumnFormationTycho has several copies of the Prutenic Tables bought at his own expense and distributed to the poorer students at his Copenhagen lectures — ‘Curaueram autem coëmi proprio ære aliquot exemplaria tabularum Prutenicarum’ (Tycho Brahe)TBOO I 173 (the appendix to the Oratio de disciplinis mathematicis, first printed 1913); Thoren 1990, p. 86
1575AcquisitionAn attempt to buy the books of Dr Ambrose, a citizen of Augsburg, failsMosley 2007, p. 175 (TBOO VII, 15.24–27; 84.1–2)
1576FormationGranted Hven; Uraniborg begun; the T.B.O. 1576 binding cohortPrandtl 1932, Heft 8; Norlind 1970, p. 335; Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 81
1576AcquisitionAn attempt, through Camerarius, to buy Brechtalius’s mathematical books: already soldMosley 2007, p. 175 (TBOO VII, 42.14–16)
May 1579AcquisitionMarks 13 titles in a Frankfurt fair catalogue for procurementMosley 2007, p. 167 (TBOO VII, 54.38–42); Norlind 1970, p. 333
October 1580AcquisitionGives Wittich the Apian Astronomicum Caesareum (departure gift)Mosley 2007, p. 176; Gingerich 2002, p. 327Apianus, Petrus, Astronomicum Caesareum (Ingolstadt 1540) — Tycho's presentation copy to Paul Wittich (1540)
1586The pressFirst book from the Uraniborg press: Morsing’s Diarium astrologicum for 1586, its dedication dated 1 January 1586 (the first imprints, the poems to Pratensis and Ulfeldt, are of late 1584)Nielsen 1921, pp. 178–179, 186; Christianson 2000, p. 377
1586The marksThe engraved portrait dated 1586, from which Mortensen derived the supralibros portrait stampMortensen 1931, p. 142
September 1587AcquisitionTycho learns of Wittich's death (from Rothmann)Mosley 2007, p. 175
1588AcquisitionBruno's Camoeracensis acrotismus received (author gift)Mosley 2007, p. 168; Šolc 2002, p. 331Bruno, Giordano, Camoeracensis acrotismus seu Rationes articulorum physicorum (Wittenberg, Z. Crato 1588) (1588)
20 March 1588The marksEarliest dated binding with the gilt supralibros portrait: the Sascerides De mundi (KB Copenhagen)Mortensen 1931, p. 142; Gigas 1900, no. 1, pp. 31–33
1589AcquisitionFirst attempt to buy Wittich’s library, through noble emissaries at Wrocław, failsMosley 2007, pp. 175–176 (TBOO VII, 166.10–17); Christianson 2000, pp. 223, 378
March 1592AcquisitionSeeks Rheticus’s and Copernicus’s papers from HageciusMosley 2007, p. 174 (TBOO VII, 333.39–334.1)
1595AcquisitionSecond attempt to buy Wittich’s library, through Hagecius and Monau, failsChristianson 2000, pp. 223, 378
21 March 1597ExileThe whole library inventoried on Hven (‘all the junker's books’)Friis (ed.) 1876, p. 263; TBOO IX, p. 146; Thoren 1990, p. 371
29 March 1597ExileTycho leaves Hven for the last time: 29 March on Dreyer’s reading of the observing ledger’s ‘29 Aprilis’ (Easter fell on 27 March), followed by Thoren; Nielsen keeps 29 AprilDreyer 1890, p. 238 n. 2; Thoren 1990, p. 371; Nielsen 1921, p. 204
2 June 1597ExileDeparts Copenhagen into exileChristianson 2000, p. 314
1597-06-beforeAcquisitionTycho has bought four copies of the Rheticus–Otho Opus Palatinum (1596) before Landgrave Moritz presents a fifth — ‘cuius quidem antea quaterna exemplaria coëmeram’ (Tycho Brahe)TBOO XIV 105–108 — Tycho to Moritz, Rostock, 17 June 1597 (epistolarium brahe-t_15970617001); VIII 386–388Rheticus, Georg Joachim (completed by Lucius Valentinus Otho), Opus palatinum de triangulis (1596)
October 1597ExileAt Wandsbek with Rantzau; the travelling press prints the MechanicaDreyer 1890, pp. 253–260; Norlind 1970, p. 334
1598AcquisitionThird attempt, through Longomontanus and Monau: the library found intact; negotiation opensChristianson 2000, pp. 223, 314, 378Copernicus, Nicolaus, De revolutionibus orbium coelestium (1566)
1598ExileWinter at WittenbergChristianson 2000, p. 300; Norlind 1970, p. 334
March 1598AcquisitionKepler's Mysterium cosmographicum arrives (with Ursus's tract)Mosley 2007, pp. 168–169 (TBOO VIII, 14.27–33; 46.37–40)Kepler, Johannes, Prodromus dissertationum cosmographicarum (Mysterium cosmographicum) (1596)
1599PragueEnters Rudolf II's service; assigned Benátky castleChristianson 2000, p. 300
1600PragueThe library, shipped up the Elbe and held at Magdeburg since 1599, reaches Prague in mid-NovemberNorlind 1970, p. 334 (TBOO VIII, 192; 305; 343)
16 May 1600AcquisitionAt Benátky, Baron Karl von Wartenberg shows Tycho the catalogue of the whole library of the late Andreas Dudith; Tycho keeps it to return on a visit to the baron's castle ‘seven miles’ away and asks Monau whether the heirs would let him see, and sell, the books he had markedTBOO VIII, 320.37–321.5 — Tycho to Jacob Monau, Benátky, 16 May 1600 (epistolarium brahe-t_16000516001); Mosley 2007, p. 175, nn. 281–282
14 June 1600AcquisitionMonau answers that Dudith's library ‘now hangs as if between heaven and earth’ — no longer the heirs', ‘not so much sold as pawned’ to another for a sum of money — and the pursuit ends; the Dudith copy of the De mundi that survives at Stockholm is Tycho's gift of 1588, not a purchaseTBOO VIII, 325.39–326.6 — Jacob Monau to Tycho, Wrocław, 14 June 1600 (epistolarium brahe-t_16000614001); Mosley 2007, p. 175, n. 283
October 1600AcquisitionMonau in Prague (his attestation of 23 October); the Wittich Copernicus copies presumed, not documented, to have come with him — no letter records a price, a payment or a deliveryGingerich 2002, p. 325 (‘presumably’); Gingerich & Westman 1988, p. 22 (‘the end of the story’); Monau to Tycho, 14 June 1600, TBOO VIII 325–326Copernicus, Nicolaus, De revolutionibus orbium coelestium (1566)
24 October 1601DeathTycho Brahe dies at Prague; the library remains with his heirsChristianson 2000, p. 304; Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76
26 October 1601DispersalKepler named imperial mathematician (charged with the manuscripts and instruments)Christianson 2000, p. 304; Dreyer 1890, Appendix, p. 365
December 1601DispersalThe sale to Rudolf II is dated by the king's own bond of 1614 to ‘the end of the year 1601’: Matthias acknowledges owing the six children 15,000 kop míšeňských ‘for some rare astronomical instruments and books left by their father and bought from them at the end of 1601’ (‘za některá vzáctná instrumenta astronomická a knihy … při konci léta 1601 koupené’), of which 4,000 were paid in 1603 and 1,000 in 1604; the word is ‘knihy’ — the observation books in the house's reading, the bond itself not saying which books (Rudolf II; the heirs)Dvorský 1883, pp. 70, 72 (the bond of 23 April 1614)
1602DispersalThe family, and with it the library, leaves Curtius's house for the Old Town before July 1602 (Magdalene Brahe to Eske Bille, Danske Magazin II, p. 361 ff.); a year or two before her death in 1604 the widow buys a country property towards the Saxon frontier, where the elder son marries in March 1604 — the heirs' orbit after 1602 is the Old Town and the Saxon border, the Chomutov side of BohemiaDreyer 1890, Appendix, pp. 366–368
10 January 1603DispersalThe heirs — Tengnagel with Elisabeth, Tycho and Jørgen — assign 2,000 thaler of the purchase money to Bernhard Fürst, burgher of Kiel, Tengnagel's creditor, who cedes the claim to Jan Rebeník of the Malá Strana; Rudolf orders the first 4,000 thaler paid on 23 September 1603 (receipted by Tycho and Jørgen on the 25th, Tengnagel not signing); Rebeník asks on 14 October that the heirs be gaoled until paid, and on 13 April 1604 Tengnagel pleads that he has pawned all he could and borrowed 800 thaler anew — the heirs' first documented sales of their possessionsDvorský 1883, pp. 70–71
September 1603DispersalOf the 20,000 thalers Rudolf II agreed to pay for the instruments and manuscripts, only 4,000 paidDreyer 1890, Appendix, p. 368
1604DispersalThe instruments ‘cum libris observationum’ moved to Vienna on Rudolf II’s order, ‘for greater safety’, according to Kleinschnitzová; Dreyer keeps the instruments in Prague, in a vault under Curtius’s house, until their destruction in 1619, and has the observation books pass to Kepler under his contract with Tengnagel of 1604; the library itself stays with the heirsKleinschnitzová 1933, p. 75; Dreyer 1890, Appendix, pp. 365, 370
23 April 1614DispersalMatthias's bond to the six heirs for the 15,000 kop outstanding, payable at St George 1615 and 1616 with 6,312 kop of interest in five terms — never honoured; the heirs' name is absent from the Diet's debt schedule of 1615, and the war of 1618 followsDvorský 1883, pp. 72–73
November 1620DispersalAfter the White Mountain the Protestant heirs must in time leave Bohemia — Dvorský gives no date, and Georg and Rudolf Tycho were still in Prague in November–December 1624 (KGW XIX nos. 9–10): ‘Kam se uchýlili, nevíme’ — where they went, Dvorský could not say (the children's later papers place them in Bohemia and Saxony); only Tengnagel, councillor of appeal and convert, remains, dying 1 December 1622 — where the library stood between 1620 and 1642 is undocumentedDvorský 1883, pp. 73–74; Dreyer 1890, Appendix, p. 367
1622DispersalTengnagel dies; the book-dispersal acceleratesKleinschnitzová 1933, p. 76; Dreyer 1890, Appendix, p. 367
1623DispersalA Brahe book already in private hands (Budějovice)Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 76Gessner, Conrad, Bibliotheca instituta et collecta. Tiguri 1574.
26 September 1623DispersalThe heirs' claim on the Bohemian Chamber is assigned to the tax arrears of four royal towns — Žatec (1,000 thaler), Kadaň (1,000), Rakovník (950) and Chomutov (950) — the instructions to the towns to pay from their arrears dated Chomutov 26 September 1623 and Kadaň 3 July 1626 — and the towns, unable to pay, send small instalments until 1654: a documented tie between the heirs and the two towns of the second Jesuit road and of Sophie Brahe's bequest; whether it carried books is undocumentedVolf 1932, part 2, p. 23
16 November 1624DispersalKepler urges Georg Brahe to have a careful catalogue made of all that remains of Tycho's library in books and manuscripts, and asks for the Greek Hipparchus with Scaliger's handKepler, GW XIX (1975), Nr. 7, pp. 202–203Hipparchus (ed. Petrus Victorius), the copy annotated by Joseph Justus Scaliger, In Arati et Eudoxi Phaenomena libri III (the Greek editio princeps, with Scaliger’s annotations) (1567)
18 December 1628DispersalFerdinand II allows one creditor of the Brahe heirs to come to Prague; the family sends Jørgen (Tycho the younger having died 2 September 1627); the reformation commissioners press him weekly to leave, and through the 1630s he goes every half year to Rakovník and to Chomutov to collect the interest on the towns' arrears — a Brahe heir on the road to Chomutov in the years before the first dated Tycho accession there (1645); his sister Sophie joins him during the Saxon invasion of 1631 and later turns CatholicDvorský 1883, pp. 74–76
10 November 1631DispersalFerdinand II orders part of the interest on the 70,000 thaler granted by the Diet paid to the heirs; the Saxon invasion of the same month stops the payment. In the same invasion the Chomutov college, which the Jesuits had left before the occupation, is plundered and its library confiscated — valued by the Jesuits at 10,000 gulden, the soldiers' sale realising 100 — and partly bought back in 1632; Banér holds the town in 1639, Wrangel takes it in 1645 and 1647: the Tycho volumes first dated there in 1645 entered a library being rebuilt after plunderVolf 1932, part 2, p. 24; Veselá 2025, pp. 27–29 (Schmidl 1754, p. 119; the NK survey of 2021 in n. 71)
1638The Jesuit housesA Musaeum mathematicum exists at the Clementinum: the Ryff Sammelband NK 14 E 3 is inscribed ‘Collegii Caesarei Soctis JESU Pragae Musaei Mathem: A.1638’ — the institution the Tycho books joined four years laterMačák 1995/96, pp. 74–78
1640DispersalJørgen Brahe, the heir who had pursued the debt in Bohemia, dies below Křivoklát after his last visit to Rakovník; his Rakovník bond passes by will to Rudolf Tycho Gansneb Tengnagel, imperial councillor, reformation commissioner and from 1642 captain of the Malá Strana — the family's Prague presence in the year of the Clementinum gift is now a Catholic grandson and a Catholic daughterDvorský 1883, pp. 74 n. 11, 76
1642The Jesuit housesThe surviving core passes to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, Prague (‘A. 1642’) — a gift according to Volf, Kleinschnitzová and Šolc, a purchase from the heirs according to TobolkaŠolc 2002, p. 329; Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 76–78; Volf 1932, part 2, p. 24; Fabian, Handbuch (Prague), §1.13
1642The Jesuit housesThe Opus palatinum and a Regiomontanus now at Strahov receive the Jesuit inscription with the rest of the coreStraka 1913; Boldan 2025; Strahov Katalog TritiusRheticus, Georg Joachim (completed by Lucius Valentinus Otho), Opus palatinum de triangulis (1596); Regiomontanus, Johannes, Ephemerides ab anno 1492 ad annum 1506 (Almanach ad annos XV accuratissime calculata), preceded by the gatherings a4 a10 (Ratdolt's dedication, Regiomontanus's preface, Mariensüss's Expositio) of the Venice 1481 Ephemerides ab anno 1482 ad annum 1506 (1492)
1642The Jesuit housesIn the year of the Clementinum gift Sophie Brahe bequeaths her claim on the Chamber to the Franciscans of Kadaň (15,000 fl. by Dvorský; 9,942 fl. by Volf) and Rudolf Tycho Tengnagel cedes his mother Elisabeth's share to the Dominicans of St Giles (17,500 fl. by Dvorský; Ferdinand III's assecuration of 14 March 1643 for 22,534 fl. by Volf): the heirs' three gifts to religious houses of 1642–43 are of one pieceDvorský 1883, p. 77; Volf 1932, part 2, pp. 24–25
14 March 1643DispersalFerdinand III's assecuration to the Dominicans of St Giles, Prague, for 22,534 fl. 22 kr. 4 d. — Rudolf Tycho Gansneb Tengnagel's share of the heirs' claim, given to the convent (Arch. min. vnitra, Bekennen u. Verträge 1642/65); Sophie Brahe's share (9,942 fl.) went the same way to the Franciscans of Kadaň, and both houses were paid in iron in 1672: in the year after the Clementinum gift the heirs were giving their claims, as they had given their books, to religious housesVolf 1932, part 2, pp. 24–25
1645The Jesuit housesThe incunable Sammelband 44 F 38 (d’Ailly’s Imago mundi and the Ratdolt Euclid of 1482, bound 1576, with Tycho’s monogram) is entered in the catalogue of the Jesuit college at Chomutov — the earliest dated Chomutov accession of a Tycho volume, unless the note on 14 B 11, read 1675 by Kleinschnitzová and Šolc and 1645 by the library’s cataloguer, is also of 1645Boldan & Kazanskii 2023, p. 28Ailly, Pierre d’, Imago mundi, with his astronomical treatises (the first edition) (Louvain: Johannes de Westfalia, c. 1477–1483 (GW M31954)); Euclid (Campanus recension), Elementa geometriae (the first printed Euclid) (Venice: Erhard Ratdolt, 1482); 44 F 38
26 July 1648War bootyThe Swedish capture of Hradčany and the Malá Strana; the Rudolfine collections carried to Sweden (26 July 1648 New Style; 16 July Old Style) (H. C. Königsmarck)Gingerich 2002, p. 325; Veselá 2025, pp. 133, 199–203
October 1648War bootyThe Castle’s books removed before 8 October and the Kunstkammer on 1–2 November; shipped in casks by the Vltava and the Elbe to Dömitz, then Wismar, reaching Stockholm at the end of May 1649 — two Tycho manuscripts and a Tycho print of Rudolf II’s collection among themVeselá 2025, pp. 133, 142, 202–205
1650War bootyVossius’s recataloguing of the Stockholm royal library (1650–51) enters the two Tycho manuscripts under Frans Tengnagel’s name and strips the booty’s spine marksVeselá 2025, pp. 142 n. 494, 208–214; Vossius–Callmer 1971, p. 19 no. 2 and p. 18 no. 4
10 February 1652DispersalThe last archival word on the heirs: the reformation commissioners report from the Brandýs nad Orlicí estate that Otto Tycho Brahe, the astronomer's grandson and an imperial Wachtmeister, explains at Těchlovice why his sister Kristina Barbara von Salhausen has stayed six years in Bohemia against the imperial order — she came with the Elector of Saxony's safe-conduct to collect the debt; Rakovník's envoys pay Tengnagel 35 kop on account on 9 November 1654Dvorský 1883, pp. 76–77
1654The Jesuit housesCrusius gives two Tycho volumes to the Chomutov JesuitsKleinschnitzová 1933, p. 765 G 92; 5 J 103
1654War bootyChristina abdicates; takes loot (incl. a Tychonic Copernicus) to RomeGingerich 2002, p. 325Copernicus, Nicolaus, De revolutionibus orbium coelestium (1543)
1655DispersalLudwig Kepler sells the observation-originals to Frederick III (Copenhagen)Mortensen 1955, pp. 31–32 (Dreyer 1890, Appendix, p. 373: by early 1662 at the latest)
1657DispersalThe Vienna set of observation copies in the Hofbibliothek by about 1657Friis 1868–69, p. 265 (after Mosel)
1722The Jesuit housesThe Museum's formal foundation under the rector Retz, with the astronomical tower; Caspar Pflieger first prefect (1722/23–1729/30)Seydl 1951, pp. 1–3; Mačák 1995/96, pp. 74–75 (Fischer 1978 for Pflieger, p. 74; Retz and the tower p. 75, the link offered as a possibility, n. 8 = Seydl 1938)
1773The Jesuit housesThe Jesuit suppression reunites the Chomutov/Krumlov fragments at the ClementinumKleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 78, 81
1775DispersalStrahov buys the library of Jan Josef Klauser — Tycho’s Euclid comes with it, without any Jesuit markNeškudla 2021, p. 229Euclid (ed. Bartolomeo Zamberti and Campanus of Novara; comm. Theon, Hypsicles), Euclidis Megarensis mathematici clarissimi Elementorum geometricorum libri XV. Cum expositione Theonis in priores XIII a Barthol. Zamberto Veneto latinitate donata, Campani in omnes, et Hypsiclis Alexandrini in duos postremos (1558)
1780The Jesuit housesThe anonymous Neue Chronik von Böhmen (Prague: Schönfeld 1780, ‘Beschreibung der Hauptstadt Prag’, pp. 65 and 88) sends whoever wants to see the Museum's collections to the university librarian, then Karel Rafael Ungar — a statement Seydl sets against Strnad's own petition of 1782 to the court study commission, which recalls the raises promised him in 1778, 1780 and 1781 ‘because he voluntarily took over the professorship and because he administers the museum’; Seydl's reading: the librarian received the visitors, the astronomer kept the collectionsSeydl 1951, pp. 4–5, 26, n. 13 and n. 39
1780sThe Jesuit housesAt Karel Rafael Ungar's cataloguing of the 1780s the Tycho volumes are placed in the University Library's thematically corresponding departments, predominantly department 14 — Šolc's sequence of division, moving and loss after 1778; he does not say what the first element of a present shelfmark denotesŠolc 2006, p. 192
1785The Jesuit housesThe Mathematical Museum dissolved as a whole, the University Library needing its rooms for the books of the suppressed monasteries; its portrait prints had gone to the library in 1781, when Strnad's list of its contents still ended with ‘some books’Seydl 1951, pp. 6, 26–30, 51, 57–58
1799DispersalAntonín Strnad dies; Strahov buys the substantial part of his library, into which Clementinum surplus had passed after 1773Munzar 2001, pp. 269–271; Boldan & Vackářová 2024, p. 143Regiomontanus, Johannes, Ephemerides ab anno 1492 ad annum 1506 (Almanach ad annos XV accuratissime calculata), preceded by the gatherings a4 a10 (Ratdolt's dedication, Regiomontanus's preface, Mariensüss's Expositio) of the Venice 1481 Ephemerides ab anno 1482 ad annum 1506 (1492); Rheticus, Georg Joachim (completed by Lucius Valentinus Otho), Opus palatinum de triangulis (1596)
1847DispersalBy c. 1847 the Heidenstein of 1588 (Cim.Qu.2812), inscribed by the Chomutov college in 1671, stands in Kielisiński's catalogue at Kórnik with Václav Hanka's red stamp — the one Chomutov volume known to have left Bohemia, by way of Hanka's PragueMuszyński 1977, no. 583 and p. 253; BolewskaCim.Qu.2812
1868RediscoveryFriis surveys the Tychonic manuscripts in Vienna and PragueFriis 1868–69, pp. 250–268
1868RediscoveryCount Franz von Klebelsberg, descendant of Rudolf Tycho Tengnagel's daughter, gives the Bohemian National Museum a collection of books and manuscripts concerning the Brahe and Tengnagel families, the Stammbuch of 1598 among them; no printed book from Tycho's library is named in the giftMortensen, ‘Tycho Brahe Minder i Prag’; Mitteilungen des Österr. Vereins für Bibliothekswesen 5 (1901), pp. 51–52
1881RediscoveryŠafařík distributes photolithographs of the standing-Tycho watercolour in the Házmburk Progymnasmata at StrahovŠafařík 1881, p. 273
1901RediscoveryPrusík lists the Clementinum Tychoniana after the recataloguing: four manuscripts and sixteen printed works in four groups by bindingPrusík 1901, pp. 197–201
1906RediscoveryKukula counts five manuscripts and fifty printed works in twenty-eight volumes, seven of them found since 1902; Ludwig Rosenthal's Zwinger volume with the plaques is published in the same number, and Bargum answers that its binding is Danish workKukula 1906–07, pp. 17–25; ZfB 1906–07 (binding note), pp. 42–43; Bargum 1906–07, pp. 124–126Zwinger, Theodor, Theatri humanae vitae volumen decimum-octavum [the last tome, volumina XVIII–XXIX: 33 books, pp. 3251–4373 and the index] (1587)
1913RediscoveryStraka publishes the weather note in the Strahov Regiomontanus and attributes it to Tycho's handStraka 1913Regiomontanus, Johannes, Ephemerides ab anno 1492 ad annum 1506 (Almanach ad annos XV accuratissime calculata), preceded by the gatherings a4 a10 (Ratdolt's dedication, Regiomontanus's preface, Mariensüss's Expositio) of the Venice 1481 Ephemerides ab anno 1482 ad annum 1506 (1492)
1915RediscoveryHjalmar Wijk gives Per Hierta's collection of bookbindings to the Röhsska museum, Göteborg — most probably the road of the Zwinger with Tycho's plaques, which Prandtl still placed at Hierta's Främmestad in 1932, eight years after Hierta's deathSBL 19, p. 32; Nordisk familjebok, 4th ed., p. 528Göteborg, Röhsska Museum — Theatri humanae vitae volumen decimum-octavum
1926RediscoveryNorlind's first list from the letters: thirty-two printed works, the unprinted writings and the loans that Tycho's own statements place on HvenNorlind 1926, pp. 211–218
1932RediscoveryPrandtl publishes the first printed catalogue of the libraryPrandtl 1932
1933RediscoveryKleinschnitzová’s census of the Clementinum Tychoniana: 97 works in 47 volumesKleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 81, 83
1938RediscoveryWalde publishes the Braunsberg copy of Scaliger's De emendatione temporum (Leiden 1598) in blind-stamped parchment with the plaques, and the books of Tycho's amanuensis Johannes Eriksen in Queen Christina's libraryWalde 1938, pp. 11–17Scaliger, Joseph Justus, De emendatione temporum (revised ed.; Leiden, Plantin 1598) (1598)
1940RediscoveryFelix Mainx prints a three-page notice on the Strahov library: its original editions of Copernicus, Tycho Brahe and Kepler ‘from the possession of the Prague astronomer A. Strnad’, two Stammbücher with entries of Melanchthon and of Brahe, and no supralibros volume — three years before his report of the eight volumesMainx 1940, printed pp. 41–43; the Tycho sentences printed p. 43
1942RediscoveryMortensen's intermediate count: 110 works in 57 volumes (the 47 Clementinum volumes with those at Göteborg, Braunsberg, Dresden, Gotha and Mnichovo Hradiště, the Mainx, Prandtl and Mortensen volumes, the Uppsala Sammelband of 1563 and the volume of 1561), superseded in 1955 by 67 volumes with 121 worksMortensen 1942, p. 25; Mortensen 1955, p. 31
1943RediscoveryMainx reports eight supralibros volumes in a Prague monastery; they have not been traced sinceMortensen 1955, p. 30(eight unidentified authors), [Eight unidentified Tycho-owned books, superexlibris and autograph marginalia, found in a Prague monastery, 1943]
1945War bootyThe Dresden Sammelband (Paulus Alexandrinus 1588 – Rantzau 1588 – Boiemus 1587, in Tycho's parchment with his plaques) is lost: the SLUB's war-loss register carries the Boiemus under Lit.Graec.B.1976 (earlier Phil. gr. B. 93a. 12Definitions and conventions

How an entry is to be read — its status, its two grades, its units, its road — what each figure in this chapter counts, what each source attests, and what is known of the size of the library the figures describe.

How to read the entries

Status. Located: a physical copy identified as Tycho’s own survives and is recorded with its shelfmark. Attested, not located: a document names the book as Tycho’s, but no copy has been found; within this class, retired as unlocatable marks a mass-survival text whose copy would carry no known mark to search by. Disputed: ownership or identity is contested and the entry is kept out of the located count. Lost: a copy is recorded as destroyed, or as having vanished after being seen. Tychoniana, not his: a book that came down among the Tychoniana without having been Tycho’s — bound into one of his volumes after it left the library, or carrying the Clementinum’s Tychoniana note though printed after his death (Kleinschnitzová’s Kein Tychonianum); it belongs to the history of the Jesuits’ Tychoniana, not to his library, and carries no grade.

Grades. Two independent A–D scales are used. An entry’s confidence grades how securely the book can be asserted to have been Tycho’s: A, secure (a surviving copy with his marks, or an unambiguous document); B, probable; C, possible, resting on inference; D, doubtful. A surviving volume’s identification grades how securely that particular copy is his: A, his marks or hand on the copy itself; B, a catalogue or scholarly identification without a mark checked at first hand; C, circumstantial; D, doubtful. A located entry may still stand at C where the volume is identified by its marks but the text bound in it is not. The grades are never rounded or removed; the entries marked Tychoniana, not his, carry none.

Units. Entries count works, not volumes: every separately printed work, and every manuscript, bound in a volume identified as Tycho’s has an entry of its own — the works bound in after the volume left his library included, and so marked; a part of one imprint (a second title within the same edition) is not a separate entry. A Sammelband therefore holds several entries. Volumes count physical objects. No ratio of located to attested entries is a survival rate: a work enters the located tier because a copy was found, and most of that tier was compiled from the surviving Prague volumes in the first place.

Roads and custody. Each located volume is assigned to one road: the route by which it passed from the library to its present holder, named for the custody that determined it — a gift of Tycho’s lifetime, the Jesuit houses — the Clementinum’s own gift of 1642 and the colleges whose libraries it gathered after 1773, the imperial collections and the Swedish booty of 1648, the observation books, private hands of the seventeenth century; where no step out of the library is documented the road is recorded as unknown. Each volume carries a chain of custody: one station per documented custodian, with the dates the record gives, the basis of the step and its source. A gap in the record is a station of its own, route unknown; a contested step is marked disputed. Roads are counted in volumes, never in entries, and the counts sum to the volumes identified as Tycho’s. An acquisition channel — how a book came to Tycho — is recorded only where a document names the route; most entries carry none.

Numbers. Every entry carries a fixed number, assigned once in the alphabetical order of 19 October 2026 and never re-assigned: an entry added later takes the next free number, a retired entry keeps its number and is listed, with the reason, in the register of retired entries under the concordance. Every surviving volume likewise carries a volume number. Cite an entry as ‘Bibliotheca Tychoniana no. N’ with its record key, a volume by its number and shelfmark.

The other indexes. The concordance is read by entry, by volume, and by each earlier catalogue’s own numbers (Prandtl’s, Kleinschnitzová’s, Šolc’s, Norlind’s and the National Library’s former-owner index), each number answered by an entry or by the reason it has none; one search box narrows all its tables at once. The owners and custodians stand in an index of their own, each with the volumes that passed through their hands.

The roads

The codes used in the Road column of the holdings, in the volume records and in §9:

  1. 0 Left the library in Tycho’s lifetime: gifts and exchanges
  2. I The Jesuit road: the Clementinum (1642), the colleges at Chomutov and Krumlov and the professed house, reunited in the Clementinum after 1773
  3. II The heirs’ dispersal into private hands (after 1601)
  4. III The Swedish booty of 1648 (Königsmarck’s capture of the west bank of Prague)
  5. IV Rudolfine-imperial absorption
  6. V Attrition / loss
  7. VI Out of the Jesuit stock after 1773 without staying in the Clementinum: Strahov (Strnad), Teplá, Kórnik
  8. VIII With the observation books: Kepler, Ludwig Kepler, Frederik III (after 1604)
  9. U Route out of the library unknown

The size of the library

The library’s original size is unresolved: the estimates run from Mortensen’s ceiling of 1,000 volumes to Christianson’s ‘over three thousand’, and the higher figure rests on a single shelf-number.

EstimateProposed byBasis
over 3,000 volumesChristianson (2000), pp. 102, 201, 404 n. 12the shelf-number 2781 that Studnička read in 1901 on the spine of the Gesner of 1565, now in Austin, where the spine shows no number; reported by Norlind
‘at best speculative’Gingerich (2002), pp. 323–324‘similar numbers are apparently not found in the other surviving volumes, so Norlind’s deduction is at best speculative’; nevertheless a library of 3,000 titles ‘would not be unreasonable’ beside Rantzau’s 6,000 and Dee’s about 4,000
at most 1,000 volumes (about 2,000 works)Mortensen (1955), p. 31what the circular Museum room at Uraniborg, 5 m across and also holding the great globe and the smaller instruments, could have held, and the argument that a larger library would have left more survivors: ‘Forsigtig tør man maaske sætte Antallet af Bind til højst 1000 svarende til omkring 2000 Skrifter’
about 5,000 volumesO. Walde (letter to Mortensen, 1938)the figure Mortensen printed without attribution in 1942, p. 25 (‘Tallet har vel naaet circ. 5000 Bd.’), gave in 1955, p. 31, as Walde’s estimate in a private letter of 1938, and judged probably too large (‘vistnok for stort’): it would need more room than the Museum had, and more books would have survived

Norlind himself wrote that it is impossible to form any estimate of the library’s size, crediting the 2781 inference to Studnička (Norlind 1970, p. 335).

What each source attests

The two tiers are built in opposite directions: the located tier works backwards, from a surviving volume to the entry it proves; the attested tier works forwards, from Norlind’s catalogue and Tycho’s letters to a book that has not been found.

Outside the count: Eight unidentified Tycho-owned books, superexlibris and autograph marginalia, found in a Prague monastery, 1943 (Mortensen 1955) is a placeholder record, with a page of its own and a place in the chronology, but no entry of the catalogue.

The Clementinum count

Kleinschnitzová (1933) records 97 works in 47 volumes; Šolc (2002) extends this to about 110 titles in 50 volumes, counting the volumes his survey added and several bound-in parts as titles. This edition itemises 106 works in 52 National Library volumes. 94 of them carry her numbers — her 34:3, Ptolemy’s Centiloquium, being the Liber fructus appended to the Bonatus of 1550 and counted with it — and 12 stand beyond her list: the pieces the library’s own records add to her volumes (the Strabo of 14 F 8, Peurbach’s Tractatus of 7 B 22, Apianus’s Instrumentum of 14 A 63, the Grynaeus and the Erastus of 14 H 192), the three volumes Šolc found (XV K 22, XXXI H 26, XIV B 38) and the two incunables of 44 F 38. The works she marks Kein Tychonianum are entered as not his, the Apianus Cosmographia of 14 J 164 as disputed, and the parts of one imprint that Šolc counted as titles — Rantzau’s praedictiones, Commandino’s De horologiorum descriptione, the De regibus Bohemicis, the Maurolico dialogues, Brucaeus’s sine doctrine — are not counted.

13Desiderata

What remains to be found or resolved. 108 attested titles have no located copy: 58 carry a trace worth following (a title, an attestation, a last-known location), 42 are retired as unlocatable because the text survives in quantity and Tycho’s copy would carry no known mark to search by, and 8 are recorded as lost. The disputed identifications and the open questions attached to individual records follow. A scholar who can settle any of these is invited to write.

Aslakssön, Cort); Zinner no. 3699; VD16 A 3899Cort Aslakssøn (Cunradus Aslacus, Cort Axelsen; Bergen 1564–1624), Tycho’s famulus on Hven 1590–93 and later the first Norwegian professor at Copenhagen. Full title: De natura caeli triplicis libelli tres, quorum I. de caelo aëreo, II. de caelo sidereo, III. de caelo perpetuo, e sacrarum litterarum & praestantium philosophorum thesauris concinnati (Siegen [Sigenae Nassoviorum]: Christoph Rab, Christophorus Corvinus, 1597). VD16 A 3899; Zinner 3699; [7] leaves and 214 pages, octavo (VD16; the ‘4°’ at Norlind, p. 339, is an error). Written and printed while Aslakssøn was abroad as tutor to Otto Brahe (matriculated at Basel 1596/97). The book is dedicated to Tycho (Norlind, p. 339; Store norske leksikon), whence Norlind’s inference that it ‘har väl alltså befunnit sig i Tychos bibliotek’. The ownership rests on that inference alone: no copy with Tycho’s marks and no presentation copy is recorded in the inventories of Prandtl, Kleinschnitzová, Šolc or Mortensen, or in the trade. In the preface Aslakssøn declares for Copernicus, a position Tycho rejected, so that the dedication stands in tension with the book’s own position. The work is a ‘Mosaic physics’, a synthesis of astronomy and scripture on the three heavens (elemental or aerial, astronomical or sidereal, eternal or perpetual); Comenius later listed Aslakssøn among the Mosaic physicists who preceded him. Book III, De caelo perpetuo, was translated into English as ‘The Description of Heaven … Composed in Latine by Cunradus Aslachus, and conuerted into English by Raph [Ralph] Iennings’ (London 1623; EEBO A22193). Copies of the edition survive in Munich (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek), Vienna (Österreichische Nationalbibliothek) and Copenhagen (Royal Library); none is Tycho’s. The dedicatory epistle, read in the Munich copy, is addressed ‘Tychoni Brahe de Knudstrup, fundatori Arcis Uraniburgicae … sideralis scientiae scrutatori, instauratori, conservatori unico’, dated Basel, 16 November 1596, and signed ‘Cunradus Aslachus Bergensis’; it hails Tycho as ‘indefessus Caeli scrutator & Atlas’ and pays eyewitness homage to his celestial globe and astronomical instruments.

The purchase was conditional: the bookseller had deposited the books with Brucaeus at the beginning of the winter and would take them back if Tycho did not want them or already had them (‘Emi autem hac conditione, ut si tibi forte non placerent, aut forte eosdem iam esses nactus, Bibliopola ad se recipiat … Iam enim libros ineunte hyeme apud me deposuit’, VII, 100); whether this copy reached Hven is not recorded (Norlind 1926, p. 214, no. 3). That Tycho had the work is his own statement to Rantzau of 22 February 1597: Clavius’s writings on Euclid, on Sacrobosco and on gnomonics ‘in promptu habeo, et iamdudum introspexi’ (VII, 381). In December 1584 the Rostock bookseller, back from Frankfurt without the books Tycho had ordered, had sold his one copy, valued at nearly five Joachimsthaler, to Heinrich Rantzau (Opera omnia VII, 88; Norlind 1926, p. 214, no. 3), so Tycho’s first order went unfilled.

Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C).

Copernicus, Nicolaus)Norlind 1970, p. 343: the letter Copernicus wrote at the request of Bernard Wapowski, canon of Kraków, on Johann Werner’s De motu octavae sphaerae; the comet book quotes a passage from it, and Tycho says there that he owns the text in a second- or third-hand transcript (Opera omnia IV, 292). No manuscript from his library is identified; the surviving transcripts of the letter have not been examined for the question.
66Cramer, DanielIsagoge in Metaphysicam AristotelisHanau, 1594, 8°BNorlind 1970, p. 344 (s.v. Cramer, Daniel)Dedicated to Tycho on the title page; Cramer visited Hven in the summer of 1592; Tycho is praised in an epigram on p. 13 and his world-system is named on pp. 217–218. Norlind (p. 344): the book ‘bör alltså ha funnits i biblioteket på Hven’ — must therefore have been in the Hven library. The ownership rests on the dedication alone; no copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified. Norlind (p. 344) transcribes the dedication ‘Ad Tychonem Brahe, Danum, virum nobilem et in astronomia facile principem’. Imprint: Hanau (Hanoviae), 1594, octavo.
69Digges, ThomasAlae seu scalae mathematicae (on the radius/cross-staff)Londini, 1573, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 344 (s.v. Diggesæus, Thomas); Tycho’s correspondence, letter of 8 December 1576 (tekstnet.dk)Brucaeus asked Tycho in December 1576 to send him ‘the noble Englishman’s book on the radius’, Digges’s Alae seu scalae mathematicae of 1573 (Opera omnia VII, 44; Norlind 1926, no. 7), which implies that Tycho owned it. Norlind 1970 lists Digges only as discussed in the Progymnasmata (III, 167–203).
70Dresser, MatthäusHistoria LutheriLeipzig, 1598, 8°BNorlind 1970, p. 344 (s.v. Dresserus, Matthias)A parcel of nine copies of the Historia Lutheri reached Tycho from Wittenberg with two letters for Rosenkrantz; he forwarded it and kept one copy to read at leisure (‘behåller han ett exemplar av boken för att i lugn och ro kunna studera den’; Tycho to Rosenkrantz, September 1598, Opera omnia VIII, 115). Dresser is not named in the letter; the identification is Norlind’s. The book was printed at Leipzig; only the parcel came from Wittenberg. Tycho’s copy has not been identified.
71Du Chesne, Joseph (Quercetanus)Ad Iacobi Auberti Vindonis de ortu et causis metallorum ... brevis responsioLugduni, 1575, 8°BNorlind 1970, p. 359 (s.v. Quercetanus, Josephus)Quercetanus (Joseph Du Chesne), Ad Iacobi Auberti … brevis responsio (Lyon 1575, 8vo): a Paracelsian book Tycho owned only briefly. Its preface is dated 1 April 1575, and he gave the copy to Thaddaeus Hagecius at their meeting in Regensburg in the autumn of that year; in August 1585 he asked Hagecius for another copy, unable to recall author or title (Tycho to Hagecius, August 1585, Opera omnia VII, 95). The work is identified from Hagecius’s marginal note ‘Libellus est Josephi Quercetani’ on Tycho’s letter (autograph in Vienna, Österreichische Nationalbibliothek), not from the book; Norlind gives the title as ‘med största sannolikhet’ (Norlind 1970, p. 359). The copy passed into Hagecius’s library; a copy recovered from it would carry his marks, not Tycho’s. Status attested, passed on, since 20 October 2026: the copy left the library in his lifetime as a gift to Hagecius (road 0), which is why no copy is sought — not a mass-survival text retired as unlocatable.
79Euclid (ed./comm. Christoph Clavius)Elementorum libri XV (with Clavius' commentary)CNorlind 1970, p. 345 (s.v. Euclides)Norlind: 'Någon av de tre första upplagorna (1574-91) har Tycho sannolikt ägt' — probably owned one of the first three editions. The Euclid found at Strahov (AV II 2, stamped TYCHO BRAHE 1567; Pařez 2009) is the Basel 1558 Zamberti–Campanus edition and is entered separately; no copy of a Clavius edition has been located.
80Everaert, Martin (Everhardus)Ephemerides novae et exactae 1590-1610 ex novis tabulis BelgicisLeiden, 1597, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 345 (s.v. Everartus, Martinus)Dedicated to Christian IV. Tycho received the tables at Wandsbek on 7 May 1598 (Tycho to Rosenkrantz, May 1598, Opera omnia VIII, 61), perhaps brought by Longomontanus (Tycho to Longomontanus, March 1598, Opera omnia VIII, 35), and criticised them sharply in the same letter. No copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified.
90Flemløse, Peder JacobsenÆgloga de eclipsi solari anno 1574 ... futuraHafniæ, 1574, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 346 (s.v. Flemlöse, Peder Jacobsen)That Tycho owned the work is well founded: the Aegloga is dedicated to him (17 October 1574), and Flemløse came to Hven early in 1578 as one of his very first pupils (Norlind 1970, p. 346). This copy, however, is not demonstrably Tycho’s. The only surviving copy known (a unicum, according to L. Nielsen as cited by Norlind 1970, p. 346) is KB Hielmst. 1226 4, an eighteenth-century Hielmstierne Danica acquisition carrying no mark of Tycho’s. No Prague or Clementinum copy is known: the work appears in none of Kleinschnitzová, Prandtl or Šolc, and the Czech National Library’s index of former owners records no copy of Brahe’s. Norlind uses no verb of ownership: he infers only that a copy was ‘högst troligt’ on Hven, from the dedication, not that the Copenhagen copy is Tycho’s. The copy is therefore rejected as Tycho’s, while ownership of the work is retained at grade C. Status attested, B, since 20 October 2026: the work-level ownership is sound on the dedication; the Royal Library's copy, judged in its own volume record, is not shown to be his.
107Gessner, ConradThierbuch (German, transl. C. Forer)Zürich, 1563, 2°BNorlind 1970, p. 348 (s.v. Gesner, Conradus)Norlind: ‘Tycho, som också hade Gesners Thierbuch’ — Tycho, who also had Gessner’s Thierbuch. The book is attested only by Tycho’s own letter to Landgrave Wilhelm of September 1591, which places the Oryx description on fol. 68 (Opera omnia VI, 244). No copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified. Whether his copy was the 1563 or the 1583 edition is unrecorded; Norlind holds it immaterial, the two editions being in his words identical: Zurich, Christoph Froschauer, 1563 (VD16 G 1728), reissued 1583 (VD16 G 1729), folio. It is a different book from the surviving Gessner, De omni rerum fossilium genere (Zurich 1565; Prandtl, Verzeichnis A no. 46; now at the University of Texas at Austin). The only Thierbuch physically traced in Tycho’s orbit is Landgrave Wilhelm’s own Kassel copy, not Tycho’s, destroyed in an air raid in September 1941.
113Hagecius, Thaddaeus (Hájek)Apodixis physica et mathematica de cometisGörlitz, 1581, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 348 (s.v. Hagecius, Thaddæus); Zinner no. 2979 (after Norlind); Kleinschnitzová 1933A copy was sent to Tycho by Scultetus in Görlitz (Tycho to Hagecius, October 1581, Opera omnia VII, 64). Tycho discusses the work in his book on the comet (Opera omnia IV, 293–295). No copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified, and the work belongs to the Hagecius gap: Tycho owned at least four works of Hagecius, each documented by a letter, and not one survives in the Clementinum. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 78) remarked on the absence: among the Clementinum Tychoniana there is not a single work of Hagecius, though his long friendship with Tycho and Norlind’s list make it likely that Tycho had many if not all of his works, and none of the Clementinum’s Hagecius copies carries a provenance note pointing to him. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 80) names the mechanism by which such a copy could lose its provenance: composite volumes from Tycho’s library were broken up and rebound with pieces of other provenance (5 G 42, 14 J 164, 19 G 20, XII A 12), and Richard Kukula, director of the university library 1897–1918, had old Sammelbände dissolved as a matter of principle, among them, to judge by its modern binding, the Scultetus of 14 F 284. Whether Tycho’s Hagecius copies were lost or survive unrecognised remains an open question. The National Library of the Czech Republic holds three copies of the Görlitz 1581 edition — in a Luther convolute, in a convolute from the Jesuit college at Litoměřice, and as the host volume (record 000030653) of the Hagecius composite owned by the Jesuit college at Chomutov — and none bears a Tycho mark.
114Hagecius, Thaddaeus (Hájek)Descriptio cometae qui apparuit 1577Prague, 1578, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 349 (s.v. Hagecius, Thaddæus); Zinner no. 2824 (after Norlind); Kleinschnitzová 1933Sent to Tycho by Paul Hainzel in Augsburg (Hainzel to Tycho, March 1579, Opera omnia VII, 50). Tycho discusses the work in his book on the comet (Opera omnia IV, 261–296). No copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified, and the work belongs to the Hagecius gap: the receipt is documented by letter (Norlind, p. 349), yet no Hagecius copy of Tycho’s survives in any inventory, an absence Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 78) remarked on herself. Imprint: Prague, Jiří Melantrich z Aventinu, 1578, 4to (Zinner 2824; Hellman 48), issued with the Spongia contra … Hannibalis Raymundi. The National Library of the Czech Republic holds two copies — 14 K 191, and a second (record 000030662) bound as the second tract in the Hagecius composite from the Jesuit college at Chomutov (host volume, record 000030653) — and neither bears a Tycho mark.
115Hagecius, Thaddaeus (Hájek)Dialexis de novae et prius incognitae stellae ... apparitioneFrankfurt am Main, 1574, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 349 (s.v. Hagecius, Thaddæus); Zinner no. 2673 (after Norlind); Kleinschnitzová 1933; Dreyer 1890; Mosley 2007Norlind: ‘Måste Tycho ha ägt’ — Tycho must have owned it, since the Progymnasmata treat the work at length (Opera omnia III, 19–43). Hájek sent Tycho a copy with many manuscript corrections and additions in his own hand, hoping that Tycho would print the revised text or take selections into his own account of the nova; Tycho discussed the revised text in the Progymnasmata and did not print it (Dreyer 1890, p. 58 n. 2; Mosley 2007, p. 124 n. 42; Opera omnia VII, 99). Tycho’s copy, which would carry Hájek’s autograph corrections, has not been identified. The National Library of the Czech Republic’s two copies of the Frankfurt 1574 edition — one inscribed for the Chomutov Jesuit college in 1671 (‘Collegij Soctis IESV Commotonij Ao. 1671’, record 000154680), one stamped ‘REGIAE BIBLIOTH: ACAD: PRAGEN.’ (record 000014579) — have no earlier owner in the library’s records.
116Hagecius, Thaddaeus (Hájek)Responsio ad ... Hannibalis Raimundi scriptumPrague, 1576, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 349 (s.v. Hagecius, Thaddæus); Zinner no. 2736 (after Norlind)Two copies reached Tycho: one sent by the author in August 1576 (Hájek to Tycho, Opera omnia VII, 38), a second in Maior’s parcel of June 1584 (VII, 83). A reply to Hannibal Raimundus of Verona, who held that the star of 1572 was not new. Neither copy is located. The National Library’s copy of the work, the first tract (record 000030657) of a Hájek composite from the Chomutov Jesuit college (record 000030653), carries no Tycho mark in the library’s record. The second copy came inside Maior's priced parcel of June 1584 (Opera omnia VII 83), so was probably bought, not given; the first copy of August 1576 was the author's gift (register dossier of 27 October 2026, §18).
118Heerbrand, JakobDisputatio de adiaphoris et calendario Gregoriano (resp. Corbinus)Tübingen, 1584, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 349 (s.v. Heerbrandus, Jacobus); Zinner no. 3137 (after Norlind)Sent to Tycho by Maior June 1584 (Opera VII,83).
119Hegelund, Jens Pedersen (Johannes Hegelius)Themata pro disputatione quarta psychologiae (praes. Jacobus Cocus)Wittenberg, 1599, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 349 (s.v. Hegelius, Iohannes)Dedicated to Tycho by the author, a son of Tycho’s friend Bishop Peder Jacobsen Hegelund of Ribe; Norlind: ‘har säkerligen befunnit sig i hans bibliotek’ — certainly in his library. The author enrolled at Wittenberg in November 1598, some months before Tycho and his sons.
124Hipparchus (ed. Petrus Victorius), the copy annotated by Joseph Justus ScaligerIn Arati et Eudoxi Phaenomena libri III (the Greek editio princeps, with Scaliger’s annotations)Florence (Giunta), 1567, 2°BNorlind 1970, p. 349 (s.v. Hipparchus Bithynus); Tycho’s correspondence, letter of 17 April 1599 (tekstnet.dk); Kepler, GW XIX (1975)Hipparchus’s commentary on the Phaenomena of Aratus and Eudoxus in the Greek editio princeps of Petrus Victorius (Florence 1567), Scaliger’s own copy, annotated in his hand. Christiernus Johannis Ripensis, formerly in Tycho’s service on Hven, met Scaliger in Holland and reported that he owned the Greek text. Tycho asked in August 1598 for the book or for transcripts of the passages he needed (Opera omnia VIII, 102); Scaliger sent excerpts, acknowledged in March 1599 (Opera omnia VIII, 151); and in April 1599 Tycho thanked him for two books granted him (‘pro utroque autem libro mihi tam benigne concesso’), of which the Hipparchus is the one identified. Norlind (1970, p. 362) considers that the other may be the Cyclometrica elementa duo of 1594 with Scaliger’s dedication, now Sign. 14 A 59 (Prandtl A 42). That Tycho had the annotated book itself Kepler states to Herwart von Hohenburg in January 1603: Scaliger had once sent Tycho his Hipparchus with his own notes, and it was still in the possession of the heirs (Norlind 1970, p. 350, citing the letter as Caspar nr. 242, p. 354). On 16 November 1624 Kepler asked Tycho’s son Georg Brahe for ‘Hipparchum de fixis graecè, ist ein klains folium, vnd vil drinnen manu Scaligerj’ (KGW XIX, no. 7, pp. 202–203), so the annotated book was still with the heirs two years after Tengnagel’s death. Whether Kepler obtained it is not recorded, and no copy has been traced since.
125Horst, Dethard (Horstius)Prognosticon de eventu belli Turcici1601ATycho’s correspondence, letter of 18 April 1601 (tekstnet.dk)The Prognosticon reached Tycho as a gift through Georg Rollenhagen in April 1601; the letter of 18 April 1601 calls it ‘prognosticon de eventu belli Turcici, sane gratissimum’. It was among the last books to enter Tycho’s library. Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C).
127Jöstel, MelchiorLunae deliquium ad hunc Christi annum 1599Wittenberg, 1599, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 350 (s.v. Jœstelius, Melchior); Zinner no. 3817 (after Norlind)Jöstel was Tycho’s collaborator in Prague, and the eclipse times in the tract were computed by Tycho’s lunar theory. Norlind: ‘Att Jöstelius’ skrift ingått i hans bibliotek är otvivelaktigt’ (that Jöstel’s tract entered his library is beyond doubt). The discrepancy at the eclipse of 31 January 1599 forced Tycho to revise his lunar theory, delaying the Progymnasmata.
129Kepler, JohannesProdromus dissertationum cosmographicarum (Mysterium cosmographicum)Tübingen, 1596, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 350 (s.v. Kepler, Johannes); Zinner no. 3664 (after Norlind)Kepler to Tycho, Graz, 13 December 1597 (Opera omnia VIII, 14–15), sent no copy of the Mysterium cosmographicum (Tübingen 1596), supposing that Tycho already had one: ‘Exemplaria non dubito, quin antea habeas: quare facile patior, ut difficultas transmittendi per tantum intervallum a mittendo me avocet’. Tycho to Kepler, Wandsbek, 1 April 1598 (Opera omnia VIII, 44), replied that he had seen and read the book before: ‘Librum tuum, quem Prodromum vocas Dissertationum Cosmographicarum, iam ante videram et … perlegeram’. So already Norlind 1970, p. 350. How and when his copy reached him is not recorded; no copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified.
135Liddel, Duncan[Themata][Helmstedt], [1595]BNorlind 1970, p. 351 (s.v. Liddelius, Duncanus)Norlind: ‘Tycho har ägt ett exemplar, ty han citerar’ — Tycho owned a copy, since he cites its proposition 2 in a letter to Cramer of September 1599 (Opera omnia VIII, 185), where Liddel, in a section ‘Parerga mathematica’, names Tycho in connection with the new world-system in terms that leave the reader unsure whether Tycho was its author. Title and imprint are Norlind’s conjecture, bracketed by him and unverified (‘Omöjlig att belägga’); the tract is not the Themata de melancholia (Helmstedt 1596) that P. J. Anderson’s Liddel bibliography (1910) lists as no. 4, and Anderson did not know it.
137Lycosthenes, ConradProdigiorum ac ostentorum chroniconBasel, 1557, 2°BNorlind 1970, p. 352 (s.v. Lycosthenes, Conradus); Zinner no. 2177 (after Norlind)Norlind: 'Endera av upplagorna ägdes av Tycho (sannolikt den latinska)' — owned (probably the Latin ed.); to Brucaeus Nov 1588 (Opera VII,155) Tycho writes he leafed through the whole book.
140Maestlin, MichaelAusführlicher und gründlicher Bericht von der Jahrrechnung (de emendatione Calendarii)Heidelberg, 1583, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 352 (s.v. Mæstlinus, Michael); Zinner no. 3087 (after Norlind)Brucaeus sent Tycho 'Maestlini de emendatione Calendarii' in June 1584 (Opera omnia VII, 86). Whether the parcel held the Heidelberg edition of 1583 (Zinner 3087) or its reprint of 1584 within the Nothwendige und gründtliche Bedenckhen von dem allgemeinen römischen Kalender (Heidelberg 1584; Zinner 3144) cannot be decided; Norlind takes the former as the likelier. Against the Gregorian reform.
141Maestlin, MichaelConsideratio et observatio cometae aetherei 1580Heidelberg, 1581, 8°BNorlind 1970, p. 352 (s.v. Mæstlinus, Michael); Zinner no. 2990 (after Norlind)Norlind: 'Ägdes av Tycho' — owned, per Tycho to Rothmann Aug 1588 (Opera VI,142-143).
145Maestlin, MichaelObservatio et demonstratio cometae aetherei 1577-1578Tübingen, 1578, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 352 (s.v. Mæstlinus, Michael); Zinner no. 2836 (after Norlind)Sent March 1579 with several other comet tracts by Paul Hainzel in Augsburg (Opera VII,50). Extensive discussion in comet-book IV,207-238.
146Magini, Giovanni AntonioEphemerides coelestium motuum (latest 10-year ed.)ATycho’s correspondence, letter of 24 January 1601 (tekstnet.dk)Tycho received Magini’s most recently published ten-year Ephemerides by way of the Frankfurt fair early in 1601 (Tycho to Magini, 24 January 1601: ‘Ephemerides tuas 10 Annorum postremo emissas Francofurto accepi’). It was among the last books to reach him. Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C).
148Magini, Giovanni AntonioTabula tetragonicaVenice, 1592, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 352 (s.v. Maginus, Johannes Antonius)Magini dedicated the work to Tycho and sent a copy (Mechanica; Opera V,127), but it 'aldrig nådde sin bestämmelseort' (never reached its destination); 'Först långt senare erhöll Tycho ett exemplar från Frankfurtmässan' — Tycho only much later got a copy from the Frankfurt fair via an amanuensis (to Magini Nov 1598, Opera VIII,120).
149Magini, Giovanni AntonioTabulae novae + Ephemerides (ad calendarii emendationem)Venice, 1585BTycho’s correspondence, letter of 15 March 1586 (tekstnet.dk)Brucaeus bought for Tycho Magini’s Tabulae novae and the Ephemerides at Rostock in March 1586, the two valued together at eleven or twelve Joachimsthaler, on the condition that the bookseller, who had deposited the books with him at the beginning of the winter, would take them back if Tycho did not want them or already had them (Brucaeus to Tycho, 15 March 1586; Opera omnia VII, 100: ‘Emi autem hac conditione …’). These are distinct from the Tabula tetragonica and from the Ephemerides of 1601. Whether the books reached Hven is not recorded.
150Manilius, Marcus (ed. Joseph Justus Scaliger)Astronomicon a Jos. Scaligero repurgatumLeiden, 1600, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 353 (s.v. Manilius, Marcus)Sent by Scaliger March 1600 (Opera VIII,264) to Tycho, who thanked him July 1600 (VIII,329). May relate to the books Scaliger sent him.
163Offusius, JofrancusDe divina astrorum facultate in larvatam astrologiamParis, 1570, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 355 (s.v. Offusius, Iofrancus); Tycho’s correspondence (DSL)Norlind 1970, p. 355: Tycho received a copy of the printed book from Hagecius at their meeting at Regensburg in November 1575 (Opera omnia VII, 184; II, 421) and was particularly taken with its section on the planets’ influence at their varying distances from the earth; in May 1588 he wrote to Hagecius that he could no longer find the book in his library and asked him to procure another copy (VII, 121; Hagecius’s answers of November 1588 and May 1589, VII, 147 and 184). A book that left the library, or was mislaid in it, in Tycho’s own lifetime. Norlind adds that a copy stood in Queen Christina’s library which he could not find among the Reginenses in the Vatican — a lead he did not pursue, and one worth the question, since books from Prague reached her library in 1648. The store's separate entry for ‘Francius, De astris’ (the Regensburg gift of 1575, lost by 1589) was this book: Hagecius describes the book he gave as ‘librum … de astris … IO. FRANCI, Parisijs impressum, et Reginae Galliae dedicatum’ (20 May 1589, Opera omnia VII 184), ‘Io. Franci’ being Iofrancus, Offusius's given name; Tycho's account of its content (3 May 1588, VII 120–121) fits Offusius, and Norlind (p. 355) already read it so. The two entries were
168Paracelsus (Theophrastus von Hohenheim)Commentationes in integra Biblia (manuscript), ManuskriptCNorlind 1970, p. 356 (s.v. Paracelsus, Theophrastus)The only authority is Joachim Morsius, who in 1625 — in the dedication to the pseudo-Paracelsian lion-prophecy — reported on Cort Aslakssøn’s word that Tycho had owned a copy, and who further supposed that the manuscript was by then in Prague with Tycho’s heirs. Norlind relays both. No inventory and no Clementinum catalogue records it, and no copy has been identified: the ownership is attested at second hand only and remains unverified. Status attested, not located, since 20 October 2026: no one contests the ownership — Norlind relays only Morsius's report — so the Definitions' 'disputed' does not fit.
181Praetorius, JohannesDe cometis qui antea visi sunt et de eo qui ... Novembri apparuit, narratioNürnberg, 1578, 4°CNorlind 1970, p. 357 (s.v. Prætorius, Johannes); Zinner no. 2845 (after Norlind)Tycho treats the work at length in the comet book (Opera omnia IV, 356–358; cf. Progymnasmata, Opera omnia III, 153–157). Thorndike (History of Magic and Experimental Science VI, p. 84) held that neither Tycho nor Hagecius owned a copy. Norlind shows that Thorndike misread the three passages of the correspondence on which he relied (Opera omnia VII, 120, 147 and 212), which concern Apianus and Pena and not this book, and so defends Tycho’s ownership against Thorndike’s denial. The Czech National Library holds the work as the fourth tract of a Hagecius composite volume from the Jesuit college at Chomutov; its record notes no mark of Tycho’s.
185Ptolemaeus, ClaudiusAlmagest (old Venetian edition, c. 1515)Venetiis, 1515, 2°ANorlind 1970, p. 358 (s.v. Ptolemæus, Claudius); Tycho’s correspondence, letter of 20 January 1587 (tekstnet.dk); Fund og Forskning 1965Tycho states that he owns an old Venetian Almagest, some seventy years old in 1587 (letter of 20 January 1587: ‘vetus quoddam exemplar Almagesti, ante annos proxime 70. Venetijs editum’), that is, the Latin Almagest printed at Venice by Petrus Liechtenstein in about 1515. It is distinct from the Ptolemy volumes among the Clementinum copies — the Opera (Basel), the Geographia (Cologne 1597) and the De analemmate (Rome 1562). Norlind identified the edition in print (Fund og Forskning XII, 1965, p. 156, ‘Efterslæt’): the Latin Almagest printed at Venice in 1515 (Petrus Liechtenstein; Gerard of Cremona’s version), whose prefatory life of Ptolemy — ‘indledningen til en oversættelse af Almagesten, trykt i Venedig 1515, som Tycho Brahe har ejet og nævner i et brev’ — is the source of the royal descent and the physical description of Ptolemy in Tycho’s elegy In effigiem Cl. Ptolemaei (Epistolae astronomicae, 1596, p. 239). No copy of the Venice Almagest with Tycho’s marks has been identified. Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C).
193Rantzau, Heinrich (Ranzovius)Rantzovianum calendarium ad elevationem poli 55. grad. tam in usum medicorum quam astrologorumHamburg, 1590, 2°BNorlind 1970, p. 360 (s.v. Rantzau, Henrik); Zinner no. 3399 (after Norlind)Norlind records the book as received from the author (‘Erhöll Tycho av förf.’), on the evidence of Tycho to Rantzau, April 1590 (Opera omnia VII, 243). Rantzau’s own copy, into which a transcript of Tycho’s elegy to Denmark was bound and which King Christian leafed through on a visit to Rantzau (Opera omnia VIII, 63), is a different book. Two copies of the 1590 edition in the Royal Library, Hielmst. 547 2° and Hielmst. 146 2°, examined in facsimile, descend from Henrik Hielmstierne and bear neither a mark of Tycho’s nor the bound-in transcript. No copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified.

234Ursus, Nicolaus Reimers (Bär)De astronomicis hypothesibus, seu de systemate mundanoPrague, 1597, 4°ANorlind 1970, p. 365 (s.v. Ursus, Nicolaus Raimarus); Zinner no. 3739 (after Norlind); Jardine et al. 2005; Jardine & Segonds 2008; Švédská knižní kořist (database)Norlind records that Tycho received the book (‘erhöll boken’). It was printed ‘Absque omni privilegio’; in it Ursus denies having stolen the system, dedicates the work to Landgrave Moritz, prints a laudatory letter from Kepler (Graz, 15 November 1595), and violently attacks Tycho and Rothmann. Tycho lent his copy, with the offending passages marked, to Holger Rosenkrantz in 1598 and complained that it was not returned (Opera omnia VIII, 126). Jardine, Launert, Segonds, Mosley and Tybjerg (2005, pp. 98–103) found the Royal Library’s copy from the Rosenkrantz sale of 1695 unmarked; the copy now in the Danish National Library of Science and Medicine, 4° Astr. 8050, perhaps transferred from the Royal Library between 1918 and 1926, is inscribed ‘Donum Autoris’ on the title and carries sixteen clear marginal marks, all against passages insulting to Tycho and all but two of them in the dedication to Landgrave Moritz or in the invective poem that follows it. They argue that this is the copy prepared for Lange and lent to Rosenkrantz. The identification rests on the pattern of the marks, not on a mark of ownership; the hand of the marks has not been compared with Tycho’s or with those of his assistants. A book lent out of the library in 1598 and never returned is a survivor of the library’s lifetime, not of its dispersal. The Czech National Library holds a copy of the Prague 1597 edition, 14 J 81/adl.2, bound second in a re-bound convolute after della Faille’s Theoremata (Antwerp 1632); its record, recatalogued under Kukula, carries no provenance. Jardine and Segonds restate the identification in 2008: the copy is the one Caspar Lehmann obtained from Ursus himself and sent through Rollenhagen in the spring of 1598; Tycho had the marks made for Erik Lange’s testimony and lent the volume to Holger Rosenkrantz, who did not return it despite the demands of 9 September 1598 (Opera omnia VIII, p. 112) and 5 December 1598 (pp. 125–126); their ‘about a dozen’ marked passages answers to the twelve puncta Lange attested, the article of 2005 counting sixteen clear marks and two doubtful (2008, pp. 175, 195–196, 243 n. 3). Three copies of the book reached Tycho in the spring of 1598 — from a student of Helmstedt, from Lehmann through Rollenhagen, and from Hagecius (pp. 157 n. 3, 191–192). A second surviving copy of the book Jardine and Segonds call rare: Västerås Stadsbibliotek, from the Olomouc Jesuit college (‘Collegij Olomu. Soctis JESV Catalogo inscriptus an: 1604’), through the Stockholm royal library of 1650–51, in a parchment binding cut from a coloured Hebrew manuscript (the Swedish-booty database, record SJ 203; Gawryś, Slavica Arosiensia III, no. 213). Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C).
235Ursus, Nicolaus Reimers (Bär)Fundamentum astronomicum, id est nova doctrina sinuum et triangulorumStrasbourg, 1588, 4°BNorlind 1970, p. 365 (s.v. Ursus, Nicolaus Raimarus); Zinner no. 3316 (after Norlind); Jardine & Segonds 2008; Balsem 2020Ursus set out in this book a world-system that, in Norlind’s words, differs only slightly from Tycho’s. Tycho held that Ursus had taken it from a sketch seen during his stay at Uraniborg in the autumn of 1584, in Erik Lange’s company, and pressed the charge of plagiarism in the correspondence with the Landgrave and Rothmann printed in 1596; Norlind, with Dreyer, holds the charge probably unwarranted. Tycho received several copies: one sent by Rantzau (Tycho to Rantzau, December 1588; Opera omnia VII, 387), a second probably from Christian Ripensis, which may be the other copy Tycho mentions in that letter, and one from Georg Rollenhagen in Magdeburg (Tycho to Rothmann, February 1589; Opera omnia VI, 179). Rollenhagen sent a copy to Rantzau on 16 October 1588 (Landesarchiv Schleswig-Holstein, Breitenburg-Archiv Abt. 127.21, Hss. 293, p. 552); Tycho already had one from elsewhere, ‘aliunde’ (to Rantzau, 21 December 1588, Opera omnia VII, p. 387) (Jardine & Segonds 2008, pp. 120–121). A copy with a Prague provenance of 1595 — ‘Daniel Muller à Mollenberg, '95 Prag’ on the title, ‘Raymari’ on the fore-edge, interleaved and annotated in a hand the Kepler-Kommission declared in 1964 not to be Kepler's — is at Leiden, 538 E 2, from Isaac Vossius's library; Balsem declines to call it Swedish booty for want of any trace of Christina's shelfmark on its ruined spine (2020, p. 37 and Cat. Math. 730). Not Tycho's copy, but a Prague copy of the year of the quarrel.
238Viète, François (Vieta)Two tracts newly published in 1600 (‘libelli duo’), one of them probably the Apollonius Gallus1600ATycho’s correspondence, letter of 26 April 1600 (tekstnet.dk)Herwart von Hohenburg sent Tycho from Munich two booklets Viète had just published, without naming them (Herwart to Tycho, 26 April 1600; Opera omnia VIII, 305: ‘libelli duo, quos … FRANCISCUS VIETA, nuper in lucem prodire voluit … his iunctos ad te mitto’); Tycho acknowledged receipt in his letter to Herwart of 28 August 1600. Norlind (1970, p. 208) identifies one of them from Kepler’s letter to Herwart of July 1600 (Caspar no. 168), which reports that Kepler had seen at Tycho’s Viète’s ‘Opus de aequationibus’: not the De aequationum recognitione, printed only in 1615, but the Apollonius Gallus of 1600, whose second appendix (problems I and IV) determines a planet’s apogee and eccentricity from three observations. On 8 November 1600 Herwart described Viète’s Canon mathematicus under the title ‘Francisci Vietaei opera Mathematica’ and offered to procure it if Tycho wished (Herwart to Tycho, 8 November 1600; Opera omnia VIII, 386: ‘Quod si eum desideres, curabo omnino, ut habeas’) — an offer, not a sending, and not the Opera of 1646. Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C).
241Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-KasselObservations of the comet of 1577 (sent to Tycho)CTycho’s correspondence, letter of 11 June 1588 (tekstnet.dk); Schrimpf & Verbunt 2021Wilhelm IV’s observations of the comet of 1577 reached Tycho through the Rothmann and Kassel correspondence (Tycho to Rothmann, 11 June 1588: ‘Recensui etiam in hoc libro... Observationes’) and were collated into his comet book, the Progymnasmata; they were not held as a discrete Wilhelm IV codex. Wilhelm IV’s own observation manuscripts survive at the Universitätsbibliothek Kassel — Landesbibliothek und Murhardsche Bibliothek, in the ‘2 Ms. astron.’ series (the observation corpus 1–7; the star catalogue 2 Ms. astron. 74; the handbook 2 Ms. astron. 5; Schrimpf and Verbunt 2021), with Wilhelm’s correspondence at the Hessisches Staatsarchiv, Marburg; those are Wilhelm’s copies, not Tycho’s. Status attested since 20 October 2026: nothing is contested — the observations reached Tycho and were collated into the comet book; no discrete codex was ever held. They had reached him earlier than the 1588 letter: through Paul Hainzel in March 1579 (Opera omnia VII 50) and from Kassel with Rothmann's letter dated in its own text ‘Cassellis 18 Calend. Maij … 1586’ = 14 April 1586 (VI 53–58; the Epistolarium's brahe-t_15850518001, re-dated) — register dossier of 27 October 2026, §18.
246(eight unidentified authors)[Eight unidentified Tycho-owned books, superexlibris and autograph marginalia, found in a Prague monastery, 1943]BMortensen 1955Felix Mainx reported to Mortensen that in 1943 he had found, in a Prague monastery library, eight further books, not further specified, bearing Tycho’s superexlibris and many autograph marginalia; he intended to describe the find in a later paper (Mortensen 1955, p. 30: ‘otte andre ikke nærmere angivne Bøger, som foruden Tycho Brahes Superexlibris havde mange egenhændige Marginalnoter’). The books have not been traced since.
250(ancient geographers, ed. David Hoeschel)Geographica — ancient minor Greek geographers, newly first-published (incl. Scylax of Caryanda)Augsburg, 1600BTycho’s correspondence, letter of 8 September 1600 (tekstnet.dk)Herwart von Hohenburg sent Tycho a newly published edition of the ancient minor Greek geographers with his letter of 8 September 1600 (‘veteres quosdam Geographos nunc primum in lucem editos’), that is, Hoeschel’s Geographica (Augsburg 1600). The book was Tycho’s own.
253Typus pompae funebris 5. Junii anno 1588 habitae Rodtschildii in exequiis Friderici II Daniae regis, opera et consilio Henrici Rantzovii efformatus (Frans Hogenberg and Simon Novellanus, twenty engravings)1588, 2°BNorlind 1970, p. 364 (s.v. Typus pompæ funebris 5. Junii Anno 1588 …)Norlind 1970, p. 364: twenty engravings of the funeral procession of Frederik II at Roskilde on 5 June 1588, made at Rantzau’s instance and dedicated to Christian IV. Tycho acknowledged the gift to Rantzau in December 1588 — ‘delineationem exequiarum ac sepulturae regiae Hamburgi per te aeneis figuris procuratam’ (Opera omnia VII, 386). A print series from the Rantzau connection rather than a book of the study; no copy with a mark of Tycho’s is known.

Tycho owned a single copy and therefore sent Cramer a transcript (Tycho to Cramer, September 1599 (Opera omnia VIII, 186)). Norlind could not trace the print itself. No copy of the programme is traced, and a copy of Tycho’s would carry no known mark by which it could be recognised.

258Boiemus, Michael (Böhm)Historia de somniisWittenberg, 1587BNorlind 1970, Bilaga I; Falkenstein 1839; Šolc 2018; Kleinschnitzová 1933; SLUB war-loss registerMichael Boiemus (Michael Böhm), Historia de somniis (Wittenberg 1587, 4°), the third piece of the Dresden Sammelband (Falkenstein 1839, pp. 574–575: ‘Michaelis Boiemi historia de somniis, Witteb. 1587. 4.’), with two distichs on the flyleaf in the hand of a M. Johannes Schmidt sending the book to a nobleman he addresses as Smil — ‘Promissum transmitto librum, Doctissime Smile … Generositatis tuae officioss. M. Johannes Schmidt’ (read on the page image 29 October 2026; the OCR had ‘Praemissum’ and lost the name) — so the leaf records a presentation to a Smil, not to Tycho; who Schmidt and Smil were is not known, and no source reconciles the leaf with Tycho's portrait binding on the volume. Šolc 2018 (pp. 201–202) quotes Falkenstein's lines as ‘ein weiteres Tychonisches Buch in Dresden’; Falkenstein's ‘Daran:’ chain places the Boiemus in the same binding as the Paulus Alexandrinus and the Horoscopographia. Lost with them in 1945 (Norlind 1970, p. 356). Grade B. The SLUB's war-loss register carries a card for the Boiemus — Lit.Graec.B.1976, earlier ‘Phil. gr. B. 93a. Misc. 3’, and ‘Misc. 3’ matches Falkenstein's order, in which the Boiemus is the third piece; no card was found under the other two headings, and the register does not say whether the volume was removed in 1945–46 or destroyed (Nachweiskatalog image 00504111, read 27 October 2026; the identification with the Tycho volume is inference, C).
36Brasch, MartinCarmen epicum de Varadino (manuscript poem)1600CNorlind 1970, p. 340 (s.v. Brasch, Martinus)Brasch sent the manuscript poem, which celebrates Melchior von Roedern’s defence of Grosswardein (Várad) in 1598, to Tycho twice: in August 1600, when it was lost in transit (Opera omnia VIII, 337), and as a replacement in September 1600 that ‘probably reached’ him (Opera omnia VIII, 380; Norlind p. 340); von Roedern died on 20 September 1600. No surviving manuscript codex has been located in any catalogue. Martin Brasch the Younger also published a printed Varadini Hungariae propugnaculi... anni 1598 (1598) on the same subject — plausibly the same matter in print beside an authorial manuscript redaction of 1600, though no source collates the two. The first copy never arrived, the replacement only ‘probably’ did, no codex survives, and no ownership mark that could be looked for attaches to the item; the entry therefore rests on the correspondence alone. Status lost since 20 October 2026: a unique manuscript sent and probably received, not a mass-survival text — the class retired as unlocatable does not fit it.

The extant Copenhagen University Library copy is not Tycho's: it is the author's dedication copy to Jacob Ulfeldt. Tycho's copy (ex-Rostgaard) is lost. The earlier witness is Oluf Bang, Samling af nyttige Materier, 7. Stykke (1745), p. 531, from which Mortensen (1955, pp. 30–31) takes the copy: in Rostgaard's library at his death in 1745, bequeathed to the University, and not found there.
