Mortensen (1942, pp. 14–15) dates the note 5 April 1592 at Uraniborg and gives its text in Høst's Danish rendering (Chronos 1822, p. 24): ‘Private og indvortes Ulykker lettes ikke ved Omskiftelse af Sted og Himmelegn; thi, hvorsomhelst nogen maatte gaa hen, bringer han sig selv med. Men offentlige Elendigheder undgaaes ofte ved at forandre Sted’.
154Methodius (pseudo-)Revelatio (Revelationes Methodii) — a manuscript copy made for Tycho1600BTycho’s correspondence, letter of 10 December 1600 (tekstnet.dk)Herwart had the Revelatio ascribed to Methodius transcribed for Tycho because the volume that contained it was too bulky to send, and despatched the copy from Munich with the Alphonsine tables (Herwart to Tycho, 10 December 1600; Opera omnia VIII, 393: ‘METHODIJ uti fertur Revelationem, quam describi curavi, cum liber, cui inserta fuerat, ob molem transferri nequeat’). The transcript is not among the Clementinum volumes and has not been identified at the Royal Library, Copenhagen, or the Austrian National Library; the text survives in many copies, and a transcript without Tycho’s own mark cannot be told from them. Status lost since 20 October 2026: a unique transcript made for Tycho and sent, not a mass-survival text.
170Paulus AlexandrinusEisagoge eis ten apotelesmatiken seu Rudimenta in doctrinam de praedictis natalitiis ex Henrici Rantzovii bibliotheca primum graece et latine edita et nunc denuo correctaWittenberg, 1588, 4°BKleinschnitzová 1933, p. 78 n. 1; Norlind 1970, p. 356 (s.v. Paulus Alexandrinus); Zinner no. 3309 (after Norlind); Šolc 1999; Šolc 2006; Collijn 1933 (as Kleinschnitzová printed it); Falkenstein 1839; Šolc 2018; SLUB war-loss register; Mortensen 1955A book by another author that Tycho owned (Paulus Alexandrinus, edited from Heinrich Rantzau’s library, Wittenberg 1588), in its original Tychonic binding. Reported by Isak Collijn to Flora Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 78 n. 1) as a Tychonianum in the Landesbibliothek Dresden, the companion to the Waldstein (Mnichovo Hradiště) copy of Tycho’s own De nova stella, which, as a copy of one of Tycho’s own works, lies outside this library. The volume is lost: Norlind (1970, p. 356) records the Dresden library’s own communication that the copy ‘gått förlorat under senaste världskrig’ — was lost in the Second World War. Šolc still lists the volume in Dresden — ‘befand sich … in der Sächsischen Landesbibliothek Dresden’ (1999, § 2.533, printed p. 150) and, in the present tense, ‘se nachází v Zemské knihovně v Drážďanech’ (2006, p. 192) — and nowhere mentions the loss Norlind reports from the library itself; neither text cites a sighting. The entry keeps ‘lost’ on Norlind's report; a question to the SLUB (its war-loss records, and whether a Paulus Alexandrinus, Wittenberg 1588, in a Tychonic binding has since been acquired) would close it. Falkenstein's description of the Dresden library (1839, pp. 574–575; quoted by Šolc 2018, pp. 194 and 201–202) shows what the volume was: a Sammelband of three works — this Paulus Alexandrinus first, then Rantzau's own Horoscopographia (Wittenberg 1588, 4°) and Michael Boiemus's Historia de somniis (Wittenberg 1587, 4°) — in a parchment binding with Tycho's portrait stamp on the front board (‘Hic patet exterior Tychonis forma Brahei. Pulchrius eniteat quae latet interior’) and his arms on the back, and on the flyleaf two distichs by a M. Johannes Schmidt sending the book to a nobleman he addresses as Smil (‘Promissum transmitto librum, Doctissime Smile, / Invenies, legito, quae Tibi forte placent, / Somnia pars narrat, sed somnia vera loquuntur / Interdum. Ast illis credere multa cave. — Generositatis tuae officioss. M. Johannes Schmidt’; read on the page image 29 October 2026 — the OCR's ‘Praemissum’ and the elided name corrected). The address is to a Smil, not to Tycho: Schmidt's leaf and Tycho's portrait binding are the two facts recorded on the object, and no source reconciles them. Šolc presents the Boiemus as a further Dresden volume; Falkenstein's ‘Daran:’ makes it the third piece of this one. The loss of 1945 therefore covers all three works, which this library enters as the two bound companions. The SLUB's war-loss register carries a card for the Boiemus — Lit.Graec.B.1976, earlier ‘Phil. gr. B. 93a. Misc. 3’, and ‘Misc. 3’ matches Falkenstein's order, in which the Boiemus is the third piece; no card was found under the other two headings, and the register does not say whether the volume was removed in 1945–46 or destroyed (Nachweiskatalog image 00504111, read 27 October 2026; the identification with the Tycho volume is inference, C). The whole literature on the volume was read on 29 October 2026 (the volumelit table, nine passages): the attribution is Collijn's, printed by Kleinschnitzová in 1933 on the binding alone and naming only the Paulus; Mortensen 1955 (p. 28, the ‘two books’ Collijn reported, no title), Norlind 1970 and Šolc 1999, 2006 and 2018 repeat her — Šolc copying her misprint ‘natalatiis’ in all three, writing ‘leather bindings’ in 2006 where Falkenstein has a parchment binding, and in 2018 counting the one volume as two (the Paulus–Rantzau pair on p. 194, the Boiemus as ‘ein weiteres Tychonisches Buch’ on p. 201) while omitting the verses. Falkenstein himself, the only writer who had the volume in hand, makes no statement about Tycho's library; nobody after 1839 reports seeing it. The Rantzau literature (Oestmann 2004, Zeeberg, Lohmeier 2000, Ilsøe 2005) and the Tycho biographies name the editions, not this copy.
257Rantzau, HeinrichHoroscopographia, sive de inveniendo stellarum situ astrologiaWittenberg, 1588BNorlind 1970, Bilaga I; Falkenstein 1839; Šolc 2018; Kleinschnitzová 1933; SLUB war-loss registerHeinrich Rantzau's Horoscopographia (Wittenberg 1588, 4°), bound after the Paulus Alexandrinus in the Dresden Sammelband that Falkenstein described in 1839 (pp. 574–575: ‘Daran: Henrici Rancovii (v. Ranzau) Horoscopographia, Wit. 1588. 4.’) — the volume in Tycho's portrait-and-arms parchment binding that Collijn reported to Kleinschnitzová and that the Dresden library reported lost in the Second World War (Norlind 1970, p. 356). Rantzau's book of the same year as the Paulus edited from his library, in the same binding: a pair that reached Tycho together, by gift or purchase, in 1588 or soon after. Entered on 20 October 2026 from Šolc 2018 (p. 194) and Falkenstein's entry; grade B by the document rule — Tycho's binding described by a librarian, the copy not seen since 1945. The SLUB's war-loss register carries a card for the Boiemus — Lit.Graec.B.1976, earlier ‘Phil. gr. B. 93a. Misc. 3’, and ‘Misc. 3’ matches Falkenstein's order, in which the Boiemus is the third piece; no card was found under the other two headings, and the register does not say whether the volume was removed in 1945–46 or destroyed (Nachweiskatalog image 00504111, read 27 October 2026; the identification with the Tycho volume is inference, C). Šolc 2018 (p. 194) infers from the words ‘ex Henrici Rantzovii bibliotheca’ that the volume's ‘paths once led through both libraries’, Rantzau's and Tycho's; the words belong to the Paulus edition's title (its Greek text printed from a manuscript in Rantzau's library) and Falkenstein records no Rantzau mark on the volume, so nothing documents that this copy was ever Rantzau's.
213Scaliger, Joseph JustusDe emendatione temporum (revised ed.; Leiden, Plantin 1598)Lugduni Batav., 1598, 2°ANorlind 1970, p. 362 (s.v. Scaliger, Joseph Justus); Tycho’s correspondence, letter of 14 March 1598 (tekstnet.dk); Walde 1938; Norlind 1926; Mortensen 1955Sought in 1584 through Johannes Maior, Tycho’s agent at the Frankfurt fairs; the first edition of 1583 then reached Tycho twice in June 1584, from Maior at Augsburg on 8 June (Maior to Tycho, 8 June 1584, Opera omnia VII, 83: ‘Inprimis autem mihi curae fuit SCALIGERI de emendatione temporum’) and from Heinrich Brucaeus at Rostock on 12 June (Brucaeus to Tycho, 12 June 1584, Opera omnia VII, 86: ‘Mitto IOSEPHUM SCALIGERUM de emendatione temporum’). One of the two copies survives: Prague, National Library, Sign. 19 A 46, initialled ‘T. B.’ on the title-page; Kleinschnitzová (no. 41, p. 92) could not say which: ‘Dürfte das von Brucaeus oder Major an Brahe gesandte Exemplar sein.’ The entry concerns the revised edition of 1598, which Tycho acknowledged to Scaliger from Wandsbeck on 14 March 1598 (Tycho to Scaliger, 14 March 1598: ‘redintegratum de Temporum Emendatione... primum accepi’); Norlind (1926, no. 28) read the copy as the author’s gift, Walde (1938, p. 14 n. 2) as an ordinarily procured copy, the letter containing no thanks. A copy of this edition from Tycho’s library was found by Walde in the summer of 1937 in the library of the Staatliche Akademie at Braunsberg: white parchment with Tycho’s portrait on the upper and his arms on the lower board, both blind-stamped, and the decor usual on his bindings; not bound on Hven, which he left in 1597, perhaps at Wandsbeck in 1598; many marginalia in several hands, photographs of which Hans Ræder judged not to be Tycho’s; no dedication; the only later note ‘M. Braunhardt i Gotha 1761 … Ex bibliotheca Oppeliana’, which Walde could not explain (a person named Oppel, or the town of Oppeln near Neisse, where Tycho’s great globe was found in 1632). Mortensen cited the find in 1955 without the title; nothing later is recorded of the volume, and Norlind’s catalogue of 1970 does not include it. Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C).

Dreyer denied that the hand is Tycho’s and found no sign that the manuscript had ever been his (Opera omnia I, p. 317); Norlind (1970, p. 340) reports both views. 61Copernicus, NicolausCommentariolus (De hypothesibus motuum coelestium ... commentariolus) — manuscript, ManuskriptCNorlind 1970, p. 343 (s.v. Copernicus, Nicolaus); Walde 1938; Jardine & Segonds 2008; Vackářová 2026; Gingerich & Westman 1988; Westman 2011A manuscript of the Commentariolus in the Österreichische Nationalbibliothek, Vienna, attributed to Tycho’s library by Norlind. Tycho owned the text: Hagecius gave him a copy at Regensburg in 1575, and he printed it in the Progymnasmata (Opera omnia II, 428). Whether the Vienna manuscript is that copy rests on Norlind’s attribution and on the Uraniborg-circle contents of the same Sammelhandschrift; the volume carries no mark of his, and its catalogue record names no former owner, so both the entry and the identification of the copy are graded C. Walde (1938) showed the Vienna manuscript to have been Longomontanus’s gift to the amanuensis Johannes Eriksen at Benátky on 18 July 1600 and left open whether it passed from Eriksen to Tycho; Eriksen’s books otherwise went into Queen Christina’s library with the Prague booty. The witness therefore belongs to the Uraniborg circle rather than, on present evidence, to Tycho’s own shelves. Jardine and Segonds note the copy that came from Hagecius (2008, p. 187 n. 4). The National Library's account of 2026 adds two points to the Regensburg gift: that the original Hájek exemplar is untraced (the same object as Norlind's ‘Tycho's exemplar not located’ if the Regensburg transfer was a gift), and the conjecture that it was Tycho who had Copernicus's name — absent from the anonymous letter as it circulated — set at the head of the transcripts he distributed (Vackářová 2026, printed p. 22; ‘zřejmě’, her conjecture, not a documented fact). The three surviving transcripts she names (Vienna, Stockholm, Aberdeen; p. 20) are those the history essay already records. Status disputed since 20 October 2026: the witness belongs to the Uraniborg circle rather than, on present evidence, to Tycho's shelves (Walde 1938 against the transfer), and a located C with the ownership in doubt is the Definitions' disputed, not located. Westman (2011, p. 248) describes the Regensburg manuscript as one ‘that evidently had been in Hagecius's family for many years’, citing TBOO II 428, which records the gift and nothing of the manuscript's earlier history.
88Fincke, ThomasGeometriae rotundi libri XIIII (Basel 1583)Basileæ, 1583, 4°CNorlind 1970, p. 345 (s.v. Fincke, Thomas)Thomas Fincke, Geometriae rotundi libri XIIII (Basel: S. Henricpetri, 1583), dedicated to Frederik II. Both copies in the Royal Library, Copenhagen, have been examined in digital reproduction, and neither bears any mark of Tycho’s ownership. The first copy (LN 599 4, ex. 1) carries the autograph ‘Horrebow’ (the eighteenth-century family of Danish Royal Astronomers) on the title page and royal-cipher and BRH stamps, in an eighteenth-century marbled-board binding. The second (Hielmst. 1661a 4, ex. 2) is a contemporary Sammelband (Fincke 1583 with Ursus, Fundamentum astronomicum, Strasbourg 1588) in limp vellum, inscribed ‘Severinus Pauli[?] … Lipsiae Anno Dni 158[3]’ (mottoes ‘Superna curato, Humana contemnito’ and ‘Mens generosa ultra polos’) and ‘Christiernus Joannis Hafniensis Anno 1620’ (motto ‘Ex uno omnia’), later Hielmstierne’s. Norlind nonetheless placed the book in Tycho’s library — ‘fanns säkerligen i biblioteket på Uraniborg’ (Bilaga I, p. 346) — but his whole basis is Fincke’s printed praise of Tycho in the preface, a compliment present in every copy rather than a mark in any copy. No inventory, inscription or ownership mark attests Tycho’s ownership, and neither surviving Copenhagen copy is his.

255Schöner, JohannThe edition and the completeness of the Schöner — Gingerich names the author and the year only; the volume's collation is to be read on the copy.
234Ursus, Nicolaus Reimers (Bär)Whether the marginal marks in 4° Astr. 8050 (Royal Danish Library, formerly the Danish National Library of Science and Medicine) are in Tycho’s hand or in that of an assistant, and by what route the volume left the Royal Library; the ink and hand of the marks set against the Uraniborg hands, the binding and any earlier shelfmark would test the identification argued by Jardine et al. 2005.
238Viète, François (Vieta)Which was the second of the two tracts of 1600: Norlind identifies only the Apollonius Gallus, and the De numerosa potestatum resolutione, printed at Paris the same year, is the other candidate; a letter naming it, or a copy with Tycho’s marks, would decide.
245Zwinger, TheodorHow the volume came to the Röhsska museum — with Hjalmar Wijk’s donation of Hierta’s books in 1915, or from the sale of Hierta’s library after his death (Björck & Börjesson, 1932, catalogue 272) — is not established; the museum’s accession record would decide.
246(eight unidentified authors)Which Prague monastery held the eight Tycho books Mainx saw in 1943, and whether he published them; the monastery's catalogue or Mainx's papers would settle it.
246(eight unidentified authors)Strahov is excluded: its only Tycho volume with autograph-attributed marginalia and a mark on the binding is the Euclid AV II 2, and its mark is a blind-stamped name and date of 1567 (Pařez 2009), not the gilt portrait plaque Mortensen ascribes to all eight; the Regiomontanus DR VII 19 has the 1642 inscription and no supralibros. Strahov's Tychoniana were surveyed by its own librarian in 1996 and 2009 and its bindings by Straka (1919, 1920), Hamanová–Nuska (1966) and Voit (2020). On Mortensen's description Strahov is not Mainx's monastery; the question stays open for Emauzy, Břevnov and the others. Mainx's own notice on Strahov of 1940 (S_MAINX1940) names no supralibros volume and predates the find: it neither names nor excludes Strahov, the exclusion resting on Mortensen's description; the leaves of the three plaque volumes — Σ V 5/a and Σ VI 3 unexamined, AG XIV 7 with one reader's note recorded — are the residual test.

  1. 5 B 70 hand comparison 2026
    The purchase note of 30 November 1560 and the marginalia of NK ČR 5 B 70 compared, on the Manuscriptorium facsimile, with the two ‘Iohannes Pratensis’ signatures on the same title page, with Tycho's dated specimens of 1583 (KB GKS 1823) and 1599 (the album leaf of 8 May), and with the two hands of the volume of 1561 at Helsingør, on 25 October 2026: the scribe-compare method (each specimen's features extracted blind, the vectors compared, every claim audited against the images), with the pipeline's three verdict bands. Every pair returned ‘inconclusive’: the note against the signatures with a weak lean against identity (the h built on different limbs, pointed against rounded minims; the shared capital I the period's standard form), against Tycho's specimens with a weak lean against (the capital I without the J-descender, the final s at x-height against his descending final s), against the hands of 1561 with a weak lean against; the marginalia against Tycho's specimens with a weak-to-moderate lean against (the u-marks and the looped g agree; the open e, the 3-shaped final s, the absence of the ſt/ct arch and the j-form final i do not — a German-cursive repertoire the secure hands show nowhere). Sample lengths below the forensic floor; the facsimile's c. 15–20 px x-height for the note is the binding constraint. Unpublished; the crops, the claims and the audits are kept with the edition's working papers.

It records the gift (January 1957, from civilingeniør Oskar Ekman; further provenance unknown), the stamps TVCHO BRADE and ANNO 1561, the spine number 204 (‘formodentlig katalognummeret i Tychos eller et senere bibliotek’), the forperm's inscriptions as he reads them — ‘Tyge Brahe’ struck through, ‘tico brahe ven’ struck through (‘en lidt barnlig skrift’), in another hand ‘Sum Paul…’ with the rest lost on the torn-off part, the price ‘… 4 taliro & 4 Gross.’ under a struck line where ‘Brade’ can be glimpsed — short astronomical notes in Tycho's hand inside the binding, on the forperm's back and in the margin of the preface's tenth page, and the herbarium: Latin plant names at the head of 36 unpaginated pages in a hand other than Tycho's, plant remains in the gutter of 26 of them identified by Jette Baagøe and re-housed in envelopes, one plant name unattested before c. 1623 (Peter Wagner and Baagøe), hence a user who ‘formentlig ikke har haft kontakt med Tycho’.   164. Volf 1932
    Josef Volf, ‘Tycho Brahe a jeho hvězdářská pozůstalost’, Říše hvězd 13 (1932), no. 1, pp. 1–9, and no. 2, pp. 21–29 (with a German summary); first printed in Český bibliofil (1931), not seen. From the Bohemian chamber records: the instruments and the manuscript observations bought for Rudolf's collections, ‘kdežto knihovna zbyla dědicům’; the 4,000 thaler of September 1603; the rescript of 9 July 1609; the heirs assigned from 1623 to the arrears of the towns Žatec, Kadaň, Rakovník and Chomutov, with payments until 1654; the heirs turned Catholic, and ‘putuje část slavné bibliotéky Brahovy s nádhernými vazbami a se supralibros do klementinské knihovny jako dar’; Rudolf Tycho Gansneb Tengnagel, captain of the Malá Strana from 1642, gave his share of the debt to the Dominicans of St Giles (Ferdinand III's assurance of 14 March 1643 for 22,534 fl.), Sophie Brahe hers (9,942 fl.) to the Kadaň Franciscans; iron instead of money in 1672; debts still claimed in 1685 and 1688; the Czechoslovak restitution claims of the 1920s against Vienna, with the documents. Read on the page 27 October 2026: part 2, p. 23, the four towns with their sums and dates — Žatec (1,000 thaler), Kadaň (1,000), Rakovník (950), Chomutov (950), ‘ze starých berních nedoplatků (Chomutov, 26. září 1623, Kadaň, 3. července 1626 a j.)’, the instalments running to 1654; p. 24, Ferdinand II's order of 10 November 1631 to pay part of the interest, stopped by the Saxon invasion, and the assecuration of 14 March 1643 to the Dominicans of St Giles for 22,534 fl. 22 kr. 4 d. (Arch. min. vnitra, Bekennen u. Verträge 1642/65); p. 25, Sophie Brahe's 9,942 fl. to the Kadaň Franciscans and the iron of 30 July 1672.
    Contributes The Czech archival account of the estate; the Clementinum transfer called a gift.
    Available online Říše hvězd archive (part 1: RH-1932-01.pdf)

    Otto Walde, Storhetstidens litterära krigsbyten: en kulturhistorisk-bibliografisk studie, II (Uppsala, 1920), p. 329: the first report of the Uppsala volume of 1563 (Prandtl’s Band III) with Vedel’s name on the first title. Cited here after Mortensen 1942 (p. 25) and Mortensen 1955 (p. 27, n. 4).
    Contributes The first report of the Uppsala volume of 1563.
  166. Walde 1938
    Otto Walde, ‘Några böcker från Tycho Brahes krets’, Nordisk tidskrift för bok- och biblioteksväsen 25 (1938), pp. 11–17. The Braunsberg find: in the library of the Staatliche Akademie at Braunsberg a copy of Scaliger's De emendatione temporum in the revised Leiden edition of 1598, bound in white parchment with Tycho's arms on the lower and his portrait on the upper board, both blind-stamped, with the decor usual on his bindings; not bound on Hven, perhaps at Wandsbeck in 1598; many marginalia in several hands, photographs of which Hans Ræder judged not Tycho's; no dedication; the later note ‘M. Braunhardt i Gotha 1761 … Ex bibliotheca Oppeliana’. Also the Uppsala volume of 1563 given to Vedel and the Glareanus Vedel bought in 1564, now in Prague; the 2781 spine number and its uncertainty; and the books of Johannes Eriksen Hamburgensis, Tycho's amanuensis, which went into Queen Christina's library with the Prague booty (a Pitiscus bought at Prague on 14 August 1601, now at Hanover; two chemical manuscripts at Leiden; a Lull of 1593 at Västerås) — and, apart from them, the Vienna Commentariolus manuscript, Longomontanus's gift to Eriksen at Benátky on 18 July 1600, whose supposed passage to Tycho and with his papers to Vienna Walde doubted.
    Contributes The identity of the Braunsberg volume and the Eriksen provenance of the Vienna Commentariolus.
    Available online Projekt Runeberg — p. 11
  167. Westman 2011
    Robert S. Westman, The Copernican Question: Prognostication, Skepticism, and Celestial Order (Berkeley and Los Angeles: University of California Press, 2011; first paperback printing 2020).     Contributes The one modern study to read two of Tycho's bindings of 1576 for their contents — the Bellanti of 14 A 66 and the Naibod of 5 J 2 — and the only printed refusal of the figure of three thousand volumes.

    Contributes The first item printed on the Uraniborg press, from Tycho's own observation protocol.
  169. ZfB 1906–07 (binding note)
    ‘Ein Bucheinband Tycho Brahes’, Zeitschrift für Bücherfreunde 10 (1906/07), Heft 1, Chronik, pp. 42–43, with three facsimile plates of the two supralibros (signed ‘—W—’ in the contents). The Munich antiquarian bookseller Ludwig Rosenthal had sent the volume: the eighteenth volume of Zwinger's Theatrum humanae vitae (Basel 1587) in wooden boards covered in brown leather, two chased brass clasps, seven raised bands, three blind-tooled frames, the innermost with fourteen portrait medallions of scholars, four gilt rosettes, and the gilt portrait and arms medallions with their distichs; a manuscript note inside the board called it a ‘Schweizer Ledereinband mit Blinddruck und Goldmedaillons’, and the writer supposed it made at Basel for Tycho. The volume is the one now at the Röhsska museum, Göteborg.
    Contributes The 1906 description and the Rosenthal step in the provenance of the Röhsska volume.
    Available online Internet Archive
